# Main hypothesis
Can an Au/Prussian-blue/colistin/BSA silent-region SERS probe combine bacterial monitoring with light-activated antibacterial treatment and improved healing of Gram-negative infected wounds?
System: Au-core/Prussian-blue-shell SERS probes loaded with colistin sulfate and stabilized with BSA, evaluated against E. coli and P. aeruginosa in vitro, in infected BALB/c and db/db mouse wounds, and in 36 infected human wound samples.
Conditions: 650 nm irradiation at 200 mW/cm2 for treatment assays; primarily Gram-negative laboratory strains and acute eight-day wound experiments; silent-region Raman readout near 2133 cm−1
Scope limits: figure pixels and supplementary files were not inspected; the JATS reports both 5-mm wounds in Methods and 8-mm wounds in Results; large-animal, long-term biodistribution, clearance, and repeated-dose safety were not tested; clinical gold-standard details are referenced in uninspected Table S1
Validation requirements:
- R1: Evaluate bacterial detection and clinical classification only at the reported analytical and sample scope. (aspects: H1, H8)
- R2: Separate light-dependent antibacterial efficacy from candidate ROS, antibiotic, and membrane-damage mechanisms. (aspects: H2, H3, H4)
- R3: Assess wound closure, bacterial clearance, immune polarization, matrix reconstruction, and angiogenesis as distinct in-vivo endpoints. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)

# Main hypothesis
Compare coating-substrate systems for polymer injection-mould tooling across mechanical, surface, tribological, corrosion, and optical performance, while identifying application-dependent trade-offs.
System: BALINIT LUMENA, BALINIT CROVEGA, BALINIT CROMA PLUS, and BALITHERM PRIMEFORM on tool steels 1.2343, 1.2083, 1.2378 HH, and Toolox 44
Conditions: laboratory material-characterization assays; hydrothermal corrosion at 80°C in distilled water for 14 days; reciprocating ball-on-flat tribology for LUMENA and CROMA PLUS
Scope limits: assay coverage differs across properties; tribology excludes CROVEGA and PRIMEFORM; gloss and XRF comparisons are limited to steel 1.2378; figure pixels were not inspected

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Load-dependent hardness performance of each coating-substrate system.
Links: composition ← H3; refinement ← H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Resistance to degradation during 14-day hydrothermal incubation.
Links: composition ← H3

## H3 (claim)
Statement: No coating universally maximizes all measured properties; selection depends on the functional priority.
Links: composition → H1; composition → H2

## H4 (limitation)
Statement: HV1 measures a coating-substrate composite response, whereas HV0.1 is more surface-sensitive and reduces substrate influence.
Links: refinement → H1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Vickers microhardness compared uncoated and coated steels at HV1 and, for selected samples, HV0.1.
Manipulation: Apply each coating and indent coated and uncoated samples at the reported loads.
Measurements: HV1 mean and standard deviation; HV0.1 mean and standard deviation
Comparison: groups: uncoated; LUMENA; CROVEGA; CROMA PLUS; PRIMEFORM | endpoint: Vickers hardness | varied: coating; steel grade; indentation load | held fixed: Vickers method; at least three indentations per sample | unit: indentation/sample | units: HV0.1 or HV1 | uncertainty: The Results contain conflicting statements about the low-load leader.
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: Hydrothermal incubation evaluated coating degradation in hot distilled water.
Manipulation: Immerse coated samples in distilled water at 80°C for 14 days.
Measurements: visual corrosion; pH; electrical conductivity
Comparison: groups: LUMENA; CROVEGA; CROMA PLUS; PRIMEFORM | endpoint: visual corrosion with solution pH and conductivity | varied: coating; steel grade; incubation time | held fixed: distilled water; 80°C | unit: coated steel sample/solution | window: daily visual inspection; solution measures on days 1, 7, and 14 | units: pH and µS cm−1 | uncertainty: Table 5 day cells are empty in supplied JATS; narrative Results provide outcomes.
Observations: O3

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)

# Main hypothesis
Does topical rHDL improve healing of full-thickness excisional wounds in diabetic mice, and does efficacy translate to a topical Pluronic F-127 formulation in diabetic Yucatan miniature pigs?
System: Streptozotocin-induced diabetic C57BL/6J mice and alloxan-induced diabetic male Yucatan miniature pigs with full-thickness excisional wounds
Conditions: Topical rHDL compared with matched controls; Mouse treatment begun at wounding or two days later; pig treatment begun immediately and given daily; Mouse follow-up through day 10 and pig follow-up through day 18
Scope limits: Preclinical excisional wounds, not chronic human diabetic foot ulcers; Only one sex was used in each efficacy model; The pig formulation could not exceed 10 mg/mL rHDL
Validation requirements:
- R1: Assess wound-closure efficacy separately in diabetic mice and diabetic pigs against the relevant vehicle control.
- R2: Use tissue-level measurements to distinguish closure from histological or inflammatory changes.
- R3: Interpret cross-species differences within the tested formulation, exposure, model, and endpoint constraints.

# Main hypothesis
Can grafting sulfonate-type zwitterionic side chains onto the hard segments of an IPDI/PTMG/MDEA polyurethane (ZESTPU) and swelling it with the ionic liquid [EMIM]+[BF4]− give an ionogel (ZESTI) that simultaneously has high tensile strength, stretchability and toughness, autonomous self-healing under ambient conditions, and high ionic conductivity, and can this ionogel serve as the active material of self-reporting packaging and strain-sensing iontronic devices?
System: ZESTI: zwitterionic side-chain engineered polyurethane (ZESTPU, made by reacting PMPU with 1,3-propanesultone) containing [EMIM]+[BF4]− ionic liquid; references are the unmodified polyurethane PMPU, IL-free ZESTPU, and the non-zwitterionic ionogel i-PMPU (PMPU + IL).
Conditions: IL content expressed as IL/(IL + PU) weight ratio; 30 wt% IL unless otherwise specified (10, 30 and 50 wt% also prepared); Tensile tests at room temperature, 10 mm min−1, three independent specimens; Self-healing at room temperature (24 h for cut-and-rejoin tests); scratch tests at ambient 20–40% relative humidity; EIS at room temperature, 0.1 Hz–1 MHz, 10 mV; temperature-dependent conductivity over 293.15–353.15 K
Scope limits: Single ionic liquid ([EMIM]+[BF4]−) and a single hard/soft segment ratio and zwitterion grafting condition; Autonomous self-healing is stated to be mainly applicable under ambient conditions and strongly limited at sub-zero temperatures; Device demonstrations are described as proof-of-concept rather than optimized products
Validation requirements:
- R1: Chemical and structural verification of zwitterionic side-chain incorporation, of its interactions with the IL, and of the resulting nanostructure (aspects: H1)

Statement: Molecular and nanostructural basis of ZESTI properties

Links: composition ← H1

Statement: Dynamic dipole–dipole interactions among zwitterionic side chains
Links: composition ← H1

Links: composition ← H1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Chemical verification of the zwitterionic modification: ATR-FTIR, XPS and elemental analysis of PMPU versus ZESTPU, plus temperature-dependent FTIR
Manipulation: PMPU reacted with 1,3-propanesultone (PS/MDEA molar ratio 1:1.5) to give ZESTPU; spectra compared with unmodified PMPU; FTIR also recorded at increasing temperature (Fig. S2b)
Measurements: ATR-FTIR spectra (Bruker, ZnSe, absorption mode); XPS (K-Alpha Plus, monochromatic Al Kα); Elemental analysis (FLASH SMART); Temperature-dependent FTIR
Comparison: groups: PMPU; ZESTPU | endpoint: FTIR characteristic peaks; XPS S 2p and N 1s signals; sulfur content by elemental analysis; temperature shift of the 963 cm−1 band | varied: zwitterionic modification (PS reaction); temperature (temperature-dependent FTIR only) | held fixed: IL-free polymers | unit: polymer film spectrum
Observations: O1, O2, O3, O4

## E2
Statement: ATR-FTIR of neat [EMIM]+[BF4]−, i-PMPU@30% and ZESTI@30%, and XPS S 2p/N 1s of ZESTI, to probe interactions between zwitterionic side chains and the IL
Manipulation: IL (30 wt%) incorporated into PMPU (i-PMPU) or ZESTPU (ZESTI); IL characteristic peak positions compared with neat IL
Measurements: ATR-FTIR spectra; XPS S 2p and N 1s (Fig. S3e, f)
Comparison: groups: [EMIM]+[BF4]−; i-PMPU@30%; ZESTI@30% | endpoint: Positions of [EMIM]+ (3163, 3123 cm−1) and [BF4]− (1053 cm−1) bands; XPS S 2p shape/position and N 1s components in ZESTI | varied: presence of zwitterionic side chains in the host polymer | held fixed: IL type; 30 wt% IL | unit: film spectrum
Observations: O5, O6

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: Compared with PMPU, ZESTPU showed three new ATR-FTIR peaks at 1483 and 963 cm−1, assigned to quaternary ammonium groups, and at 1178 cm−1, assigned to asymmetric S=O stretching of sulfonate groups.
Scope: IL-free PMPU vs ZESTPU; peak assignments from cited literature [30–32]; spectra in Fig. 2a and S2a not inspected
Comparison: groups: PMPU; ZESTPU | endpoint: Presence of characteristic FTIR peaks | varied: zwitterionic modification | held fixed: IL-free polymers | unit: film spectrum | units: cm−1 | result: Three new peaks in ZESTPU (1483, 963, 1178 cm−1)
Bears on: H2, H3

## O2 (from E1)
Statement: In temperature-dependent FTIR (Fig. S2b), the 963 cm−1 band gradually shifted to higher wavenumber with increasing temperature.
Scope: Sample not named explicitly in the sentence (reported in the ZESTPU vs PMPU paragraph); temperature range and shift magnitude not stated in text
Comparison: groups: spectra at increasing temperatures | endpoint: Position of the 963 cm−1 band | varied: temperature | units: cm−1 | result: Gradual shift to higher wavenumber with increasing temperature
Bears on: H4

## O3 (from E1)
Statement: Compared with PMPU, ZESTPU showed a distinct S 2p XPS signal attributed to sulfonate sulfur in –SO3− groups and a shift of the N 1s signal to higher binding energy, associated with quaternary ammonium formation (Fig. S3).
Scope: IL-free polymers; Fig. S3 not inspected; binding-energy values not stated in text
Comparison: groups: PMPU; ZESTPU | endpoint: XPS S 2p and N 1s signals | varied: zwitterionic modification | held fixed: IL-free polymers | result: S 2p signal present in ZESTPU; N 1s shifted to higher binding energy
Bears on: H2, H3

## O4 (from E1)
Statement: Elemental analysis detected sulfur from the zwitterionic side chains in ZESTPU (Table S3).
Scope: Numerical values in Table S3 not inspected; comparison with PMPU not stated in text
Comparison: groups: ZESTPU | endpoint: Sulfur content | result: Sulfur present in ZESTPU
Bears on: H2, H3

## O5 (from E2)
Statement: The [EMIM]+ C(4,5)H symmetric stretching (3163 cm−1) and NC(H)NCH ring (3123 cm−1) bands and the [BF4]− band (1053 cm−1) showed negligible shifts in i-PMPU but redshifts in ZESTI.
Scope: Shift magnitudes not stated in text; Fig. 2b not inspected
Comparison: groups: [EMIM]+[BF4]− band positions; i-PMPU@30%; ZESTI@30% | endpoint: Shift of IL characteristic bands | varied: presence of zwitterionic side chains in the host polymer | held fixed: IL type; 30 wt% IL | units: cm−1 | result: Negligible shifts in i-PMPU; redshifts in ZESTI
Bears on: H5

## O6 (from E2)

Scope: Reference spectrum for the S 2p shift not named in the sentence; Fig. S3e, f not inspected

# Main hypothesis
How efficiently do four lignocellulosic byproducts (walnut shell, chestnut shell, pine wood and burnt pine wood) remove Pb ions from water by adsorption under selected pH conditions, and what do kinetic and isotherm models and material characterization (SEM, BET, PXRD) indicate about the adsorption process?
System: Batch adsorption of Pb from Pb(NO3)2 solutions in distilled water onto milled walnut shell, chestnut shell, Pinus pinaster wood and burnt P. pinaster wood collected in the Viseu region, central Portugal
Conditions: pH 7.5 for chestnut shell, pine wood and burnt pine wood; pH 6.5 for walnut shell; Initial-concentration tests: 5-200 mg L⁻¹ Pb, adsorbent dose 4 g L⁻¹, 12 h agitation; Kinetic tests: 25 mg L⁻¹ Pb, agitation times from 10 to 1440 min; Room temperature; triplicate adsorption tests; Adsorbent particle size <80 mesh (<0.177 mm)
Scope limits: Single-metal Pb(NO3)2 solutions prepared in distilled water; One temperature (room temperature)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Describe the adsorption rate with pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order, Elovich and intraparticle diffusion models. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Evaluate the adsorption mechanisms through the kinetic and isotherm models. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Assess Pb retained in the solid samples by EDX, with thermogravimetric and SEM analyses. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Pb removal from water by adsorption onto walnut shell, chestnut shell, pine wood and burnt pine wood byproducts.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Pb uptake over contact time (10-1440 min at 25 mg L⁻¹) and its description by pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order, Elovich and intraparticle diffusion models.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E2

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Detection and quantification of Pb retained in the adsorbent solids.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Attempted detection of Pb in the solid samples by EDX, with complementary thermogravimetric and SEM analyses.

Measurements: EDX elemental composition; TGA mass loss
Comparison: groups: Pb-exposed adsorbent samples | endpoint: presence and amount of Pb in the solids | held fixed: EDX, TGA and SEM instrument settings | unit: material sample
Links: experimental target → H3

## E2
Statement: Kinetic adsorption tests with linearized PFO, PSO, Elovich and intraparticle diffusion model fits.

Comparison: groups: walnut shell; chestnut shell; pine wood; burnt pine wood | endpoint: adsorbed Pb over time and fitted kinetic parameters with R² | varied: contact time; kinetic model; adsorbent material | held fixed: initial Pb 25 mg L⁻¹; material-specific pH | unit: material dataset | window: 10-1440 min | units: mg g⁻¹ | uncertainty: Parameter standard errors not reported

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

## H2 (aspect)

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Under the tested conditions, S. oneidensis-associated MtrC and OmcA contribute to consortium leaching and extracellular electron-transfer capacity, while cell-free reduced riboflavin is oxidized after NCM addition; together these observations are consistent with cytochrome- and riboflavin-associated routes, but do not directly establish their relative or in vivo electron flux to NCM.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: In the tested SO3-BS3 background, deletion of mtrC, omcA, or both was associated with markedly lower 14-day metal leaching than SO3-BS3, supporting a contribution of these cytochromes under the tested conditions but not establishing that they are individually required for NCM reduction.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: In the tested SO3-BS3 deletion series, loss of MtrC, OmcA, or both was associated with substantially lower MFC power and metal leaching than SO3-BS3, supporting a contribution but not establishing essentiality for NCM reduction; separately, reduced riboflavin shifted toward its oxidized spectrum after NCM contact in a cell-free anoxic assay.
Links: refinement ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement ← H7

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6; refinement ← H7

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis were essential for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching, and riboflavin in its reduced form could be oxidised by NCM.
Links: refinement → H4; refinement → H2

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis contribute to electron transfer to NCM during metal oxide leaching, as their deletion lowers power density and metal leaching; the double-deletion value is indistinguishable from strain BS3 alone, so the cytochromes are not shown to be required for the reaction to occur.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis were essential for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching, and riboflavin in its reduced form could be oxidised by NCM.
Links: refinement ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can a W-shaped piezoresistive pressure sensor that couples a rigid aluminum sheet (inspired by the rigid outer wall and soft porous interior of Bambusa textilis) with a carbon-ink-coated melamine sponge and a micro-protruded MWCNT/PU film (inspired by the surface protrusions of Salvia plebeia R.Br.) address the poor stability and long recovery times of porous flexible pressure sensors, while providing a broad pressure range, usable sensitivity, fine load resolution, and terrain discrimination when mounted on a robot foot?
System: W-shaped layered sensor: aluminum sheet, insulating double-sided tape, carbon-black-ink-coated melamine sponge, MWCNT/PU film with sandpaper-replicated micro-protrusions, copper electrodes; 80 mm x 20 mm strip
Conditions: Bench loading with a motorized linear stage; resistance read with a Keithley DAQ6510 multimeter; force with a 1 kN gauge; Applied pressures up to 31.5 kPa; Robot tests on a six-legged robot with the sensor on the ventral side of one foot
Scope limits: Bench tests and one robot platform; Figure images and supplementary figures are not part of this text record
Validation requirements:
- R1: Broad effective pressure range with usable sensitivity and a predictable resistance-pressure relationship.
- R2: Resolution of small load changes.
- R3: Fast response and recovery and faithful tracking of dynamic loads.
- R4: Reversibility and long-term stability under repeated loading.
- R5: Discrimination of ground surfaces when mounted on a robot foot.

# Main hypothesis
How does Ni grain size in electrodeposited coatings on CF evolve with heat-treatment temperature, heating mode and HD deposition duration?
System: PAN-based T300 3K carbon fiber plain-weave fabric, sizing removed and HNO3-etched, Ni electrodeposited from a Watts bath at 0.02 A/cm2 (LD) or 0.04 A/cm2 (HD), vacuum heat-treated, and cured into 4674 epoxy CFRP panels

Scope limits: LH applied only at 700 °C

- R1: Characterize Ni grain growth in the coatings during vacuum heat treatment. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4, H5)

Links: composition ← H1

Links: composition ← H1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: SEM morphology and grain-size statistics of Ni-coated fabrics after IH at 500-900 °C
Manipulation: Quartz tube with as-deposited samples (HD 30, 20 and 10 min; LD 30 min) inserted into a furnace preheated to 500, 600, 700, 800 or 900 °C (IH), then held 2 h
Measurements: SEM surface morphology; average grain size and size distribution
Comparison: groups: IH 500 °C; IH 600 °C; IH 700 °C; IH 800 °C; IH 900 °C | endpoint: surface morphology and average Ni grain size from SEM image statistics (Figures S4-S6) | varied: heat-treatment temperature; coating type (LD 30 min; HD 30, 20, 10 min) | held fixed: vacuum below 5 × 10^-3 Pa, 2 h isothermal hold; IH heating mode | unit: coated fabric sample | window: after 2 h isothermal treatment | units: nm
Observations: O1, O2, O4

## E2
Statement: Comparison of LH and IH heating modes at 700 °C for the grain size of different coatings
Manipulation: LH: tube placed in the furnace at room temperature and heated at 5 °C/min to 700 °C, then held 2 h; IH: tube inserted into the furnace preheated to 700 °C, then held 2 h; applied to HD 30, 20, 10 min and LD 30 min coatings
Measurements: SEM surface morphology; average grain size and size distribution
Comparison: groups: LH to 700 °C; IH at 700 °C | endpoint: average Ni grain size and size distribution width (SEM statistics, Figure 2u) | varied: heating mode | held fixed: 700 °C final temperature; vacuum below 5 × 10^-3 Pa, 2 h isothermal hold; coating type within each pair | unit: coated fabric sample | window: after 2 h hold at 700 °C | units: nm
Observations: O3, O5

## E3
Statement: XRD phase analysis and Scherrer crystallite-size calculation for LD and HD Ni-coated fabrics after heat treatment
Manipulation: Heat treatment of LD (0.02 A/cm2) and HD (0.04 A/cm2) coated fabrics at 500-900 °C, including LH and IH modes
Measurements: XRD patterns; Scherrer crystallite size with K = 0.89, λ = 0.154056 nm, FWHM corrected for instrumental broadening
Comparison: groups: LD coatings at 500-900 °C; HD coatings at 500-900 °C; LH versus IH | endpoint: Ni, NiO and C diffraction peaks; Ni crystallite size D = Kλ/(β cos θ) from Ni (111), (200), (220) peaks | varied: heat-treatment temperature; current density; heating mode | held fixed: Cu Kα radiation (Rigaku MiniFlex600) | unit: coated fabric sample | units: nm (crystallite size)
Observations: O6

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: For the LD coating, grain size was 98.1 nm at 500 °C and about 345.3 nm at 600 °C with severe agglomeration; after IH at 700 °C the coating was continuous but non-dense with visible bare CF sites; many exposed sites appeared at 800 °C; at 900 °C Ni spheroidized into isolated particles averaging 185.8 nm, with molten pits on the CF surface.
Scope: LD coating after IH; grain distributions in Figure S4 not inspected
Comparison: groups: LD IH 500 °C; LD IH 600 °C; LD IH 700 °C; LD IH 800 °C; LD IH 900 °C | endpoint: SEM morphology and average Ni grain size | varied: heat-treatment temperature | held fixed: LD 30 min; vacuum below 5 × 10^-3 Pa, 2 h isothermal hold | unit: coated fabric | window: after 2 h isothermal treatment | units: nm
Bears on: H2

## O2 (from E1)
Statement: For the HD 30 min coating, average grain size was ~136.3 nm at 500 °C and ~237.2 nm at 600 °C (continuous, no obvious porosity), ~619.3 nm with a broad distribution after IH at 700 °C, ~1.25 µm with polyhedral grains at 800 °C, and ~1.05 µm at 900 °C with a suspected outwardly protruding carbon recrystallization overlayer.
Scope: HD 30 min coating after IH
Comparison: groups: HD IH 500 °C; HD IH 600 °C; HD IH 700 °C; HD IH 800 °C; HD IH 900 °C | endpoint: SEM morphology and average Ni grain size | varied: heat-treatment temperature | held fixed: HD 30 min; vacuum below 5 × 10^-3 Pa, 2 h isothermal hold | unit: coated fabric | window: after 2 h isothermal treatment | units: nm / µm
Bears on: H2

## O3 (from E2)
Statement: At 700 °C, the HD 30 min coating had an average grain size of ~619.3 nm with a broad distribution after IH, versus ~479.7 nm with a narrow distribution and enhanced compactness after LH at 5 °C/min.
Scope: HD 30 min coating at 700 °C
Comparison: groups: HD 30 min IH 700 °C; HD 30 min LH 700 °C | endpoint: average Ni grain size and distribution width | varied: heating mode | held fixed: HD 30 min; 700 °C; 2 h hold | unit: coated fabric | window: after 2 h hold at 700 °C | units: nm
Bears on: H4

## O4 (from E1)
Statement: For HD coatings, grain size rose overall monotonically with deposition duration and heat-treatment temperature; for 30 min deposits the grain size exceeded 1200 nm after 900 °C treatment.
Scope: HD coatings; the 900 °C value for 30 min deposits differs from the ~1.05 µm value given in the coating restructuring section
Comparison: groups: HD 10 min; HD 20 min; HD 30 min; 500-900 °C | endpoint: average Ni grain size (Figure 2t) | varied: deposition duration; heat-treatment temperature | held fixed: 0.04 A/cm2 | unit: coated fabric | units: nm
Bears on: H2, H5

## O5 (from E2)
Statement: All LH-treated specimens had smaller average grain sizes and narrower size distributions than IH-treated specimens; the effect was particularly prominent for thin Ni coatings.
Scope: All coatings compared in Figure 2u
Comparison: groups: LH 700 °C; IH 700 °C | endpoint: average grain size and distribution width | varied: heating mode | held fixed: coating type within each pair | unit: coated fabric
Bears on: H4

## O6 (from E3)
Statement: Scherrer analysis: LD grains grew mainly along the (200) normal, changing only slightly below 600 °C and increasing monotonically above 700 °C; HD coatings had stronger XRD signals with (111) preferred orientation, grew rapidly from 600 °C, plateaued at 700 °C and grew near-linearly from 800 to 900 °C; under LH, Ni peaks were weaker, grains remained fine and uniform, and the C(110) peak was more intense than under IH.
Scope: Crystallite size from XRD line broadening
Comparison: groups: LD 500-900 °C; HD 500-900 °C; LH versus IH | endpoint: Ni crystallite size from Ni (111), (200), (220) peak widths (Figure 4c,d) | varied: heat-treatment temperature; current density; heating mode | held fixed: K = 0.89; λ = 0.154056 nm | unit: coated fabric | units: nm
Bears on: H3

System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Molecular processes related to oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, mitochondrial homeostasis and cell survival are characterized, including by cardiac proteomics. (aspects: H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserves left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation limits left ventricular structural remodeling in MI rats (hypertrophy, dilation, interstitial fibrosis and ECM protein accumulation).
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac superoxide levels in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac inflammatory marker expression in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation attenuates cardiac ER stress activation in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H7 (claim)
Statement: In male MI rats 4 weeks after LAD ligation, the preserved LV function and reduced hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis after mitochondrial transplantation were accompanied by lower cardiac superoxide, inflammatory gene expression (CCL2, TLR4, sST2) and ER stress proteins (BiP, CHOP, ATF4, ATF6α); whether these changes mediate the benefits was not tested.
Links: analysis derivation ← H4; analysis derivation ← H5; analysis derivation ← H6; analysis derivation ← H2; analysis derivation ← H3

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Molecular processes related to oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, mitochondrial homeostasis and cell survival are characterized, including by cardiac proteomics. (aspects: H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserves left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation limits left ventricular structural remodeling in MI rats (hypertrophy, dilation, interstitial fibrosis and ECM protein accumulation).
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac superoxide levels in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac inflammatory marker expression in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation attenuates cardiac ER stress activation in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Cardiac superoxide, inflammatory markers and ER stress proteins are altered by mitochondrial transplantation in MI rats, and these changes are associated with the functional and structural benefits observed. Whether these changes mediate the benefits requires pathway-specific intervention.
Links: analysis derivation ← H4; analysis derivation ← H5; analysis derivation ← H6; analysis derivation ← H2; analysis derivation ← H3

Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Molecular processes related to oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, mitochondrial homeostasis and cell survival are characterized, including by cardiac proteomics. (aspects: H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserves left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation limits left ventricular structural remodeling in MI rats (hypertrophy, dilation, interstitial fibrosis and ECM protein accumulation).
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac superoxide levels in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac inflammatory marker expression in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation attenuates cardiac ER stress activation in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H7 (claim)
Statement: In MI rats, cardiac superoxide levels, inflammatory gene expression and ER stress markers are altered in the same direction as the functional and remodeling benefits, and these alterations are prevented by mitochondrial transplantation. These findings are consistent with, but do not establish, that oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling and ER stress responses mediate the functional and remodeling benefits of mitochondrial transplantation.
Links: analysis derivation ← H4; analysis derivation ← H5; analysis derivation ← H6; analysis derivation ← H2; analysis derivation ← H3

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the exposure protocol produces the intended hypertensive phenotype, with systolic blood pressure compared between week 0 and week 8 in each group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Quantify aortic lipid peroxidation products and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities across the exposure levels. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Chronic oral CdCl2 exposure (40 or 80 ppm for 8 weeks) produces a hypertensive phenotype in male Wistar rats, accompanied by changes in body weight and blood glucose.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Vasomotor function of isolated thoracic aortic rings is altered in cadmium-exposed hypertensive rats relative to controls.
Links: composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Contraction to the TXA2 analogue U46619 in aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H6

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Aortic redox balance, measured as lipid peroxidation products (MDA, 4-HDA) and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities (GPx, GR), changes with cadmium exposure level.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5; refinement → H7

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species within the vascular wall mediate the altered vasomotor responses of cadmium-exposed aortas; the proposed mechanism is probed by incubating rings with the NADPH oxidase inhibitor apocynin.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; proposed mechanism → H4

## H6 (claim)
Statement: TXA2 induces hypercontractility in aortas from cadmium-exposed hypertensive animals, an effect associated with oxidative stress and reversed after NADPH oxidase inhibition.
Links: refinement ← H3

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure produces dose-related aortic lipid peroxidation together with altered glutathione-cycle enzyme activity, described by the authors as a compensatory antioxidant response at the lower exposure followed by depletion at the higher one.
Links: refinement ← H4

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure protocol with in vivo follow-up of body weight, blood glucose and systolic blood pressure at week 0 and week 8.
Manipulation: Male Wistar rats of about 200 g were randomly assigned with a digital randomiser to control, CdCl2 40 ppm or CdCl2 80 ppm; cadmium chloride was given in the drinking water for 8 weeks. Animals were housed under controlled temperature and humidity with a 12-h light/dark cycle and ad libitum food and water. Systolic blood pressure was measured in conscious rats by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography after a 7-day acclimatisation to restraint, with multiple consecutive recordings per animal and exclusion of recordings with movement artefacts or unstable pulse detection.
Measurements: body weight (g); blood glucose (mg/dL); systolic blood pressure by tail-cuff plethysmography (mmHg)
Comparison: groups: control (CTRL); CdCl2 40 ppm; CdCl2 80 ppm | endpoint: Body weight, blood glucose and systolic blood pressure, each recorded at week 0 and week 8 | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm); time (week 0 versus week 8) | held fixed: male Wistar rats of about 200 g at entry; same housing, light/dark cycle and ad libitum food and water; same quiet temperature-controlled room on the measurement day; same tail-cuff system and LabChart acquisition | unit: individual animal (n = 12 per group in Table 1) | window: Week 0 (baseline) and week 8 (end of exposure) | units: g for body weight, mg/dL for glucose, mmHg for systolic blood pressure | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; Methods state paired tests for within-group week 0 versus week 8 comparisons and between-group tests at each time point, while the Table 1 footnote reports Student's t test with asterisks marking p < 0.05 versus week 0

## E2
Statement: U46619 (TXA2 analogue) concentration-response curves in aortic rings, with and without apocynin preincubation.
Manipulation: Aortic rings prepared as in the other reactivity protocols were exposed to cumulative U46619 concentrations from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M, with contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl. ## E3
Statement: Spectrophotometric quantification of aortic lipid peroxidation products MDA and 4-HDA.
Manipulation: Aortic tissue from each rat was mechanically homogenised in potassium phosphate buffer (0.05 M, pH 7.8). Homogenates were centrifuged at 10,000 x g for 15 min at 4 degrees C, total protein was quantified by the Lowry method, and MDA and 4-HDA concentrations were measured in the supernatant at 586 nm.

## E4
Statement: Spectrophotometric assay of aortic glutathione peroxidase activity.
Manipulation: Homogenate fraction (0.1 mL) was added to a freshly prepared buffer containing 50 mM K2HPO4 (pH 7.1), 1 mM EDTA, a catalase inhibitor, 0.2 mM NADPH, 1 unit of glutathione reductase and 1 mM reduced glutathione, incubated 5 min at room temperature; hydrogen peroxide (0.25 mM, 0.1 mL) was added, the mixture was centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 degrees C, and activity was quantified in the supernatant at 340 nm.

## E5
Statement: Spectrophotometric assay of aortic glutathione reductase activity.
Manipulation: Tissue homogenate was mixed with potassium phosphate buffer (139 mM, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 degrees C; the supernatant was combined with NADPH (2.5 mmol/mL) and FAD (315 micromol/L), initial absorbance was read at 340 nm after 3.3 min, glutathione disulfide (22 mmol/L) was added, and absorbance was read again after 2.9 min, activity being calculated from the difference.

Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the exposure protocol produces the intended hypertensive phenotype, with systolic blood pressure compared between week 0 and week 8 in each group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Quantify aortic lipid peroxidation products and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities across the exposure levels. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Chronic oral CdCl2 exposure (40 or 80 ppm for 8 weeks) produces a hypertensive phenotype in male Wistar rats, accompanied by changes in body weight and blood glucose.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Vasomotor function of isolated thoracic aortic rings is altered in cadmium-exposed hypertensive rats relative to controls.
Links: composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Contraction to the TXA2 analogue U46619 in aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H6

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Aortic redox balance, measured as lipid peroxidation products (MDA, 4-HDA) and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities (GPx, GR), changes with cadmium exposure level.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5; refinement → H7

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species within the vascular wall mediate the altered vasomotor responses of cadmium-exposed aortas; the proposed mechanism is probed by incubating rings with the NADPH oxidase inhibitor apocynin.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; proposed mechanism → H4; competing explanation ← H8

## H6 (claim)
Statement: TXA2 induces hypercontractility in aortas from cadmium-exposed hypertensive animals, an effect associated with oxidative stress and reversed after NADPH oxidase inhibition.
Links: refinement ← H3; competing explanation ← H8

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure produces dose-related aortic lipid peroxidation together with altered glutathione-cycle enzyme activity, described by the authors as a compensatory antioxidant response at the lower exposure followed by depletion at the higher one.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate alternative, unverified: the dose-graded rise in circulating glucose that accompanied cadmium exposure (98.5 mg/dL in controls versus 110.0 mg/dL at 40 ppm and 115.5 mg/dL at 80 ppm at week 8) may itself drive the aortic lipid peroxidation, the decline in glutathione-cycle enzyme activity and the amplified maximal contraction to U46619, so the vascular phenotype need not require a cadmium-specific action on TXA2-receptor-mediated contraction or on NADPH oxidase. The present design cannot separate the two accounts because glycaemia and cadmium exposure vary together across the only three groups.
Links: competing explanation → H5; competing explanation → H6

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure protocol with in vivo follow-up of body weight, blood glucose and systolic blood pressure at week 0 and week 8.
Manipulation: Male Wistar rats of about 200 g were randomly assigned with a digital randomiser to control, CdCl2 40 ppm or CdCl2 80 ppm; cadmium chloride was given in the drinking water for 8 weeks. Animals were housed under controlled temperature and humidity with a 12-h light/dark cycle and ad libitum food and water. Systolic blood pressure was measured in conscious rats by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography after a 7-day acclimatisation to restraint, with multiple consecutive recordings per animal and exclusion of recordings with movement artefacts or unstable pulse detection.
Measurements: body weight (g); blood glucose (mg/dL); systolic blood pressure by tail-cuff plethysmography (mmHg)

Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: U46619 (TXA2 analogue) concentration-response curves in aortic rings, with and without apocynin preincubation.
Manipulation: Aortic rings prepared as in the other reactivity protocols were exposed to cumulative U46619 concentrations from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M, with contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl. Selected rings were incubated with apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction.
Measurements: isometric tension of aortic rings; Emax of U46619 contraction; pD2 of U46619 contraction
Comparison: groups: CTRL; CTRL/APO; Cd2+ 40 ppm; Cd2+ 40 ppm/APO; Cd2+ 80 ppm; Cd2+ 80 ppm/APO | endpoint: Emax and pD2 of the U46619 contraction curve, fitted per animal by nonlinear regression | varied: cadmium exposure level of the donor animal; presence of apocynin in the bath | held fixed: 3-mm thoracic aortic rings; Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; cumulative U46619 range 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; normalisation to the 80 mM KCl maximal contraction | unit: individual animal (n = 6 per condition in Table 2 and Figure 3) | window: Ex vivo, after 8 weeks of exposure | units: Emax relative to the 80 mM KCl contraction; pD2 as log of the half-maximal effective concentration | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test, p < 0.05
Observations: O3, O4, O5, O6

## E3
Statement: Spectrophotometric quantification of aortic lipid peroxidation products MDA and 4-HDA.
Manipulation: Aortic tissue from each rat was mechanically homogenised in potassium phosphate buffer (0.05 M, pH 7.8). Homogenates were centrifuged at 10,000 x g for 15 min at 4 degrees C, total protein was quantified by the Lowry method, and MDA and 4-HDA concentrations were measured in the supernatant at 586 nm.
Measurements: malondialdehyde concentration; 4-hydroxyalkenal concentration; total protein (Lowry)
Comparison: groups: CTRL; Cd2+ 40 ppm; Cd2+ 80 ppm | endpoint: MDA and 4-HDA concentration per mg protein | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm) | held fixed: thoracic aortic tissue homogenate; potassium phosphate buffer 0.05 M, pH 7.8; centrifugation at 10,000 x g, 15 min, 4 degrees C; absorbance read at 586 nm; normalisation to total protein by the Lowry method | unit: individual animal (n = 8 per group in Figure 4) | window: Aortic tissue collected after 8 weeks of exposure | units: micromol/mg | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test, p < 0.05
Observations: O7, O8

## E4
Statement: Spectrophotometric assay of aortic glutathione peroxidase activity.
Manipulation: Homogenate fraction (0.1 mL) was added to a freshly prepared buffer containing 50 mM K2HPO4 (pH 7.1), 1 mM EDTA, a catalase inhibitor, 0.2 mM NADPH, 1 unit of glutathione reductase and 1 mM reduced glutathione, incubated 5 min at room temperature; hydrogen peroxide (0.25 mM, 0.1 mL) was added, the mixture was centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 degrees C, and activity was quantified in the supernatant at 340 nm.
Measurements: glutathione peroxidase activity at 340 nm
Comparison: groups: CTRL; Cd2+ 40 ppm; Cd2+ 80 ppm | endpoint: Glutathione peroxidase activity per mg protein | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm) | held fixed: aortic homogenate fraction; assay buffer composition and 5-min room-temperature incubation; hydrogen peroxide 0.25 mM as substrate; absorbance read at 340 nm | unit: individual animal (n = 8 per group in Figure 4) | window: Aortic tissue collected after 8 weeks of exposure | units: U/mg | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test, p < 0.05
Observations: O9

## E5
Statement: Spectrophotometric assay of aortic glutathione reductase activity.
Manipulation: Tissue homogenate was mixed with potassium phosphate buffer (139 mM, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 degrees C; the supernatant was combined with NADPH (2.5 mmol/mL) and FAD (315 micromol/L), initial absorbance was read at 340 nm after 3.3 min, glutathione disulfide (22 mmol/L) was added, and absorbance was read again after 2.9 min, activity being calculated from the difference.
Measurements: glutathione reductase activity at 340 nm
Comparison: groups: CTRL; Cd2+ 40 ppm; Cd2+ 80 ppm | endpoint: Glutathione reductase activity per mg protein | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm) | held fixed: aortic homogenate supernatant; potassium phosphate buffer 139 mM, pH 7.4; NADPH and FAD concentrations; fixed absorbance timing at 340 nm | unit: individual animal (n = 8 per group in Figure 4) | window: Aortic tissue collected after 8 weeks of exposure | units: U/mg | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test, p < 0.05
Observations: O10

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the exposure protocol produces the intended hypertensive phenotype, with systolic blood pressure compared between week 0 and week 8 in each group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Quantify aortic lipid peroxidation products and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities across the exposure levels. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Chronic oral CdCl2 exposure (40 or 80 ppm for 8 weeks) produces a hypertensive phenotype in male Wistar rats, accompanied by changes in body weight and blood glucose.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Vasomotor function of isolated thoracic aortic rings is altered in cadmium-exposed hypertensive rats relative to controls.
Links: composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Contraction to the TXA2 analogue U46619 in aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H6

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Aortic redox balance, measured as lipid peroxidation products (MDA, 4-HDA) and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities (GPx, GR), changes with cadmium exposure level.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5; refinement → H7

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species within the vascular wall mediate the altered vasomotor responses of cadmium-exposed aortas; the proposed mechanism is probed by incubating rings with the NADPH oxidase inhibitor apocynin.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; proposed mechanism → H4

## H6 (claim)
Statement: TXA2 induces hypercontractility in aortas from cadmium-exposed hypertensive animals, an effect associated with oxidative stress and reversed after NADPH oxidase inhibition.
Links: refinement ← H3

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure produces dose-related aortic lipid peroxidation together with altered glutathione-cycle enzyme activity, described by the authors as a compensatory antioxidant response at the lower exposure followed by depletion at the higher one.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: Cadmium may increase post-receptor contractile capacity in aortic smooth muscle, contributing to the higher U46619 Emax, while the lipid-peroxidation and glutathione-enzyme changes are parallel tissue responses rather than the cause of hypercontractility. Apocynin's effect could include actions independent of NADPH oxidase inhibition.

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the exposure protocol produces the intended hypertensive phenotype, with systolic blood pressure compared between week 0 and week 8 in each group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Quantify aortic lipid peroxidation products and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities across the exposure levels. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Chronic oral CdCl2 exposure (40 or 80 ppm for 8 weeks) produces a hypertensive phenotype in male Wistar rats, accompanied by changes in body weight and blood glucose.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Vasomotor function of isolated thoracic aortic rings is altered in cadmium-exposed hypertensive rats relative to controls.
Links: composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Contraction to the TXA2 analogue U46619 in aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H6

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Aortic redox balance, measured as lipid peroxidation products (MDA, 4-HDA) and glutathione-cycle enzyme activities (GPx, GR), changes with cadmium exposure level.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5; refinement → H7

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species within the vascular wall mediate the altered vasomotor responses of cadmium-exposed aortas; the proposed mechanism is probed by incubating rings with the NADPH oxidase inhibitor apocynin.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; proposed mechanism → H4; competing explanation ← H8

## H6 (claim)
Statement: TXA2 induces hypercontractility in aortas from cadmium-exposed hypertensive animals, an effect associated with oxidative stress and reversed after NADPH oxidase inhibition.
Links: refinement ← H3

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure produces dose-related aortic lipid peroxidation together with altered glutathione-cycle enzyme activity, described by the authors as a compensatory antioxidant response at the lower exposure followed by depletion at the higher one.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: The greater U46619 hypercontractility of rings from Cd2+ 80 ppm animals is explained not by NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species but by the marked fall in glutathione peroxidase activity at 80 ppm, which leaves reactive oxygen species unchecked and reduces the sensitivity of the rings to apocynin inhibition, so the apocynin arm cannot establish NADPH oxidase involvement.
Links: competing explanation → H5

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure protocol with in vivo follow-up of body weight, blood glucose and systolic blood pressure at week 0 and week 8.
Manipulation: Male Wistar rats of about 200 g were randomly assigned with a digital randomiser to control, CdCl2 40 ppm or CdCl2 80 ppm; cadmium chloride was given in the drinking water for 8 weeks. Animals were housed under controlled temperature and humidity with a 12-h light/dark cycle and ad libitum food and water. Systolic blood pressure was measured in conscious rats by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography after a 7-day acclimatisation to restraint, with multiple consecutive recordings per animal and exclusion of recordings with movement artefacts or unstable pulse detection.
Measurements: body weight (g); blood glucose (mg/dL); systolic blood pressure by tail-cuff plethysmography (mmHg)
Comparison: groups: control (CTRL); CdCl2 40 ppm; CdCl2 80 ppm | endpoint: Body weight, blood glucose and systolic blood pressure, each recorded at week 0 and week 8 | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm); time (week 0 versus week 8) | held fixed: male Wistar rats of about 200 g at entry; same housing, light/dark cycle and ad libitum food and water; same quiet temperature-controlled room on the measurement day; same tail-cuff system and LabChart acquisition | unit: individual animal (n = 12 per group in Table 1) | window: Week 0 (baseline) and week 8 (end of exposure) | units: g for body weight, mg/dL for glucose, mmHg for systolic blood pressure | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; Methods state paired tests for within-group week 0 versus week 8 comparisons and between-group tests at each time point, while the Table 1 footnote reports Student's t test with asterisks marking p < 0.05 versus week 0
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: U46619 (TXA2 analogue) concentration-response curves in aortic rings, with and without apocynin preincubation.
Manipulation: Aortic rings prepared as in the other reactivity protocols were exposed to cumulative U46619 concentrations from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M, with contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl. Selected rings were incubated with apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction.
Measurements: isometric tension of aortic rings; Emax of U46619 contraction; pD2 of U46619 contraction

## E3
Statement: Spectrophotometric quantification of aortic lipid peroxidation products MDA and 4-HDA.
Manipulation: Aortic tissue from each rat was mechanically homogenised in potassium phosphate buffer (0.05 M, pH 7.8). Homogenates were centrifuged at 10,000 x g for 15 min at 4 degrees C, total protein was quantified by the Lowry method, and MDA and 4-HDA concentrations were measured in the supernatant at 586 nm.
Measurements: malondialdehyde concentration; 4-hydroxyalkenal concentration; total protein (Lowry)
Comparison: groups: CTRL; Cd2+ 40 ppm; Cd2+ 80 ppm | endpoint: MDA and 4-HDA concentration per mg protein | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm) | held fixed: thoracic aortic tissue homogenate; potassium phosphate buffer 0.05 M, pH 7.8; centrifugation at 10,000 x g, 15 min, 4 degrees C; absorbance read at 586 nm; normalisation to total protein by the Lowry method | unit: individual animal (n = 8 per group in Figure 4) | window: Aortic tissue collected after 8 weeks of exposure | units: micromol/mg | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test, p < 0.05
Observations: O7, O8

## E4
Statement: Spectrophotometric assay of aortic glutathione peroxidase activity.
Manipulation: Homogenate fraction (0.1 mL) was added to a freshly prepared buffer containing 50 mM K2HPO4 (pH 7.1), 1 mM EDTA, a catalase inhibitor, 0.2 mM NADPH, 1 unit of glutathione reductase and 1 mM reduced glutathione, incubated 5 min at room temperature; hydrogen peroxide (0.25 mM, 0.1 mL) was added, the mixture was centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 degrees C, and activity was quantified in the supernatant at 340 nm.
Measurements: glutathione peroxidase activity at 340 nm
Comparison: groups: CTRL; Cd2+ 40 ppm; Cd2+ 80 ppm | endpoint: Glutathione peroxidase activity per mg protein | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm) | held fixed: aortic homogenate fraction; assay buffer composition and 5-min room-temperature incubation; hydrogen peroxide 0.25 mM as substrate; absorbance read at 340 nm | unit: individual animal (n = 8 per group in Figure 4) | window: Aortic tissue collected after 8 weeks of exposure | units: U/mg | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test, p < 0.05
Observations: O9

## E5
Statement: Spectrophotometric assay of aortic glutathione reductase activity.
Manipulation: Tissue homogenate was mixed with potassium phosphate buffer (139 mM, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 degrees C; the supernatant was combined with NADPH (2.5 mmol/mL) and FAD (315 micromol/L), initial absorbance was read at 340 nm after 3.3 min, glutathione disulfide (22 mmol/L) was added, and absorbance was read again after 2.9 min, activity being calculated from the difference.
Measurements: glutathione reductase activity at 340 nm
Comparison: groups: CTRL; Cd2+ 40 ppm; Cd2+ 80 ppm | endpoint: Glutathione reductase activity per mg protein | varied: cadmium concentration in drinking water (0, 40, 80 ppm) | held fixed: aortic homogenate supernatant; potassium phosphate buffer 139 mM, pH 7.4; NADPH and FAD concentrations; fixed absorbance timing at 340 nm | unit: individual animal (n = 8 per group in Figure 4) | window: Aortic tissue collected after 8 weeks of exposure | units: U/mg | uncertainty: Mean +/- SEM; one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni test, p < 0.05

Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure protocol with in vivo follow-up of body weight, blood glucose and systolic blood pressure at week 0 and week 8.
Manipulation: Male Wistar rats of about 200 g were randomly assigned with a digital randomiser to control, CdCl2 40 ppm or CdCl2 80 ppm; cadmium chloride was given in the drinking water for 8 weeks. Systolic blood pressure was measured in conscious rats by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography after a 7-day acclimatisation to restraint, with multiple consecutive recordings per animal and exclusion of recordings with movement artefacts or unstable pulse detection.

# Main hypothesis
Can Ni electrodeposition on HNO3-activated CF fabric followed by vacuum heat treatment simultaneously enhance the EMI shielding and the mechanical properties of CFRP, and which interfacial microstructural changes accompany these property changes?
System: PAN-based T300 3K carbon fiber plain-weave fabric, sizing removed and HNO3-etched, Ni electrodeposited from a Watts bath at 0.02 A/cm2 (LD) or 0.04 A/cm2 (HD), vacuum heat-treated, and cured into 4674 epoxy CFRP panels
Conditions: LD 0.02 A/cm2 and HD 0.04 A/cm2 electrodeposition; IH at 500-900 °C or LH to 700 °C, 2 h, vacuum; EMI in the X band; quasi-static tensile tests of cured panels
Scope limits: LH applied only at 700 °C; EMI measured only in the X band
Validation requirements:
- R1: Enhance the X-band EMI shielding effectiveness of the CF reinforcement relative to pristine CF. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Improve the mechanical properties of the CFRP relative to pristine CFRP. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses

Statement: X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz) EMI shielding effectiveness (average and maximum SE_R, SE_A, SE_T) of Ni-coated, heat-treated CF compared with pristine CF
Links: refinement → H4

## H4 (claim)
Statement: LH at 700 °C is the optimal processing condition; it triggers morphological reconstruction and interfacial lattice rearrangement and overcomes the performance trade-off between EMI shielding capacity and mechanical ductility.

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H3)
- R2: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H2)
