# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H3)
- R2: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H2)

Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H5; refinement → H6; experimental target ← E2

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.

# Main hypothesis
By which mechanism do circulating factors of heart failure reach and damage the retinal neurovascular unit? The study tests whether elevated circulating TGFβ2 drives retinal endothelial epigenetic senescence through pSMAD2/EP300-H3K9ac-P21, whether senescent endothelium activates retinal microglia and neuroinflammation, and whether neutralizing TGFβ2 or depleting microglia preserves retinal structure and function.
System: Pressure-overload heart failure in C57BL/6J mice (TAC versus sham), parabiosis with sham- or TAC-operated partners, transfer of donor plasma onto cultured human endothelial cells (HUVECs and primary HRMECs), plasma from heart failure patients and healthy controls, and public human cardiac snRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets
Conditions: Surgery at 2 months of age; retinal assessment at 5 months in most mouse cohorts and at 6 months in the Tgfbr2 conditional knockout cohort; Dialyzed plasma applied to endothelial cells at 1% (v/v) for 48 h; Recombinant TGFβ2 at 6 ng/mL in culture and 6 ng per mouse by tail vein every 2 days for 2 months; Anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 mg/kg in vivo (six injections, intravitreal or tail vein) or 1 μg/mL on cells, against isotype IgG
Scope limits: Retinal readouts are electroretinography amplitudes, optical coherence tomography layer thickness, lectin vascular density and diameter, and immunostaining of senescence and microglial markers; Human material is limited to plasma, cultured endothelial cells and public transcriptomic datasets; Cardiac endpoints are echocardiographic and histological; no survival or systemic hemodynamic outcomes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish that the TAC model produces heart failure and that it damages retinal structure, function and the retinal vasculature. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Define the endothelial signaling route from TGFβ2 to senescence and test whether endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can directional freeze-drying of regenerated silk fibroin (RSF)/poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/Ti3C2Tx MXene mixtures produce ultralight aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture that provide efficient X-band EMI shielding, and how do MXene content and the lamellar architecture relate to shielding effectiveness and to the balance of absorption and reflection?
System: RSF/PVA/Ti3C2Tx MXene composite aerogels (RPM-20, RPM-40, RPM-60, RPM-80) prepared from Bombyx mori silk-derived RSF, PVA and LiF/HCl-etched Ti3C2Tx
Conditions: MXene content 20, 40, 60 and 80 wt% of total RSF + PVA + MXene solids; RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; EMI shielding measured by waveguide vector network analyzer over 8.2-12.4 GHz (X-band); Specimens 22.86 mm x 10.16 mm x 3 mm
Scope limits: Shielding was measured only in the X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Fabricate RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture and characterize MXene synthesis, incorporation and distribution in the RSF/PVA matrix. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine how Ti3C2Tx MXene content (20, 40, 60 and 80 wt%) affects X-band EMI shielding effectiveness (SE_T), shielding efficiency, and the absorption (A) and reflection (R) contributions. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Evaluate the lightweight shielding capability of the aerogels. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Reveal the relationship between the lamellar architecture and EMI shielding performance. (aspects: H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Directional freeze-drying produces an ordered lamellar architecture in the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Ti3C2Tx MXene is uniformly distributed throughout the aerogel framework.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: X-band EMI shielding effectiveness of the aerogels depends on MXene content (20-80 wt%) and on frequency.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The balance of shielding shifts from surface reflection toward internal absorption as MXene content increases, with RPM-60 absorption-dominated.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The aerogels are ultralight and provide high density-normalized (specific) shielding effectiveness.

## H6 (claim)
Statement: The enhanced EMI shielding of the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels originates from the combined effect of multiple internal reflections within the ordered lamellar channels, ohmic (conductive) loss from the MXene nanosheets, and polarization loss from MXene surface terminations and heterogeneous interfaces.

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Preparation of RPM-x aerogels by directional freezing and vacuum freeze-drying, with cross-sectional SEM and EDS elemental mapping of the composite aerogel.
Manipulation: Silk from Bombyx mori cocoons was degummed in 0.5 wt% Na2CO3 at 100 C for 30 min (2-3 times), dissolved in CaCl2/ethanol/water (molar ratio 1:2:8) at 80 C for 40 min, dialyzed for 72 h and freeze-dried to an RSF sponge. The RSF sponge was dissolved in 10 wt% aqueous PVA to an RSF:PVA mass ratio of 1:1, and Ti3C2Tx dispersion was added to give 20, 40, 60 or 80 wt% MXene in total solids. Each mixture was poured into a 3 cm x 3 cm x 3 cm PTFE mold with a copper template at the bottom, frozen by slowly injecting liquid nitrogen around the mold (freezing rate -10 C/min), and freeze-dried for 72 h (-70 C, <2 Pa).

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: The ordered lamellar structure is formed via directional freezing, with MXene uniformly distributed throughout the framework (supported by O1, O2).

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Shielding transitions from surface reflection to internal absorption with increasing MXene content, with RPM-60 dominated by absorption (supported by O5, O6).

# Main hypothesis
Can directional freeze-drying of regenerated silk fibroin (RSF)/poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/Ti3C2Tx MXene mixtures produce ultralight aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture that provide efficient X-band EMI shielding, and how do MXene content and the lamellar architecture relate to shielding effectiveness and to the balance of absorption and reflection?
System: RSF/PVA/Ti3C2Tx MXene composite aerogels (RPM-20, RPM-40, RPM-60, RPM-80) prepared from Bombyx mori silk-derived RSF, PVA and LiF/HCl-etched Ti3C2Tx
Conditions: MXene content 20, 40, 60 and 80 wt% of total RSF + PVA + MXene solids; RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; EMI shielding measured by waveguide vector network analyzer over 8.2-12.4 GHz (X-band); Specimens 22.86 mm x 10.16 mm x 3 mm
Scope limits: Shielding was measured only in the X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Fabricate RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture and characterize MXene synthesis, incorporation and distribution in the RSF/PVA matrix. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine how Ti3C2Tx MXene content (20, 40, 60 and 80 wt%) affects X-band EMI shielding effectiveness (SE_T), shielding efficiency, and the absorption (A) and reflection (R) contributions. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Evaluate the lightweight shielding capability of the aerogels. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Reveal the relationship between the lamellar architecture and EMI shielding performance. (aspects: H6)

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: X-band EMI shielding effectiveness of the aerogels depends on MXene content (20-80 wt%) and on frequency.

## H4 (aspect)

## H5 (aspect)

## H6 (claim)
Statement: The enhanced X-band EMI shielding of the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels is proposed to originate from the combined effect of multiple internal reflections within the ordered lamellar channels, ohmic (conductive) loss from the MXene nanosheets, and polarization loss from MXene surface terminations and heterogeneous interfaces; this remains a proposed explanation based on the available observations.

# Main hypothesis
Can directional freeze-drying of regenerated silk fibroin (RSF)/poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/Ti3C2Tx MXene mixtures produce ultralight aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture that provide efficient X-band EMI shielding, and how do MXene content and the lamellar architecture relate to shielding effectiveness and to the balance of absorption and reflection?
System: RSF/PVA/Ti3C2Tx MXene composite aerogels (RPM-20, RPM-40, RPM-60, RPM-80) prepared from Bombyx mori silk-derived RSF, PVA and LiF/HCl-etched Ti3C2Tx
Conditions: MXene content 20, 40, 60 and 80 wt% of total RSF + PVA + MXene solids; RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; EMI shielding measured by waveguide vector network analyzer over 8.2-12.4 GHz (X-band); Specimens 22.86 mm x 10.16 mm x 3 mm
Scope limits: Shielding was measured only in the X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Fabricate RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture and characterize MXene synthesis, incorporation and distribution in the RSF/PVA matrix. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine how Ti3C2Tx MXene content (20, 40, 60 and 80 wt%) affects X-band EMI shielding effectiveness (SE_T), shielding efficiency, and the absorption (A) and reflection (R) contributions. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Evaluate the lightweight shielding capability of the aerogels. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Reveal the relationship between the lamellar architecture and EMI shielding performance. (aspects: H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Directional freeze-drying produces an ordered lamellar architecture in the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Ti3C2Tx MXene is uniformly distributed throughout the aerogel framework.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: X-band EMI shielding effectiveness of the aerogels depends on MXene content (20-80 wt%) and on frequency.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The balance of shielding shifts from surface reflection toward internal absorption as MXene content increases, with RPM-60 absorption-dominated.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The aerogels are ultralight and provide high density-normalized (specific) shielding effectiveness.

## H6 (claim)
Statement: The enhanced EMI shielding of the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels is proposed to originate from the combined effect of multiple internal reflections within the ordered lamellar channels, ohmic (conductive) loss from the MXene nanosheets, and polarization loss from MXene surface terminations and heterogeneous interfaces. The polarization loss component is inferred from the material properties and is not directly measured in the visible evidence.

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine which signal processing strategy extracts the most information from the noisy composite signal. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine which signal processing strategy extracts the most information from the noisy composite signal. (aspects: H2)

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Among the four detection metrics (full RMS, 1 s moving-average RMS, residual RMS after 1 s moving-average subtraction, Chebyshev noise spectroscopy coefficients), residual RMS is the lowest threshold in all ten configurations of the factorial Monte Carlo study at the baseline worst-case coating (Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, 30 s recordings). # Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7; composition → H8

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Reduced riboflavin transfers electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension, and MtrC and OmcA are required for NCM reduction by the SO3-BS3 consortium; that S. oneidensis loads electrons onto riboflavin through MtrC and OmcA during leaching is a proposal taken from an earlier report and was not measured here, so the share of leaching carried by the shuttle rather than by direct cytochrome contact remains open.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: The relative contribution of direct MtrC/OmcA contact with NCM and of riboflavin shuttling to metal oxide leaching can be separated, for example by supplying reduced riboflavin to a consortium lacking both cytochromes or by titrating riboflavin at fixed cell density.
Links: composition ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7; composition → H8

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: In a cell-free anoxic suspension, reduced riboflavin becomes oxidised after NCM is added, consistent with electron transfer from reduced riboflavin to NCM. In the engineered SO3-BS3 consortium, deletion of mtrC or omcA individually, or both together, lowers total metal leaching relative to the intact consortium; the double-deletion value is indistinguishable from the BS3-only reference. These results support a role for MtrC and OmcA in the consortium’s enhanced leaching, but do not establish that they are required for all NCM reduction or that they load electrons onto riboflavin during leaching. Cytochrome-mediated riboflavin reduction was proposed in an earlier report, but was not measured here; the relative contributions of riboflavin shuttling and other electron-transfer routes remain unresolved.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: The relative contribution of direct MtrC/OmcA contact with NCM and of riboflavin shuttling to metal oxide leaching can be separated, for example by supplying reduced riboflavin to a consortium lacking both cytochromes or by titrating riboflavin at fixed cell density.
Links: composition ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can a W-shaped piezoresistive pressure sensor that couples a rigid aluminum sheet (inspired by the rigid outer wall and soft porous interior of Bambusa textilis) with a carbon-ink-coated melamine sponge and a micro-protruded MWCNT/PU film (inspired by the surface protrusions of Salvia plebeia R.Br.) address the poor stability and long recovery times of porous flexible pressure sensors, while providing a broad pressure range, usable sensitivity, fine load resolution, and terrain discrimination when mounted on a robot foot?
System: W-shaped layered sensor: aluminum sheet, insulating double-sided tape, carbon-black-ink-coated melamine sponge, MWCNT/PU film with sandpaper-replicated micro-protrusions, copper electrodes; 80 mm x 20 mm strip
Conditions: Bench loading with a motorized linear stage; resistance read with a Keithley DAQ6510 multimeter; force with a 1 kN gauge; Applied pressures up to 31.5 kPa; Robot tests on a six-legged robot with the sensor on the ventral side of one foot
Scope limits: Bench tests and one robot platform; Figure images and supplementary figures are not part of this text record
Validation requirements:
- R1: Fast response and recovery and faithful tracking of dynamic loads. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Main hypothesis
Does oral Oxystorm, given alone at a low and a high dose or combined with BCM-95, reduce infarct size and cardiac injury biomarkers after LAD ligation ischemia-reperfusion in Wistar rats, in a preventive (pre-treatment) model and a treatment (post-reperfusion) model?
System: Adult Wistar rats (150-200 g; equal numbers of males and females) with LAD ligation (45 min ischemia) followed by reperfusion
Conditions: Preventive model: daily oral dosing for 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31; Treatment model: 45 min ischemia, reperfusion for 7 days; dosing from 4 h after reperfusion, once daily until day 7; Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg (preventive) and 90 or 180 mg/kg (treatment); combination Oxystorm 90 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (preventive) or Oxystorm 180 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (treatment); Controls: vehicle (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control, verapamil 10 mg/kg LAD positive control
Scope limits: Single rat LAD ischemia-reperfusion model; Endpoints: TTC infarct size and cardiac injury biomarkers (LDH, CK-MB, myoglobin, troponin I)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Measure TTC infarct size in each group of both models. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Measure the cardiac injury biomarkers LDH, CK-MB, myoglobin and troponin I in each group of both models. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, protects the rat myocardium against LAD ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; refinement → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce TTC-defined infarct size relative to the LAD control.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce cardiac injury biomarkers (LDH, CK-MB, myoglobin, troponin I) relative to the LAD control.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (claim)
Statement: The combination of Oxystorm with curcuminoid-enriched turmeric extract (BCM-95) has a synergic cardioprotective effect against myocardial ischemia in vivo.
Links: refinement ← H1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: TTC infarct size in the preventive and treatment LAD ischemia-reperfusion models.
Manipulation: In each model, 56 adult Wistar rats (150-200 g) were randomly assigned to 7 groups of 8 (4 male, 4 female): vehicle control (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control (ischemia-reperfusion alone), verapamil 10 mg/kg (LAD positive control), low-dose Oxystorm, high-dose Oxystorm, and Oxystorm + BCM-95. LAD ligation: 45 min ischemia, then reperfusion. Preventive model: Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg in water, orally, daily for 30 days; combination Oxystorm 90 mg/kg (in water) + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (in dimethyl sulfoxide), orally, 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31. Treatment model: Oxystorm 90 or 180 mg/kg; combination Oxystorm 180 mg/kg + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (2:1); dosing started 4 h after reperfusion and continued once daily until day 7 of reperfusion.
Measurements: Hearts sectioned horizontally into 4-5 slices, stained with 2% TTC (pH 7.8, 37 C, 30 min), fixed in paraformaldehyde and photographed; unstained and stained areas quantified in ImageJ as % of total myocardial area; Outcome assessment blinded to treatment allocation; one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc test

# Main hypothesis
How does the substrate temperature used during RF-magnetron sputtering (room temperature, 150, 250 and 350 °C) affect the structure, nickel/oxygen defect chemistry, Li+ transport and electrochromic performance of nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films intended as counter electrodes for smart windows?
System: Nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films sputtered from an 82%:18% target onto FTO-coated glass
Conditions: Substrate temperature during deposition: RT, 150, 250 and 350 °C; 100 W RF power, 30 min deposition, Ar working pressure 5 × 10^-2 mbar; Electrochemical tests in 1 M LiClO4 in propylene carbonate
Scope limits: One target composition and one deposition time; Li+ electrolyte only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize crystallinity and local bonding structure of the films at each substrate temperature (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine nickel oxidation states and lattice versus defect oxygen as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H3)
- R3: Quantify Li+ diffusion and inserted charge as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H4, H5, H6)
- R4: Compare optical modulation and coloration/bleaching times across substrate temperatures (aspects: H7, H8)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Film structure of NWT films across substrate temperatures (crystallinity, local bonding, thickness)
Links: composition → H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: NWT films are amorphous across substrate temperatures, as assessed by X-ray diffraction
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Nickel oxidation state and oxygen-defect content of NWT films change with substrate temperature

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Li+ transport and charge insertion in NWT films vary with substrate temperature
Links: composition → H5; composition → H6

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Li+ diffusion coefficient derived from the CV anodic peak current varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Charge inserted per potential step (chronocoulometry) varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H4

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Optical modulation and switching kinetics of NWT films vary with substrate temperature
Links: composition → H8

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: Optical modulation (ΔT at 550 nm) varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H7; proposed mechanism ← H9

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: Deposition above 150 °C makes the films denser and more compact, which constrains Li+ diffusion pathways and lowers optical modulation
Links: proposed mechanism → H8

# Main hypothesis
How does the substrate temperature used during RF-magnetron sputtering (room temperature, 150, 250 and 350 °C) affect the structure, nickel/oxygen defect chemistry, Li+ transport and electrochromic performance of nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films intended as counter electrodes for smart windows?
System: Nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films sputtered from an 82%:18% target onto FTO-coated glass
Conditions: Substrate temperature during deposition: RT, 150, 250 and 350 °C; 100 W RF power, 30 min deposition, Ar working pressure 5 × 10^-2 mbar; Electrochemical tests in 1 M LiClO4 in propylene carbonate
Scope limits: One target composition and one deposition time; Li+ electrolyte only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize crystallinity and local bonding structure of the films at each substrate temperature (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine nickel oxidation states and lattice versus defect oxygen as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H3)
- R3: Quantify Li+ diffusion and inserted charge as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H4, H5, H6)
- R4: Compare optical modulation and coloration/bleaching times across substrate temperatures (aspects: H7, H8)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Film structure of NWT films across substrate temperatures (crystallinity, local bonding, thickness)
Links: composition → H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: NWT films are amorphous across substrate temperatures, as assessed by X-ray diffraction
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Nickel oxidation state and oxygen-defect content of NWT films change with substrate temperature

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Li+ transport and charge insertion in NWT films vary with substrate temperature
Links: composition → H5; composition → H6

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Li+ diffusion coefficient derived from the CV anodic peak current varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Charge inserted per potential step (chronocoulometry) varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H4

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Optical modulation and switching kinetics of NWT films vary with substrate temperature
Links: composition → H8

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: Optical modulation (ΔT at 550 nm) varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H7; proposed mechanism ← H9; proposed mechanism ← H10

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: Deposition above 150 °C makes the films denser and more compact, which constrains Li+ diffusion pathways and lowers optical modulation
Links: proposed mechanism → H8; competing explanation ← H10

## H10 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate (unverified): films deposited at 250 and 350 °C have fewer electrochemically active Ni redox sites, reflected in lower Ni3+ (nickel-vacancy-related) and defect-oxygen fractions, so less Ni2+/Ni3+ switching charge is available and the optical contrast is smaller, independently of whether Li+ transport pathways are restricted by densification.
Links: competing explanation → H9; proposed mechanism → H8

# Main hypothesis
How does the substrate temperature used during RF-magnetron sputtering (room temperature, 150, 250 and 350 °C) affect the structure, nickel/oxygen defect chemistry, Li+ transport and electrochromic performance of nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films intended as counter electrodes for smart windows?
System: Nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films sputtered from an 82%:18% target onto FTO-coated glass
Conditions: Substrate temperature during deposition: RT, 150, 250 and 350 °C; 100 W RF power, 30 min deposition, Ar working pressure 5 × 10^-2 mbar; Electrochemical tests in 1 M LiClO4 in propylene carbonate

Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize crystallinity and local bonding structure of the films at each substrate temperature (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine nickel oxidation states and lattice versus defect oxygen as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
How does the substrate temperature used during RF-magnetron sputtering (room temperature, 150, 250 and 350 °C) affect the structure, nickel/oxygen defect chemistry, Li+ transport and electrochromic performance of nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films intended as counter electrodes for smart windows?
System: Nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films sputtered from an 82%:18% target onto FTO-coated glass
Conditions: Substrate temperature during deposition: RT, 150, 250 and 350 °C; 100 W RF power, 30 min deposition, Ar working pressure 5 × 10^-2 mbar; Electrochemical tests in 1 M LiClO4 in propylene carbonate

Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize crystallinity and local bonding structure of the films at each substrate temperature (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine nickel oxidation states and lattice versus defect oxygen as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H3)
- R3: Quantify Li+ diffusion and inserted charge as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H4, H5, H6)

# Main hypothesis
How does the substrate temperature used during RF-magnetron sputtering (room temperature, 150, 250 and 350 °C) affect the structure, nickel/oxygen defect chemistry, Li+ transport and electrochromic performance of nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films intended as counter electrodes for smart windows?
System: Nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films sputtered from an 82%:18% target onto FTO-coated glass
Conditions: Substrate temperature during deposition: RT, 150, 250 and 350 °C; 100 W RF power, 30 min deposition, Ar working pressure 5 × 10^-2 mbar; Electrochemical tests in 1 M LiClO4 in propylene carbonate
Scope limits: One target composition and one deposition time; Li+ electrolyte only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize crystallinity and local bonding structure of the films at each substrate temperature (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Determine nickel oxidation states and lattice versus defect oxygen as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H3)
- R3: Quantify Li+ diffusion and inserted charge as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H4, H5, H6)
- R4: Compare optical modulation and coloration/bleaching times across substrate temperatures (aspects: H7, H8)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Film structure of NWT films across substrate temperatures (crystallinity, local bonding, thickness)
Links: composition → H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: NWT films are amorphous across substrate temperatures, as assessed by X-ray diffraction
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Nickel oxidation state and oxygen-defect content of NWT films change with substrate temperature

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Li+ transport and charge insertion in NWT films vary with substrate temperature
Links: composition → H5; composition → H6

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Li+ diffusion coefficient derived from the CV anodic peak current varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Charge inserted per potential step (chronocoulometry) varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H4

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Optical modulation and switching kinetics of NWT films vary with substrate temperature
Links: composition → H8

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: Optical modulation (ΔT at 550 nm) varies with substrate temperature
Links: composition ← H7; proposed mechanism ← H9

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: Deposition above 150 °C makes the films denser and more compact, which constrains Li+ diffusion pathways and lowers optical modulation
Links: proposed mechanism → H8

## H10 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate alternative: The lower optical modulation at 250 °C and 350 °C is partly due to reduced Li+ insertion capacity (Qin) rather than only the dense film structure constraining Li+ diffusion pathways.

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature

# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?
System: 411 patients with confirmed superficial LNTB, Xi'an Chest Hospital, November 30, 2018 to June 17, 2024; tissue and purulent specimens tested with a Mycobacterium nucleic acid detection kit (PCR-fluorescent probe) on an ABI7500 real-time PCR system
Conditions: Retrospective extraction of electronic medical records; Blood for laboratory tests, including T lymphocyte subsets, collected within 24 hours of admission; PCR-fluorescent probe result as the dependent variable in logistic regression
Scope limits: Single center (Xi'an Chest Hospital); Superficial LNTB only; other extrapulmonary TB forms not studied; Observational retrospective design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Screen candidate factors (demographic characteristics, TB-related information, comorbidities, laboratory data, T lymphocyte subsets and number of samples) for association with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. (aspects: H1, H4, H5)
- R2: Explore the dose-response relationships of age, total T lymphocytes (CD3+), T helper lymphocytes (CD3+CD4+) and the T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models combined with logistic regression. (aspects: H4, H6, H7, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Specimen acquisition factors (how and how many specimens were obtained) are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result in LNTB patients.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Samples obtained through surgery, compared with samples not obtained through surgery, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Double samples, compared with a single sample, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Age is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H10

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Peripheral T lymphocyte subsets measured within 24 hours of admission are associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition → H6; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Total T lymphocyte count (CD3+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: T helper lymphocyte count (CD3+CD4+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5; proposed mechanism ← H11

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: T suppressor lymphocyte count (CD3+CD8+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H5

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: The T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5

## H10 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' proposed mechanism: the age pattern reflects combined effects of immune maturation, mycobacterial burden and disease activity; young adults have an active immune response and relatively higher mycobacterial burden, and after about 28 years cellular immunity stabilizes and mycobacterial clearance increases, lowering tissue MTB nucleic acid load.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

## H11 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' proposed mechanism: stronger CD4+-mediated immune clearance reduces mycobacterial nucleic acid content in lesions and thereby lowers PCR positivity, with no further effect once a protective threshold (about 858 cells/uL) is reached.
Links: proposed mechanism → H7

# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?
System: 411 patients with confirmed superficial LNTB, Xi'an Chest Hospital, November 30, 2018 to June 17, 2024; tissue and purulent specimens tested with a Mycobacterium nucleic acid detection kit (PCR-fluorescent probe) on an ABI7500 real-time PCR system
Conditions: Retrospective extraction of electronic medical records; Blood for laboratory tests, including T lymphocyte subsets, collected within 24 hours of admission; PCR-fluorescent probe result as the dependent variable in logistic regression
Scope limits: Single center (Xi'an Chest Hospital); Superficial LNTB only; other extrapulmonary TB forms not studied; Observational retrospective design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Screen candidate factors (demographic characteristics, TB-related information, comorbidities, laboratory data, T lymphocyte subsets and number of samples) for association with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. (aspects: H1, H4, H5)
- R2: Explore the dose-response relationships of age, total T lymphocytes (CD3+), T helper lymphocytes (CD3+CD4+) and the T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models combined with logistic regression. (aspects: H4, H6, H7, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Specimen acquisition factors (how and how many specimens were obtained) are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result in LNTB patients.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Samples obtained through surgery, compared with samples not obtained through surgery, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Double samples, compared with a single sample, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Age is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H10

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Peripheral T lymphocyte subsets measured within 24 hours of admission are associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition → H6; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Total T lymphocyte count (CD3+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: T helper lymphocyte count (CD3+CD4+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5; proposed mechanism ← H11

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: T suppressor lymphocyte count (CD3+CD8+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H5

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: The T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5

## H10 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' proposed mechanism: the age pattern reflects combined effects of immune maturation, mycobacterial burden and disease activity; young adults have an active immune response and relatively higher mycobacterial burden, and after about 28 years cellular immunity stabilizes and mycobacterial clearance increases, lowering tissue MTB nucleic acid load.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

## H11 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' proposed mechanism: stronger CD4+-mediated immune clearance reduces mycobacterial nucleic acid content in lesions and thereby lowers PCR positivity, with no further effect once a protective threshold (about 858 cells/uL) is reached.
Links: proposed mechanism → H7

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: Pre-sampling prediction: in patients with suspected LNTB assessed before specimen collection, age and admission CD3+CD4+ count predict whether the PCR-fluorescent probe result will be positive, with useful accuracy beyond what the planned sampling route and number of samples already predict.
Links: composition → H13; composition → H14; composition → H15

## H13 (aspect)
Statement: Discrimination and incremental value: a model with age and CD3+CD4+ count separates PCR-positive from PCR-negative patients (C-statistic with 95% CI), and adding them to a model with sampling route and number of samples improves discrimination.
Links: composition ← H12

## H14 (aspect)
Statement: Calibration and cut-offs: predicted probabilities agree with observed positivity across risk groups, and pre-specified cut-offs (e.g., age 28 years, CD3+CD4+ 858 cells/uL) give stated sensitivity and specificity for a positive result.
Links: composition ← H12

## H15 (aspect)
Statement: Transportability: discrimination and calibration hold in an independent cohort of patients with suspected LNTB sampled at other centers, including patients later not confirmed as TB.
Links: composition ← H12

Statement: Multivariate logistic regression of the PCR-fluorescent probe result (Table 3). Methods state that covariates with P < .05 in univariate regression were included, with covariate selection also based on clinical relevance and prior evidence. ## E2
Statement: Quartile logistic regression models for age, total CD3+, CD3+CD4+ and CD4+/CD8+ ratio (Table 4) with three adjustment levels: Model 1 unadjusted; Model 2 adjusted for sex/gender, BMI, smoking, drinking (plus age for the T lymphocyte indicators); Model 3 adjusted for gender, BMI, sampling through surgery, treatment regimen, course of disease, 'treatmite' (as printed), initial treatment, smoking, drinking, anemia, hypoproteinemia, TB of other organs, diabetes, hypertension, hepatobiliary disease, number of samples, CD4+/CD8+ and adenosine deaminase (plus age for the T lymphocyte indicators). Trend tests entered the median of each quartile as a continuous variable.
Manipulation: None (observational factors).
Measurements: OR (95% CI); P; P for trend

# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?
System: 411 patients with confirmed superficial LNTB, Xi'an Chest Hospital, November 30, 2018 to June 17, 2024; tissue and purulent specimens tested with a Mycobacterium nucleic acid detection kit (PCR-fluorescent probe) on an ABI7500 real-time PCR system
Conditions: Retrospective extraction of electronic medical records; Blood for laboratory tests, including T lymphocyte subsets, collected within 24 hours of admission; PCR-fluorescent probe result as the dependent variable in logistic regression
Scope limits: Single center (Xi'an Chest Hospital); Superficial LNTB only; other extrapulmonary TB forms not studied; Observational retrospective design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Screen candidate factors (demographic characteristics, TB-related information, comorbidities, laboratory data, T lymphocyte subsets and number of samples) for association with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. (aspects: H1, H4, H5)
- R2: Explore the dose-response relationships of age, total T lymphocytes (CD3+), T helper lymphocytes (CD3+CD4+) and the T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models combined with logistic regression. (aspects: H4, H6, H7, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Specimen acquisition factors (how and how many specimens were obtained) are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result in LNTB patients.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Samples obtained through surgery, compared with samples not obtained through surgery, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Double samples, compared with a single sample, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Age is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H10; proposed mechanism ← H12; composition → H13

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Peripheral T lymphocyte subsets measured within 24 hours of admission are associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition → H6; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Total T lymphocyte count (CD3+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: T helper lymphocyte count (CD3+CD4+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5; proposed mechanism ← H11; proposed mechanism ← H12; composition → H13

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: T suppressor lymphocyte count (CD3+CD8+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H5

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: The T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) is associated with the PCR-fluorescent probe result, by quartile and as a dose-response relationship.
Links: composition ← H5

## H10 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' proposed mechanism: the age pattern reflects combined effects of immune maturation, mycobacterial burden and disease activity; young adults have an active immune response and relatively higher mycobacterial burden, and after about 28 years cellular immunity stabilizes and mycobacterial clearance increases, lowering tissue MTB nucleic acid load.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

## H11 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' proposed mechanism: stronger CD4+-mediated immune clearance reduces mycobacterial nucleic acid content in lesions and thereby lowers PCR positivity, with no further effect once a protective threshold (about 858 cells/uL) is reached.
Links: proposed mechanism → H7

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: Age and CD3+CD4+ count predict the PCR-fluorescent probe result before specimen collection; the prediction rule is based on the nonlinear age relationship and the linear CD3+CD4+ relationship.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4; proposed mechanism → H7

## H13 (aspect)
Statement: A decision rule: if a patient is below 28 years, the model predicts a positive PCR result; above 28 years, the model predicts a negative result, so fewer specimens are needed.
Links: composition ← H4; composition ← H7; proposed mechanism → H14

## H14 (mechanism)
Statement: Proposed mechanism for the threshold: below about 858 cells/uL, CD3+CD4+ count lowers the risk of a positive result; above it, no significant further change in risk is seen.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H13

# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?
System: 411 patients with confirmed superficial LNTB, Xi'an Chest Hospital, November 30, 2018 to June 17, 2024; tissue and purulent specimens tested with a Mycobacterium nucleic acid detection kit (PCR-fluorescent probe) on an ABI7500 real-time PCR system
Conditions: Retrospective extraction of electronic medical records; Blood for laboratory tests, including T lymphocyte subsets, collected within 24 hours of admission; PCR-fluorescent probe result as the dependent variable in logistic regression
Scope limits: Single center (Xi'an Chest Hospital); Superficial LNTB only; other extrapulmonary TB forms not studied; Observational retrospective design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Screen candidate factors (demographic characteristics, TB-related information, comorbidities, laboratory data, T lymphocyte subsets and number of samples) for association with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. (aspects: H1, H4, H5)
- R2: Explore the dose-response relationships of age, total T lymphocytes (CD3+), T helper lymphocytes (CD3+CD4+) and the T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models combined with logistic regression. (aspects: H4, H6, H7, H9)

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H2)
- R2: The Ni-P diffusion barrier layer on the TE element surface is uniform and defect-minimized. (aspects: H2)
- R3: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H2)
- R4: The Ni-P layer suppresses Cu diffusion and intermetallic compound formation between the Cu layer and the TE element after heat treatment. (aspects: H1)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: SDS-assisted selective electroless Ni-P plating forms a uniform Ni-P layer on the exposed TE element surface of polymer-coated cylindrical TE elements, and this layer acts as a Cu diffusion barrier.
Links: composition → H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: SDS addition to the electroless Ni-P bath affects plating selectivity, the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and Cu diffusion barrier performance.
Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H2)
- R2: The Ni-P diffusion barrier layer on the TE element surface is uniform and defect-minimized. (aspects: H2)
- R3: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H2)
- R4: The Ni-P layer suppresses Cu diffusion and intermetallic compound formation between the Cu layer and the TE element after heat treatment. (aspects: H1)

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H2)
- R2: The Ni-P diffusion barrier layer on the TE element surface is uniform and defect-minimized. (aspects: H2)
- R3: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H2)
- R4: The Ni-P layer suppresses Cu diffusion and intermetallic compound formation between the Cu layer and the TE element after heat treatment. (aspects: H1)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Under the reported plating conditions, electroless Ni-P plating from Bath B (0.5 g/L SDS) forms a uniform, continuous layer on the exposed TE element region while deposition on the adjacent polymer region is effectively suppressed. For Cu/Ni-P specimens using this layer, EPMA detected no Cu beyond the Ni-P layer or in the Bi/Te regions and reported no intermetallic compound formation in the as-deposited or 100 °C and 200 °C Ar-treated specimens; this supports barrier performance at the reported detection and exposure scope, with heat-treatment duration unspecified.
Links: composition → H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: SDS addition to the electroless Ni-P bath affects plating selectivity, the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and Cu diffusion barrier performance.
Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Sn is incorporated as Sn4+ into the bulk of the single-crystalline particles, preferentially on transition-metal sites.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: A residual Li2SnO3 phase is present on the surface of SC-Sn-NCA90 particles.

## H4 (claim)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 shows higher rate capability and 500-cycle capacity retention than PC-NCA90 in half-cells cycled to 4.5 V and to 4.7 V.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: The dual-site Sn modification, bulk Sn doping plus the residual surface Li2SnO3 layer, produces the improved high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Sn is incorporated as Sn4+ into the bulk of the single-crystalline particles, preferentially on transition-metal sites.
Links: composition ← H6

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: A residual Li2SnO3 phase is present on the surface of SC-Sn-NCA90 particles.
Links: composition ← H7

## H4 (claim)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 shows higher rate capability and 500-cycle capacity retention than PC-NCA90 in half-cells cycled to 4.5 V and to 4.7 V.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5; proposed mechanism ← H8

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: The dual-site Sn modification, bulk Sn doping plus the residual surface Li2SnO3 layer, produces the improved high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4; composition → H6; composition → H7

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Bulk Sn4+ on transition-metal sites anchors lattice oxygen and keeps the H2-H3 transition reversible during cycling to 4.5 V, limiting layered-to-rock-salt transformation and capacity fade.
Links: composition ← H5; composition → H2

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: The surface Li2SnO3 layer lowers cathode-electrolyte interphase resistance and suppresses electrolyte decomposition and Ni dissolution during high-voltage cycling.
Links: composition ← H5; composition → H3

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: Independently of Sn chemistry, the grain-boundary-free single-crystalline morphology of SC-Sn-NCA90 prevents intergranular cracking and the associated exposure of fresh surface to electrolyte, contributing to its higher retention and lower impedance growth relative to polycrystalline PC-NCA90.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Sn is incorporated as Sn4+ into the bulk of the single-crystalline particles, preferentially on transition-metal sites.
Links: proposed explanation → H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: A residual Li2SnO3 phase is present on the surface of SC-Sn-NCA90 particles.

## H4 (claim)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 shows higher rate capability and 500-cycle capacity retention than PC-NCA90 in half-cells cycled to 4.5 V and to 4.7 V.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: The dual-site Sn modification, bulk Sn doping plus the residual surface Li2SnO3 layer, produces the improved high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4; proposed mechanism → H6; proposed mechanism → H7

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: The structural component of the dual-site Sn modification: bulk Sn doping reduces the voltage hysteresis and intensity loss of the H2-H3 oxidation peak, lowers the fitted interfacial charge-transfer resistance (Rct) and charge-transfer-inhibiting layer resistance (RCEI), and preserves the apparent Li+ diffusion coefficient (DLi+) during cycling.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: The interfacial component of the dual-site Sn modification: a residual surface Li2SnO3 phase of about 8 nm forms a thin, protective CEI that attenuates oxidative decomposition products (LiF2-, PO3-, C2HO-) and suppresses transition-metal dissolution (NiF3-), preventing intergranular cracking.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5; proposed explanation ← H2

Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H4, H5)

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Sn is incorporated as Sn4+ into the bulk of the single-crystalline particles, preferentially on transition-metal sites.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: A residual Li2SnO3 phase is present on the surface of SC-Sn-NCA90 particles.

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H2, H3, H6, H7)

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H2, H3, H6, H7)
