# Main hypothesis
Can chimeric antigen receptors that combine an aducanumab-derived anti-Aβ scFv with a TAM-family (TYRO3, AXL, MERTK) intracellular domain increase amyloid-β engulfment by macrophages and microglia while limiting pro-inflammatory activation, and does the selected design reduce Aβ burden after transplantation of human iPSC-derived CAR microglia-like cells into an AD mouse brain?
System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed
Validation requirements:
- R1: CAR constructs must increase oAβ engulfment relative to cells lacking a TAM intracellular signalling domain. (aspects: H1)
- R2: The selected design must limit pro-inflammatory cytokine induction under acute co-stimulation, LPS priming and prolonged oAβ exposure. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Anti-Aβ CARs carrying a TAM-family intracellular domain increase oAβ engulfment by macrophage and microglial cell lines relative to control constructs.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The second-version CAR architecture, in which the FNIII repeats and native transmembrane segment replace the CD8 hinge and transmembrane module, changes TAM downstream signalling relative to the first-version architecture.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: TAM-CAR expression limits pro-inflammatory cytokine transcript induction in myeloid and microglial lines under acute LPS plus oAβ co-stimulation, LPS priming followed by oAβ, and prolonged oAβ exposure.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H4

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Engagement of the CAR by Aβ induces STAT1 phosphorylation, which promotes SOCS1 and SOCS3 upregulation and thereby suppresses inflammatory gene expression.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3; proposed mechanism → H2

## H5 (claim)
Statement: The structural basis for the differential anti-inflammatory activity of V1 and V2 AXL-CAR constructs has been confirmed by AlphaFold2 prediction: the V2 design exhibits enhanced interfacial stability at the dimer interface, which underlies its stronger downstream signalling and upregulation of anti-inflammatory regulators like Socs3.
Links: refinement ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can chimeric antigen receptors that combine an aducanumab-derived anti-Aβ scFv with a TAM-family (TYRO3, AXL, MERTK) intracellular domain increase amyloid-β engulfment by macrophages and microglia while limiting pro-inflammatory activation, and does the selected design reduce Aβ burden after transplantation of human iPSC-derived CAR microglia-like cells into an AD mouse brain?
System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed
Validation requirements:
- R1: CAR constructs must increase oAβ engulfment relative to cells lacking a TAM intracellular signalling domain. (aspects: H1)
- R2: The selected design must limit pro-inflammatory cytokine induction under acute co-stimulation, LPS priming and prolonged oAβ exposure. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Anti-Aβ CARs carrying a TAM-family intracellular domain increase oAβ engulfment by macrophage and microglial cell lines relative to control constructs.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The second-version CAR architecture, in which the FNIII repeats and native transmembrane segment replace the CD8 hinge and transmembrane module, changes TAM downstream signalling relative to the first-version architecture.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: TAM-CAR expression limits pro-inflammatory cytokine transcript induction in myeloid and microglial lines under acute LPS plus oAβ co-stimulation, LPS priming followed by oAβ, and prolonged oAβ exposure.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H4

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Engagement of the CAR by Aβ induces STAT1 phosphorylation, which promotes SOCS1 and SOCS3 upregulation and thereby suppresses inflammatory gene expression.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3; proposed mechanism → H2

## H5 (claim)
Statement: The second-version AXL-CAR architecture, in which the FNIII repeats and native transmembrane segment replace the CD8 hinge and transmembrane module, is predicted to have greater interfacial stability at the dimer interface than the first-version architecture. This structural prediction is consistent with the stronger phospho-STAT1 and Socs1/Socs3 induction observed in RAW264.7 cells expressing V2 AXL-CAR relative to V1 AXL-CAR cells; the RAW264.7 engulfment result is not reported for the V1/V2 comparison, and the BV2 engulfment result shows no difference between the two constructs. The claim does not extend to other TAM-family constructs or to all cell types.
Links: refinement ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can chimeric antigen receptors that combine an aducanumab-derived anti-Aβ scFv with a TAM-family (TYRO3, AXL, MERTK) intracellular domain increase amyloid-β engulfment by macrophages and microglia while limiting pro-inflammatory activation, and does the selected design reduce Aβ burden after transplantation of human iPSC-derived CAR microglia-like cells into an AD mouse brain?
System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed
Validation requirements:
- R1: CAR constructs must increase oAβ engulfment relative to cells lacking a TAM intracellular signalling domain. (aspects: H1)
- R2: The selected design must limit pro-inflammatory cytokine induction under acute co-stimulation, LPS priming and prolonged oAβ exposure. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Anti-Aβ CARs carrying a TAM-family intracellular domain increase oAβ engulfment by macrophage and microglial cell lines relative to control constructs.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The second-version CAR architecture, in which the FNIII repeats and native transmembrane segment replace the CD8 hinge and transmembrane module, changes TAM downstream signalling relative to the first-version architecture.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: TAM-CAR expression limits pro-inflammatory cytokine transcript induction in myeloid and microglial lines under acute LPS plus oAβ co-stimulation, LPS priming followed by oAβ, and prolonged oAβ exposure.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H4

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Engagement of the CAR by Aβ induces STAT1 phosphorylation, which promotes SOCS1 and SOCS3 upregulation and thereby suppresses inflammatory gene expression.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3; proposed mechanism → H2

## H5 (claim)
Statement: The second-version AXL-CAR (V2) differs from the first-version AXL-CAR (V1) in its predicted dimer structure, which includes multiple interfacial hydrogen bonds at the dimer interface. This structural difference may contribute to the stronger downstream signalling and induction of anti-inflammatory regulators observed in V2 cells, but the visible data do not show a difference in phagocytic efficiency between the V1 and V2 constructs.
Links: refinement ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can enzymatic hydrolysis of coconut kernel fiber (CKF), a coconut-processing by-product, yield a low-molecular-weight (1-3 kDa) hydrolysate fraction (LW-CKFH) that inhibits alpha-glucosidase, improves glucose metabolism in IR-HepG2 cells and in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, retains activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions, and contains identifiable alpha-glucosidase inhibitory peptides?
System: CKF protein hydrolysates (CKFH) and their ultrafiltration/gel-filtration fractions; in vitro alpha-glucosidase (pNPG) assay; HepG2 and insulin-induced IR-HepG2 cells; male Kunming mice with high-sugar high-fat diet plus streptozotocin (HSHFD/STZ) induced T2DM; simulated digestion and bread model; LC-MS/MS, in silico screening, molecular docking and synthetic peptides.
Conditions: Ultrasound-assisted sequential neutral then alkaline protease hydrolysis (8000 U/g, 2 h each); LW-CKFH = 1-3 kDa ultrafiltration fraction; Mice: oral gavage for 4 weeks with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, or LW-CKFH 200, 400, 800 mg/kg bw; n = 6 per group; Stability/matrix outcomes expressed as retention relative to untreated LW-CKFH (20 mg/mL, pH 7.0, 25 C) set to 100%
Scope limits: Single mouse strain and sex (male Kunming), one T2DM induction model, one 4-week treatment period; Insulin resistance and sensitivity assessed by HOMA surrogate indices from fasting glucose and insulin; Peptide binding assessed by molecular docking; synthetic peptides tested only for in vitro alpha-glucosidase inhibition; Food feasibility assessed in vitro (simulated digestion, one bread formulation)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Assess resistance to simulated gastrointestinal digestion, processing stability (heat, pH, metal ions), food-matrix effects, and glucose release from a food containing LW-CKFH. (aspects: H1)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: LW-CKFH is feasible as a hypoglycemic functional-food ingredient: it retains alpha-glucosidase inhibitory activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions and slows glucose release from a food.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: LW-CKFH retains alpha-glucosidase inhibitory activity after exposure to pH 2.0-11.0.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: LW-CKFH alpha-glucosidase inhibitory activity depends on the metal ion present (K+, Ca2+, Al3+, Mg2+, Fe3+).
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Metal ions act as oxidizing agents that oxidatively modify amino-acid residues of LW-CKFH peptides, lowering their inhibitory activity (explanation drawn from a cited prior report).
Links: proposed mechanism → H3

- R2: Assess OER durability of NiFe-LDH-4 in alkaline seawater, including at high current density. (aspects: H2, H3)

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10; composition → H11; composition → H13

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H6

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: The Al-doping level sets the rate of in-situ dry reforming of the adsorbed CO2.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping increases the CO2 capture rate of the DFMs (fast carbonation and diffusion through the CaCO3 product layer) relative to CaO and across x, in proportion to oxygen-vacancy content.

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10; composition → H11; composition → H13

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10; composition → H11

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H6

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: The Al-doping level sets the rate of in-situ dry reforming of the adsorbed CO2.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping increases the CO2 capture rate of the DFMs (fast carbonation and diffusion through the CaCO3 product layer) relative to CaO and across x, in proportion to oxygen-vacancy content.

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10; composition → H11

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism. (aspects: H1, H2, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR induces ferroptosis-associated changes in bacteria: intracellular ROS, lipid peroxidation, GSH oxidation and reduced GSH-Px activity.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H6

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR interferes with the bacterial ETC and energy metabolism.
Links: composition → H3; composition → H4; proposed mechanism ← H6

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR lowers bacterial ATP content.
Links: composition ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR inhibits the activity of bacterial respiratory chain complexes.
Links: composition ← H2

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx(+NIR) changes the E. coli transcriptome, including energy-metabolism, iron-transport and glutathione-metabolism genes.

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' mechanism: under NIR, sulfur-vacancy-rich Fe-WS2@GOx generates abundant ROS (with GOx-derived H2O2), which oxidizes GSH, inactivates GSH-Px and drives lipid peroxidation (bacterial ferroptosis) while inhibiting ETC complexes and ATP synthesis, leading to bacterial death.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1; proposed mechanism → H2

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism. (aspects: H1, H2, H5)

Links: composition → H3; composition → H4; proposed mechanism ← H6

Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR lowers bacterial ATP content.
Links: composition ← H2

Links: composition ← H2

Links: proposed mechanism → H1; proposed mechanism → H2

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Molecular processes related to oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, mitochondrial homeostasis and cell survival are characterized, including by cardiac proteomics. (aspects: H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H8

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserves left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation limits left ventricular structural remodeling in MI rats (hypertrophy, dilation, interstitial fibrosis and ECM protein accumulation).
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: At 4 weeks after MI, mitochondrial transplantation prevented the reported MI-associated increase in cardiac DHE fluorescence (used as a superoxide estimate); SOD1 and SOD2 mRNA were unchanged across groups.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 4 weeks after MI, mitochondrial transplantation reportedly prevented increases in cardiac CCL2, TLR4, and sST2 mRNA; IL-33 and ST2L mRNA were unchanged.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: At 4 weeks after MI, mitochondrial transplantation attenuated or prevented reported increases in cardiac BiP, CHOP, ATF4, and ATF6α protein.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserved LV function, reduced cardiac hypertrophy, and attenuated interstitial fibrosis 4 weeks after MI, effects that were accompanied by decreases in oxidative stress, inflammation, and ER stress activation.
Links: analysis derivation ← H4; analysis derivation ← H5; analysis derivation ← H6; analysis derivation ← H2; analysis derivation ← H3

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: At 4 weeks after MI, no difference in CMR-measured infarct size was reported between vehicle-treated and mitochondria-treated MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Molecular processes related to oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, mitochondrial homeostasis and cell survival are characterized, including by cardiac proteomics. (aspects: H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserves left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation limits left ventricular structural remodeling in MI rats (hypertrophy, dilation, interstitial fibrosis and ECM protein accumulation).
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: In MI rats, cardiac superoxide was not increased with mitochondrial transplantation at 4 weeks; SOD1 and SOD2 mRNA were unchanged in all groups.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac inflammatory marker expression in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation attenuates cardiac ER stress activation in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; analysis derivation → H7

## H7 (claim)
Statement: In MI rats, mitochondrial transplantation was associated with preserved LV function, reduced LV mass and fibrosis, and lower cardiac superoxide, inflammation and ER stress activation at 4 weeks after MI; the functional benefits were observed in the absence of differences in infarct size. No differences were found in non-infarcted rats in any of the parameters evaluated. These associations do not establish sustained effects beyond 4 weeks, prevention of heart failure or a causal chain in which the superoxide decrease mediates the other improvements.
Links: analysis derivation ← H4; analysis derivation ← H5; analysis derivation ← H6; analysis derivation ← H2; analysis derivation ← H3

# Main hypothesis
Does SIRT1 act as the deacetylase for GAPDH lysine 254 in microglia, and does the K254 acetylation state thereby set glycolytic flux and pro-inflammatory output during LPS/IFN-gamma activation?
System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH
Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+
Scope limits: in vitro only; no in vivo, aged or chronic low-grade inflammatory model was studied; GAPDH replacement reaches 75-80%, leaving residual endogenous wild-type protein; acetylation states are represented by K254Q and K254R substitutions rather than by enzymatically controlled acetylation in cells; figure images and supplementary files were not inspected during this extraction
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine whether the K254 acetylation state controls GAPDH catalytic activity and glycolytic flux. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Distinguish cell-autonomous from paracrine contributions of GAPDH K254 deacetylation to microglial inflammatory responses. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Show that the reported treatment and genotype differences are not produced by loss of cell viability. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: The acetylation state of GAPDH K254 sets GAPDH catalytic activity and glycolytic flux in microglia.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The amplified inflammatory phenotype of K254R microglia reaches naive neighbouring microglia through secreted mediators.

## H3 (claim)
Statement: The treatment- and genotype-associated differences reported in this study occur without loss of cell viability.

# Main hypothesis
How does the substrate temperature used during RF-magnetron sputtering (room temperature, 150, 250 and 350 °C) affect the structure, nickel/oxygen defect chemistry, Li+ transport and electrochromic performance of nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films intended as counter electrodes for smart windows?
System: Nickel-tungsten oxide (NWT) thin films sputtered from an 82%:18% target onto FTO-coated glass
Conditions: Substrate temperature during deposition: RT, 150, 250 and 350 °C; 100 W RF power, 30 min deposition, Ar working pressure 5 × 10^-2 mbar; Electrochemical tests in 1 M LiClO4 in propylene carbonate
Scope limits: One target composition and one deposition time; Li+ electrolyte only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify Li+ diffusion and inserted charge as a function of substrate temperature (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Compare optical modulation and coloration/bleaching times across substrate temperatures (aspects: H4, H5, H6)

# Main hypothesis
Do mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles carrying the DPEP1 inhibitor cilastatin sodium and surface-modified with L-serine (CTT/MPDA@L-Ser NPs) accumulate in injured kidney tissue and mitigate cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury by suppressing DPEP1 and restoring GPX4/SLC7A11-dependent ferroptosis defence?
System: Human proximal tubular HK-2 cells treated with cisplatin (DDP) and male/female-unspecified C57BL/6J mice given cisplatin 20 mg/kg intraperitoneally
Conditions: Cell work: 40 ug/mL nanoparticles for 24 h unless stated otherwise; the source reports this as equivalent to about 15 ug/mL cilastatin, a ratio that matches the reported encapsulation efficiency of 36.74% rather than the reported drug loading of 18.37%, from which 40 ug/mL would carry about 7 ug/mL, so the basis of the conversion is not stated; Animal work: dosing 30 min before cisplatin and on days 1 and 2, sacrifice 72 h after model establishment; the Methods give 10 mg/kg for the C/M-Ser group only, state no dose for the free CTT or C/M arms, and do not say whether the figure is nanoparticle mass or cilastatin-equivalent mass; Formulations compared: free CTT, CTT/MPDA (C/M) and CTT/MPDA@L-Ser (C/M-Ser)
Scope limits: Single cisplatin AKI model; no other AKI aetiology tested; Follow-up ends 72 h after model establishment for efficacy and 14 days for safety; Tumour-bearing animals and chemotherapy efficacy were not part of the reported design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Treatment must reduce ferroptosis-associated readouts in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells and in AKI kidneys. (aspects: H1, H5)
- R2: Protection must be shown to depend on the DPEP1-GPX4 axis rather than on unspecified cytoprotection. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Treatment must improve kidney histology and renal function in cisplatin AKI mice. (aspects: H5)

# Main hypothesis
Do mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles carrying the DPEP1 inhibitor cilastatin sodium and surface-modified with L-serine (CTT/MPDA@L-Ser NPs) accumulate in injured kidney tissue and mitigate cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury by suppressing DPEP1 and restoring GPX4/SLC7A11-dependent ferroptosis defence?
System: Human proximal tubular HK-2 cells treated with cisplatin (DDP) and male/female-unspecified C57BL/6J mice given cisplatin 20 mg/kg intraperitoneally
Conditions: Cell work: 40 ug/mL nanoparticles for 24 h unless stated otherwise; the source reports this as equivalent to about 15 ug/mL cilastatin, a ratio that matches the reported encapsulation efficiency of 36.74% rather than the reported drug loading of 18.37%, from which 40 ug/mL would carry about 7 ug/mL, so the basis of the conversion is not stated; Animal work: dosing 30 min before cisplatin and on days 1 and 2, sacrifice 72 h after model establishment; the Methods give 10 mg/kg for the C/M-Ser group only, state no dose for the free CTT or C/M arms, and do not say whether the figure is nanoparticle mass or cilastatin-equivalent mass; Formulations compared: free CTT, CTT/MPDA (C/M) and CTT/MPDA@L-Ser (C/M-Ser)
Scope limits: Single cisplatin AKI model; no other AKI aetiology tested; Follow-up ends 72 h after model establishment for efficacy and 14 days for safety; Tumour-bearing animals and chemotherapy efficacy were not part of the reported design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Treatment must reduce ferroptosis-associated readouts in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells and in AKI kidneys. (aspects: H1, H5)
- R2: Protection must be shown to depend on the DPEP1-GPX4 axis rather than on unspecified cytoprotection. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Treatment must improve kidney histology and renal function in cisplatin AKI mice. (aspects: H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles reduce ferroptosis-associated damage in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment lowers intracellular reactive oxygen species in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H9

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment limits lipid peroxidation and glutathione depletion in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Cytoprotection by CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles depends on suppression of DPEP1 and restoration of GPX4.
Links: refinement → H8

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles reduce kidney ferroptosis markers, histological injury and functional impairment in cisplatin AKI mice.
Links: composition → H6; composition → H7; proposed mechanism ← H8; proposed mechanism ← H10

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment lowers kidney iron deposition and restores GPX4 and SLC7A11 protein levels in AKI mice.
Links: composition ← H5

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment reduces tubular injury scores, injury-marker staining and serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen in AKI mice.
Links: composition ← H5

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: Cilastatin released from the nanoparticles inhibits DPEP1, which raises GPX4 and SLC7A11 levels and thereby suppresses ferroptotic tubular injury.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5; refinement ← H4; competing explanation ← H10

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: The polydopamine carrier itself scavenges reactive oxygen species and so contributes to the reduction of oxidative stress observed after treatment.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

## H10 (alternative)
Statement: A substantial part of the renal benefit in AKI mice could come from the L-serine-modified polydopamine carrier itself rather than from its cilastatin cargo: an antioxidant carrier concentrated in injured tubules would lower lipid peroxidation and iron-linked tubular damage, and the resulting reduction in injury would by itself lower DPEP1 and injury-marker staining and raise GPX4 and SLC7A11, reproducing the reported group ordering without a cilastatin-specific DPEP1 step in vivo. This is an untested candidate explanation, not an established finding.
Links: competing explanation → H8; proposed mechanism → H5

# Main hypothesis
Do mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles carrying the DPEP1 inhibitor cilastatin sodium and surface-modified with L-serine (CTT/MPDA@L-Ser NPs) accumulate in injured kidney tissue and mitigate cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury by suppressing DPEP1 and restoring GPX4/SLC7A11-dependent ferroptosis defence?
System: Human proximal tubular HK-2 cells treated with cisplatin (DDP) and male/female-unspecified C57BL/6J mice given cisplatin 20 mg/kg intraperitoneally
Conditions: Cell work: 40 ug/mL nanoparticles for 24 h unless stated otherwise; the source reports this as equivalent to about 15 ug/mL cilastatin, a ratio that matches the reported encapsulation efficiency of 36.74% rather than the reported drug loading of 18.37%, from which 40 ug/mL would carry about 7 ug/mL, so the basis of the conversion is not stated; Animal work: dosing 30 min before cisplatin and on days 1 and 2, sacrifice 72 h after model establishment; the Methods give 10 mg/kg for the C/M-Ser group only, state no dose for the free CTT or C/M arms, and do not say whether the figure is nanoparticle mass or cilastatin-equivalent mass; Formulations compared: free CTT, CTT/MPDA (C/M) and CTT/MPDA@L-Ser (C/M-Ser)
Scope limits: Single cisplatin AKI model; no other AKI aetiology tested; Follow-up ends 72 h after model establishment for efficacy and 14 days for safety; Tumour-bearing animals and chemotherapy efficacy were not part of the reported design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Treatment must reduce ferroptosis-associated readouts in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells and in AKI kidneys. (aspects: H1, H5)
- R2: Protection must be shown to depend on the DPEP1-GPX4 axis rather than on unspecified cytoprotection. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Treatment must improve kidney histology and renal function in cisplatin AKI mice. (aspects: H5)

# Main hypothesis
Do mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles carrying the DPEP1 inhibitor cilastatin sodium and surface-modified with L-serine (CTT/MPDA@L-Ser NPs) accumulate in injured kidney tissue and mitigate cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury by suppressing DPEP1 and restoring GPX4/SLC7A11-dependent ferroptosis defence?
System: Human proximal tubular HK-2 cells treated with cisplatin (DDP) and male/female-unspecified C57BL/6J mice given cisplatin 20 mg/kg intraperitoneally
Conditions: Cell work: 40 ug/mL nanoparticles for 24 h unless stated otherwise; the source reports this as equivalent to about 15 ug/mL cilastatin, a ratio that matches the reported encapsulation efficiency of 36.74% rather than the reported drug loading of 18.37%, from which 40 ug/mL would carry about 7 ug/mL, so the basis of the conversion is not stated; Animal work: dosing 30 min before cisplatin and on days 1 and 2, sacrifice 72 h after model establishment; the Methods give 10 mg/kg for the C/M-Ser group only, state no dose for the free CTT or C/M arms, and do not say whether the figure is nanoparticle mass or cilastatin-equivalent mass; Formulations compared: free CTT, CTT/MPDA (C/M) and CTT/MPDA@L-Ser (C/M-Ser)
Scope limits: Single cisplatin AKI model; no other AKI aetiology tested; Follow-up ends 72 h after model establishment for efficacy and 14 days for safety; Tumour-bearing animals and chemotherapy efficacy were not part of the reported design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Treatment must reduce ferroptosis-associated readouts in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells and in AKI kidneys. (aspects: H1, H5)
- R2: Protection must be shown to depend on the DPEP1-GPX4 axis rather than on unspecified cytoprotection. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Treatment must improve kidney histology and renal function in cisplatin AKI mice. (aspects: H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles reduce ferroptosis-associated damage in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment lowers intracellular reactive oxygen species in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H9

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment limits lipid peroxidation and glutathione depletion in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Cytoprotection by CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles depends on suppression of DPEP1 and restoration of GPX4.
Links: refinement → H8

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles reduce kidney ferroptosis markers, histological injury and functional impairment in cisplatin AKI mice.
Links: composition → H6; composition → H7; proposed mechanism ← H8

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment lowers kidney iron deposition and restores GPX4 and SLC7A11 protein levels in AKI mice.
Links: composition ← H5

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment reduces tubular injury scores, injury-marker staining and serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen in AKI mice.
Links: composition ← H5

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: Cilastatin released from the nanoparticles inhibits DPEP1, which raises GPX4 and SLC7A11 levels and thereby suppresses ferroptotic tubular injury.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5; refinement ← H4; competing explanation ← H10

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: The polydopamine carrier itself scavenges reactive oxygen species and so contributes to the reduction of oxidative stress observed after treatment.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; proposed mechanism ← H10

## H10 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate alternative: the observed reduction in DPEP1, iron and ferroptosis markers and the improved injury and function in AKI mice may partly result from the polydopamine carrier or its surface modification, or from residual free cilastatin not encapsulated, rather than from cilastatin released from the nanoparticles. This remains untested because the visible evidence does not measure cilastatin release in kidney tissue or exclude a carrier- or surface-related contribution.
Links: competing explanation → H8; proposed mechanism → H9

# Main hypothesis
Do mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles carrying the DPEP1 inhibitor cilastatin sodium and surface-modified with L-serine (CTT/MPDA@L-Ser NPs) accumulate in injured kidney tissue and mitigate cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury by suppressing DPEP1 and restoring GPX4/SLC7A11-dependent ferroptosis defence?
System: Human proximal tubular HK-2 cells treated with cisplatin (DDP) and male/female-unspecified C57BL/6J mice given cisplatin 20 mg/kg intraperitoneally
Conditions: Cell work: 40 ug/mL nanoparticles for 24 h unless stated otherwise; the source reports this as equivalent to about 15 ug/mL cilastatin, a ratio that matches the reported encapsulation efficiency of 36.74% rather than the reported drug loading of 18.37%, from which 40 ug/mL would carry about 7 ug/mL, so the basis of the conversion is not stated; Animal work: dosing 30 min before cisplatin and on days 1 and 2, sacrifice 72 h after model establishment; the Methods give 10 mg/kg for the C/M-Ser group only, state no dose for the free CTT or C/M arms, and do not say whether the figure is nanoparticle mass or cilastatin-equivalent mass; Formulations compared: free CTT, CTT/MPDA (C/M) and CTT/MPDA@L-Ser (C/M-Ser)
Scope limits: Single cisplatin AKI model; no other AKI aetiology tested; Follow-up ends 72 h after model establishment for efficacy and 14 days for safety; Tumour-bearing animals and chemotherapy efficacy were not part of the reported design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Treatment must reduce ferroptosis-associated readouts in cisplatin-injured HK-2 cells and in AKI kidneys. (aspects: H1, H5)
- R2: Protection must be shown to depend on the DPEP1-GPX4 axis rather than on unspecified cytoprotection. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Treatment must improve kidney histology and renal function in cisplatin AKI mice. (aspects: H5)

Links: refinement → H8

Links: composition → H6; composition → H7; proposed mechanism ← H8

Links: composition ← H5

Links: composition ← H5

## H8 (mechanism)

Links: proposed mechanism → H5; refinement ← H4; competing explanation ← H10

## H9 (mechanism)

## H10 (alternative)

Links: competing explanation → H8; refinement → H9

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES to the carbon paste changes the photovoltaic performance (PCE, JSC, VOC, FF, Rs, Rsh, hysteresis) of p-i-n C-PSCs relative to the pure carbon paste control.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Stability of p-i-n C-PSCs made with and without additive-containing carbon electrodes.
Links: refinement → H3

## H3 (claim)
Statement: p-i-n C-PSCs with SiC-APTES carbon electrodes combine the maximum PCE of 18.43% with excellent operational stability under ambient operation.

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H3)
- R2: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the Sn(OH)2-coated precursor forms single crystals under the calcination schedule that gives polycrystalline NCA90, and establish the mechanism and the role of Sn specifically. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H2; proposed mechanism ← H3; composition → H4

## H2 (mechanism)
Statement: During heating to 700 °C, Sn(OH)2 converts to SnO2 that diffuses into the secondary particles and localizes at primary-particle grain boundaries.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Boundary-localized SnO2 reacts with adjacent NCA (LiMO2 + αSnO2 -> Li1-2αMO2-2α + αLi2SnO3 + α/2 O2), and the released O2 increases the separation between primary particles, lowering van der Waals adhesion and driving exfoliation.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Among the tested coating elements, only Sn produces single-crystalline NCA90 at 750 °C.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Sn's effectiveness at 750 °C, compared with other oxides, reflects early grain-boundary occupation by 700 °C and chemical inertness toward the LiOH flux, together with favorable interfacial oxygen release; oxygen-release thermodynamics alone do not distinguish Sn.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells

## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H2; proposed mechanism ← H3; composition → H4

## H2 (mechanism)
Statement: During heating to 700 °C, Sn(OH)2 converts to SnO2 that diffuses into the secondary particles and localizes at primary-particle grain boundaries.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1; competing explanation → H3; competing explanation ← H3

## H3 (mechanism)

## H4 (aspect)

## H5 (mechanism)

# Main hypothesis
Does active immunization of mice with purified recombinant murine keratin 14 (K14) or keratin 17 (K17) fusion protein produce an antigen-specific psoriasis-like disease model, that is, psoriasis-like skin lesions together with the histopathological and antigen-specific immune features reported for psoriasis?
System: Female wild-type BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice, 6-8 weeks old at purchase, immunized with Escherichia coli-expressed murine K14 or K17 fused to a GST or a His-Trigger-factor (TF) tag.
Conditions: Primary immunization: antigen emulsified in complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), injected intradermally into shaved dorsal skin (about 25 uL per site, 200 uL total per mouse; 350 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Booster immunization 3-4 weeks later: same antigen emulsified in incomplete Freund's adjuvant (IFA), injected subcutaneously (450 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Comparator groups: tag-only protein with the same adjuvant, an adjuvant-only group injected with CFA intradermally or IFA subcutaneously without protein, mice only anesthetized and hair-clipped (C57BL/6J additionally depilated), and topical imiquimod (IMQ; 10 mg/day to the tail base in BALB/c, 62.5 mg/day to dorsal skin in C57BL/6J, 7 consecutive days); no outcome is reported for the adjuvant-only group in the retrieved text.; Five independent experiments per mouse strain (two with GST-tagged proteins, three with TF-tagged proteins); per experiment 5 mice in the control and in the tag-control group and 10 mice in each of the K14 and K17 groups.

## H1 (aspect)

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Clinical psoriasis-like lesions were reported in female BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice in the described K14/K17 GST- and TF-fusion immunization series. Lesion site, timing, incidence, and duration varied by series and observation point; these reports document occurrence in the two tested backgrounds but do not establish strain-independent generalizability or a regimen-independent effect.
Links: refinement ← H1

## H3 (claim)
Statement: Reported clinical incidence varied across the tested female-mouse series: after primary immunization, BALB/c mice had incidences of 40% for GST-K14 and 70% for GST-K17, and 40% for each TF-tagged antigen; C57BL/6J mice had incidences of 20% for GST-K14 and 10% for GST-K17 after primary immunization, rising in that GST series to 30% and 40%, respectively, after booster immunization. In the C57BL/6J TF series, no symptoms were observed 21 days after primary immunization, while incidence was 50% for each antigen four days after the booster. Reported duration also differed by series: BALB/c TF symptoms persisted through day 35, whereas C57BL/6J lesions in the GST and TF reports lasted about five days. # Main hypothesis
Does integrating an in situ polymerized polypyrrole-coated carbon cloth (PPy/CC) electrode with a sodium alginate/poly(acrylamide-co-acrylic acid) supramolecular gel electrolyte containing NaCl give a flexible symmetric supercapacitor (FSGSC) whose electrochemical performance depends on the NaCl content of the gel, with an optimal NaCl content?
System: Symmetric sandwich supercapacitor with two identical PPy/CC electrodes (1 cm x 1 cm carbon cloth pieces) and an SA/P(AM-AA) supramolecular gel electrolyte prepared with 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3 g NaCl (S-gel0.1, S-gel0.2, S-gel0.3)
Conditions: Gel precursor: 4.5 g of 3 wt% SA solution, 1.0 g acrylamide, 2.0 g acrylic acid, 2.0 mL water, 0.1/0.2/0.3 g NaCl and APS; polymerized at 55 °C for 8 h; PPy/CC electrode alone tested in a three-electrode cell with aqueous NaCl electrolyte; Device tests at room temperature with a 0.7 V potential window
Scope limits: Three NaCl levels in one gel formulation; One electrode preparation (FeCl3-initiated pyrrole polymerization for 24 h)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that PPy is deposited on the carbon cloth and characterize the electrochemical performance of the PPy/CC electrode relative to bare carbon cloth. (aspects: H1)

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether MG53 regulates corneal sensory nerve regeneration after alkali burn injury and define the macrophage-associated molecular route through which it acts.
System: Mouse alkali-burn corneal injury in wild-type, MG53 global knockout (mg53-/-) and tPA-MG53 transgenic mice, with bone marrow-derived and immortalized macrophage cultures and HEK-293T/HEK293 reconstitution systems.
Conditions: Central corneal alkali burn produced with a 2 mm filter paper soaked in 2 uL of 1 M NaOH for 30 s; Corneal readouts between 3 h and day 10 after injury; M2 polarization of macrophages induced with 20 ng/mL IL-4 for 24 h; Recombinant human MG53 (rhMG53) or modified RNA used to raise MG53 levels
Scope limits: Mouse cornea and cultured mouse macrophages, with human membrane proteins and tagged constructs expressed in HEK-293T/HEK293 cells; MG53 levels are varied by global genotype (mg53-/-, tPA-MG53), recombinant protein or modified RNA rather than by cell type-restricted manipulation; Macrophages are identified by surface markers (CD68, CD206, CD80, CD192, CD11b) without separation of CCR2+ and CCR2- subsets
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether MG53 abundance changes corneal nerve loss and regrowth after alkali injury in vivo. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Establish whether macrophages are required for corneal epithelial healing and nerve regeneration after injury. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Define the intracellular route by which MG53 changes macrophage polarization. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R4: Determine how extracellular MG53 enters macrophages and mediates its biological functions.

System: Mouse alkali-burn corneal injury in wild-type, MG53 global knockout (mg53-/-) and tPA-MG53 transgenic mice, with bone marrow-derived and immortalized macrophage cultures and HEK-293T/HEK293 reconstitution systems.

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether MG53 regulates corneal sensory nerve regeneration after alkali burn injury and define the macrophage-associated molecular route through which it acts.
System: Mouse alkali-burn corneal injury in wild-type, MG53 global knockout (mg53-/-) and tPA-MG53 transgenic mice, with bone marrow-derived and immortalized macrophage cultures and HEK-293T/HEK293 reconstitution systems.
Conditions: Central corneal alkali burn produced with a 2 mm filter paper soaked in 2 uL of 1 M NaOH for 30 s; Corneal readouts between 3 h and day 10 after injury; M2 polarization of macrophages induced with 20 ng/mL IL-4 for 24 h; Recombinant human MG53 (rhMG53) or modified RNA used to raise MG53 levels
Scope limits: Mouse cornea and cultured mouse macrophages, with human membrane proteins and tagged constructs expressed in HEK-293T/HEK293 cells; MG53 levels are varied by global genotype (mg53-/-, tPA-MG53), recombinant protein or modified RNA rather than by cell type-restricted manipulation; Macrophages are identified by surface markers (CD68, CD206, CD80, CD192, CD11b) without separation of CCR2+ and CCR2- subsets

# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?
System: Glycerol-plasticized cast chitosan film combined with electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwovens as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH and CH/PCLm/CH trilayers; comparator: monolayer chitosan film without PCL fibers
Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Hydrophilic properties: moisture content, swelling degree, total soluble matter and water contact angle. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Degradation: mass loss of films incubated in PBS at 37 °C over 72 h. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Trilayer films of cast chitosan and electrospun PCL nonwovens joined by heating have enhanced packaging-relevant properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4

Statement: PCL layers reduce the hydrophilicity of the films relative to chitosan.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H3

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Gravimetric moisture content, swelling degree and total soluble matter of the neat chitosan film and the trilayer films.
Manipulation: Neat chitosan film: solution-cast from 2% w/v chitosan in 1% v/v aqueous acetic acid with 30% w/w glycerol. Trilayers: 10 x 10 cm pieces of chitosan film and electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwoven stacked between aluminum foils as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH or CH/PCLm/CH and heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side (2 min total), then cooled to room temperature and the foil removed. Measurements: MC; SD; TSM
Comparison: groups: neat chitosan film (CH); PCLt/CH/PCLt; PCLm/CH/PCLm; CH/PCLt/CH; CH/PCLm/CH | endpoint: moisture content (MC), swelling degree (SD), total soluble matter (TSM) | varied: presence of PCL nonwoven layers; layer arrangement; PCL grade | held fixed: drying at 100 °C for 24 h; 24 h immersion in 100 mL distilled water | unit: film sample; replicate number not reported | window: 24 h drying; 24 h immersion; 24 h re-drying | units: %
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: Mass loss of films incubated in phosphate-buffered saline at 37 °C.
Manipulation: Neat chitosan film: solution-cast from 2% w/v chitosan in 1% v/v aqueous acetic acid with 30% w/w glycerol.
