Neat chitosan film, neat PCLm and PCLt fiber mats and the four trilayers were weighed before immersion, incubated in PBS (pH 7.4) at 37 °C, removed after 12 h, dried at 100 °C and reweighed; the procedure was repeated at 24, 36, 48 and 72 h.

# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?
System: Glycerol-plasticized cast chitosan film combined with electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwovens as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH and CH/PCLm/CH trilayers; comparator: monolayer chitosan film without PCL fibers
Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Mechanical performance: tensile strength and elongation at break (ASTM D882) of trilayer films compared with the monolayer chitosan film. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Hydrophilic properties: moisture content, swelling degree, total soluble matter and water contact angle. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Barrier properties: water vapor, oxygen and carbon dioxide permeability. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Structural properties: SEM of fiber and film surfaces and cross-sections. (aspects: H9)
- R5: Optical properties: transparency from UV-VIS spectra. (aspects: H6)
- R6: Thermal properties: DSC of pure PCL, chitosan and trilayer films. (aspects: H7)
- R7: Degradation: mass loss of films incubated in PBS at 37 °C over 72 h. (aspects: H8)
- R8: Both configurations evaluated with PCL fibers from medical-grade and technical-grade polymers to compare the influence of PCL grade, quality and purity.
- R9: Two configurations compared: PCL nonwoven between chitosan sheets (CH/PCL/CH) and chitosan sheet between two PCL nonwovens (PCL/CH/PCL). (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?
System: Glycerol-plasticized cast chitosan film combined with electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwovens as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH and CH/PCLm/CH trilayers; comparator: monolayer chitosan film without PCL fibers
Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Mechanical performance: tensile strength and elongation at break (ASTM D882) of trilayer films compared with the monolayer chitosan film. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Hydrophilic properties: moisture content, swelling degree, total soluble matter and water contact angle. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Barrier properties: water vapor, oxygen and carbon dioxide permeability. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Structural properties: SEM of fiber and film surfaces and cross-sections. (aspects: H9)
- R5: Optical properties: transparency from UV-VIS spectra. (aspects: H6)
- R6: Thermal properties: DSC of pure PCL, chitosan and trilayer films. (aspects: H7)
- R7: Degradation: mass loss of films incubated in PBS at 37 °C over 72 h. (aspects: H8)
- R8: Both configurations evaluated with PCL fibers from medical-grade and technical-grade polymers to compare the influence of PCL grade, quality and purity.
- R9: Two configurations compared: PCL nonwoven between chitosan sheets (CH/PCL/CH) and chitosan sheet between two PCL nonwovens (PCL/CH/PCL). (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?
System: Glycerol-plasticized cast chitosan film combined with electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwovens as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH and CH/PCLm/CH trilayers; comparator: monolayer chitosan film without PCL fibers
Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Mechanical performance: tensile strength and elongation at break (ASTM D882) of trilayer films compared with the monolayer chitosan film. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Hydrophilic properties: moisture content, swelling degree, total soluble matter and water contact angle. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Barrier properties: water vapor, oxygen and carbon dioxide permeability. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Structural properties: SEM of fiber and film surfaces and cross-sections. (aspects: H9)
- R5: Optical properties: transparency from UV-VIS spectra. (aspects: H6)
- R6: Thermal properties: DSC of pure PCL, chitosan and trilayer films. (aspects: H7)
- R7: Degradation: mass loss of films incubated in PBS at 37 °C over 72 h. (aspects: H8)
- R8: Both configurations evaluated with PCL fibers from medical-grade and technical-grade polymers to compare the influence of PCL grade, quality and purity.
- R9: Two configurations compared: PCL nonwoven between chitosan sheets (CH/PCL/CH) and chitosan sheet between two PCL nonwovens (PCL/CH/PCL). (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Can a 2 x 2 single-chip SnO2 MEMS gas sensor array whose four units run at different temperatures under one heating voltage, combined with a physics-informed Hierarchical Kolmogorov-Arnold Mixture-of-Experts (HK-MoE) model, detect target-gas presence, classify, and determine the concentration of the lithium-ion-battery thermal-runaway gases H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, including after aging-induced sensor drift and in gas mixtures?
System: Solution-synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles dispensed on a 1.8 x 1.8 x 0.5 mm3 2 x 2 MEMS microheater array (Pt heating electrode line widths 8, 12, 16 and 20 um), read out as four resistance channels and analyzed by the HK-MoE model
Conditions: H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 at 100-500 ppm in discrete 100 ppm steps, balance nitrogen, with background air between injections; Heating voltage 1.9 V during gas sensing; Laboratory gas delivery; 25 C and 60% RH unless otherwise noted; Fresh array (Source Domain) and the same array after 30 days (Target Domain) and 60 days of continuous operational aging; Four mixtures of the four gases at 1000 ppm total concentration
Scope limits: Laboratory gas-delivery conditions; no measurement during actual battery thermal runaway; Aging studied on one array up to 60 days
Validation requirements:
- R1: The array must respond to H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and produce distinct temperature-modulated response patterns across its four units. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: The model must perform three tasks: target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination.
- R3: Discrimination must remain usable after sensor drift caused by aging of the array. (aspects: H3)
- R4: Discrimination must be demonstrated for multi-component gas mixtures. (aspects: H5)
- R5: The device must be miniaturized, low-power and single-chip. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can a 2 x 2 single-chip SnO2 MEMS gas sensor array whose four units run at different temperatures under one heating voltage, combined with a physics-informed Hierarchical Kolmogorov-Arnold Mixture-of-Experts (HK-MoE) model, detect target-gas presence, classify, and determine the concentration of the lithium-ion-battery thermal-runaway gases H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, including after aging-induced sensor drift and in gas mixtures?

Conditions: H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 at 100-500 ppm in discrete 100 ppm steps, balance nitrogen, with background air between injections; Heating voltage 1.9 V during gas sensing; Laboratory gas delivery; 25 C and 60% RH unless otherwise noted; Fresh array (Source Domain) and the same array after 30 days (Target Domain) and 60 days of continuous operational aging; Four mixtures of the four gases at 1000 ppm total concentration
Scope limits: Laboratory gas-delivery conditions; no measurement during actual battery thermal runaway; Aging studied on one array up to 60 days

- R1: The array must respond to H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and produce distinct temperature-modulated response patterns across its four units. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can a 2 x 2 single-chip SnO2 MEMS gas sensor array whose four units run at different temperatures under one heating voltage, combined with a physics-informed Hierarchical Kolmogorov-Arnold Mixture-of-Experts (HK-MoE) model, detect target-gas presence, classify, and determine the concentration of the lithium-ion-battery thermal-runaway gases H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, including after aging-induced sensor drift and in gas mixtures?
System: Solution-synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles dispensed on a 1.8 x 1.8 x 0.5 mm3 2 x 2 MEMS microheater array (Pt heating electrode line widths 8, 12, 16 and 20 um), read out as four resistance channels and analyzed by the HK-MoE model
Conditions: H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 at 100-500 ppm in discrete 100 ppm steps, balance nitrogen, with background air between injections; Heating voltage 1.9 V during gas sensing; Laboratory gas delivery; 25 C and 60% RH unless otherwise noted; Fresh array (Source Domain) and the same array after 30 days (Target Domain) and 60 days of continuous operational aging; Four mixtures of the four gases at 1000 ppm total concentration
Scope limits: Laboratory gas-delivery conditions; no measurement during actual battery thermal runaway; Aging studied on one array up to 60 days
Validation requirements:
- R1: The array must respond to H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and produce distinct temperature-modulated response patterns across its four units. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: The model must perform three tasks: target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination.
- R3: Discrimination must remain usable after sensor drift caused by aging of the array. (aspects: H3)
- R4: Discrimination must be demonstrated for multi-component gas mixtures. (aspects: H5)
- R5: The device must be miniaturized, low-power and single-chip. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: The SnO2 array detects H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and gives gas-specific response patterns across its four temperature zones.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Four microheater units with heating-electrode line widths of 8, 12, 16 and 20 um reach four distinct temperatures under one constant heating voltage.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: HK-MoE discrimination remains usable after aging-induced drift of the same array.
Links: composition → H4

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Task-wise HK-MoE performance after 60 days of aging.
Links: composition ← H3

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: HK-MoE discriminates gases and concentrations in multi-component mixtures of H2, CO, CH4 and CO2.
Links: refinement → H8; proposed mechanism ← H11; proposed alternative ← H12; proposed alternative ← H13; proposed alternative ← H14

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Baseline resistance and response of the four units under ambient humidity and ambient temperature different from 25 C and 60% RH.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H9; proposed mechanism ← H10

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Independently fabricated arrays reproduce the unit-to-unit baseline and response pattern.

## H8 (claim)
Statement: The framework can decouple the overlapping responses of multiple characteristic gases and identify both the dominant gas species and its concentration in multi-component gas mixtures.
Links: refinement ← H5

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: Competitive adsorption of water on SnO2 reduces active sites for oxygen and target gas, lowering baseline resistance and response at higher RH.
Links: proposed mechanism → H6

## H10 (mechanism)
Statement: Higher ambient temperature reduces the microheater-to-air temperature gradient and heat dissipation, so at constant heating voltage the operating temperature rises slightly, lowering baseline resistance and response.
Links: proposed mechanism → H6

## H11 (mechanism)
Statement: The upward shift of baseline resistance of all units in the mixed-gas runs relative to the single-gas runs is attributed to the change of gas distribution system, which used 1000 sccm instead of 100 sccm.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

## H12 (alternative)
Statement: Cross-gas adsorption competition: In multi-component mixtures, multiple gases competing for adsorption sites on SnO₂ reduces baseline resistance more than water alone.
Links: proposed alternative → H5

## H13 (alternative)
Statement: Sensor saturation: Higher total gas concentration (1000 ppm) leads to increased baseline resistance due to partial desorption of already adsorbed gases.
Links: proposed alternative → H5

## H14 (alternative)
Statement: Device-to-device variability: Differences in baseline resistance between mixed-gas and single-gas runs vary across independently fabricated arrays, indicating device-level contributions.
Links: proposed alternative → H5

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether raising riboflavin supply in the consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached. (aspects: H1)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin biosynthesis in the two-species consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached from NCM.
Links: composition → H3; composition → H5; composition → H6

## H2 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: refinement → H4

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Engineering the riboflavin biosynthesis pathway raises the riboflavin concentration that the consortium accumulates in brewing wastewater as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin supply raises the electrical output of the consortium in a microbial fuel cell, measured as maximum power density.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: The engineered consortia accumulate a higher riboflavin concentration in brewing wastewater than the SO1-BS1 consortium, which raises the amount of electron shuttle available for EET.
Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether raising riboflavin supply in the consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached. (aspects: H1)

# Main hypothesis
Does active immunization of mice with purified recombinant murine keratin 14 (K14) or keratin 17 (K17) fusion protein produce an antigen-specific psoriasis-like disease model, that is, psoriasis-like skin lesions together with the histopathological and antigen-specific immune features reported for psoriasis?
System: Female wild-type BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice, 6-8 weeks old at purchase, immunized with Escherichia coli-expressed murine K14 or K17 fused to a GST or a His-Trigger-factor (TF) tag.
Conditions: Primary immunization: antigen emulsified in complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), injected intradermally into shaved dorsal skin (about 25 uL per site, 200 uL total per mouse; 350 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Booster immunization 3-4 weeks later: same antigen emulsified in incomplete Freund's adjuvant (IFA), injected subcutaneously (450 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Comparator groups: tag-only protein with the same adjuvant, an adjuvant-only group injected with CFA intradermally or IFA subcutaneously without protein, mice only anesthetized and hair-clipped (C57BL/6J additionally depilated), and topical imiquimod (IMQ; 10 mg/day to the tail base in BALB/c, 62.5 mg/day to dorsal skin in C57BL/6J, 7 consecutive days); no outcome is reported for the adjuvant-only group in the retrieved text.; Five independent experiments per mouse strain (two with GST-tagged proteins, three with TF-tagged proteins); per experiment 5 mice in the control and in the tag-control group and 10 mice in each of the K14 and K17 groups.
Scope limits: Female mice only; applicability to male mice was not evaluated.; Proof-of-concept study; no T-cell depletion, transfer or blocking experiment was performed.; Systematic longitudinal clinical scoring was not performed.; Figure images, supplementary figures and the supplementary table were not inspected for this workspace; values are taken from Results text and figure captions.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Immunization with K14 or K17 must produce psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, scales) in immunized mice, recorded with incidence, onset and duration alongside the adjuvant/tag and untreated comparator groups.
- R2: Lesional skin of immunized mice must show the histopathological hallmarks attributed to psoriasis (epidermal hyperplasia or thickening and inflammatory cell infiltration) relative to skin from comparator mice sampled at the same anatomical site.
- R3: Immunized mice must mount a measurable antigen-specific antibody response against K14/K17, resolved by isotype and time point.
- R4: Immunized mice must show an antigen-specific T-cell response, and the systemic inflammatory cytokine profile after immunization must be characterized.
- R5: The induced phenotype must be attributable to the keratin moiety rather than to the fusion tag used to express it.
- R6: Whether the antigen-specific disease obtained in BALB/c mice can be generalized to another mouse genetic background must be determined.
- R7: The immunogens and their tag-only counterparts must be produced with verified identity, assessed purity and controlled endotoxin before immunization.

## H1 (aspect)

Statement: Lesional histopathology: skin sections from lesional sites of immunized mice show epidermal hyperplasia with increased epidermal thickness and inflammatory cell infiltration, compared with sections from comparator mice sampled at the same anatomical site and processed identically.

# Main hypothesis
Does SIRT1 act as the deacetylase for GAPDH lysine 254 in microglia, and does the K254 acetylation state thereby set glycolytic flux and pro-inflammatory output during LPS/IFN-gamma activation?
System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH
Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+
Scope limits: in vitro only; no in vivo, aged or chronic low-grade inflammatory model was studied; GAPDH replacement reaches 75-80%, leaving residual endogenous wild-type protein; acetylation states are represented by K254Q and K254R substitutions rather than by enzymatically controlled acetylation in cells; figure images and supplementary files were not inspected during this extraction
Validation requirements:
- R1: Distinguish cell-autonomous from paracrine contributions of GAPDH K254 deacetylation to microglial inflammatory responses. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show that the reported treatment and genotype differences are not produced by loss of cell viability. (aspects: H2)

## E1
Statement: Lactate dehydrogenase release assay run in parallel with the metabolic experiments, comparing experimental release with spontaneous-release and maximal-lysis controls.
Manipulation: Conditioned medium clarified at 500 x g for 5 min; LDH activity read colorimetrically at 490 nm with a 680 nm reference; matched wells lysed with the assay lysis reagent provided the maximum-release control; assays run in duplicate for each experiment. The assay was run in parallel with the metabolic and transfer experiments, including the reconstituted K254R and K254Q cultures whose supernatants were profiled for extracellular mediators.

Statement: Trypan blue exclusion counting run in parallel with the metabolic experiments.

## E3
Statement: Conditioned-medium transfer from stimulated K254R or K254Q donor microglia to naive wild-type recipients, with parallel aliquots depleted of individual mediators before transfer.
Manipulation: Donor BV-2 or primary microglia (K254R, K254Q or WT with or without SRT1720/EX-527) stimulated with LPS/IFN-gamma for 24 h; medium cleared by sequential centrifugation (500 x g 5 min; 2,000 x g 10 min) and applied to naive WT recipients undiluted or 1:1 in fresh medium for a further 24 h; parallel aliquots pre-treated with lactate oxidase (1 U/mL, 30 min, 37 C), apyrase (10 U/mL), neutralizing anti-HMGB1 (2G7, 10 ug/mL) or heat inactivation (95 C, 10 min).
Measurements: recipient multiplex ELISA cytokine panel; recipient Nos2 and Il1b qPCR; recipient glycoPER; recipient HIF-1alpha immunoblot
Comparison: groups: recipients of K254R conditioned medium; recipients of K254Q conditioned medium; recipients of mediator-depleted K254R conditioned medium | endpoint: recipient TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-1beta secretion, Nos2 and Il1b transcripts, glycoPER and HIF-1alpha immunoblot | varied: donor genotype at GAPDH position 254; depletion of an individual mediator from the transferred medium | held fixed: cell-free transferred medium; 24-h donor stimulation and 24-h recipient exposure; naive wild-type recipients | unit: independent biological replicate: a separately seeded microglial culture treated and harvested on a distinct day, from an independent BV-2 passage or an independent litter | window: 24 h after transfer | units: fold difference between recipient groups; percent reduction

# Main hypothesis
Does SIRT1 act as the deacetylase for GAPDH lysine 254 in microglia, and does the K254 acetylation state thereby set glycolytic flux and pro-inflammatory output during LPS/IFN-gamma activation?
System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH
Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+
Scope limits: in vitro only; no in vivo, aged or chronic low-grade inflammatory model was studied; GAPDH replacement reaches 75-80%, leaving residual endogenous wild-type protein; acetylation states are represented by K254Q and K254R substitutions rather than by enzymatically controlled acetylation in cells; figure images and supplementary files were not inspected during this extraction
Validation requirements:
- R1: Distinguish cell-autonomous from paracrine contributions of GAPDH K254 deacetylation to microglial inflammatory responses. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show that the reported treatment and genotype differences are not produced by loss of cell viability. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: The amplified inflammatory phenotype of K254R microglia reaches naive neighbouring microglia through secreted mediators.
Links: composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H7

## H2 (claim)
Statement: The treatment- and genotype-associated differences reported in this study occur without loss of cell viability.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Donor-derived extracellular L-lactate is the arm of the transferred signal that drives recipient TNF-alpha and IL-6 output and recipient HIF-1alpha stabilization: K254R medium contains 1.9-fold more lactate, and enzymatic depletion of L-lactate from it removes 55-60% of the recipient TNF-alpha and IL-6 response and abolishes recipient HIF-1alpha stabilization.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Donor-derived extracellular ATP acting on recipient P2X7 drives recipient IL-1beta specifically: K254R medium contains 1.8-fold more ATP, and either hydrolysis of ATP in the medium or blockade of recipient P2X7 reduces recipient IL-1beta by about 40% while leaving TNF-alpha unchanged.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)

Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+
Scope limits: in vitro only; no in vivo, aged or chronic low-grade inflammatory model was studied; GAPDH replacement reaches 75-80%, leaving residual endogenous wild-type protein; acetylation states are represented by K254Q and K254R substitutions rather than by enzymatically controlled acetylation in cells; figure images and supplementary files were not inspected during this extraction
Validation requirements:
- R1: Distinguish cell-autonomous from paracrine contributions of GAPDH K254 deacetylation to microglial inflammatory responses. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show that the reported treatment and genotype differences are not produced by loss of cell viability. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)

# Main hypothesis
Can an ultrafast Na–benzophenone/diglyme chemical pre-sodiation compensate the initial Na+ loss of CaV8O20 (CVO450) anodes, and can it be carried out in a roll-to-roll process?
System: CVO450 (CaV8O20 annealed at 450 °C) electrodes (CVO:carbon black:PVDF 8:1:1 on Al foil) pre-sodiated with a Na–benzophenone/diglyme (Na–BPh/Dgy) solution and tested in CR2032 half-cells against Na metal.
Conditions: Electrolyte 1 M NaPF6 in EC:DEC (1:1 by volume) with 5 vol% FEC; Whatman filter separator; Half-cell voltage window 0.01–3 V; room temperature; Pre-sodiation reagent: 1 mmol benzophenone and 1 mmol Na metal in 1 mL diglyme; electrodes immersed for minutes and rinsed with diglyme
Scope limits: Laboratory coin cells; Computational results refer to DFT-optimized bulk CaV8O20 models
Validation requirements:
- R1: A pre-sodiation step must compensate the active Na+ lost during first-cycle SEI formation and raise the initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) within minutes. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: The pre-sodiation must be performed ex situ and avoid the gas-evolving reactions associated with sacrificial pre-sodiation additives. (aspects: H4)
- R3: The pre-sodiation must be transferable to continuous, large-area (roll-to-roll) electrode production.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Na metal and benzophenone in diglyme form a stable, strongly reducing Na–benzophenone ketyl-radical reagent.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Soaking time in Na–BPh/Dgy controls the amount of Na+ inserted into CVO450 electrodes and raises their initial coulombic efficiency.
Links: refinement → H3

## H3 (claim)
Statement: Soaking CVO450 electrodes in Na–BPh/Dgy for 2 min inserts enough Na+ to raise the half-cell initial coulombic efficiency from 60.86% to 98.03%.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The Na–BPh/Dgy route pre-sodiates the anode ex situ, using only Na metal, without the gas-evolving high-voltage decomposition of sacrificial additives.

System: CVO450 (CaV8O20 annealed at 450 °C) electrodes (CVO:carbon black:PVDF 8:1:1 on Al foil) pre-sodiated with a Na–benzophenone/diglyme (Na–BPh/Dgy) solution and tested in CR2032 half-cells against Na metal.
Conditions: Electrolyte 1 M NaPF6 in EC:DEC (1:1 by volume) with 5 vol% FEC; Whatman filter separator; Half-cell voltage window 0.01–3 V; room temperature; Pre-sodiation reagent: 1 mmol benzophenone and 1 mmol Na metal in 1 mL diglyme; electrodes immersed for minutes and rinsed with diglyme
Scope limits: Laboratory coin cells; Computational results refer to DFT-optimized bulk CaV8O20 models
Validation requirements:
- R1: A pre-sodiation step must compensate the active Na+ lost during first-cycle SEI formation and raise the initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) within minutes. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: The pre-sodiation must be performed ex situ and avoid the gas-evolving reactions associated with sacrificial pre-sodiation additives. (aspects: H4)
- R3: The pre-sodiation must be transferable to continuous, large-area (roll-to-roll) electrode production.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Na metal and benzophenone in diglyme form a stable, strongly reducing Na–benzophenone ketyl-radical reagent.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Soaking time in Na–BPh/Dgy controls the amount of Na+ inserted into CVO450 electrodes and raises their initial coulombic efficiency.
Links: refinement → H3

## H3 (claim)
Statement: Soaking CVO450 electrodes in Na–BPh/Dgy for 2 min inserts enough Na+ to raise the half-cell initial coulombic efficiency from 60.86% to 98.03%.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The Na–BPh/Dgy route pre-sodiates the anode ex situ, using only Na metal, without the gas-evolving high-voltage decomposition of sacrificial additives.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Verify that the Na–BPh/Dgy pre-sodiation can be transferred to continuous, large-area roll-to-roll electrode production, including uniform coverage, process speed, and retention of the pre-sodiated state.
Links: refinement ← R3

# Experiments
## E1

Manipulation: Addition of Na metal to BPh/Dgy; storage time
Measurements: optical photographs; EPR
Comparison: groups: BPh/Dgy; Na–BPh/Dgy | endpoint: Solution colour; EPR signal | varied: Na addition; storage time | held fixed: composition | unit: solution | window: minutes after Na addition; 6 months
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: CVO450 electrodes soaked in Na–BPh/Dgy for 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 4 min (Methods: immersion 1–4 min, then rinsing with diglyme) and compared with non-sodiated (0 min) electrodes, whose handling (e.g., any rinse) is not described; all assembled into half-cells against Na metal; OCV, initial discharge capacity and ICE recorded.
Manipulation: Soaking time (0–4 min)
Measurements: OCV; first-cycle GCD; ICE
Comparison: groups: 0 min (non-sodiated); 1 min; 1.5 min; 2 min; 3 min; 4 min | endpoint: OCV; initial discharge capacity; ICE | varied: soaking time | held fixed: CVO450 electrode; reagent composition; half-cell configuration | unit: half-cell per soaking time | window: first cycle | units: V; mAh g−1; %

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: Molecular processes related to oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, mitochondrial homeostasis and cell survival are characterized, including by cardiac proteomics. (aspects: H2, H3, H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac superoxide levels in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation lowers cardiac inflammatory marker expression in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation counteracts MI-associated changes in cardiac mitochondrial markers.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: The lower cardiac superoxide in transplanted MI rats appears independent of antioxidant defense, since SOD1/SOD2 mRNA did not change, and may be related to changes in mitochondrial superoxide generation.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Cardiac superoxide and antioxidant enzyme expression: DHE fluorescence of 14 μm cardiac sections (mean fluorescence density in a target region, region not specified; three sections per animal averaged) and qPCR of SOD1 and SOD2 mRNA.
Manipulation: Permanent ligation of the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery (MI) or sham operation (suture passed without fastening); at the time of surgery, PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria from hearts of healthy donor rats (180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL) injected with a 29-gauge needle at four points around the ligature, in half of the animals of each surgical group.
Measurements: DHE fluorescence density; SOD1 mRNA; SOD2 mRNA
Comparison: groups: Sham + PBS vehicle; Sham + mitochondria; MI + PBS vehicle; MI + mitochondria | endpoint: mean DHE fluorescence density in the target region; SOD1 and SOD2 mRNA | varied: surgery: permanent LAD ligation (MI) vs sham operation; intramyocardial injection at surgery: isolated mitochondria vs PBS vehicle | held fixed: male Wistar rats, 10 weeks old at surgery, standard diet; mitochondrial dose 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL, delivered at four points around the ligature at the time of surgery; sacrifice 4 weeks after MI induction; DHE 2 × 10^-6 M, 30 min, 37°C; 40× fluorescence microscopy | unit: animal | window: 4 weeks after MI induction and injection | units: n-fold over control group (arbitrary units) | uncertainty: two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni multiple comparisons; mean ± SEM

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of NHLFs, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether DCLK1 expression and phosphorylation differ in fibrotic human lung tissue relative to nonfibrotic control lung tissue, and identify which lung cell populations express DCLK1. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)
- R4: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H6; composition → H8

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 protein expression and DCLK1 phosphorylation are higher in lung tissue from patients with IPF than in nonfibrotic control lung tissue.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H11

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: In human lung, DCLK1 transcript is detectable across endothelial, epithelial, lymphoid, myeloid and stromal populations, with the greatest expression in stromal cells and particularly in myofibroblasts.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion reduces bleomycin-induced lung infiltration, collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression in mouse lung at day 21.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5; scoped evidence ← H10

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion attenuates bleomycin-induced impairment of lung mechanics and lung structure and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 21.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: TGF-β stimulation of normal human lung fibroblasts increases DCLK1 protein expression at 8 h and DCLK1 phosphorylation at 30 min.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H7

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: TGF-β-responsive Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupy their response elements in the DCLK1 promoter region, linking canonical and noncanonical TGF-β signalling to DCLK1 expression.
Links: refinement ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 knockdown reduces TGF-β-induced expression of fibronectin, collagen 1A1, α-SMA and CTGF in normal human lung fibroblasts, indicating that DCLK1 contributes to their induction.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H9

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: DCLK1 alters Smad3 phosphorylation, associates with Smad3 and is enriched at the Smad3-binding region of the CTGF promoter, consistent with DCLK1-Smad3-associated signalling linked to CTGF expression.
Links: refinement ← H8

## H10 (limitation)
Statement: The Pgk1-Cre/ERT2 system used here mediates global tamoxifen-inducible deletion of Dclk1 rather than cell-type-targeted deletion, and DCLK1 is expressed across fibroblasts, immune cells, alveolar epithelial type II cells and endothelial cells, so the contributions of individual lung cell populations to fibrogenesis were not distinguished.
Links: scoped evidence → H4

## H11 (limitation)
Statement: Human control lung tissue was heterogeneous, comprising tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD and commercially sourced normal lung slides, and potential confounding could not be fully excluded.
Links: scoped evidence → H2

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of NHLFs, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether DCLK1 expression and phosphorylation differ in fibrotic human lung tissue relative to nonfibrotic control lung tissue, and identify which lung cell populations express DCLK1. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)
- R4: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H6; composition → H8; composition → H12

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 protein expression and DCLK1 phosphorylation are higher in lung tissue from patients with IPF than in nonfibrotic control lung tissue.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H11

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: In human lung, DCLK1 transcript is detectable across endothelial, epithelial, lymphoid, myeloid and stromal populations, with the greatest expression in stromal cells and particularly in myofibroblasts.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion reduces bleomycin-induced lung infiltration, collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression in mouse lung at day 21.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5; scoped evidence ← H10

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion attenuates bleomycin-induced impairment of lung mechanics and lung structure and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 21.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: TGF-β stimulation of normal human lung fibroblasts increases DCLK1 protein expression at 8 h and DCLK1 phosphorylation at 30 min.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H7

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: TGF-β-responsive Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupy their response elements in the DCLK1 promoter region, linking canonical and noncanonical TGF-β signalling to DCLK1 expression.
Links: refinement ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 knockdown reduces TGF-β-induced expression of fibronectin, collagen 1A1, α-SMA and CTGF in normal human lung fibroblasts, indicating that DCLK1 contributes to their induction.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H9; refinement → H13

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: DCLK1 alters Smad3 phosphorylation, associates with Smad3 and is enriched at the Smad3-binding region of the CTGF promoter, consistent with DCLK1-Smad3-associated signalling linked to CTGF expression.
Links: refinement ← H8

## H10 (limitation)
Statement: The Pgk1-Cre/ERT2 system used here mediates global tamoxifen-inducible deletion of Dclk1 rather than cell-type-targeted deletion, and DCLK1 is expressed across fibroblasts, immune cells, alveolar epithelial type II cells and endothelial cells, so the contributions of individual lung cell populations to fibrogenesis were not distinguished.
Links: scoped evidence → H4

## H11 (limitation)
Statement: Human control lung tissue was heterogeneous, comprising tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD and commercially sourced normal lung slides, and potential confounding could not be fully excluded.
Links: scoped evidence → H2

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: Pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 in bleomycin-treated mice, begun after fibrosis has been induced, reduces fibrotic remodelling and preserves lung mechanics and lung structure relative to vehicle-treated bleomycin controls.
Links: composition ← H1

## H13 (aspect)
Statement: Pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 in TGF-beta-stimulated normal human lung fibroblasts reduces profibrotic protein expression (for example CTGF, fibronectin and alpha-SMA) relative to vehicle-treated stimulated cells.

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of NHLFs, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether DCLK1 expression and phosphorylation differ in fibrotic human lung tissue relative to nonfibrotic control lung tissue, and identify which lung cell populations express DCLK1. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)
- R4: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H6; composition → H8; composition → H12

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 protein expression and DCLK1 phosphorylation are higher in lung tissue from patients with IPF than in nonfibrotic control lung tissue.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H11

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: In human lung, DCLK1 transcript is detectable across endothelial, epithelial, lymphoid, myeloid and stromal populations, with the greatest expression in stromal cells and particularly in myofibroblasts.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion reduces bleomycin-induced lung infiltration, collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression in mouse lung at day 21.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5; scoped evidence ← H10

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion attenuates bleomycin-induced impairment of lung mechanics and lung structure and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 21.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: TGF-β stimulation of normal human lung fibroblasts increases DCLK1 protein expression at 8 h and DCLK1 phosphorylation at 30 min.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H7

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: TGF-β-responsive Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupy their response elements in the DCLK1 promoter region, linking canonical and noncanonical TGF-β signalling to DCLK1 expression.
Links: refinement ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 knockdown reduces TGF-β-induced expression of fibronectin, collagen 1A1, α-SMA and CTGF in normal human lung fibroblasts, indicating that DCLK1 contributes to their induction.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H9

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: DCLK1 alters Smad3 phosphorylation, associates with Smad3 and is enriched at the Smad3-binding region of the CTGF promoter, consistent with DCLK1-Smad3-associated signalling linked to CTGF expression.
Links: refinement ← H8

## H10 (limitation)
Statement: The Pgk1-Cre/ERT2 system used here mediates global tamoxifen-inducible deletion of Dclk1 rather than cell-type-targeted deletion, and DCLK1 is expressed across fibroblasts, immune cells, alveolar epithelial type II cells and endothelial cells, so the contributions of individual lung cell populations to fibrogenesis were not distinguished.
Links: scoped evidence → H4

## H11 (limitation)
Statement: Human control lung tissue was heterogeneous, comprising tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD and commercially sourced normal lung slides, and potential confounding could not be fully excluded.
Links: scoped evidence → H2

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: Pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 reduces TGF-β-induced fibrotic protein expression in cultured normal human lung fibroblasts and attenuates bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, lung mechanics impairment and lung structure in mice, without altering the genetic background of Dclk1.

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of NHLFs, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether DCLK1 expression and phosphorylation differ in fibrotic human lung tissue relative to nonfibrotic control lung tissue, and identify which lung cell populations express DCLK1. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)
- R4: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H6; composition → H8; composition → H12

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 protein expression and DCLK1 phosphorylation are higher in lung tissue from patients with IPF than in nonfibrotic control lung tissue.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H11

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: In human lung, DCLK1 transcript is detectable across endothelial, epithelial, lymphoid, myeloid and stromal populations, with the greatest expression in stromal cells and particularly in myofibroblasts.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion reduces bleomycin-induced lung infiltration, collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression in mouse lung at day 21.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5; scoped evidence ← H10

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion attenuates bleomycin-induced impairment of lung mechanics and lung structure and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 21.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: TGF-β stimulation of normal human lung fibroblasts increases DCLK1 protein expression at 8 h and DCLK1 phosphorylation at 30 min.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H7

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: TGF-β-responsive Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupy their response elements in the DCLK1 promoter region, linking canonical and noncanonical TGF-β signalling to DCLK1 expression.
Links: refinement ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 knockdown reduces TGF-β-induced expression of fibronectin, collagen 1A1, α-SMA and CTGF in normal human lung fibroblasts, indicating that DCLK1 contributes to their induction.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H9

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: DCLK1 alters Smad3 phosphorylation, associates with Smad3 and is enriched at the Smad3-binding region of the CTGF promoter, consistent with DCLK1-Smad3-associated signalling linked to CTGF expression.

## H10 (limitation)
Statement: The Pgk1-Cre/ERT2 system used here mediates global tamoxifen-inducible deletion of Dclk1 rather than cell-type-targeted deletion, and DCLK1 is expressed across fibroblasts, immune cells, alveolar epithelial type II cells and endothelial cells, so the contributions of individual lung cell populations to fibrogenesis were not distinguished.
Links: scoped evidence → H4

## H11 (limitation)
Statement: Human control lung tissue was heterogeneous, comprising tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD and commercially sourced normal lung slides, and potential confounding could not be fully excluded.
Links: scoped evidence → H2

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: The objective includes pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition as a distinct evaluation of DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target, including DCLK1-IN-1 (10 mg/kg orally once daily from day 7 after BLM induction) in the mouse model. The supplied observations report no outcome for this pharmacological arm and no pharmacological-inhibitor result in fibroblasts.

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of NHLFs, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether DCLK1 expression and phosphorylation differ in fibrotic human lung tissue relative to nonfibrotic control lung tissue, and identify which lung cell populations express DCLK1. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)
- R4: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H6; composition → H8; composition → H12

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 protein expression and DCLK1 phosphorylation are higher in lung tissue from patients with IPF than in nonfibrotic control lung tissue.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H11

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: In human lung, DCLK1 transcript is detectable across endothelial, epithelial, lymphoid, myeloid and stromal populations, with the greatest expression in stromal cells and particularly in myofibroblasts.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion reduces bleomycin-induced lung infiltration, collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression in mouse lung at day 21.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5; scoped evidence ← H10

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion attenuates bleomycin-induced impairment of lung mechanics and lung structure and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 21.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: TGF-β stimulation of normal human lung fibroblasts increases DCLK1 protein expression at 8 h and DCLK1 phosphorylation at 30 min.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H7

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: TGF-β-responsive Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupy their response elements in the DCLK1 promoter region, linking canonical and noncanonical TGF-β signalling to DCLK1 expression.
Links: refinement ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 knockdown reduces TGF-β-induced expression of fibronectin, collagen 1A1, α-SMA and CTGF in normal human lung fibroblasts, indicating that DCLK1 contributes to their induction.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H9; refinement → H12

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: DCLK1 alters Smad3 phosphorylation, associates with Smad3 and is enriched at the Smad3-binding region of the CTGF promoter, consistent with DCLK1-Smad3-associated signalling linked to CTGF expression.
Links: refinement ← H8

## H10 (limitation)
Statement: The Pgk1-Cre/ERT2 system used here mediates global tamoxifen-inducible deletion of Dclk1 rather than cell-type-targeted deletion, and DCLK1 is expressed across fibroblasts, immune cells, alveolar epithelial type II cells and endothelial cells, so the contributions of individual lung cell populations to fibrogenesis were not distinguished.
Links: scoped evidence → H4; scoped evidence → H12

## H11 (limitation)
Statement: Human control lung tissue was heterogeneous, comprising tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD and commercially sourced normal lung slides, and potential confounding could not be fully excluded.
Links: scoped evidence → H2

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: Pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition by DCLK1-IN-1 reduces BLM-induced fibrotic remodelling and lung function impairment in C57BL/6 mice at day 21, with the caveat that the genetic arm is global and tamoxifen-inducible, so cell-type contributions are not separated.
Links: composition ← H1; scoped evidence ← H10; refinement ← H8

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of NHLFs, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether DCLK1 expression and phosphorylation differ in fibrotic human lung tissue relative to nonfibrotic control lung tissue, and identify which lung cell populations express DCLK1. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)
- R4: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H6; composition → H8; composition → H12

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 protein expression and DCLK1 phosphorylation are higher in lung tissue from patients with IPF than in nonfibrotic control lung tissue.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H11

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: In human lung, DCLK1 transcript is detectable across endothelial, epithelial, lymphoid, myeloid and stromal populations, with the greatest expression in stromal cells and particularly in myofibroblasts.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion reduces bleomycin-induced lung infiltration, collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression in mouse lung at day 21.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5; scoped evidence ← H10; refinement ← H12

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion attenuates bleomycin-induced impairment of lung mechanics and lung structure and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 21.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: TGF-β stimulation of normal human lung fibroblasts increases DCLK1 protein expression at 8 h and DCLK1 phosphorylation at 30 min.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H7

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: TGF-β-responsive Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupy their response elements in the DCLK1 promoter region, linking canonical and noncanonical TGF-β signalling to DCLK1 expression.
Links: refinement ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 knockdown reduces TGF-β-induced expression of fibronectin, collagen 1A1, α-SMA and CTGF in normal human lung fibroblasts, indicating that DCLK1 contributes to their induction.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H9; refinement ← H12

## H9 (mechanism)
Statement: DCLK1 alters Smad3 phosphorylation, associates with Smad3 and is enriched at the Smad3-binding region of the CTGF promoter, consistent with DCLK1-Smad3-associated signalling linked to CTGF expression.
Links: refinement ← H8

## H10 (limitation)
Statement: The Pgk1-Cre/ERT2 system used here mediates global tamoxifen-inducible deletion of Dclk1 rather than cell-type-targeted deletion, and DCLK1 is expressed across fibroblasts, immune cells, alveolar epithelial type II cells and endothelial cells, so the contributions of individual lung cell populations to fibrogenesis were not distinguished.
Links: scoped evidence → H4

## H11 (limitation)
Statement: Human control lung tissue was heterogeneous, comprising tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD and commercially sourced normal lung slides, and potential confounding could not be fully excluded.
Links: scoped evidence → H2

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: Test whether pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition by DCLK1-IN-1 alters fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in the bleomycin model, in addition to the genetic Dclk1-deletion arm.

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of NHLFs, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether DCLK1 expression and phosphorylation differ in fibrotic human lung tissue relative to nonfibrotic control lung tissue, and identify which lung cell populations express DCLK1. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)
- R4: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H6; composition → H8; composition → H12

## H2 (aspect)

# Main hypothesis
Does oral Oxystorm, a nitrate-enriched water extract of Amaranthus leaves, given alone at a low and a high dose or combined with the curcuminoid-enriched turmeric extract BCM-95, reduce myocardial injury after left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) ligation ischemia-reperfusion in Wistar rats, in a preventive (pre-treatment) model and a treatment (post-reperfusion) model, and which mechanisms might underlie any protection?
System: Adult Wistar rats (150-200 g; equal numbers of males and females) with LAD ligation (45 min ischemia) followed by reperfusion
Conditions: Preventive model: daily oral dosing for 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31; Treatment model: 45 min ischemia, reperfusion for 7 days; dosing from 4 h after reperfusion, once daily until day 7; Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg (preventive) and 90 or 180 mg/kg (treatment); combination Oxystorm 90 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (preventive) or Oxystorm 180 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (treatment); Controls: vehicle (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control, verapamil 10 mg/kg LAD positive control
Scope limits: Single rat LAD ischemia-reperfusion model; Endpoints: TTC infarct size, cardiac injury biomarkers (LDH, CK-MB, myoglobin, troponin I), IL-6 and TNF-alpha, MDA, SOD and GSH
Validation requirements:
- R1: Assess protection in a preventive model (30-day oral pre-treatment before LAD ischemia-reperfusion) and in a treatment model (dosing initiated 4 h after reperfusion and continued for 7 days).
- R2: Test Oxystorm at a low and a high dose in each model (45 and 90 mg/kg preventive; 90 and 180 mg/kg treatment).
- R3: Evaluate the combination of Oxystorm with BCM-95 for synergistic effects.
- R4: Measure infarct size by TTC staining, cardiac injury biomarkers (LDH, CK-MB, myoglobin, troponin I), inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha) and oxidative stress markers.
- R5: Explicate the probable mechanisms underlying any cardioprotective effect.
- R6: Include vehicle, sham and LAD control groups and a verapamil-treated LAD positive control group.

Does oral Oxystorm, a nitrate-enriched water extract of Amaranthus leaves, given alone at a low and a high dose or combined with the curcuminoid-enriched turmeric extract BCM-95, reduce myocardial injury after left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) ligation ischemia-reperfusion in Wistar rats, in a preventive (pre-treatment) model and a treatment (post-reperfusion) model, and which mechanisms might underlie any protection?
System: Adult Wistar rats (150-200 g; equal numbers of males and females) with LAD ligation (45 min ischemia) followed by reperfusion
Conditions: Preventive model: daily oral dosing for 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31; Treatment model: 45 min ischemia, reperfusion for 7 days; dosing from 4 h after reperfusion, once daily until day 7; Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg (preventive) and 90 or 180 mg/kg (treatment); combination Oxystorm 90 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (preventive) or Oxystorm 180 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (treatment); Controls: vehicle (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control, verapamil 10 mg/kg LAD positive control
Scope limits: Single rat LAD ischemia-reperfusion model; Endpoints: TTC infarct size, cardiac injury biomarkers (LDH, CK-MB, myoglobin, troponin I), IL-6 and TNF-alpha, MDA, SOD and GSH
Validation requirements:
- R1: Assess protection in a preventive model (30-day oral pre-treatment before LAD ischemia-reperfusion) and in a treatment model (dosing initiated 4 h after reperfusion and continued for 7 days).
- R2: Test Oxystorm at a low and a high dose in each model (45 and 90 mg/kg preventive; 90 and 180 mg/kg treatment).
- R3: Evaluate the combination of Oxystorm with BCM-95 for synergistic effects.
- R4: Measure infarct size by TTC staining, cardiac injury biomarkers (LDH, CK-MB, myoglobin, troponin I), inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha) and oxidative stress markers.
- R5: Explicate the probable mechanisms underlying any cardioprotective effect.
- R6: Include vehicle, sham and LAD control groups and a verapamil-treated LAD positive control group.

Statement: Cardioprotective efficacy of Oxystorm doses in the treatment model

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Synergistic effects of Oxystorm + BCM-95 combination

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Mechanistic underpinnings of cardioprotection (infarct size, biomarkers, cytokines, oxidative stress)
