# Experiments
# Observations

# Main hypothesis
Can directional freeze-drying of regenerated silk fibroin (RSF)/poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/Ti3C2Tx MXene mixtures produce ultralight aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture that provide efficient X-band EMI shielding, and how do MXene content and the lamellar architecture relate to shielding effectiveness and to the balance of absorption and reflection?
System: RSF/PVA/Ti3C2Tx MXene composite aerogels (RPM-20, RPM-40, RPM-60, RPM-80) prepared from Bombyx mori silk-derived RSF, PVA and LiF/HCl-etched Ti3C2Tx
Conditions: MXene content 20, 40, 60 and 80 wt% of total RSF + PVA + MXene solids; RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; EMI shielding measured by waveguide vector network analyzer over 8.2-12.4 GHz (X-band); Specimens 22.86 mm x 10.16 mm x 3 mm
Scope limits: Shielding was measured only in the X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Fabricate RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture and characterize MXene synthesis, incorporation and distribution in the RSF/PVA matrix. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine how Ti3C2Tx MXene content (20, 40, 60 and 80 wt%) affects X-band EMI shielding effectiveness (SE_T), shielding efficiency, and the absorption (A) and reflection (R) contributions. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Evaluate the lightweight shielding capability of the aerogels. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Directional freeze-drying produces an ordered lamellar architecture in the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: X-band EMI shielding effectiveness of the aerogels depends on MXene content (20-80 wt%) and on frequency.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The balance of shielding shifts from surface reflection toward internal absorption as MXene content increases, with RPM-60 absorption-dominated.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The aerogels are ultralight and provide high density-normalized (specific) shielding effectiveness.

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Preparation of RPM-x aerogels by directional freezing and vacuum freeze-drying, with cross-sectional SEM and EDS elemental mapping of the composite aerogel.
Manipulation: Silk from Bombyx mori cocoons was degummed in 0.5 wt% Na2CO3 at 100 C for 30 min (2-3 times), dissolved in CaCl2/ethanol/water (molar ratio 1:2:8) at 80 C for 40 min, dialyzed for 72 h and freeze-dried to an RSF sponge. The RSF sponge was dissolved in 10 wt% aqueous PVA to an RSF:PVA mass ratio of 1:1, and Ti3C2Tx dispersion was added to give 20, 40, 60 or 80 wt% MXene in total solids. Each mixture was poured into a 3 cm x 3 cm x 3 cm PTFE mold with a copper template at the bottom, frozen by slowly injecting liquid nitrogen around the mold (freezing rate -10 C/min), and freeze-dried for 72 h (-70 C, <2 Pa).
Measurements: Cross-sectional SEM images; EDS elemental mapping
Comparison: groups: RSF/PVA/MXene composite aerogel (MXene content of the imaged sample not stated) | endpoint: Cross-sectional morphology; spatial distribution of C, N, O and Ti | held fixed: RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; Directional freezing on a copper template at -10 C/min; Freeze-drying 72 h at -70 C, <2 Pa | unit: Aerogel cross-section
Observations: O1

## E2
Statement: X-band EMI shielding measurement of RPM-20, RPM-40, RPM-60 and RPM-80 with a waveguide vector network analyzer, calculating R, A and T coefficients and SE_T, SE_A and SE_R from S11 and S21.
Manipulation: MXene content of the aerogel (20, 40, 60, 80 wt% of total solids)
Measurements: S11 and S21 scattering parameters; SE_T, SE_A, SE_R spectra and X-band averages; R and A coefficients; Shielding efficiency at 12.4 GHz
Comparison: groups: RPM-20; RPM-40; RPM-60; RPM-80 | endpoint: SE_T, SE_A and SE_R (dB); R, A and T power coefficients; shielding efficiency (%) | varied: MXene content | held fixed: RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; Directional freezing on a copper template and 72 h vacuum freeze-drying; Specimen size 22.86 mm x 10.16 mm x 3 mm; Waveguide VNA measurement over 8.2-12.4 GHz | unit: Rectangular specimen per composition; number of specimens per composition not reported | window: 8.2-12.4 GHz | units: dB; dimensionless coefficients; % | uncertainty: Error bars in X-band averaged plots are standard deviations over frequency-dependent data points
Observations: O2, O3, O4, O5

## E3
Statement: Apparent density of each RPM-x aerogel (Table S1) and calculation of specific shielding effectiveness (SSE) and thickness-normalized SSE (SSE/t) over the X-band.
Manipulation: MXene content of the aerogel (20, 40, 60, 80 wt% of total solids)
Measurements: Apparent density; SSE spectra; SSE/t spectra
Comparison: groups: RPM-20; RPM-40; RPM-60; RPM-80 | endpoint: Apparent density (g cm^-3); SSE (dB cm^3 g^-1); SSE/t | varied: MXene content | held fixed: Specimen thickness about 3 mm; Same preparation route | unit: Aerogel per composition; density measurement procedure not described in Methods | window: 8.2-12.4 GHz | units: g cm^-3; dB cm^3 g^-1
Observations: O6, O7, O8

# Main hypothesis
Can directional freeze-drying of regenerated silk fibroin (RSF)/poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/Ti3C2Tx MXene mixtures produce ultralight aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture that provide efficient X-band EMI shielding, and how do MXene content and the lamellar architecture relate to shielding effectiveness and to the balance of absorption and reflection?
System: RSF/PVA/Ti3C2Tx MXene composite aerogels (RPM-20, RPM-40, RPM-60, RPM-80) prepared from Bombyx mori silk-derived RSF, PVA and LiF/HCl-etched Ti3C2Tx
Conditions: MXene content 20, 40, 60 and 80 wt% of total RSF + PVA + MXene solids; RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; EMI shielding measured by waveguide vector network analyzer over 8.2-12.4 GHz (X-band); Specimens 22.86 mm x 10.16 mm x 3 mm
Scope limits: Shielding was measured only in the X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Fabricate RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture and characterize MXene synthesis, incorporation and distribution in the RSF/PVA matrix. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine how Ti3C2Tx MXene content (20, 40, 60 and 80 wt%) affects X-band EMI shielding effectiveness (SE_T), shielding efficiency, and the absorption (A) and reflection (R) contributions. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Evaluate the lightweight shielding capability of the aerogels. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Directional freeze-drying produces an ordered lamellar architecture in the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: X-band EMI shielding effectiveness of the aerogels depends on MXene content (20-80 wt%) and on frequency.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The balance of shielding shifts from surface reflection toward internal absorption as MXene content increases, with RPM-60 absorption-dominated.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The aerogels are ultralight and provide high density-normalized (specific) shielding effectiveness.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: RPM-60 maintains lamellar structure under mechanical stress and thermal cycling.

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: RPM-60 exhibits consistent X-band shielding effectiveness across 8.2-12.4 GHz without frequency-dependent degradation.

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: RPM-60 outperforms commercial MXene/PVA composites in specific shielding effectiveness (SSE) and thickness-normalized performance.

# Main hypothesis
Can directional freeze-drying of regenerated silk fibroin (RSF)/poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/Ti3C2Tx MXene mixtures produce ultralight aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture that provide efficient X-band EMI shielding, and how do MXene content and the lamellar architecture relate to shielding effectiveness and to the balance of absorption and reflection?
System: RSF/PVA/Ti3C2Tx MXene composite aerogels (RPM-20, RPM-40, RPM-60, RPM-80) prepared from Bombyx mori silk-derived RSF, PVA and LiF/HCl-etched Ti3C2Tx
Conditions: MXene content 20, 40, 60 and 80 wt% of total RSF + PVA + MXene solids; RSF:PVA mass ratio 1:1; EMI shielding measured by waveguide vector network analyzer over 8.2-12.4 GHz (X-band); Specimens 22.86 mm x 10.16 mm x 3 mm
Scope limits: Shielding was measured only in the X-band (8.2-12.4 GHz)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Fabricate RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels with an ordered lamellar architecture and characterize MXene synthesis, incorporation and distribution in the RSF/PVA matrix. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine how Ti3C2Tx MXene content (20, 40, 60 and 80 wt%) affects X-band EMI shielding effectiveness (SE_T), shielding efficiency, and the absorption (A) and reflection (R) contributions. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Evaluate the lightweight shielding capability of the aerogels. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Directional freeze-drying produces an ordered lamellar architecture in the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: X-band EMI shielding effectiveness of the aerogels depends on MXene content (20-80 wt%) and on frequency.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The balance of shielding shifts from surface reflection toward internal absorption as MXene content increases, with RPM-60 absorption-dominated.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The aerogels are ultralight and provide high density-normalized (specific) shielding effectiveness.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The lamellar thickness and orientation of the RSF/PVA/MXene aerogels vary with MXene content.

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: The X-band EMI shielding effectiveness remains stable over a range of temperatures relevant to portable device operation (e.g., -20°C to 40°C).

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: The aerogels exhibit sufficient mechanical integrity and flexibility for integration into portable electronic devices.

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: Moisture exposure does not significantly degrade the EMI shielding effectiveness of the aerogels.

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: The EMI shielding effectiveness of the RPM-60 aerogel compares favorably with commercially available shielding materials for portable electronics.

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES to the carbon paste changes the photovoltaic performance (PCE, JSC, VOC, FF, Rs, Rsh, hysteresis) of p-i-n C-PSCs relative to the pure carbon paste control.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H7

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the cross-sectional structure of the carbon electrode and its contact with the underlying C60/Cr layers.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the interfacial charge-transport resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon contact.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the bulk conductivity of the carbon electrode.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change leakage and recombination behaviour of the devices (shunt resistance, reverse-bias dark current, recombination resistance, trap density).

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: APTES added directly (not anchored to SiC) to the carbon paste changes device performance.

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: APTES functionalization disperses SiC and keeps the paste flowable, giving void-free carbon films in intimate contact with C60; the resulting reduction of contact resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon interface is the primary origin of the PCE gain.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES to the carbon paste changes the photovoltaic performance (PCE, JSC, VOC, FF, Rs, Rsh, hysteresis) of p-i-n C-PSCs relative to the pure carbon paste control.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H7

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the cross-sectional structure of the carbon electrode and its contact with the underlying C60/Cr layers.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the interfacial charge-transport resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon contact.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the bulk conductivity of the carbon electrode.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change leakage and recombination behaviour of the devices (shunt resistance, reverse-bias dark current, recombination resistance, trap density).

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: APTES added directly (not anchored to SiC) to the carbon paste changes device performance.

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: APTES functionalization disperses SiC and keeps the paste flowable, giving void-free carbon films in intimate contact with C60; the resulting reduction of contact resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon interface is the primary origin of the PCE gain.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1; competing explanation ← H8

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate (unverified): APTES-derived amine/silane species migrate from the SiC-APTES paste through the thin Cr/C60 layers during coating and the 80 °C anneal and passivate defects at the perovskite/C60 interface, contributing to the lower trap density, lower dark current and larger recombination resistance independently of the carbon contact.
Links: competing explanation → H7

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES to the carbon paste changes the photovoltaic performance (PCE, JSC, VOC, FF, Rs, Rsh, hysteresis) of p-i-n C-PSCs relative to the pure carbon paste control.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H7

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the cross-sectional structure of the carbon electrode and its contact with the underlying C60/Cr layers.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the interfacial charge-transport resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon contact.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the bulk conductivity of the carbon electrode.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change leakage and recombination behaviour of the devices (shunt resistance, reverse-bias dark current, recombination resistance, trap density).

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: APTES added directly (not anchored to SiC) to the carbon paste changes device performance.

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: APTES functionalization disperses SiC and keeps the paste flowable, giving void-free carbon films in intimate contact with C60; the resulting reduction of contact resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon interface is the primary origin of the PCE gain.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: Suppression of shunt leakage and recombination, potentially associated with lower trap density, may contribute to the device-performance changes with SiC-APTES independently of, or in addition to, the reduced C60/Cr/carbon contact resistance proposed in H7.

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5, H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES to the carbon paste changes the photovoltaic performance (PCE, JSC, VOC, FF, Rs, Rsh, hysteresis) of p-i-n C-PSCs relative to the pure carbon paste control.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H7; competing explanation ← H8

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the cross-sectional structure of the carbon electrode and its contact with the underlying C60/Cr layers.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the interfacial charge-transport resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon contact.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the bulk conductivity of the carbon electrode.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change leakage and recombination behaviour of the devices (shunt resistance, reverse-bias dark current, recombination resistance, trap density).

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: APTES added directly (not anchored to SiC) to the carbon paste changes device performance.

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: APTES functionalization disperses SiC and keeps the paste flowable, giving void-free carbon films in intimate contact with C60; the resulting reduction of contact resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon interface is the primary origin of the PCE gain.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate alternative: the dense, uniform carbon film formed by SiC-APTES at its optimal loading lowers Rs and raises Rsh, and this film effect accounts for the PCE gain, without requiring the SiC-APTES layer to lower the interfacial contact resistance.
Links: competing explanation → H1

# Main hypothesis
Can chimeric antigen receptors that combine an aducanumab-derived anti-Aβ scFv with a TAM-family (TYRO3, AXL, MERTK) intracellular domain increase amyloid-β engulfment by macrophages and microglia while limiting pro-inflammatory activation, and does the selected design reduce Aβ burden after transplantation of human iPSC-derived CAR microglia-like cells into an AD mouse brain?
System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed

# Main hypothesis
Can chimeric antigen receptors that combine an aducanumab-derived anti-Aβ scFv with a TAM-family (TYRO3, AXL, MERTK) intracellular domain increase amyloid-β engulfment by macrophages and microglia while limiting pro-inflammatory activation, and does the selected design reduce Aβ burden after transplantation of human iPSC-derived CAR microglia-like cells into an AD mouse brain?
System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed
Validation requirements:
- R1: Transplanted CAR-iMGLs must engraft and lower hippocampal Aβ burden in an AD mouse model without evident adverse effects. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intrahippocampal transplantation of hCSF1-expressing AXL-CAR-iMGLs lowers hippocampal Aβ plaque burden in 5xFAD mice within the analysed region at three weeks.
Links: refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H4; scoped evidence ← H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: AXL-CAR-iMGL transplantation into 5xFAD mice is not accompanied by detectable neuronal or synaptic loss in hippocampal CA1 and dentate gyrus relative to PBS treatment; synaptophysin density did not differ across the compared groups; and neither EGFP-iMGL- nor AXL-CAR-iMGL-treated mice lost body weight over 21 days.

## H3 (claim)
Statement: At three weeks after transplantation, 5xFAD mice treated with AXL-CAR-iMGLs show a lower hippocampal Aβ-positive area than mice treated with EGFP-iMGLs.
Links: refinement ← H1; refinement → H6

## H4 (limitation)
Statement: The in vivo work used xenogeneic transplantation with a three-week endpoint, and donor-derived cells accounted for only a minority (~15%) of the local microglial population.
Links: scoped evidence → H1

## H5 (limitation)
Statement: Transplanted microglia had not completely reacquired a homeostatic state at three weeks post-transplantation, which may contribute to the Aβ-clearing activity observed in control iMGLs.
Links: scoped evidence → H1

## H6 (alternative)
Statement: AXL-CAR-iMGLs may reduce Aβ-positive area through enhanced spatial engagement with Aβ deposits via amoeboid morphology, rather than increased per-cell clearance.
Links: refinement ← H3

System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed
Validation requirements:
- R1: Transplanted CAR-iMGLs must engraft and lower hippocampal Aβ burden in an AD mouse model without evident adverse effects. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intrahippocampal transplantation of hCSF1-expressing AXL-CAR-iMGLs lowers hippocampal Aβ plaque burden in 5xFAD mice within the analysed region at three weeks.
Links: refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H4; scoped evidence ← H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: AXL-CAR-iMGL transplantation into 5xFAD mice is not accompanied by detectable neuronal or synaptic loss in hippocampal CA1 and dentate gyrus relative to PBS treatment; synaptophysin density did not differ across the compared groups; and neither EGFP-iMGL- nor AXL-CAR-iMGL-treated mice lost body weight over 21 days.

## H3 (claim)
Statement: At three weeks after transplantation, 5xFAD mice treated with AXL-CAR-iMGLs show a lower hippocampal Aβ-positive area than mice treated with EGFP-iMGLs.
Links: refinement ← H1; competing explanation ← H6

## H4 (limitation)
Statement: The in vivo work used xenogeneic transplantation with a three-week endpoint, and donor-derived cells accounted for only a minority (~15%) of the local microglial population.
Links: scoped evidence → H1

## H5 (limitation)
Statement: Transplanted microglia had not completely reacquired a homeostatic state at three weeks post-transplantation, which may contribute to the Aβ-clearing activity observed in control iMGLs.
Links: scoped evidence → H1

## H6 (alternative)
Statement: At three weeks, the lower Aβ-positive area in AXL-CAR-iMGL-treated mice relative to EGFP-iMGL-treated mice reflects a greater contribution of transplanted cells to Aβ clearance, either through a higher fraction of the local microglial population or through a higher number of transplanted cells reaching the hippocampus, rather than through a higher per-cell Aβ-clearing activity of AXL-CAR-iMGLs.
Links: competing explanation → H3

## E2

# Main hypothesis
Can chimeric antigen receptors that combine an aducanumab-derived anti-Aβ scFv with a TAM-family (TYRO3, AXL, MERTK) intracellular domain increase amyloid-β engulfment by macrophages and microglia while limiting pro-inflammatory activation, and does the selected design reduce Aβ burden after transplantation of human iPSC-derived CAR microglia-like cells into an AD mouse brain?
System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed
Validation requirements:
- R1: Transplanted CAR-iMGLs must engraft and lower hippocampal Aβ burden in an AD mouse model without evident adverse effects. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intrahippocampal transplantation of hCSF1-expressing AXL-CAR-iMGLs lowers hippocampal Aβ plaque burden in 5xFAD mice within the analysed region at three weeks.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: AXL-CAR-iMGL transplantation into 5xFAD mice is not accompanied by detectable neuronal or synaptic loss in hippocampal CA1 and dentate gyrus relative to PBS treatment; synaptophysin density did not differ across the compared groups; and neither EGFP-iMGL- nor AXL-CAR-iMGL-treated mice lost body weight over 21 days.

## H3 (claim)

## H4 (limitation)

# Main hypothesis
Can chimeric antigen receptors that combine an aducanumab-derived anti-Aβ scFv with a TAM-family (TYRO3, AXL, MERTK) intracellular domain increase amyloid-β engulfment by macrophages and microglia while limiting pro-inflammatory activation, and does the selected design reduce Aβ burden after transplantation of human iPSC-derived CAR microglia-like cells into an AD mouse brain?
System: Mouse RAW264.7 macrophage and BV2 microglial lines, human HMC3 microglial line, and human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs); synthetic oligomeric Aβ1-42 (oAβ); microglia-depleted, tacrolimus-treated C57BL/6J and 5xFAD recipient mice.
Conditions: Lentiviral CAR transduction with an EGFP reporter; truncated CAR without intracellular domain, EGFP vector and WT cells as controls; oAβ-pHrodo engulfment assays at 5 μg/mL; Inflammatory paradigms: LPS plus oAβ for 6 h, LPS priming for 2 h followed by oAβ for 4 h, and oAβ alone for 16 h; PLX5622 diet for 14 days to deplete host microglia and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/kg) from one day before transplantation; Bilateral intrahippocampal injection of 2 μL at 50,000 cells/μL
Scope limits: Xenogeneic transplantation of human cells into mouse brain; In vivo analyses restricted to three weeks post-transplantation; Aβ quantification limited to three coronal sections spanning the injection site; Synthetic oAβ preparations in vitro; tau pathology and behaviour were not assessed
Validation requirements:
- R1: Transplanted CAR-iMGLs must engraft and lower hippocampal Aβ burden in an AD mouse model without evident adverse effects. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intrahippocampal transplantation of hCSF1-expressing AXL-CAR-iMGLs lowers hippocampal Aβ plaque burden in 5xFAD mice within the analysed region at three weeks.
Links: refinement → H3; scoped evidence ← H4; scoped evidence ← H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: AXL-CAR-iMGL transplantation into 5xFAD mice is not accompanied by detectable neuronal or synaptic loss in hippocampal CA1 and dentate gyrus relative to PBS treatment; synaptophysin density did not differ across the compared groups; and neither EGFP-iMGL- nor AXL-CAR-iMGL-treated mice lost body weight over 21 days.

## H3 (claim)
Statement: At three weeks after transplantation, 5xFAD mice treated with AXL-CAR-iMGLs show a lower hippocampal Aβ-positive area than mice treated with EGFP-iMGLs.
Links: refinement ← H1; competing explanation ← H6; scoped evidence ← H6

## H4 (limitation)
Statement: The in vivo work used xenogeneic transplantation with a three-week endpoint, and donor-derived cells accounted for only a minority (~15%) of the local microglial population.
Links: scoped evidence → H1

## H5 (limitation)
Statement: Transplanted microglia had not completely reacquired a homeostatic state at three weeks post-transplantation, which may contribute to the Aβ-clearing activity observed in control iMGLs.
Links: scoped evidence → H1

## H6 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate alternative explanation: The lower Aβ-positive area in the AXL-CAR-iMGL group compared with the EGFP-iMGL group at three weeks may reflect a greater contribution of transplanted AXL-CAR-iMGLs to local Aβ clearance, either through their own Aβ-engulfing activity or through a greater local microglial response, rather than a per-cell increase in Aβ clearance conferred by the CAR.
Links: competing explanation → H3; scoped evidence → H3

# Main hypothesis
What role does doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) play in fibroblast activation and pulmonary fibrosis, and does genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of DCLK1 alter fibrotic progression and lung function?
System: Human IPF and control lung tissue, a published human lung single-cell RNA sequencing data set (GSE136831), cultured normal human lung fibroblasts (NHLFs), and bleomycin (BLM)-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice with tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion or oral DCLK1-IN-1 treatment
Conditions: TGF-β 10 ng/mL stimulation of normal human lung fibroblasts, with readouts from 30 min to 24 h; Intratracheal BLM 3 mg/kg or PBS in C57BL/6 mice, analysed on day 21 (genetic arm) or day 28 (pharmacological arm); DCLK1-IN-1 10 mg/kg once daily by oral gavage from day 7 after BLM induction
Scope limits: Dclk1 deletion is global and tamoxifen-inducible rather than cell-type specific; Human control lung tissue is heterogeneous (tumour-adjacent lung, lung with COPD, commercially sourced normal slides); Fibrosis progression was studied; resolution or regeneration of established fibrosis was not
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine whether loss of DCLK1 alters bleomycin-induced fibrotic remodelling, lung structure and lung function in mice. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R2: Determine how TGF-β regulates DCLK1 in lung fibroblasts and how DCLK1 acts on profibrotic gene expression. (aspects: H4, H5, H6)
- R3: Evaluate DCLK1 as a candidate therapeutic target by testing pharmacological DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts and in the bleomycin model. (aspects: H7, H8)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: DCLK1 is associated with fibroblast activation and fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and is a candidate therapeutic target warranting further investigation.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H7; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion reduces bleomycin-induced lung infiltration, collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression in mouse lung at day 21.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H3

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Tamoxifen-inducible global Dclk1 deletion attenuates bleomycin-induced impairment of lung mechanics and lung structure and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 21.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: TGF-β-responsive Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupy their response elements in the DCLK1 promoter region, linking canonical and noncanonical TGF-β signalling to DCLK1 expression.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: DCLK1 knockdown reduces TGF-β-induced expression of fibronectin, collagen 1A1, α-SMA and CTGF in normal human lung fibroblasts, indicating that DCLK1 contributes to their induction.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H6; refinement → H8

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: DCLK1 alters Smad3 phosphorylation, associates with Smad3 and is enriched at the Smad3-binding region of the CTGF promoter, consistent with DCLK1-Smad3-associated signalling linked to CTGF expression.
Links: refinement ← H5

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Oral DCLK1-IN-1 (10 mg/kg daily) begun on day 7 after bleomycin slows fibrotic progression, preserves lung function and reduces the blood neutrophil percentage at day 28.
Links: composition ← H1

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: Pretreatment of normal human lung fibroblasts with DCLK1-IN-1 reduces TGF-β-induced CTGF expression.
Links: refinement ← H5

# Main hypothesis

Conditions: HMC3 human microglial cells exposed to LPS 100 ng/mL + nigericin 30 uM for 24 h with maltol 12.5, 25 or 50 uM; male C57BL/6J mice given LPS 0.5 mg/kg i.p. daily for 14 days, with maltol 50 or 100 mg/kg by oral gavage or donepezil 2 mg/kg i.p. 3 h after each LPS injection; in vivo readouts taken from the hippocampus

- R1: Oxidative stress and ferroptosis-associated changes are reversed by maltol. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Main hypothesis
How efficiently do four lignocellulosic byproducts (walnut shell, chestnut shell, pine wood and burnt pine wood) remove Pb ions from water by adsorption under selected pH conditions, and what do kinetic and isotherm models and material characterization (SEM, BET, PXRD) indicate about the adsorption process?
System: Batch adsorption of Pb from Pb(NO3)2 solutions in distilled water onto milled walnut shell, chestnut shell, Pinus pinaster wood and burnt P. pinaster wood collected in the Viseu region, central Portugal
Conditions: pH 7.5 for chestnut shell, pine wood and burnt pine wood; pH 6.5 for walnut shell; Initial-concentration tests: 5-200 mg L⁻¹ Pb, adsorbent dose 4 g L⁻¹, 12 h agitation; Kinetic tests: 25 mg L⁻¹ Pb, agitation times from 10 to 1440 min; Room temperature; triplicate adsorption tests; Adsorbent particle size <80 mesh (<0.177 mm)
Scope limits: Single-metal Pb(NO3)2 solutions prepared in distilled water; One temperature (room temperature)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify Pb removal by each material across initial Pb concentrations under the selected pH conditions. (aspects: H3)
- R2: Describe the equilibrium adsorption of Pb on each material with the Langmuir and Freundlich isotherm models. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Characterize the adsorbent materials by SEM, BET surface area analysis and powder X-ray diffraction. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
How efficiently do four lignocellulosic byproducts (walnut shell, chestnut shell, pine wood and burnt pine wood) remove Pb ions from water by adsorption under selected pH conditions, and what do kinetic and isotherm models and material characterization (SEM, BET, PXRD) indicate about the adsorption process?
System: Batch adsorption of Pb from Pb(NO3)2 solutions in distilled water onto milled walnut shell, chestnut shell, Pinus pinaster wood and burnt P. pinaster wood collected in the Viseu region, central Portugal
Conditions: pH 7.5 for chestnut shell, pine wood and burnt pine wood; pH 6.5 for walnut shell; Initial-concentration tests: 5-200 mg L⁻¹ Pb, adsorbent dose 4 g L⁻¹, 12 h agitation; Kinetic tests: 25 mg L⁻¹ Pb, agitation times from 10 to 1440 min; Room temperature; triplicate adsorption tests; Adsorbent particle size <80 mesh (<0.177 mm)
Scope limits: Single-metal Pb(NO3)2 solutions prepared in distilled water; One temperature (room temperature)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify Pb removal by each material across initial Pb concentrations under the selected pH conditions. (aspects: H3)
- R2: Describe the equilibrium adsorption of Pb on each material with the Langmuir and Freundlich isotherm models. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Characterize the adsorbent materials by SEM, BET surface area analysis and powder X-ray diffraction. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)

Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the combinations of electrode area and coating quality for which ZRA-based monitoring is feasible, given that corrosion noise, ECG interference and the instrumental floor scale differently with area.
- R2: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings.
- R3: Determine which signal processing strategy extracts the most information from the noisy composite signal.

Does SIRT1 act as the deacetylase for GAPDH lysine 254 in microglia, and does the K254 acetylation state thereby set glycolytic flux and pro-inflammatory output during LPS/IFN-gamma activation?
System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH
Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+
Scope limits: in vitro only; no in vivo, aged or chronic low-grade inflammatory model was studied; GAPDH replacement reaches 75-80%, leaving residual endogenous wild-type protein; acetylation states are represented by K254Q and K254R substitutions rather than by enzymatically controlled acetylation in cells; figure images and supplementary files were not inspected during this extraction
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how inflammatory activation changes SIRT1 protein, NAD+-dependent deacetylase activity and NAD+ cofactor availability in microglia. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show that the reported treatment and genotype differences are not produced by loss of cell viability. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: LPS/IFN-gamma activation lowers SIRT1 protein level and NAD+-dependent deacetylase activity in microglia.
Links: refinement → H2

## H2 (claim)
Statement: SIRT1 suppression by LPS/IFN-gamma is a response shared by the immortalized BV-2 line and ex vivo primary microglia.
Links: refinement ← H1

## H3 (claim)
Statement: The treatment- and genotype-associated differences reported in this study occur without loss of cell viability.

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: SIRT1 protein immunoblotting and fluorometric NAD+-dependent deacetylase activity measurement in BV-2 and CD11b+ primary microglia at 6 and 24 h of LPS/IFN-gamma stimulation, with SRT1720 or EX-527 pre-treatment arms.
Manipulation: LPS (100 ng/mL) plus IFN-gamma (10 ng/mL) for 6 or 24 h, with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM) applied 1 h before stimulation and DMSO (<=0.1%) as vehicle; activity measured on 20 ug protein of nicotinamide-free lysate with an acetylated fluorogenic peptide and 100 uM exogenous NAD+ for 30 min at 37 C, with substrate-free and no-NAD+ background controls and EX-527-treated lysates as a pharmacological specificity control.
Measurements: SIRT1 immunoblot densitometry normalized to beta-actin; fluorometric NAD+-dependent deacetylase activity (excitation/emission 360/460 nm)
Comparison: groups: untreated control; LPS/IFN-gamma 6 h; LPS/IFN-gamma 24 h; SRT1720 + LPS/IFN-gamma; EX-527 + LPS/IFN-gamma | endpoint: SIRT1 immunoblot densitometry as fold of untreated control and background-corrected deacetylase activity relative to untreated control | varied: inflammatory stimulation and its duration; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation; cell system (BV-2 or primary microglia) | held fixed: identical LPS/IFN-gamma doses in both cell systems; nicotinamide-free lysis for the activity assay; equal protein input; normalization of immunoblots to beta-actin and of activity to input protein | unit: independent biological replicate: a separately seeded microglial culture treated and harvested on a distinct day, from an independent BV-2 passage or an independent litter | window: 6 and 24 h after stimulation | units: fold of untreated control
Observations: O1, O2, O3

## E2
Statement: Lactate dehydrogenase release assay run in parallel with the metabolic experiments, comparing experimental release with spontaneous-release and maximal-lysis controls.
Manipulation: Conditioned medium clarified at 500 x g for 5 min; LDH activity read colorimetrically at 490 nm with a 680 nm reference; matched wells lysed with the assay lysis reagent provided the maximum-release control; assays run in duplicate for each experiment. The assay was run in parallel with the metabolic and transfer experiments, including the reconstituted K254R and K254Q cultures whose supernatants were profiled for extracellular mediators.
Measurements: colorimetric LDH activity at 490 nm with 680 nm reference
Comparison: groups: untreated or vehicle control wells; LPS/IFN-gamma and pharmacological treatment wells; K254R-reconstituted cultures; K254Q-reconstituted cultures; spontaneous-release low control; maximal-lysis high control | endpoint: cytotoxicity as (experimental release - low control)/(maximum release - low control) x 100 | varied: treatment condition; identity of the reconstituted GAPDH at position 254 | held fixed: matched wells from the same experiment; duplicate wells; identical medium clarification | unit: independent biological replicate: a separately seeded microglial culture treated and harvested on a distinct day, from an independent BV-2 passage or an independent litter | window: at the harvest time of the matched metabolic experiment | units: percent
Observations: O4

## E3
Statement: Trypan blue exclusion counting run in parallel with the metabolic experiments.
Manipulation: Detached and adherent cells collected, mixed 1:1 with 0.4% trypan blue and counted on a hemocytometer, with at least 200 cells scored per sample and duplicate counts per experiment. Counts were made in parallel with the metabolic and transfer experiments, including the reconstituted K254R and K254Q cultures whose supernatants were profiled for extracellular mediators.
Measurements: hemocytometer counts of trypan-blue-excluding cells
Comparison: groups: untreated or vehicle control wells; LPS/IFN-gamma and pharmacological treatment wells; K254R-reconstituted cultures; K254Q-reconstituted cultures | endpoint: percentage of unstained cells among total counted cells | varied: treatment condition; identity of the reconstituted GAPDH at position 254 | held fixed: at least 200 cells scored per sample; duplicate counts; pooled detached and adherent cells | unit: independent biological replicate: a separately seeded microglial culture treated and harvested on a distinct day, from an independent BV-2 passage or an independent litter | window: at the harvest time of the matched metabolic experiment | units: percent viable cells
Observations: O5

## O1 (from E1)
Statement: SIRT1 protein fell to 0.48 +/- 0.05-fold of control in BV-2 cells and to 0.56 +/- 0.07-fold in primary microglia at 24 h (p < 0.01 versus untreated), with no significant cell-type by treatment interaction in a two-way ANOVA (F(1.16) = 1.24, p = 0.28).
Scope: Side-by-side comparison of the two cell systems at 24 h; the F statistic is printed as F(1.16) in the source.

## O2 (from E1)
Statement: SRT1720 pre-treatment largely reversed the decline in SIRT1 protein, restoring it to 0.85 +/- 0.04-fold of control in BV-2 cells and 0.82 +/- 0.06-fold in primary microglia, whereas EX-527 further suppressed SIRT1 in both cell types.

## O3 (from E1)
Statement: NAD+-dependent deacetylase activity fell to approximately half of control by 24 h in both cell systems; SRT1720 pre-treatment restored deacetylase activity to 80-90% of the unstimulated baseline, and in primary microglia activity declined to 0.53 +/- 0.06-fold of baseline and was restored to 0.82 +/- 0.04-fold by SRT1720. Scope: Enzymatic activity measured on lysates with exogenous NAD+ supplied, so the readout reflects lysate enzyme content and intrinsic activity rather than intracellular cofactor supply. # Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show the enzyme-like catalytic activities of the nanozyme (POD-, GOx-, CAT- and GPx-like). (aspects: H1, H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can a 2 x 2 single-chip SnO2 MEMS gas sensor array whose four units run at different temperatures under one heating voltage, combined with a physics-informed Hierarchical Kolmogorov-Arnold Mixture-of-Experts (HK-MoE) model, detect target-gas presence, classify, and determine the concentration of the lithium-ion-battery thermal-runaway gases H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, including after aging-induced sensor drift and in gas mixtures?
System: Solution-synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles dispensed on a 1.8 x 1.8 x 0.5 mm3 2 x 2 MEMS microheater array (Pt heating electrode line widths 8, 12, 16 and 20 um), read out as four resistance channels and analyzed by the HK-MoE model
Conditions: H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 at 100-500 ppm in discrete 100 ppm steps, balance nitrogen, with background air between injections; Heating voltage 1.9 V during gas sensing; Laboratory gas delivery; 25 C and 60% RH unless otherwise noted; Fresh array (Source Domain) and the same array after 30 days (Target Domain) and 60 days of continuous operational aging; Four mixtures of the four gases at 1000 ppm total concentration
Scope limits: Laboratory gas-delivery conditions; no measurement during actual battery thermal runaway; Aging studied on one array up to 60 days
Validation requirements:
- R1: The array must respond to H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and produce distinct temperature-modulated response patterns across its four units.
- R2: The model must perform three tasks: target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination. (aspects: H1)
- R3: Discrimination must remain usable after sensor drift caused by aging of the array. (aspects: H2)
- R4: Discrimination must be demonstrated for multi-component gas mixtures.
- R5: The device must be miniaturized, low-power and single-chip.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: On the fresh array, HK-MoE performs target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HK-MoE discrimination remains usable after aging-induced drift of the same array.
Links: composition → H3; composition → H4; proposed mechanism ← H8

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Task-wise HK-MoE performance on the 30-day-aged Target Domain relative to the fresh Source Domain and to baseline models.
Links: composition ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Task-wise HK-MoE performance after 60 days of aging.
Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H5; refinement → H6

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Few-shot calibration with a small number of labeled samples from the aged array recovers classification and concentration performance.
Links: refinement ← H4; refinement → H7

## H6 (claim)
Statement: Under the 60-day aging condition HK-MoE reached F1 of 94.83% (presence), 53.59% (classification) and 30.65% (concentration), indicating that prolonged drift primarily degrades classification and concentration determination while presence detection, the primary requirement for early warning, remains reliable.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Although model performance noticeably degraded after 60 days of aging, the few-shot calibration strategy effectively restored F1-scores with a small number of labeled calibration samples (k = 100), confirming its practical feasibility for long-term deployment.
Links: refinement ← H5

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: Performance degradation after aging could arise from SnO2 grain growth, changes in oxygen-vacancy concentration, heater-resistance change, thermal-stress accumulation and slight changes in the temperature distribution across units.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

# Main hypothesis
How do lavender-extract AgNPs and LEO compare in the concentrations at which they inhibit growth and biofilm formation of multidrug-resistant, biofilm-forming staphylococci?
System: In vitro microtiter-plate assays with two S. aureus reference strains (CCM 4750, methicillin-resistant; CCM 4223, strong biofilm producer) and two multidrug-resistant, strong biofilm-forming NASM clinical isolates from animals (Mammaliicoccus sciuri, S. pseudintermedius); lavender-extract AgNPs and commercial L. angustifolia essential oil.
Conditions: Modified BHI broth with 1% glucose and 2% NaCl; 37 °C, 24 h exposures; AgNPs 25–200 μg/mL; LEO 0.001–1% (Methods); Triplicate wells; one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's test against the positive control
Scope limits: In vitro only; Four strains, one isolate or strain per designation; Biofilm eradication and nanoparticle characterization are outside this workspace
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the growth-inhibitory concentrations of AgNPs and LEO for each strain. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Determine the concentrations of AgNPs and LEO that inhibit biofilm formation for each strain. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the effective concentrations of AgNPs and LEO for growth inhibition and for inhibition of biofilm formation across the four strains. (aspects: H4)

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: The transplanted material consists of pure, respiration-coupled mitochondria that are taken up by host tissue after intramyocardial injection. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Renal alterations associated with MI are evaluated with and without cardiac mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H4)

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: The transplanted material consists of pure, respiration-coupled mitochondria that are taken up by host tissue after intramyocardial injection. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Renal alterations associated with MI are evaluated with and without cardiac mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Isolated donor heart mitochondria are pure and respiration-coupled, and are taken up by host tissue after intramyocardial injection.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserves left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Cardiac mitochondrial transplantation prevents renal alterations in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H5; composition → H6; proposed mechanism ← H7; proposed mechanism ← H8

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: In MI rats 4 weeks after LAD ligation, cardiac mitochondrial transplantation prevents MI-associated increases in renal injury and fibrosis markers (NGAL mRNA and interstitial collagen volume fraction); collagen IV and TGF-β protein rose only non-significantly with MI.
Links: composition ← H4

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: In MI rats 4 weeks after LAD ligation, cardiac mitochondrial transplantation prevents MI-associated increases in renal superoxide, inflammatory gene expression (Ccl2, sSt2) and ER stress proteins (BiP, ATF6α, CHOP).
Links: composition ← H4

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: Proposed direct route: mitochondria (or their components) injected into the myocardium reach the kidney and act on renal tissue.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: Proposed indirect route: renal changes follow from preserved cardiac function and reduced systemic neurohumoral signaling, such as aldosterone, after cardiac transplantation.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

Statement: Intramyocardial mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction attenuates cardiac and renal alterations 4 weeks after permanent LAD ligation in male rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: In non-infarcted Sham rats, fluorescent label from intramyocardially injected labeled mitochondria was detected in heart and kidney; these observations establish tissue-level label detection, not intact mitochondrial uptake or preparation purity and respiratory coupling.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: In male MI rats, cardiac mitochondrial transplantation at MI induction ameliorated MI-associated reductions in LVEF and global longitudinal strain at 4 weeks; the supplied result does not establish a diastolic-function effect.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: At 4 weeks in male MI rats, cardiac mitochondrial transplantation was reported to prevent or attenuate renal increases in NGAL, interstitial collagen, Ccl2 and sSt2 mRNA, and BiP, ATF6α and CHOP protein; prevention of increased renal DHE signal is stated in the Discussion. IL33 was unchanged, and the MI-associated renal collagen IV and TGF-β increases were slight and non-significant. These findings concern selected renal endpoints, not all renal alterations.
Links: composition ← H1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Tracking of injected mitochondria: isolated mitochondria stained with MitoTracker Deep Red FM were injected into the hearts of Sham rats; heart and one kidney were examined ex vivo by optical imaging and by fluorescence microscopy of 14 μm cryosections.
Manipulation: Intramyocardial injection of MitoTracker Deep Red-labeled mitochondria into Sham rats; comparison tissue from a control animal without labeled mitochondria.
Measurements: ex vivo optical imaging of heart and kidney; fluorescence microscopy of heart and kidney cryosections

# Main hypothesis
Does intramyocardial injection of isolated functional heart mitochondria at the time of permanent LAD ligation attenuate cardiac dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and MI-associated renal alterations 4 weeks after myocardial infarction in male Wistar rats, and which molecular processes accompany these effects?
System: Male Wistar rats (10 weeks old) with permanent LAD ligation or sham operation; donor mitochondria isolated from ventricles of healthy donor rats
Conditions: 2 × 2 design: Sham or MI, each receiving PBS vehicle or isolated mitochondria at surgery; 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL injected at four points around the ligature; single endpoint 4 weeks after MI; cardiac imaging in the final week; ten animals planned per group
Scope limits: male rats only; a single mitochondrial dose and a single delivery time (at MI induction); permanent ligation without reperfusion
Validation requirements:
- R1: The transplanted material consists of pure, respiration-coupled mitochondria that are taken up by host tissue after intramyocardial injection. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Cardiac function and structural remodeling are evaluated 4 weeks after MI with and without mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Renal alterations associated with MI are evaluated with and without cardiac mitochondrial transplantation. (aspects: H4)

Statement: Isolated donor heart mitochondria are taken up by host tissue after intramyocardial injection.
Links: composition ← H1

Statement: Mitochondrial transplantation preserves left ventricular systolic and diastolic function in MI rats.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Cardiac mitochondrial transplantation prevents renal alterations in MI rats.

# Main hypothesis
Can a 2 x 2 single-chip SnO2 MEMS gas sensor array whose four units run at different temperatures under one heating voltage, combined with a physics-informed Hierarchical Kolmogorov-Arnold Mixture-of-Experts (HK-MoE) model, detect target-gas presence, classify, and determine the concentration of the lithium-ion-battery thermal-runaway gases H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, including after aging-induced sensor drift and in gas mixtures?
System: Solution-synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles dispensed on a 1.8 x 1.8 x 0.5 mm3 2 x 2 MEMS microheater array (Pt heating electrode line widths 8, 12, 16 and 20 um), read out as four resistance channels and analyzed by the HK-MoE model
Conditions: H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 at 100-500 ppm in discrete 100 ppm steps, balance nitrogen, with background air between injections; Heating voltage 1.9 V during gas sensing; Laboratory gas delivery; 25 C and 60% RH unless otherwise noted; Fresh array (Source Domain) and the same array after 30 days (Target Domain) and 60 days of continuous operational aging; Four mixtures of the four gases at 1000 ppm total concentration
Scope limits: Laboratory gas-delivery conditions; no measurement during actual battery thermal runaway; Aging studied on one array up to 60 days
Validation requirements:
- R1: The array must respond to H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and produce distinct temperature-modulated response patterns across its four units. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: The model must perform three tasks: target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination.
- R3: Discrimination must remain usable after sensor drift caused by aging of the array.
- R4: Discrimination must be demonstrated for multi-component gas mixtures.
- R5: The device must be miniaturized, low-power and single-chip. (aspects: H2, H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: The SnO2 array detects H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and gives gas-specific response patterns across its four temperature zones.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H2; proposed mechanism ← H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Four microheater units with heating-electrode line widths of 8, 12, 16 and 20 um reach four distinct temperatures under one constant heating voltage.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1; composition ← H3

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The single-chip array operates at low heater power.
Links: composition → H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: At the 1.9 V heating voltage used for gas sensing, the single chip provides a different operating temperature in each of its four units, set by the heating-electrode line width.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Temperature within each microheater unit is uniform.

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Each heating electrode's resistance varies predictably with temperature.

Observations: O2, O5

# Main hypothesis
Does Ni electrodeposition on HNO3-activated CF fabric followed by vacuum heat treatment improve the tensile behaviour of the resulting epoxy CFRP, and how does the change relate to the Ni-C interfacial structure?
System: PAN-based T300 3K carbon fiber plain-weave fabric, sizing removed and HNO3-etched, Ni electrodeposited from a Watts bath at 0.02 A/cm2 (LD) or 0.04 A/cm2 (HD), vacuum heat-treated, and cured into 4674 epoxy CFRP panels
Conditions: LD 0.02 A/cm2 and HD 0.04 A/cm2 electrodeposition; IH at 500-900 °C or LH to 700 °C, 2 h, vacuum; EMI in the X band; quasi-static tensile tests of cured panels
Scope limits: LH applied only at 700 °C
Validation requirements:
- R1: Improve the mechanical properties of the CFRP relative to pristine CFRP. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Characterize the Ni/C interfacial structure that accompanies the tensile changes. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Tensile ductility (maximum fracture strain) of epoxy CFRP panels made from pristine, LD-coated and HD-coated fabrics after heat treatment
Links: refinement → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Tensile strength (maximum tensile strength) of epoxy CFRP panels made from pristine, LD-coated and HD-coated fabrics after heat treatment

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Interfacial lattice structure and strain field at Ni/NiO/AC and Ni/AC interfaces before and after LH treatment to 700 °C

## H4 (claim)
Statement: CFRP made from LD Ni-coated fabric after 700 °C vacuum heat treatment reached a maximum fracture strain of 16.96%, 201.78% above untreated uncoated CFRP (5.62%); because heat treatment of uncoated fabric alone gave 13.2%, the increment associated with the Ni coating is about 3.8 percentage points over heat-treated uncoated CFRP (heating conditions of that group not stated), and a causal contribution of the Ni-C miscible regions, Ni/NiO/C multiphases and nanopores to this increment remains unverified.
Links: refinement ← H1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Quasi-static tensile tests of epoxy CFRP panels made from pristine, LD-coated and HD-coated fabrics at RT, 700 °C and 900 °C treatment
Manipulation: Fabric (pristine, LD or HD; untreated or heat-treated at 700 °C or 900 °C) impregnated with 4674 epoxy and H-4073-3 curing agent, laid up and autoclave-cured at 70 °C for 3 h under -0.1 MPa vacuum and 75 kgf/cm2
Measurements: stress-strain curves; maximum tensile strength; elongation at break
Comparison: groups: pristine CFRP RT; pristine CFRP 700 °C; pristine CFRP 900 °C; LD CFRP RT; LD CFRP 700 °C; LD CFRP 900 °C; HD CFRP RT; HD CFRP 700 °C; HD CFRP 900 °C | endpoint: maximum tensile strength and maximum fracture strain (elongation at break) | varied: coating; heat-treatment temperature | held fixed: epoxy system and cure cycle; Instron 34TM-50 | unit: cured panel specimen | units: MPa and %
Observations: O1, O2, O3, O4, O5

## E2
Statement: HRTEM, IFFT and GPA strain mapping of FIB cross-sections at Ni/NiO/AC three-phase and Ni/AC two-phase interfaces of LD samples before and after LH to 700 °C
Manipulation: LD as-plated sample versus LD sample linearly heated to 700 °C; FIB cross-sections thinner than 100 nm prepared under a tungsten protective layer
Measurements: BF, HAADF and HRTEM imaging (JEOL JEM-F200, Tecnai G2 F30); IFFT lattice analysis; GPA strain maps; EDS mapping
Comparison: groups: LD as-plated; LD after LH to 700 °C | endpoint: lattice fringes and interplanar spacing, phase constitution, 2D strain tensors (εxx, εxy, εyx, εyy) by GPA | varied: heat treatment | held fixed: LD deposition; interface type examined (three-phase at oxygen-rich defect regions; two-phase on flat regions) | unit: imaged interfacial region | units: nm; strain dimensionless
Observations: O6, O7

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: Pristine CFRP showed brittle fracture with a maximum fracture strain of 5.62% and a maximum tensile strength of 514 MPa.
Scope: Untreated, uncoated CFRP; number of specimens not reported in the text
Comparison: groups: pristine CFRP, untreated | endpoint: maximum fracture strain and tensile strength | held fixed: epoxy system and cure | unit: panel specimen | units: % and MPa
Bears on: H1, H2

## O2 (from E1)

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H3)
- R2: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
By which mechanism do circulating factors of heart failure reach and damage the retinal neurovascular unit? The study tests whether elevated circulating TGFβ2 drives retinal endothelial epigenetic senescence through pSMAD2/EP300-H3K9ac-P21, whether senescent endothelium activates retinal microglia and neuroinflammation, and whether neutralizing TGFβ2 or depleting microglia preserves retinal structure and function.
System: Pressure-overload heart failure in C57BL/6J mice (TAC versus sham), parabiosis with sham- or TAC-operated partners, transfer of donor plasma onto cultured human endothelial cells (HUVECs and primary HRMECs), plasma from heart failure patients and healthy controls, and public human cardiac snRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets
Conditions: Surgery at 2 months of age; retinal assessment at 5 months in most mouse cohorts and at 6 months in the Tgfbr2 conditional knockout cohort; Dialyzed plasma applied to endothelial cells at 1% (v/v) for 48 h; Recombinant TGFβ2 at 6 ng/mL in culture and 6 ng per mouse by tail vein every 2 days for 2 months; Anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 mg/kg in vivo (six injections, intravitreal or tail vein) or 1 μg/mL on cells, against isotype IgG
Scope limits: Retinal readouts are electroretinography amplitudes, optical coherence tomography layer thickness, lectin vascular density and diameter, and immunostaining of senescence and microglial markers; Human material is limited to plasma, cultured endothelial cells and public transcriptomic datasets; Cardiac endpoints are echocardiographic and histological; no survival or systemic hemodynamic outcomes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Identify a circulating mediator elevated in heart failure and test whether it induces endothelial senescence and retinal dysfunction. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Define the endothelial signaling route from TGFβ2 to senescence and test whether endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Test whether endothelial senescence leads to retinal microglial activation and whether microglia are required for the retinal damage. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Heart failure plasma and TGFβ2 induce endothelial cell senescence in retinal and other endothelial cells.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H2

## H2 (mechanism)

Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Factors released by senescent endothelial cells activate retinal microglia, increasing synaptosome phagocytosis and proinflammatory cytokine expression.

# Main hypothesis
By which mechanism do circulating factors of heart failure reach and damage the retinal neurovascular unit? The study tests whether elevated circulating TGFβ2 drives retinal endothelial epigenetic senescence through pSMAD2/EP300-H3K9ac-P21, whether senescent endothelium activates retinal microglia and neuroinflammation, and whether neutralizing TGFβ2 or depleting microglia preserves retinal structure and function.
System: Pressure-overload heart failure in C57BL/6J mice (TAC versus sham), parabiosis with sham- or TAC-operated partners, transfer of donor plasma onto cultured human endothelial cells (HUVECs and primary HRMECs), plasma from heart failure patients and healthy controls, and public human cardiac snRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets
Conditions: Surgery at 2 months of age; retinal assessment at 5 months in most mouse cohorts and at 6 months in the Tgfbr2 conditional knockout cohort; Dialyzed plasma applied to endothelial cells at 1% (v/v) for 48 h; Recombinant TGFβ2 at 6 ng/mL in culture and 6 ng per mouse by tail vein every 2 days for 2 months; Anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 mg/kg in vivo (six injections, intravitreal or tail vein) or 1 μg/mL on cells, against isotype IgG
Scope limits: Retinal readouts are electroretinography amplitudes, optical coherence tomography layer thickness, lectin vascular density and diameter, and immunostaining of senescence and microglial markers; Human material is limited to plasma, cultured endothelial cells and public transcriptomic datasets; Cardiac endpoints are echocardiographic and histological; no survival or systemic hemodynamic outcomes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Identify a circulating mediator elevated in heart failure and test whether it induces endothelial senescence and retinal dysfunction. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Define the endothelial signaling route from TGFβ2 to senescence and test whether endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Test whether endothelial senescence leads to retinal microglial activation and whether microglia are required for the retinal damage. (aspects: H3)
