Does Ni in one-pot LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO dissolve into and exsolve from the perovskite across the oxidative CO2 capture and reductive CH4 conversion steps of iCCC-DRM, and does the DFM retain its performance and Ni NP size over repeated cycles?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Ni dissolves into the perovskite during CO2 capture and exsolves from it during CH4 conversion. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Determine whether LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity, CO2/CH4 conversion and Ni NP size over repeated cycles. (aspects: H3, H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H3; scoped evidence ← H6

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H3

## H6 (claim)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO shows durability over 50 cycles, with a CO2 capture capacity of 10.2 mmol gDFM−1 and conversions of 91.5% for CO2 and 93.5% for CH4.
Links: scoped evidence ← O10; scoped evidence → H4

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: In-situ XRD of H2-pretreated LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO recorded during the CO2 capture step (10 vol% CO2, 2 vol% O2 in N2) and during the subsequent CH4 conversion step with rising temperature.
Manipulation: Sequential exposure to oxidative capture gas and then reductive CH4 atmosphere
Measurements: In-situ XRD peak intensities
Comparison: groups: during CO2 capture step; during CH4 conversion step | endpoint: Intensity of CaO (200), CaCO3 (104), Ni0 (111) and LaNiO3-δ (202) reflections | varied: gas atmosphere; temperature during the conversion step | held fixed: composition x = 0.2; prior H2 pretreatment | unit: diffraction pattern series
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: Temperature-programmed surface reactions on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO: CO2-TPSR, and CH4-TPSR after CO2 pre-adsorption.
Manipulation: Programmed heating under reactive gas after H2 pretreatment
Measurements: Effluent gas concentrations by nondispersive infrared analyzer
Comparison: groups: CO2-TPSR; CH4-TPSR after CO2 pre-adsorption | endpoint: Effluent CO2, CO, CH4 and H2 concentrations versus temperature (nondispersive infrared analyzer) | varied: reactive gas; temperature ramp | held fixed: 0.1 g sample; pretreatment 10 vol% H2/N2 at 700 °C for 30 min; heating 10 °C min−1; 50 ml min−1 gas flow | unit: effluent profile | window: CO2-TPSR 200–800 °C in 10 vol% CO2/N2; CH4-TPSR in 5 vol% CH4/N2 after 30 min CO2 saturation at 650 °C and cooling to 50 °C
Observations: O3, O7

## E3
Statement: Step-resolved characterization of LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO after H2 pretreatment, after CO2 capture and after CH4 conversion: quasi-in situ O 1s and Ni 3p XPS, EPR, HAADF-STEM with EDS and HRTEM.
Manipulation: Stage of the iCCC-DRM sequence at which the sample is examined
Measurements: XPS O 1s and Ni 3p (C 1s 284.6 eV reference); EPR; HAADF-STEM/EDS; HRTEM
Comparison: groups: after H2 pretreatment; after CO2 capture; after CH4 conversion | endpoint: Surface oxygen species (OV/OL ratio), surface Ni valence fractions, Ni distribution and NP presence | varied: process stage | held fixed: composition x = 0.2 | unit: sample at each stage
Observations: O4, O5, O6, O8, O9

## E4
Statement: 50-cycle iCCC-DRM stability test of LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO at 650 °C with 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 simulated flue gas followed by 5 vol% CH4 at 30,000 mL g−1 h−1.
Manipulation: Cycle number
Measurements: Outlet gas analysis per cycle
Comparison: groups: cycle 1 to cycle 50 | endpoint: CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion per cycle | varied: cycle number | held fixed: composition x = 0.2; 650 °C; 10 vol% CO2/2 vol% O2 capture; 5 vol% CH4 conversion; 30,000 mL g−1 h−1 | unit: DFM sample | window: 50 cycles
Observations: O10

## E5
Statement: Characterization of spent DFMs after cycling: HAADF-STEM Ni NP size distributions of LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO (early state and after 50 cycles) and LaNiO3/CaO (after 25 cycles), Raman spectra and XRD of spent LaNiO3/CaO and LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO.
Manipulation: DFM composition (x = 0 versus x = 0.2) and cycling history
Measurements: HAADF-STEM size distributions; Raman (532 nm laser, three sample areas); XRD
Comparison: groups: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; LaNiO3/CaO | endpoint: Ni NP size, carbon deposits (Raman D and G bands), crystalline phases | varied: Al doping; cycle number | held fixed: iCCC-DRM stability-test conditions | unit: sample | window: after stability tests (50 cycles for x = 0.2; 25 cycles for x = 0 Ni size)
Observations: O11, O12, O13

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: During the CO2 capture step (10 vol% CO2, 2 vol% O2 in N2) after H2 pretreatment, in-situ XRD shows decreasing CaO (200, 37.359°) and Ni0 (111, 44.507°) peak intensities and stepwise increasing CaCO3 (104, 29.400°) and LaNiO3-δ (202, 47.357°) intensities.
Scope: x = 0.2, single capture step. Source: Results text describing Fig. 2a; figure pixels not inspected
Comparison: groups: start of capture step; progress of capture step | endpoint: In-situ XRD peak intensities | varied: exposure time to capture gas | held fixed: composition x = 0.2; capture gas 10 vol% CO2/2 vol% O2/N2 | unit: diffraction pattern series | window: during CO2 capture step | result: CaO and Ni0 decrease; CaCO3 and LaNiO3-δ increase
Bears on: H2

## O2 (from E1)
Statement: During the subsequent CH4 conversion step, the CaCO3 (104) peak starts to disappear at 550 °C and CaO (200) reappears; the Ni0 (111) peak appears while the LaNiO3-δ (202) intensity decreases with temperature.
Scope: x = 0.2, single conversion step. Source: Results text describing Fig. 2b; figure pixels not inspected
Comparison: groups: during conversion step at increasing temperature | endpoint: In-situ XRD peak intensities | varied: temperature | held fixed: composition x = 0.2; reductive CH4 atmosphere | unit: diffraction pattern series | window: during CH4 conversion step | result: CaCO3 lost from 550 °C with CaO return; Ni0 appears as LaNiO3-δ (202) decreases
Bears on: H2

## O3 (from E2)
Statement: The CO2-TPSR profile of LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO in 10 vol% CO2 shows a downward CO2 adsorption peak centred at 650 °C, an upward CO2 release peak at 850 °C, and an additional small downward peak at 500 °C.
Scope: x = 0.2 only. Source: Results text describing Fig. 2c; figure pixels not inspected
Comparison: groups: CO2-TPSR of LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO | endpoint: Effluent CO2 versus temperature | varied: temperature | held fixed: 10 vol% CO2/N2; prior H2 pretreatment | unit: effluent profile | window: programmed heating | units: °C | result: Adsorption peak 650 °C; release peak 850 °C; small adsorption peak 500 °C | uncertainty: Methods state heating from 200 to 800 °C, while the release peak is reported at 850 °C
Bears on: H2

## O4 (from E3)
Statement: Quasi-in situ O 1s XPS gives an OV (531.5 eV) to OL (528.5–529.5 eV) intensity ratio that decreases from 6.6 to 1.4 after CO2 adsorption and increases to 6.8 in the reductive CH4 step (Supplementary Table 1).
Scope: x = 0.2 surface (XPS). Source: Results text and Supplementary Table 1 as cited; table not inspected
Comparison: groups: before CO2 adsorption; after CO2 adsorption; after CH4 step | endpoint: OV/OL XPS intensity ratio | varied: process stage | held fixed: composition x = 0.2 | unit: sample surface | units: ratio | result: 6.6 → 1.4 → 6.8
Bears on: H2

## O5 (from E3)
Statement: After CO2 capture, the Ni0 3p3/2 XPS peak near 65.6 eV diminishes and Ni2+ (66.7 eV) and Ni3+ (68.3 eV) 3p3/2 peaks appear.
Scope: x = 0.2 surface (XPS). Source: Results text describing Fig. 2j; figure pixels not inspected
Comparison: groups: before CO2 capture; after CO2 capture | endpoint: Surface Ni valence (Ni 3p XPS) | varied: process stage | held fixed: composition x = 0.2 | unit: sample surface | units: eV (peak positions) | result: Ni0 decreases; Ni2+ and Ni3+ appear
Bears on: H2

## O6 (from E3)
Statement: After CO2 capture, HAADF and EDS maps show Ni evenly distributed with La and Al in the CaCO3 matrix; some larger Ni NPs remain in the perovskite; perovskite particles are in intimate contact with CaCO3, forming heterogeneous interfaces.
Scope: x = 0.2 imaged regions. Source: Results text describing Fig. 2d, 2e and Supplementary Fig. 7; figures not inspected
Comparison: groups: after CO2 capture | endpoint: Ni distribution and particle presence | held fixed: composition x = 0.2 | unit: imaged regions | window: after capture step | result: Ni co-located with La and Al; some larger Ni NPs remain; perovskite–CaCO3 contact
Bears on: H2

Statement: In CH4-TPSR after CO2 pre-adsorption, CH4 consumption and H2 production start at 550 °C, the onset of CO nearly coincides with that of H2, and both peaks are centred at 600–700 °C.

Bears on: H2

Scope: x = 0.2 imaged regions. Source: Results text describing Fig. 2g, 2h and Supplementary Fig. 8; figures not inspected

# Main hypothesis
Does Ni in one-pot LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO dissolve into and exsolve from the perovskite across the oxidative CO2 capture and reductive CH4 conversion steps of iCCC-DRM, and does the DFM retain its performance and Ni NP size over repeated cycles?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Ni dissolves into the perovskite during CO2 capture and exsolves from it during CH4 conversion. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Determine whether LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity, CO2/CH4 conversion and Ni NP size over repeated cycles. (aspects: H3, H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H3; scoped evidence ← H6

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Reported spent-sample comparisons show a modest mean Ni NP size increase for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO (14.3 to 15.6 nm; the early-state endpoint is inconsistently described) and no obvious Raman carbon, whereas LaNiO3/CaO shows an increase from 14.4 to 36.07 nm after 25 cycles and D/G carbon bands. # Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the combinations of electrode area and coating quality for which ZRA-based monitoring is feasible, given that corrosion noise, ECG interference and the instrumental floor scale differently with area. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H4)

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the combinations of electrode area and coating quality for which ZRA-based monitoring is feasible, given that corrosion noise, ECG interference and the instrumental floor scale differently with area. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H4)

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H4)
- R2: Establish whether residual ethanol in the brewing wastewater limits EET of S. oneidensis and whether an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that limitation. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Establish whether raising riboflavin supply in the consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The 1.8% (v/v) residual ethanol of the brewing wastewater suppresses EET by S. oneidensis, and an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that ethanol from the wastewater.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin biosynthesis in the two-species consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached from NCM.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H6; composition → H7

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: In the engineered B. subtilis, alcohol dehydrogenase oxidises ethanol to acetaldehyde and aldehyde dehydrogenase converts acetaldehyde to acetate, a dual-enzyme cascade that consumes the residual ethanol.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Engineering the riboflavin biosynthesis pathway raises the riboflavin concentration that the consortium accumulates in brewing wastewater as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H3

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin supply raises the electrical output of the consortium in a microbial fuel cell, measured as maximum power density.
Links: composition ← H3

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H4)
- R2: Establish whether residual ethanol in the brewing wastewater limits EET of S. oneidensis and whether an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that limitation. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Establish whether raising riboflavin supply in the consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H4)
- R2: Establish whether residual ethanol in the brewing wastewater limits EET of S. oneidensis and whether an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that limitation. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Establish whether raising riboflavin supply in the consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H4; candidate explanation ← H8

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The 1.8% (v/v) residual ethanol of the brewing wastewater suppresses EET by S. oneidensis, and an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that ethanol from the wastewater.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin biosynthesis in the two-species consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached from NCM.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H6; composition → H7

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: In the engineered B. subtilis, alcohol dehydrogenase oxidises ethanol to acetaldehyde and aldehyde dehydrogenase converts acetaldehyde to acetate, a dual-enzyme cascade that consumes the residual ethanol.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Engineering the riboflavin biosynthesis pathway raises the riboflavin concentration that the consortium accumulates in brewing wastewater as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H3

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin supply raises the electrical output of the consortium in a microbial fuel cell, measured as maximum power density.
Links: composition ← H3

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: Besides ethanol relief, BS1 may affect consortium EET and leaching through a direct partner contribution, such as altered culture activity or metabolic/electrical interaction with SO1; the visible comparisons do not establish this explanation.
Links: candidate explanation → H1

Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H4)
- R2: Establish whether residual ethanol in the brewing wastewater limits EET of S. oneidensis and whether an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that limitation. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Establish whether raising riboflavin supply in the consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The 1.8% (v/v) residual ethanol of the brewing wastewater suppresses EET by S. oneidensis, and an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that ethanol from the wastewater.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5; competing explanation → H8

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin biosynthesis in the two-species consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached from NCM.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H6; composition → H7

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: In the engineered B. subtilis, alcohol dehydrogenase oxidises ethanol to acetaldehyde and aldehyde dehydrogenase converts acetaldehyde to acetate, a dual-enzyme cascade that consumes the residual ethanol.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Engineering the riboflavin biosynthesis pathway raises the riboflavin concentration that the consortium accumulates in brewing wastewater as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H3

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Raising riboflavin supply raises the electrical output of the consortium in a microbial fuel cell, measured as maximum power density.
Links: composition ← H3

## H8 (alternative)
Statement: The higher EET of the SO1-BS1 consortium relative to strain SO1 is partly because the consortium has a higher cell density and the presence of the B. subtilis partner, which has its own redox species, rather than because the residual ethanol of the brewing wastewater is removed.
Links: competing explanation ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H4)
- R2: Establish whether residual ethanol in the brewing wastewater limits EET of S. oneidensis and whether an engineered ethanol-catabolising B. subtilis partner removes that limitation. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Establish whether raising riboflavin supply in the consortium raises its EET rate and the amount of metal leached. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region.
- R2: The Ni-P diffusion barrier layer on the TE element surface is uniform and defect-minimized.
- R3: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined.
- R4: The Ni-P layer suppresses Cu diffusion and intermetallic compound formation between the Cu layer and the TE element after heat treatment.

Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Links: composition → H1; composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region.
- R2: The Ni-P diffusion barrier layer on the TE element surface is uniform and defect-minimized.
- R3: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined.
- R4: The Ni-P layer suppresses Cu diffusion and intermetallic compound formation between the Cu layer and the TE element after heat treatment.

Statement: Selective deposition of the Ni-P layer on the exposed TE element surface relative to the adjacent polymer-coated region.
Links: composition ← Main hypothesis

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Uniformity and defect minimization of the Ni-P diffusion barrier layer on the TE element surface.
Links: composition ← Main hypothesis

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Effects of SDS addition on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements.
Links: composition ← Main hypothesis

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Performance of the Ni-P layer in suppressing Cu diffusion and intermetallic compound formation between the Cu layer and the TE element after heat treatment.
Links: composition ← Main hypothesis

# Experiments
# Observations

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4). (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: At each of the three wire diameters, Teflon pad wiping yields a lower zinc coating mass per unit area and thickness than wax wiping.
Links: experimental target ← E1; experimental target ← E2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Coating thickness calculated from gravimetric mass per unit area agrees with thickness measured directly on SEM cross-sections.
Links: experimental target ← E2

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Whether the two wiping techniques differ in the circumferential (angular) uniformity of coating thickness around the wire.
Links: experimental target ← E3

Statement: Gravimetric coating determination (UNE-EN ISO 1460:2021): each sample weighed before and after chemical removal of the coating in 5% HCl at room temperature; mass per unit area mt (g/m2) converted to average thickness t (µm) with a zinc density of 7.14 g/cm3; five measurements on different portions of each wire, reported as mean with relative standard deviation.

Measurements: mass before and after chemical stripping; mass per unit area mt; calculated thickness t

# Main hypothesis

Statement: SEM morphology and grain-size statistics of Ni-coated fabrics after IH at 500-900 °C
Manipulation: Quartz tube with as-deposited samples (HD 30, 20 and 10 min; LD 30 min) inserted into a furnace preheated to 500, 600, 700, 800 or 900 °C (IH), then held 2 h
Measurements: SEM surface morphology; average grain size and size distribution
Comparison: groups: IH 500 °C; IH 600 °C; IH 700 °C; IH 800 °C; IH 900 °C | endpoint: surface morphology and average Ni grain size from SEM image statistics (Figures S4-S6) | varied: heat-treatment temperature; coating type (LD 30 min; HD 30, 20, 10 min) | held fixed: vacuum below 5 × 10^-3 Pa, 2 h isothermal hold; IH heating mode | unit: coated fabric sample | window: after 2 h isothermal treatment | units: nm
Observations: O1

## E2
Statement: XRD phase analysis and Scherrer crystallite-size calculation for LD and HD Ni-coated fabrics after heat treatment
Manipulation: Heat treatment of LD (0.02 A/cm2) and HD (0.04 A/cm2) coated fabrics at 500-900 °C, including LH and IH modes
Measurements: XRD patterns; Scherrer crystallite size with K = 0.89, λ = 0.154056 nm, FWHM corrected for instrumental broadening
Comparison: groups: LD coatings at 500-900 °C; HD coatings at 500-900 °C; LH versus IH | endpoint: Ni, NiO and C diffraction peaks; Ni crystallite size D = Kλ/(β cos θ) from Ni (111), (200), (220) peaks | varied: heat-treatment temperature; current density; heating mode | held fixed: Cu Kα radiation (Rigaku MiniFlex600) | unit: coated fabric sample | units: nm (crystallite size)
Observations: O2

## E3
Statement: HRTEM, IFFT and GPA strain mapping of FIB cross-sections at Ni/NiO/AC three-phase and Ni/AC two-phase interfaces of LD samples before and after LH to 700 °C
Manipulation: LD as-plated sample versus LD sample linearly heated to 700 °C; FIB cross-sections thinner than 100 nm prepared under a tungsten protective layer
Measurements: BF, HAADF and HRTEM imaging (JEOL JEM-F200, Tecnai G2 F30); IFFT lattice analysis; GPA strain maps; EDS mapping
Comparison: groups: LD as-plated; LD after LH to 700 °C | endpoint: lattice fringes and interplanar spacing, phase constitution, 2D strain tensors (εxx, εxy, εyx, εyy) by GPA | varied: heat treatment | held fixed: LD deposition; interface type examined (three-phase at oxygen-rich defect regions; two-phase on flat regions) | unit: imaged interfacial region | units: nm; strain dimensionless
Observations: O3, O4

## E4
Statement: XPS C 1s, Ni 2p and O 1s analysis of LD and HD coated fabrics after IH at 500-900 °C and LH to 700 °C
Manipulation: LD and HD coated fabrics after IH at 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 °C and after LH to 700 °C
Measurements: C 1s spectra; Ni 2p spectra; O 1s spectra
Comparison: groups: LD IH 500-900 °C; LD LH 700 °C; HD IH 500-900 °C; HD LH 700 °C | endpoint: peak-fitted C 1s (Figure 7), Ni 2p (Figure S7) and O 1s (Figure S8) chemical states | varied: heat-treatment temperature; heating mode; current density | held fixed: Thermo Scientific Escalab 250Xi | unit: coated fabric sample
Observations: O5, O6

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: LD coating grain size increased moderately at 500-600 °C, peaked at approximately 410 nm at 700 °C, and fell below 200 nm at 900 °C, where severe spheroidization and fragmentation destroyed coating continuity.
Scope: LD coating; the heating mode of the 700 °C point is not stated in the reporting sentence
Comparison: groups: LD 500 °C; LD 600 °C; LD 700 °C; LD 900 °C | endpoint: average Ni grain size (Figure 2s) | varied: heat-treatment temperature | held fixed: LD 30 min | unit: coated fabric | units: nm
Bears on: H1

## O2 (from E2)
Statement: In LD coatings, weak NiO peaks at 37.2°, 43.3° and 62° appeared at 500-600 °C in addition to Ni and C peaks; no NiO peaks appeared for HD coatings, which the authors attribute to masking by the strong Ni signal; at 700 °C the NiO peaks of the LD coating completely vanished.
Scope: Phase detection by laboratory XRD on coated fabric
Comparison: groups: LD 500-600 °C; LD 700 °C; HD coatings | endpoint: presence of NiO diffraction peaks | varied: heat-treatment temperature; current density | held fixed: Cu Kα XRD | unit: coated fabric | units: 2θ (°)
Bears on: H2, H3

## O3 (from E3)
Statement: At an oxygen-rich defect region of the LD as-plated sample, HRTEM showed an electrodeposited polycrystalline Ni layer (d ≈ 0.203 nm), a polycrystalline NiO transition layer (d ≈ 0.209 nm, (002)NiO//(111)Ni, 2.87% lattice mismatch) and the AC matrix with sharp interfaces; GPA normal strain amplitudes exceeded 0.4, concentrated within the Ni, NiO and AC phases.
Scope: One imaged three-phase region in the LD as-plated sample
Comparison: groups: LD as-plated three-phase interface | endpoint: phase layering, interplanar spacing, strain tensors | held fixed: LD deposition | unit: imaged interfacial region | window: as-plated | units: nm; strain
Bears on: H2

## O4 (from E3)
Statement: After LH to 700 °C, the continuous NiO transition layer at the LD three-phase interface was fragmented and partly consumed into nanoscale dispersed NiO phases within the Ni-C interdiffusion region, forming a Ni/NiO/C multiphase interface; NiO-to-Ni transformation by lattice relaxation was observed at the Ni/NiO interface, graphite-like domains with ~0.425 nm interlayer spacing formed near the interface, and the peak normal strain dropped to about 0.2 with a more uniform distribution.
Scope: Imaged three-phase regions of LD samples only
Comparison: groups: LD as-plated; LD after LH to 700 °C | endpoint: NiO layer continuity, phase constitution, strain tensors | varied: heat treatment | held fixed: three-phase interface region | unit: imaged interfacial region | window: after LH to 700 °C | units: nm; strain
Bears on: H2

## O5 (from E4)
Statement: For LD coatings, O 1s spectra at 500-600 °C showed abundant C-O and C=O groups and Ni 2p showed Ni-O states; at 700 °C (IH and LH) a portion of NiO was reduced, with polar oxygen groups and NiO partly retained; at 800-900 °C the coating spheroidized and the carbon skeleton was extensively exposed.
Scope: Surface-sensitive XPS of LD coatings; fitted component fractions are in figures not inspected
Comparison: groups: LD 500-600 °C; LD IH 700 °C; LD LH 700 °C; LD 800-900 °C | endpoint: C 1s, Ni 2p and O 1s chemical states | varied: heat-treatment temperature | held fixed: LD coating | unit: coated fabric
Bears on: H2

## O6 (from E4)
Statement: For HD coatings, oxygen stayed confined to a shallow interfacial region at 500-600 °C; after 700 °C (IH and LH) total oxygen fell to a minimum and the Ni-O component was almost entirely reduced to metallic Ni; at 800-900 °C the oxygen signal rebounded slightly and the metallic Ni proportion decreased.
Scope: Surface-sensitive XPS of HD coatings
Comparison: groups: HD 500-600 °C; HD IH 700 °C; HD LH 700 °C; HD 800-900 °C | endpoint: C 1s, Ni 2p and O 1s chemical states | varied: heat-treatment temperature | held fixed: HD coating | unit: coated fabric
Bears on: H2

# Main hypothesis
How do NiO and interfacial oxygen evolve in LD and HD Ni coatings on CF during vacuum heat treatment, and how is NiO removed at 700 °C?
System: PAN-based T300 3K carbon fiber plain-weave fabric, sizing removed and HNO3-etched, Ni electrodeposited from a Watts bath at 0.02 A/cm2 (LD) or 0.04 A/cm2 (HD), vacuum heat-treated, and cured into 4674 epoxy CFRP panels
Conditions: LD 0.02 A/cm2 and HD 0.04 A/cm2 electrodeposition; IH at 500-900 °C or LH to 700 °C, 2 h, vacuum; EMI in the X band; quasi-static tensile tests of cured panels
Scope limits: LH applied only at 700 °C
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the fate of NiO and interfacial oxygen, and the accompanying Ni grain evolution, during vacuum heat treatment. (aspects: H2, H1)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Ni grain and crystallite size evolution with deposition condition and heat treatment

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Fate of NiO and interfacial oxygen in LD and HD coatings during vacuum heat treatment
Links: refinement → H3

## H3 (claim)
Statement: At 700 °C, carbon atoms diffusing at the interface reduce NiO in the LD coating in situ to metallic Ni, as shown by the complete disappearance of the XRD NiO peaks.
Links: refinement ← H2; competing explanation → H4

## H4 (alternative)
Statement: At 700 °C, the NiO layer at the LD coating interface becomes too thin to be detected by XRD, rather than being completely reduced to metallic Ni.
Links: competing explanation ← H3

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H1)

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the exposure protocol produces the intended hypertensive phenotype, with systolic blood pressure compared between week 0 and week 8 in each group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Chronic oral CdCl2 exposure (40 or 80 ppm for 8 weeks) produces a hypertensive phenotype in male Wistar rats, accompanied by changes in body weight and blood glucose.

## H2 (aspect)

Links: composition → H3; proposed mechanism ← H4

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Contraction to the TXA2 analogue U46619 in aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H5

Statement: TXA2 induces hypercontractility in aortas from cadmium-exposed hypertensive animals, an effect associated with oxidative stress and reversed after NADPH oxidase inhibition.

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the exposure protocol produces the intended hypertensive phenotype, with systolic blood pressure compared between week 0 and week 8 in each group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H4)

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3)

Statement: Cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs improves the photodetection performance of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices with untreated commercial MWCNTs.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Structural, surface and morphological changes of the MWCNTs produced by the cryogenic thermal-stress treatment relative to the commercial MWCNTs.
Links: composition → H4; composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Wavelength-resolved response of the two devices from 351 to 1600 nm at zero bias and a fixed 20 mW cm-2: photocurrent, photosensitivity, responsivity, NEP, specific detectivity and EQE.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (claim)
Statement: The cryogenic treatment produces a small increase in the Raman ID/IG ratio (1.30 vs 1.26) and reduces the ID and IG band intensities, so the Raman-assessed structural defect level is not comparable to that of the commercial MWCNTs; the entangled fibrous morphology is preserved without visible breakage, with the treated MWCNTs showing open, rougher ends and reduced entanglement, while both samples form randomly oriented, highly interconnected networks and the treated appear more homogeneously distributed with slightly reduced agglomeration.
Links: composition ← H2; scoped evidence ← O1; scoped evidence ← O3

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Raman spectra of commercial and treated MWCNTs recorded with a Renishaw inVia microscope, 532 nm laser, 0-3500 cm-1, room temperature; D, G and 2D band positions, intensities and ID/IG tabulated (Table 1).
Manipulation: Cryogenic treatment versus untreated commercial MWCNTs
Measurements: D, G and 2D band positions (cm-1); band intensities; ID/IG
Comparison: groups: commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT); cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT) | endpoint: D, G, 2D band positions and intensities; ID/IG ratio | varied: cryogenic treatment | held fixed: same commercial MWCNT source (Sigma-Aldrich); same characterization instrument and settings for both samples; 532 nm excitation; room temperature | unit: MWCNT sample | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Observations: O1

## E2
Statement: CTEM imaging (FEI Tecnai G2 Spirit Biotwin) of commercial and treated MWCNTs dispersed ultrasonically in ethanol for 1 h, deposited on a grid and dried overnight.
Manipulation: Cryogenic treatment versus untreated commercial MWCNTs
Measurements: CTEM micrographs (qualitative)
Comparison: groups: commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT); cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT) | endpoint: nanotube end structure, entanglement and length (qualitative) | varied: cryogenic treatment | held fixed: same dispersion and grid preparation | unit: imaged MWCNT sample; number of images or tubes analysed not stated | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Observations: O2

## E3
Statement: SEM imaging (ZEISS EVO LS10) of the surface morphology of commercial and treated MWCNT samples.
Manipulation: Cryogenic treatment versus untreated commercial MWCNTs
Measurements: SEM micrographs (qualitative)
Comparison: groups: commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT); cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT) | endpoint: network morphology, damage and agglomeration (qualitative) | varied: cryogenic treatment | held fixed: same SEM instrument | unit: imaged MWCNT sample; sample preparation for SEM not stated | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Observations: O3

## E4
Statement: Spectral response of both devices at zero bias (self-powered) across 351-1600 nm using 20 narrowband Thorlabs band-pass filters (average FWHM about 10 nm), with the incident power density kept at 20 mW cm-2 at every selected wavelength; Iph, K, R, NEP, D* and EQE derived at each wavelength (Table 3, Fig. 11).
Manipulation: MWCNT interlayer type and wavelength
Measurements: photocurrent; photosensitivity; responsivity; NEP; specific detectivity; EQE
Comparison: groups: Al/C-MWCNT/n-Si device; Al/Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si device | endpoint: Iph, K, R, NEP, D*, EQE versus wavelength | varied: MWCNT interlayer; wavelength (351-1600 nm, 20 filters) | held fixed: incident power density 20 mW cm-2 at each wavelength; zero applied bias | unit: device; number of devices per interlayer type not stated | units: A; mA W-1; Jones; W Hz-1/2; % | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Observations: O4

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: Raman D, G and 2D bands of the treated MWCNTs appear at positions similar to the commercial MWCNTs with slight shifts (D 1337.24 to 1333.10 cm-1; G 1577.22 to 1571.34 cm-1; 2D 2665.22 to 2648.32 cm-1); absolute intensities are lower after treatment (ID 37.48 to 16.45; IG 29.79 to 12.65; I2D 10.40 to 4.62); ID/IG is 1.26 for commercial and 1.30 for treated MWCNTs, which the authors describe as nearly identical.
Scope: One spectrum per material as tabulated (Table 1); measured on MWCNT samples, not device films.
Comparison: groups: commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT); cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT) | endpoint: Raman band positions, intensities and ID/IG | varied: cryogenic treatment | held fixed: same commercial MWCNT source (Sigma-Aldrich); same characterization instrument and settings for both samples; 532 nm excitation | unit: MWCNT sample | units: cm-1; arbitrary intensity units | result: ID/IG 1.26 (C-MWCNT) vs 1.30 (Cryo-MWCNT) | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Bears on: H2
Links: scoped evidence → H4

## O2 (from E2)
Statement: CTEM shows commercial MWCNTs predominantly terminated with closed end caps, whereas treated MWCNTs have rough, open tube ends and reduced entanglement; the authors state that the thermal stress promoted opening and functionalization of graphitic end caps, contributing to shortening of the initially long MWCNTs.
Scope: Qualitative CTEM observations (Fig. 3); no length distribution or counts reported.
Comparison: groups: commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT); cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT) | endpoint: end-cap structure, entanglement, tube length (qualitative) | varied: cryogenic treatment | held fixed: same dispersion and grid preparation | unit: imaged MWCNT sample | result: Closed caps (commercial) vs open, rough ends and reduced entanglement (treated) | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Bears on: H2

## O3 (from E3)
Statement: SEM shows that both commercial and treated MWCNT samples form randomly oriented, highly interconnected networks of entangled nanotubes; no nanotube breakage or collapse is noticeable after treatment, and the treated MWCNTs appear more homogeneously distributed with slightly reduced agglomeration.
Scope: Qualitative SEM observations of MWCNT samples (Fig. 4); spin-coated device films were not imaged.
Comparison: groups: commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT); cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT) | endpoint: network morphology, damage, agglomeration (qualitative) | varied: cryogenic treatment | held fixed: same SEM instrument | unit: imaged MWCNT sample | result: Random entangled networks in both; slightly reduced agglomeration after treatment | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Bears on: H2
Links: scoped evidence → H4

## O4 (from E4)
Statement: At zero bias and 20 mW cm-2 per wavelength, both devices give measurable photocurrent across 351-1600 nm, and the Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si device has higher photocurrent at every wavelength: C device 7.21 x 10^-7 A (351 nm), maximum 9.51 x 10^-7 A (650 nm), 4.42 x 10^-7 A (900 nm), about 2.47 x 10^-7 A (1600 nm); Cryo device 3.13 x 10^-6 A (351 nm), 8.52 x 10^-6 A (650 nm), 9.02 x 10^-6 A (900 nm), 3.39 x 10^-6 A (1600 nm).
Scope: Spectral series with band-pass filters (Fig. 10, Fig. 11a).
Comparison: groups: Al/C-MWCNT/n-Si device; Al/Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si device | endpoint: photocurrent versus wavelength | varied: MWCNT interlayer; wavelength | held fixed: 20 mW cm-2 at each wavelength; zero bias | unit: device; number of devices per interlayer type not stated | units: A | result: Cryo higher at every wavelength | uncertainty: No uncertainty, replicate count or statistical test reported
Bears on: H3

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show accelerated healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds with tissue-level bacterial clearance, repair and inflammation readouts. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5)

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show accelerated healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds with tissue-level bacterial clearance, repair and inflammation readouts. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR induces ferroptosis-associated changes in bacteria: intracellular ROS, lipid peroxidation, GSH oxidation and reduced GSH-Px activity.

Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR accelerates closure of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR reduces tissue bacterial burden and improves tissue repair (collagen, angiogenesis) in the infected diabetic wound.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR shifts the wound from a pro-inflammatory toward an anti-inflammatory state, including M2-marker-dominant macrophages.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx treatment changes the ferroptosis marker GPX4 in wound tissue.

## H6 (claim)
Statement: GPX4 staining in wound tissue decreases after Fe-WS2@GOx treatment, and the decrease is greater with Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; this is a marker signal in tissue and does not establish that Fe-WS2@GOx kills bacteria in the wound by ferroptosis.

Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism. (aspects: H1)

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR shifts the wound from a pro-inflammatory toward an anti-inflammatory state, including M2-marker-dominant macrophages.

# Main hypothesis
Does ultrafast Na–benzophenone/diglyme chemical pre-sodiation of CVO450 compensate the initial Na+ loss, and does the pre-sodiated anode give a high-performance sodium-ion capacitor?
System: CVO450 (CaV8O20 annealed at 450 °C) electrodes pre-sodiated by immersion in Na–benzophenone/diglyme (Na–BPh/Dgy), tested in CR2032 half-cells against Na metal and as anodes in full sodium-ion capacitors (SICs) with an activated carbon/soft carbon (AC/SC) cathode.
Conditions: Electrolyte 1 M NaPF6 in EC:DEC (1:1 by volume) with 5 vol% FEC; Whatman filter separator; Half-cell window 0.01–3 V; full-cell window 0.01–3.6 V; room temperature; Pre-sodiation reagent: 1 mmol benzophenone and 1 mmol Na metal in 1 mL diglyme; electrodes immersed 1–4 min and rinsed with diglyme
Scope limits: Laboratory coin cells; Computational results refer to DFT-optimized bulk CaV8O20 models
Validation requirements:
- R1: A pre-sodiation step must compensate the active Na+ lost during first-cycle SEI formation and raise the initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) within minutes. (aspects: H1)
- R2: A sodium-ion capacitor built with the pre-sodiated anode must deliver high specific energy and power together with long cycle life. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Soaking time in Na–BPh/Dgy controls the amount of Na+ inserted into CVO450 electrodes and raises their initial coulombic efficiency.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: A full SIC pairing the pre-sodiated CVO450 anode with an AC/SC composite cathode delivers high specific energy and power and long cycle life.
Links: refinement → H4

## H3 (claim)
Statement: The pre-sodiated sodium-ion capacitor delivers 100% initial coulombic efficiency alongside exceptionally high energy and ultrastable cycling.

## H4 (claim)
Statement: The fabricated SIC delivers a material-level specific energy of 176 Wh kg−1 at 380 W kg−1 (active mass of both electrodes) and retains 87% of its initial capacity after 10,000 cycles at 1 A g−1.
Links: refinement ← H2

## E1
Statement: CVO450 electrodes soaked in Na–BPh/Dgy for 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 4 min (Methods: immersion 1–4 min, then rinsing with diglyme) and compared with non-sodiated (0 min) electrodes, whose handling (e.g., any rinse) is not described; all assembled into half-cells against Na metal; OCV, initial discharge capacity and ICE recorded.
Manipulation: Soaking time (0–4 min)
Measurements: OCV; first-cycle GCD; ICE
Comparison: groups: 0 min (non-sodiated); 1 min; 1.5 min; 2 min; 3 min; 4 min | endpoint: OCV; initial discharge capacity; ICE | varied: soaking time | held fixed: CVO450 electrode; reagent composition; half-cell configuration | unit: half-cell per soaking time | window: first cycle | units: V; mAh g−1; %
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: Full SIC: pre-sodiated CVO450 anode (Methods: electrodes immersed in Na–BPh/Dgy for 1–4 min before full-cell assembly) with an AC/SC/PVDF (6:3:1) cathode at a 1:3 anode:cathode mass ratio, 0.01–3.6 V; GCD at several rates, CV at 2 mV s−1 (and 5–50 mV s−1), 10,000-cycle test at 1 A g−1; specific energy/power from active mass of both electrodes and a device-level estimate including inactive components.

# Main hypothesis
Does ultrafast Na–benzophenone/diglyme chemical pre-sodiation of CVO450 compensate the initial Na+ loss, and does the pre-sodiated anode give a high-performance sodium-ion capacitor?
System: CVO450 (CaV8O20 annealed at 450 °C) electrodes pre-sodiated by immersion in Na–benzophenone/diglyme (Na–BPh/Dgy), tested in CR2032 half-cells against Na metal and as anodes in full sodium-ion capacitors (SICs) with an activated carbon/soft carbon (AC/SC) cathode.
Conditions: Electrolyte 1 M NaPF6 in EC:DEC (1:1 by volume) with 5 vol% FEC; Whatman filter separator; Half-cell window 0.01–3 V; full-cell window 0.01–3.6 V; room temperature; Pre-sodiation reagent: 1 mmol benzophenone and 1 mmol Na metal in 1 mL diglyme; electrodes immersed 1–4 min and rinsed with diglyme
Scope limits: Laboratory coin cells; Computational results refer to DFT-optimized bulk CaV8O20 models
Validation requirements:
- R1: A pre-sodiation step must compensate the active Na+ lost during first-cycle SEI formation and raise the initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) within minutes. (aspects: H1)

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show accelerated healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds with tissue-level bacterial clearance, repair and inflammation readouts. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5)

Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show accelerated healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds with tissue-level bacterial clearance, repair and inflammation readouts. (aspects: H2, H3, H4, H5)

Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR induces ferroptosis-associated changes in bacteria: intracellular ROS, lipid peroxidation, GSH oxidation and reduced GSH-Px activity.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR accelerates closure of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR reduces tissue bacterial burden and improves tissue repair (collagen, angiogenesis) in the infected diabetic wound.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR shifts the wound from a pro-inflammatory toward an anti-inflammatory state, including M2-marker-dominant macrophages.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Wound-tissue GPX4 staining was decreased by Fe-WS2@GOx, and the decrease was greater with Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR. The cellular source (bacterial vs. host) was not identified.

## H6 (claim)
Statement: Wound-tissue GPX4 staining was lower after Fe-WS2@GOx and lower still with Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR at the day-12 collection; because the stained cell type is not identified, this is a tissue-level ferroptosis-marker change that is consistent with, but does not directly measure, ferroptosis of the infecting bacteria.

# Main hypothesis
Does Ni in one-pot LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO dissolve into and exsolve from the perovskite across the oxidative CO2 capture and reductive CH4 conversion steps of iCCC-DRM, and does the DFM retain its performance and Ni NP size over repeated cycles?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Ni dissolves into the perovskite during CO2 capture and exsolves from it during CH4 conversion. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Determine whether LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity, CO2/CH4 conversion and Ni NP size over repeated cycles. (aspects: H3, H4, H5)
