# Main hypothesis
Does Ni in one-pot LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO dissolve into and exsolve from the perovskite across the oxidative CO2 capture and reductive CH4 conversion steps of iCCC-DRM, and does the DFM retain its performance and Ni NP size over repeated cycles?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Ni dissolves into the perovskite during CO2 capture and exsolves from it during CH4 conversion. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Determine whether LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity, CO2/CH4 conversion and Ni NP size over repeated cycles. (aspects: H3, H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1; scoped evidence ← H6

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H3

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H3

## H6 (claim)
Statement: The stable CO2 capture capacity (10.2 mmol g−1, more than 98% retained) and CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiencies of LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO over 50 cycles at 650 °C (91.5% and 93.5%) are consistent with reversible Ni dissolution-exsolution during the redox-switching iCCC-DRM process, and the mean Ni NP size rises from 14.3 nm after the first cycle to 15.6 nm after 50 cycles. These observations do not themselves measure the Ni dissolution-exsolution cycle in the reactor.

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H1)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Minimum detectable coating breach fraction (two-sample test against intact baseline, alpha = 0.05) and its dependence on electrode design, sampling rate, coating resistance and number of recordings.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Dependence of the minimum detectable breach on electrode area and sampling rate at the baseline coating resistance Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Dependence of the minimum detectable breach on coating resistance Rf,sp across electrode areas at N = 30 recordings.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E2; refinement → H4

## H4 (claim)
Statement: Model prediction (Figure 7 sweep, residual RMS, N = 30 recordings of 30 s, alpha = 0.05): with a high-barrier coating of Rf,sp about 1200 ohm cm2 on a 1.0 cm2 AZ91 electrode, a breach of about 2% (0.02 cm2 of bare metal) is statistically detectable; at the worst-case baseline Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2 the predicted thresholds are far larger (about 25% at 0.05 cm2).
Links: scoped evidence ← O3; scoped evidence ← O5; refinement ← H3

## H5 (limitation)
Statement: All reported thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs (predictions), not measurements; experimental validation with ZRA recordings from implanted animals is pending.

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether MG53 regulates corneal sensory nerve regeneration after alkali burn injury and define the macrophage-associated molecular route through which it acts.
System: Mouse alkali-burn corneal injury in wild-type, MG53 global knockout (mg53-/-) and tPA-MG53 transgenic mice, with bone marrow-derived and immortalized macrophage cultures and HEK-293T/HEK293 reconstitution systems.
Conditions: Central corneal alkali burn produced with a 2 mm filter paper soaked in 2 uL of 1 M NaOH for 30 s; Corneal readouts between 3 h and day 10 after injury; M2 polarization of macrophages induced with 20 ng/mL IL-4 for 24 h; Recombinant human MG53 (rhMG53) or modified RNA used to raise MG53 levels
Scope limits: Mouse cornea and cultured mouse macrophages, with human membrane proteins and tagged constructs expressed in HEK-293T/HEK293 cells; MG53 levels are varied by global genotype (mg53-/-, tPA-MG53), recombinant protein or modified RNA rather than by cell type-restricted manipulation; Macrophages are identified by surface markers (CD68, CD206, CD80, CD192, CD11b) without separation of CCR2+ and CCR2- subsets
Validation requirements:
- R1: Define the intracellular route by which MG53 changes macrophage polarization. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: MG53 biases IL-4-stimulated bone marrow-derived macrophages toward the M2 (reparative) gene program.
Links: refinement → H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: MG53 interacts with major vault protein (MVP) and is associated with nuclear localization of MVP and STAT6 in M2-polarized macrophages.
Links: refinement ← H1; refinement → H3

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: MG53 promotes K63-linked, rather than K48-linked, ubiquitination of MVP through its E3 ligase activity.
Links: refinement ← H2; refinement → H4

## H4 (claim)
Statement: In HEK293 cells co-expressing tagged MG53 and MVP constructs, K747 is the critical MVP residue for MG53-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination, and MVP-K747R shows reduced co-localization with MG53 and reduced nuclear localization compared with wild-type MVP.
Links: refinement ← H3

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Anti-MG53 co-immunoprecipitation from IL-4-polarized (M2) BMDM lysates of tPA-MG53 and mg53-/- mice with Coomassie staining and LC-MS/MS identification of enriched bands.

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether MG53 regulates corneal sensory nerve regeneration after alkali burn injury and define the macrophage-associated molecular route through which it acts.
System: Mouse alkali-burn corneal injury in wild-type, MG53 global knockout (mg53-/-) and tPA-MG53 transgenic mice, with bone marrow-derived and immortalized macrophage cultures and HEK-293T/HEK293 reconstitution systems.
Conditions: Central corneal alkali burn produced with a 2 mm filter paper soaked in 2 uL of 1 M NaOH for 30 s; Corneal readouts between 3 h and day 10 after injury; M2 polarization of macrophages induced with 20 ng/mL IL-4 for 24 h; Recombinant human MG53 (rhMG53) or modified RNA used to raise MG53 levels
Scope limits: Mouse cornea and cultured mouse macrophages, with human membrane proteins and tagged constructs expressed in HEK-293T/HEK293 cells; MG53 levels are varied by global genotype (mg53-/-, tPA-MG53), recombinant protein or modified RNA rather than by cell type-restricted manipulation; Macrophages are identified by surface markers (CD68, CD206, CD80, CD192, CD11b) without separation of CCR2+ and CCR2- subsets
Validation requirements:
- R1: Define the intracellular route by which MG53 changes macrophage polarization. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: MG53 biases IL-4-stimulated bone marrow-derived macrophages toward the M2 (reparative) gene program.
Links: refinement → H2

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: MG53 interacts with major vault protein (MVP) and is associated with nuclear localization of MVP and STAT6 in M2-polarized macrophages.
Links: refinement ← H1; refinement → H3

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: MG53 promotes K63-linked, rather than K48-linked, ubiquitination of MVP through its E3 ligase activity.
Links: refinement ← H2; refinement ← H4

## H4 (claim)
Statement: K747 is the critical MVP residue for MG53-mediated K63 ubiquitination; MVP-K747R shows reduced co-localization with MG53 and impaired nuclear signaling.
Links: refinement → H3

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping accelerates CO2 capture kinetics of the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Oxygen vacancies in the Al-doped perovskite, in intimate contact with CaO, act as O2− migration channels that let CO2 cross the CaCO3 layer and react with inner CaO.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H4, H5)

# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?
System: Glycerol-plasticized cast chitosan film combined with electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwovens as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH and CH/PCLm/CH trilayers; comparator: monolayer chitosan film without PCL fibers
Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Mechanical performance: tensile strength and elongation at break (ASTM D882) of trilayer films compared with the monolayer chitosan film. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Structural properties: SEM of fiber and film surfaces and cross-sections. (aspects: H5)
- R3: Two configurations compared: PCL nonwoven between chitosan sheets (CH/PCL/CH) and chitosan sheet between two PCL nonwovens (PCL/CH/PCL). (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)

Links: composition → H2; composition → H5; composition → H3

Statement: Trilayer films have higher tensile strength and elongation at break than the monolayer chitosan film.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Layer arrangement (PCL between chitosan layers, CH/PCL/CH, versus PCL on the outer surfaces, PCL/CH/PCL) changes tensile performance, interlayer adhesion, surface wettability, transparency and mass loss in PBS.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Stronger interfacial adhesion when the PCL fiber layer lies between chitosan layers accounts for the better tensile performance of CH/PCL/CH films than PCL/CH/PCL films.

Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Mechanical performance: tensile strength and elongation at break (ASTM D882) of trilayer films compared with the monolayer chitosan film. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Structural properties: SEM of fiber and film surfaces and cross-sections. (aspects: H5)
- R3: Two configurations compared: PCL nonwoven between chitosan sheets (CH/PCL/CH) and chitosan sheet between two PCL nonwovens (PCL/CH/PCL). (aspects: H3)

Links: composition → H2; composition → H5; composition → H3

Links: composition ← H1; competing explanation ← H6

Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4

# Main hypothesis
Does integrating an in situ polymerized polypyrrole-coated carbon cloth (PPy/CC) electrode with a sodium alginate/poly(acrylamide-co-acrylic acid) supramolecular gel electrolyte containing NaCl give a flexible symmetric supercapacitor (FSGSC) whose electrochemical performance depends on the NaCl content of the gel, with an optimal NaCl content?
System: Symmetric sandwich supercapacitor with two identical PPy/CC electrodes (1 cm x 1 cm carbon cloth pieces) and an SA/P(AM-AA) supramolecular gel electrolyte prepared with 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3 g NaCl (S-gel0.1, S-gel0.2, S-gel0.3)
Conditions: Gel precursor: 4.5 g of 3 wt% SA solution, 1.0 g acrylamide, 2.0 g acrylic acid, 2.0 mL water, 0.1/0.2/0.3 g NaCl and APS; polymerized at 55 °C for 8 h; PPy/CC electrode alone tested in a three-electrode cell with aqueous NaCl electrolyte; Device tests at room temperature with a 0.7 V potential window
Scope limits: Three NaCl levels in one gel formulation; One electrode preparation (FeCl3-initiated pyrrole polymerization for 24 h)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that PPy is deposited on the carbon cloth and characterize the electrochemical performance of the PPy/CC electrode relative to bare carbon cloth. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterize the chemical structure of the supramolecular gel electrolyte and its ionic conductivity as a function of NaCl content. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Determine how the NaCl content of the gel electrolyte affects the electrochemical performance of the assembled device. (aspects: H3)
- R4: Establish the synergistic promotion between the modified electrode and the gel electrolyte. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: The PPy/CC electrode stores more charge and has lower impedance than bare carbon cloth in a three-electrode cell with aqueous NaCl electrolyte.
Links: composition ← H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The ionic conductivity of the supramolecular gel electrolyte depends on the NaCl content used in its preparation (0.1, 0.2 or 0.3 g).
Links: composition ← H4

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The areal specific capacitance of the assembled FSGSC depends on the NaCl content of its gel electrolyte.
Links: composition ← H4

## H4 (claim)
Statement: Combining the PPy/CC electrode with the supramolecular gel electrolyte produces a synergistic promotion of device performance beyond the contributions of the individual components.
Links: composition → H1; composition → H2; composition → H3

# Experiments

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4). (aspects: H2)
- R2: Obtain compositional profiles of the deposited layers for all six samples by SEM (Figures 3-5). (aspects: H3)
- R3: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11). (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Replacing charcoal-wax wiping (technique a) with non-asbestos Teflon pad wiping (technique b) after hot-dip galvanizing changes the zinc coating of S235JR wire and its protective performance; the study asks whether zinc use can fall without compromising anticorrosive performance.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: At each of the three wire diameters, Teflon pad wiping yields a lower zinc coating mass per unit area and thickness than wax wiping.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The Fe–Zn intermetallic (diffusion) sublayer at the steel interface persists after Teflon pad wiping with thickness similar to that under wax wiping, so it forms a larger fraction of the thinner coating.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to white rust (initial zinc oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique or wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to red rust (taken by the authors as base-metal oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique and wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6; experimental target ← E3

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Time to red rust is governed by total zinc coating thickness (the sacrificial zinc reservoir): thicker coatings give proportionally longer substrate protection.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Gravimetric coating determination (UNE-EN ISO 1460:2021): each sample weighed before and after chemical removal of the coating in 5% HCl at room temperature; mass per unit area mt (g/m2) converted to average thickness t (µm) with a zinc density of 7.14 g/cm3; five measurements on different portions of each wire, reported as mean with relative standard deviation.
Manipulation: Wiping technique after identical hot-dip galvanizing (a: wire pulled through a pile of charcoal-wax mixture; b: two non-asbestos Teflon pads pressed onto the wire at the bath exit) crossed with wire diameter (Ø3.25, 2.50, 1.50 mm): one wire sample per combination, labelled 1a, 2a, 3a, 1b, 2b, 3b.
Measurements: mass before and after chemical stripping; mass per unit area mt; calculated thickness t
Comparison: groups: 1a: Ø3.25 mm, wax wiping (technique a); 2a: Ø2.50 mm, wax wiping; 3a: Ø1.50 mm, wax wiping; 1b: Ø3.25 mm, Teflon pad wiping (technique b); 2b: Ø2.50 mm, Teflon pad wiping; 3b: Ø1.50 mm, Teflon pad wiping | endpoint: zinc mass per unit area mt (g/m2) and calculated average coating thickness t (µm) | varied: wiping technique after galvanizing (a: charcoal-wax pile wiping; b: two non-asbestos Teflon pads pressed on the wire at the bath exit); wire diameter (Ø3.25, 2.50, 1.50 mm) | held fixed: steel grade S235JR; pretreatment: in-line annealing, water cooling, 20% HCl pickling at about 23 °C, water rinse; ZnZ1 zinc bath (at least 99.995 wt% Zn) at 450 °C; immersion time 90 s (1.5 min); line speed 50 m/min | unit: five measurements on different portions of each single wire sample | window: as-produced coating, before corrosion testing | units: g/m2; µm | uncertainty: relative standard deviation (%) of the five measurements
Links: experimental target → H2
Observations: O1

The number of sections, fields or positions used for tv is not reported.

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4). (aspects: H2)
- R2: Obtain compositional profiles of the deposited layers for all six samples by SEM (Figures 3-5). (aspects: H3)
- R3: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11). (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Replacing charcoal-wax wiping (technique a) with non-asbestos Teflon pad wiping (technique b) after hot-dip galvanizing changes the zinc coating of S235JR wire and its protective performance; the study asks whether zinc use can fall without compromising anticorrosive performance.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: At each of the three wire diameters, Teflon pad wiping yields a lower zinc coating mass per unit area and thickness than wax wiping.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The Fe–Zn intermetallic (diffusion) sublayer at the steel interface persists after Teflon pad wiping with thickness similar to that under wax wiping, so it forms a larger fraction of the thinner coating.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to white rust (initial zinc oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique or wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to red rust (taken by the authors as base-metal oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique and wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6; experimental target ← E3; proposed mechanism ← H7

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Time to red rust is governed by total zinc coating thickness (the sacrificial zinc reservoir): thicker coatings give proportionally longer substrate protection.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5; competing explanation ← H7

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate (unverified): on Teflon-wiped wires, red coloration at about 120 h may mark corrosion of the Fe-bearing Fe–Zn intermetallic sublayer, which has similar thickness in all specimens and remains after the thin outer zinc is consumed, rather than attack of the steel substrate. On this reading, red-rust time tracks exposure of the common alloy sublayer, not total coating thickness.
Links: competing explanation → H6; proposed mechanism → H5

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4). (aspects: H2)
- R2: Obtain compositional profiles of the deposited layers for all six samples by SEM (Figures 3-5). (aspects: H3)
- R3: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11). (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Replacing charcoal-wax wiping (technique a) with non-asbestos Teflon pad wiping (technique b) after hot-dip galvanizing changes the zinc coating of S235JR wire and its protective performance; the study asks whether zinc use can fall without compromising anticorrosive performance.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: At each of the three wire diameters, Teflon pad wiping yields a lower zinc coating mass per unit area and thickness than wax wiping.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The Fe–Zn intermetallic (diffusion) sublayer at the steel interface persists after Teflon pad wiping with thickness similar to that under wax wiping, so it forms a larger fraction of the thinner coating.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to white rust (initial zinc oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique or wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to red rust (taken by the authors as base-metal oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique and wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6; experimental target ← E3

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Time to red rust is governed by total zinc coating thickness (the sacrificial zinc reservoir): thicker coatings give proportionally longer substrate protection.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5; alternative to ← H7

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: Red-rust onset may also depend on wiping-dependent coating architecture, such as continuity or defects in the outer zinc layer and its distribution relative to the Fe–Zn sublayer, which could affect localized access to the steel independently of total coating thickness.
Links: alternative to → H6

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4). (aspects: H2)
- R2: Obtain compositional profiles of the deposited layers for all six samples by SEM (Figures 3-5). (aspects: H3)
- R3: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11). (aspects: H4, H5)

## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Replacing charcoal-wax wiping (technique a) with non-asbestos Teflon pad wiping (technique b) after hot-dip galvanizing changes the zinc coating of S235JR wire and its protective performance; the study asks whether zinc use can fall without compromising anticorrosive performance.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: At each of the three wire diameters, Teflon pad wiping yields a lower zinc coating mass per unit area and thickness than wax wiping.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The Fe–Zn intermetallic (diffusion) sublayer at the steel interface persists after Teflon pad wiping with thickness similar to that under wax wiping, so it forms a larger fraction of the thinner coating.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to white rust (initial zinc oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique or wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Whether time to red rust (taken by the authors as base-metal oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique and wire diameter.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6; experimental target ← E3

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Time to red rust is governed by total zinc coating thickness (the sacrificial zinc reservoir): thicker coatings give proportionally longer substrate protection.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5; competing explanation ← H7; competing explanation ← H7

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: Alternative explanation: the red-rust time is governed by the thickness of the Fe–Zn intermetallic diffusion sublayer at the steel interface; Teflon pad wiping leaves this sublayer relatively thicker than wax wiping, so its oxidation contributes more strongly to the observed red-rust times than the total zinc thickness does, even though the Teflon coatings are thinner.
Links: competing explanation → H6; competing explanation → H6

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H1)

# Sub-hypotheses

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H1)

# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?

Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C

# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?
System: Glycerol-plasticized cast chitosan film combined with electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwovens as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH and CH/PCLm/CH trilayers; comparator: monolayer chitosan film without PCL fibers
Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Hydrophilic properties: moisture content, swelling degree, total soluble matter and water contact angle. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Barrier properties: water vapor, oxygen and carbon dioxide permeability. (aspects: H5, [unlisted])

# Main hypothesis
Whether implantation of HPC@Gel into a rat cortical cavity TBI, compared with PBS and with its component hydrogels (Gel, CCQDs@Gel, HB-PDA@Gel), improves neurological function and behavioral performance over 28 days.
System: Sprague-Dawley rats with a right parietal cortical cavity TBI (2 mm diameter, 2 mm depth) receiving PBS or hydrogel implants immediately after injury
Conditions: Behavioral and neurological testing on days 1-28 after surgery
Scope limits: n = 6 animals per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Assess the neurological deficit trajectory (mNSS) across groups. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Assess Y-maze performance on day 28 across groups. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Assess open-field behavior across groups. (aspects: H4)

Statement: HPC@Gel implantation improves functional recovery after cortical cavity TBI in rats.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H6

Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5

System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH

# Main hypothesis
Does SIRT1 act as the deacetylase for GAPDH lysine 254 in microglia, and does the K254 acetylation state thereby set glycolytic flux and pro-inflammatory output during LPS/IFN-gamma activation?
System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH
Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+
Scope limits: in vitro only; no in vivo, aged or chronic low-grade inflammatory model was studied; GAPDH replacement reaches 75-80%, leaving residual endogenous wild-type protein; acetylation states are represented by K254Q and K254R substitutions rather than by enzymatically controlled acetylation in cells; figure images and supplementary files were not inspected during this extraction
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine whether the K254 acetylation state controls GAPDH catalytic activity and glycolytic flux. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine whether the K254 acetylation state controls pro-inflammatory output and whether glycolytic flux is required for that output. (aspects: H2, H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: The acetylation state of GAPDH K254 sets GAPDH catalytic activity and glycolytic flux in microglia.
Links: composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The acetylation state of GAPDH K254 sets pro-inflammatory cytokine, transcript and nitric oxide output in activated microglia.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H3

## H3 (claim)
Statement: Enhanced glycolytic flux is the required intermediate through which GAPDH K254 deacetylation amplifies pro-inflammatory output.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; composition ← H1; competing explanation ← H4; competing explanation → H4

## H4 (alternative)
Statement: Alternative account: the observed cytokine difference between the high-flux (K254R) and low-flux (K254Q) genotypes is primarily a reflection of the glycolytic flux difference, and the flux difference itself is the factor that accounts for the cytokine difference, rather than a separate pathway that requires glycolytic flux.
Links: competing explanation → H3; competing explanation ← H3

# Main hypothesis
Whether NiFe-LDH-4 grown on nickel foam is suited as an OER anode for alkaline seawater (1.0 M KOH + seawater, pH 13.51) electrolysis: its activity relative to the other Ni/Fe ratios, its durability, and its behaviour with respect to chloride-related side reactions at low and high current density.
System: NiFe layered double hydroxide grown on nickel foam (NiFe-LDH-x, x = 1, 2, 4, 6) by one-step hydrothermal synthesis with urea and NH4F
Conditions: 1.0 M KOH + seawater (pH 13.51); 1.0 M KOH for high-current comparison; three-electrode half-cell tests
Scope limits: Laboratory-scale electrodes; Durability tests of 12 to 25 h in seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare OER activity of the four ratios in 1.0 M KOH + seawater. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Assess OER durability of NiFe-LDH-4 in alkaline seawater, including at high current density. (aspects: H2, H3)
- R3: Address chloride-related side reactions relevant to alkaline seawater oxidation. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: OER activity in 1.0 M KOH + seawater (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl, EIS).

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Durability of NiFe-LDH-4 for OER and HER in 1.0 M KOH + seawater in three-electrode tests.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Activity of NiFe-LDH-4 at 500 mA cm−2 in 1.0 M KOH and 1.0 M KOH + seawater, and durability at high current density (500 mA cm−2 for alkaline OER).

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Behaviour of the NiFe-LDH-4 anode with respect to chloride-related side reactions (chlorine evolution, hypochlorite formation) in alkaline seawater.
Links: refinement → H5

## H5 (claim)
Statement: At 10 mA cm−2 in 1.0 M KOH + seawater, the OER overpotential of NiFe-LDH-4 (230.5–231 mV) lies below the approximately 480 mV potential difference between hypochlorite formation and OER given by the cited Pourbaix analysis, so hypochlorite formation is not thermodynamically expected at this operating point. OER selectivity (O2 Faradaic efficiency, hypochlorite or active-chlorine formation) was not measured, and at 500 mA cm−2 the seawater OER overpotential (503.5 mV) exceeds this threshold; the stable 12-h and 25-h operation therefore supports durability but does not show that chloride side reactions are absent at industrial current density.
Links: refinement ← H4

# Main hypothesis
Can a W-shaped piezoresistive pressure sensor that couples a rigid aluminum sheet (inspired by the rigid outer wall and soft porous interior of Bambusa textilis) with a carbon-ink-coated melamine sponge and a micro-protruded MWCNT/PU film (inspired by the surface protrusions of Salvia plebeia R.Br.) address the poor stability and long recovery times of porous flexible pressure sensors, while providing a broad pressure range, usable sensitivity, fine load resolution, and terrain discrimination when mounted on a robot foot?
System: W-shaped layered sensor: aluminum sheet, insulating double-sided tape, carbon-black-ink-coated melamine sponge, MWCNT/PU film with sandpaper-replicated micro-protrusions, copper electrodes; 80 mm x 20 mm strip
Conditions: Bench loading with a motorized linear stage; resistance read with a Keithley DAQ6510 multimeter; force with a 1 kN gauge; Applied pressures up to 31.5 kPa; Robot tests on a six-legged robot with the sensor on the ventral side of one foot
Scope limits: Bench tests and one robot platform; Figure images and supplementary figures are not part of this text record
Validation requirements:

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3, H4, H5)
- R3: Investigate the photodetection performance of devices with untreated and cryogenically treated MWCNTs under solar illumination and under different UV, Vis and NIR wavelengths. (aspects: H3, H4)

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3, H4, H5)
- R3: Investigate the photodetection performance of devices with untreated and cryogenically treated MWCNTs under solar illumination and under different UV, Vis and NIR wavelengths. (aspects: H3, H4)

# Main hypothesis
Can enzymatic hydrolysis of coconut kernel fiber (CKF), a coconut-processing by-product, yield a low-molecular-weight (1-3 kDa) hydrolysate fraction (LW-CKFH) that inhibits alpha-glucosidase, improves glucose metabolism in IR-HepG2 cells and in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, retains activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions, and contains identifiable alpha-glucosidase inhibitory peptides?
System: CKF protein hydrolysates (CKFH) and their ultrafiltration/gel-filtration fractions; in vitro alpha-glucosidase (pNPG) assay; HepG2 and insulin-induced IR-HepG2 cells; male Kunming mice with high-sugar high-fat diet plus streptozotocin (HSHFD/STZ) induced T2DM; simulated digestion and bread model; LC-MS/MS, in silico screening, molecular docking and synthetic peptides.
Conditions: Ultrasound-assisted sequential neutral then alkaline protease hydrolysis (8000 U/g, 2 h each); LW-CKFH = 1-3 kDa ultrafiltration fraction; Mice: oral gavage for 4 weeks with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, or LW-CKFH 200, 400, 800 mg/kg bw; n = 6 per group; Stability/matrix outcomes expressed as retention relative to untreated LW-CKFH (20 mg/mL, pH 7.0, 25 C) set to 100%
Scope limits: Single mouse strain and sex (male Kunming), one T2DM induction model, one 4-week treatment period; Insulin resistance and sensitivity assessed by HOMA surrogate indices from fasting glucose and insulin; Peptide binding assessed by molecular docking; synthetic peptides tested only for in vitro alpha-glucosidase inhibition; Food feasibility assessed in vitro (simulated digestion, one bread formulation)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Evaluate in vivo hypoglycemic efficacy of LW-CKFH in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice relative to untreated model mice and a metformin group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterize insulin-related outcomes (serum insulin and HOMA indices of beta-cell function, insulin resistance and insulin sensitivity) in the treated T2DM mice. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Can enzymatic hydrolysis of coconut kernel fiber (CKF), a coconut-processing by-product, yield a low-molecular-weight (1-3 kDa) hydrolysate fraction (LW-CKFH) that inhibits alpha-glucosidase, improves glucose metabolism in IR-HepG2 cells and in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, retains activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions, and contains identifiable alpha-glucosidase inhibitory peptides?
System: CKF protein hydrolysates (CKFH) and their ultrafiltration/gel-filtration fractions; in vitro alpha-glucosidase (pNPG) assay; HepG2 and insulin-induced IR-HepG2 cells; male Kunming mice with high-sugar high-fat diet plus streptozotocin (HSHFD/STZ) induced T2DM; simulated digestion and bread model; LC-MS/MS, in silico screening, molecular docking and synthetic peptides.
Conditions: Ultrasound-assisted sequential neutral then alkaline protease hydrolysis (8000 U/g, 2 h each); LW-CKFH = 1-3 kDa ultrafiltration fraction; Mice: oral gavage for 4 weeks with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, or LW-CKFH 200, 400, 800 mg/kg bw; n = 6 per group; Stability/matrix outcomes expressed as retention relative to untreated LW-CKFH (20 mg/mL, pH 7.0, 25 C) set to 100%
Scope limits: Single mouse strain and sex (male Kunming), one T2DM induction model, one 4-week treatment period; Insulin resistance and sensitivity assessed by HOMA surrogate indices from fasting glucose and insulin; Peptide binding assessed by molecular docking; synthetic peptides tested only for in vitro alpha-glucosidase inhibition; Food feasibility assessed in vitro (simulated digestion, one bread formulation)

- R1: Evaluate in vivo hypoglycemic efficacy of LW-CKFH in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice relative to untreated model mice and a metformin group. (aspects: H1)

# Main hypothesis
By which mechanism do circulating factors of heart failure reach and damage the retinal neurovascular unit? The study tests whether elevated circulating TGFβ2 drives retinal endothelial epigenetic senescence through pSMAD2/EP300-H3K9ac-P21, whether senescent endothelium activates retinal microglia and neuroinflammation, and whether neutralizing TGFβ2 or depleting microglia preserves retinal structure and function.
System: Pressure-overload heart failure in C57BL/6J mice (TAC versus sham), parabiosis with sham- or TAC-operated partners, transfer of donor plasma onto cultured human endothelial cells (HUVECs and primary HRMECs), plasma from heart failure patients and healthy controls, and public human cardiac snRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets
Conditions: Surgery at 2 months of age; retinal assessment at 5 months in most mouse cohorts and at 6 months in the Tgfbr2 conditional knockout cohort; Dialyzed plasma applied to endothelial cells at 1% (v/v) for 48 h; Recombinant TGFβ2 at 6 ng/mL in culture and 6 ng per mouse by tail vein every 2 days for 2 months; Anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 mg/kg in vivo (six injections, intravitreal or tail vein) or 1 μg/mL on cells, against isotype IgG
Scope limits: Retinal readouts are electroretinography amplitudes, optical coherence tomography layer thickness, lectin vascular density and diameter, and immunostaining of senescence and microglial markers; Human material is limited to plasma, cultured endothelial cells and public transcriptomic datasets; Cardiac endpoints are echocardiographic and histological; no survival or systemic hemodynamic outcomes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Define the endothelial signaling route from TGFβ2 to senescence and test whether endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Test whether neutralizing TGFβ2 reduces endothelial senescence and retinal damage in mice, across organs, and in human retinal endothelial cells exposed to patient plasma. (aspects: H2, H3, H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo for TAC-induced retinal dysfunction, retinal vascular degeneration and retinal endothelial senescence.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Neutralizing TGFβ2 reduces endothelial senescence and retinal damage associated with heart failure.
Links: composition → H3; composition → H4

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Heart failure raises endothelial senescence in organs beyond the retina, and systemic anti-TGFβ2 antibody lowers it.
Links: composition ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Plasma from heart failure patients induces senescence in primary human retinal microvascular endothelial cells, and anti-TGFβ2 antibody reduces it.
Links: composition ← H2

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Retinal phenotyping of endothelial-specific Tgfbr2 conditional knockout and wild-type mice after Sham or TAC surgery.
Manipulation: Tgfbr2-flox mice crossed with Cdh5-CreERT2 mice, with tamoxifen administered by intraperitoneal injection before Sham or TAC surgery to induce the endothelial-specific deletion; retinal function, structure, endothelial senescence and vasculature assessed.
Measurements: electroretinography; optical coherence tomography; SA-β-gal immunostaining; lectin staining
Comparison: groups: WT-Sham; Tgfbr2 cKO-Sham; WT-TAC; Tgfbr2 cKO-TAC | endpoint: Scotopic a- and b-wave amplitudes, photopic b-wave amplitudes, OCT layer thickness, SA-β-gal in CD31+ retinal microvascular endothelial cells, retinal vascular density and diameter | varied: endothelial Tgfbr2 deletion; aortic constriction | held fixed: same C57BL/6J background; same electroretinography, OCT and staining protocols | unit: eye or mouse | window: Electroretinography and OCT at 6 months of age; tissue collection at 7 months
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: Co-treatment of endothelial cells with Sham or TAC plasma and anti-TGFβ2 antibody or IgG.
Manipulation: Endothelial cells treated for 48 h with Sham or TAC plasma together with isotype IgG or anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 μg/mL.
Measurements: immunocytochemistry
Comparison: groups: TAC plasma with anti-TGFβ2 antibody; TAC plasma with IgG; Sham plasma with anti-TGFβ2 antibody; Sham plasma with IgG | endpoint: SA-β-gal, P16Ink4a, P21 and H3K9me3 staining in endothelial cells | varied: anti-TGFβ2 antibody; heart failure status of the plasma | held fixed: 48 h treatment; 1 μg/mL antibody; same staining and imaging settings | unit: independent experiment | window: 48 h of treatment
Observations: O3

## E3
Statement: Intravitreal anti-TGFβ2 antibody in Sham and TAC mice, with retinal function, structure and endothelial senescence readouts.
Manipulation: Six intravitreal injections of anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 mg/kg in 1 μL saline, or isotype IgG, between 3 and 5 months of age after Sham or TAC surgery at 2 months.
Measurements: electroretinography; optical coherence tomography; SA-β-gal immunostaining
Comparison: groups: TAC with intravitreal anti-TGFβ2 antibody; TAC with control injection; Sham groups | endpoint: Scotopic a- and b-wave amplitudes, photopic b-wave amplitudes, OCT layer thickness, SA-β-gal in retinal vascular endothelial cells | varied: intravitreal anti-TGFβ2 antibody; aortic constriction | held fixed: six injections between 3 and 5 months; 32 G needle under microscopic guidance; 1-week recovery before assessment | unit: eye or mouse | window: Electroretinography and OCT at 5 months of age; histology at 6 months
Observations: O4, O5, O6

# Main hypothesis
By which mechanism do circulating factors of heart failure reach and damage the retinal neurovascular unit? The study tests whether elevated circulating TGFβ2 drives retinal endothelial epigenetic senescence through pSMAD2/EP300-H3K9ac-P21, whether senescent endothelium activates retinal microglia and neuroinflammation, and whether neutralizing TGFβ2 or depleting microglia preserves retinal structure and function.
System: Pressure-overload heart failure in C57BL/6J mice (TAC versus sham), parabiosis with sham- or TAC-operated partners, transfer of donor plasma onto cultured human endothelial cells (HUVECs and primary HRMECs), plasma from heart failure patients and healthy controls, and public human cardiac snRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets
Conditions: Surgery at 2 months of age; retinal assessment at 5 months in most mouse cohorts and at 6 months in the Tgfbr2 conditional knockout cohort; Dialyzed plasma applied to endothelial cells at 1% (v/v) for 48 h; Recombinant TGFβ2 at 6 ng/mL in culture and 6 ng per mouse by tail vein every 2 days for 2 months; Anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 mg/kg in vivo (six injections, intravitreal or tail vein) or 1 μg/mL on cells, against isotype IgG
Scope limits: Retinal readouts are electroretinography amplitudes, optical coherence tomography layer thickness, lectin vascular density and diameter, and immunostaining of senescence and microglial markers; Human material is limited to plasma, cultured endothelial cells and public transcriptomic datasets; Cardiac endpoints are echocardiographic and histological; no survival or systemic hemodynamic outcomes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Define the endothelial signaling route from TGFβ2 to senescence and test whether endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Test whether neutralizing TGFβ2 reduces endothelial senescence and retinal damage in mice, across organs, and in human retinal endothelial cells exposed to patient plasma. (aspects: H2, H3, H4)

Statement: Endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo for TAC-induced retinal dysfunction, retinal vascular degeneration and retinal endothelial senescence.

Statement: Heart failure raises endothelial senescence in organs beyond the retina, and systemic anti-TGFβ2 antibody lowers it.
Links: composition ← H2; supports ← H5

Statement: Plasma from heart failure patients induces senescence in primary human retinal microvascular endothelial cells, and anti-TGFβ2 antibody reduces it.

# Main hypothesis
By which mechanism do circulating factors of heart failure reach and damage the retinal neurovascular unit? The study tests whether elevated circulating TGFβ2 drives retinal endothelial epigenetic senescence through pSMAD2/EP300-H3K9ac-P21, whether senescent endothelium activates retinal microglia and neuroinflammation, and whether neutralizing TGFβ2 or depleting microglia preserves retinal structure and function.
System: Pressure-overload heart failure in C57BL/6J mice (TAC versus sham), parabiosis with sham- or TAC-operated partners, transfer of donor plasma onto cultured human endothelial cells (HUVECs and primary HRMECs), plasma from heart failure patients and healthy controls, and public human cardiac snRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets
Conditions: Surgery at 2 months of age; retinal assessment at 5 months in most mouse cohorts and at 6 months in the Tgfbr2 conditional knockout cohort; Dialyzed plasma applied to endothelial cells at 1% (v/v) for 48 h; Recombinant TGFβ2 at 6 ng/mL in culture and 6 ng per mouse by tail vein every 2 days for 2 months; Anti-TGFβ2 antibody at 1 mg/kg in vivo (six injections, intravitreal or tail vein) or 1 μg/mL on cells, against isotype IgG
Scope limits: Retinal readouts are electroretinography amplitudes, optical coherence tomography layer thickness, lectin vascular density and diameter, and immunostaining of senescence and microglial markers; Human material is limited to plasma, cultured endothelial cells and public transcriptomic datasets; Cardiac endpoints are echocardiographic and histological; no survival or systemic hemodynamic outcomes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Define the endothelial signaling route from TGFβ2 to senescence and test whether endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Test whether neutralizing TGFβ2 reduces endothelial senescence and retinal damage in mice, across organs, and in human retinal endothelial cells exposed to patient plasma. (aspects: H2, H3, H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Endothelial TGFBR2 is required in vivo for TAC-induced retinal dysfunction, retinal vascular degeneration and retinal endothelial senescence.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Neutralizing TGFβ2 reduces endothelial senescence and retinal damage associated with heart failure: in vitro the antibody attenuated endothelial senescence caused by heart failure plasma, and intravitreal injection reduced endothelial senescence and improved retinal structure and function in heart failure mice. Cultured endothelial cells treated with patient plasma show similar sensitivity to TGFβ2 blockade.
Links: composition → H3; composition → H4

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Heart failure raises endothelial senescence in organs beyond the retina, and systemic anti-TGFβ2 antibody lowers it.
Links: composition ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Plasma from heart failure patients induces senescence in primary human retinal microvascular endothelial cells, and anti-TGFβ2 antibody reduces it.
Links: composition ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Does Ni electrodeposition on HNO3-activated CF fabric followed by vacuum heat treatment improve the tensile behaviour of the resulting epoxy CFRP, and how does the change relate to the Ni-C interfacial structure?
System: PAN-based T300 3K carbon fiber plain-weave fabric, sizing removed and HNO3-etched, Ni electrodeposited from a Watts bath at 0.02 A/cm2 (LD) or 0.04 A/cm2 (HD), vacuum heat-treated, and cured into 4674 epoxy CFRP panels
Conditions: LD 0.02 A/cm2 and HD 0.04 A/cm2 electrodeposition; IH at 500-900 °C or LH to 700 °C, 2 h, vacuum; EMI in the X band; quasi-static tensile tests of cured panels
Scope limits: LH applied only at 700 °C
Validation requirements:
- R1: Improve the mechanical properties of the CFRP relative to pristine CFRP. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Characterize the Ni/C interfacial structure that accompanies the tensile changes. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Tensile ductility (maximum fracture strain) of epoxy CFRP panels made from pristine, LD-coated and HD-coated fabrics after heat treatment
Links: refinement → H4

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H3, H6)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H4, H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface without changing the SiC crystal structure, and SiC and APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Pristine SiC and SiC-APTES differ in how they change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings.
Links: composition ← H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES to the carbon paste changes the photovoltaic performance (PCE, JSC, VOC, FF, Rs, Rsh, hysteresis) of p-i-n C-PSCs relative to the pure carbon paste control.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H8

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the cross-sectional structure of the carbon electrode and its contact with the underlying C60/Cr layers.
Links: composition ← H7

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the interfacial charge-transport resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon contact.
Links: composition ← H7

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Average device PCE depends on the additive loading in the paste, with an optimal loading window for SiC and for SiC-APTES.

## H7 (claim)
Statement: APTES modification converts inert, highly agglomerating SiC into a well-dispersed filler that dramatically improves carbon paste rheology, promotes void-free contact, and reduces interfacial resistance.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: APTES functionalization disperses SiC and keeps the paste flowable, giving void-free carbon films in intimate contact with C60; the resulting reduction of contact resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon interface is the primary origin of the PCE gain.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3

Manipulation: As-received SiC nanoparticles (50 nm nominal, beta form; 200 mg) were activated in 0.5 M aqueous KOH, ultrasonically dispersed for 30 min, treated in a home-built vibro-heating reactor at 130 °C for 90 min, centrifuged and rinsed twice with water, redispersed in IPA and dried by rotary evaporation to give SiC-OH (~90% yield). SiC-OH was then redispersed by sonication in 3 mL 1-butanol, mixed with 1 mL anhydrous DMF and 1 mL APTES, vibro-heated for 90 min, washed with IPA by repeated centrifugation and dried to give SiC-APTES.

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H3, H6)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H4, H5)

System: Solvent-cast sago-starch films containing nano-ZnO (20 nm) or micro-ZnO

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4). (aspects: H2)
- R2: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11). (aspects: H3, H4)

Statement: Replacing charcoal-wax wiping (technique a) with non-asbestos Teflon pad wiping (technique b) after hot-dip galvanizing changes the zinc coating of S235JR wire and its protective performance; the study asks whether zinc use can fall without compromising anticorrosive performance.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: At each of the three wire diameters, Teflon pad wiping yields a lower zinc coating mass per unit area and thickness than wax wiping.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

Statement: Whether time to white rust (initial zinc oxidation) in neutral salt spray differs with wiping technique or wire diameter.

# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?
System: 411 patients with confirmed superficial LNTB, Xi'an Chest Hospital, November 30, 2018 to June 17, 2024; tissue and purulent specimens tested with a Mycobacterium nucleic acid detection kit (PCR-fluorescent probe) on an ABI7500 real-time PCR system
Conditions: Retrospective extraction of electronic medical records; Blood for laboratory tests, including T lymphocyte subsets, collected within 24 hours of admission; PCR-fluorescent probe result as the dependent variable in logistic regression
Scope limits: Single center (Xi'an Chest Hospital); Superficial LNTB only; other extrapulmonary TB forms not studied; Observational retrospective design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Screen candidate factors (demographic characteristics, TB-related information, comorbidities, laboratory data, T lymphocyte subsets and number of samples) for association with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Explore the dose-response relationships of age, total T lymphocytes (CD3+), T helper lymphocytes (CD3+CD4+) and the T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models combined with logistic regression.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Specimen acquisition factors (how and how many specimens were obtained) are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result in LNTB patients.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; refinement → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Samples obtained through surgery, compared with samples not obtained through surgery, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Double samples, compared with a single sample, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (claim)
Statement: A strategy of surgical sampling and submission of multiple samples (granulation tissue + granulation tissue, granulation tissue + purulent, or purulent + purulent) can nearly double the PCR-fluorescent probe positivity rate in LNTB patients.
Links: refinement ← H1; scoped evidence ← O1; scoped evidence ← O2; scoped evidence ← O5; scoped evidence ← O6

# Main hypothesis
Does controlled Ag nanoparticle deposition on Ag2NCN enhance visible-light pollutant degradation, and which optical, charge-transfer, thermal, and reactive-species mechanisms account for the enhancement?
System: Ag/Ag2NCN heterostructures degrading RhB, phenol, and tetracycline in water under visible light
Conditions: 420–800 nm irradiation from a 300 W xenon lamp; natural initial pH reported as 6.8; Ag loadings produced by NaBH4 surface reduction
Scope limits: laboratory pollutant solutions; parent-pollutant disappearance is distinct from mineralization; mechanistic attribution combines direct assays and author interpretation
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare activity and mineralization endpoints against pristine Ag2NCN. (aspects: H1, H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Pollutant disappearance kinetics and removal under visible-light irradiation.
Links: scoped evidence ← O1

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Mineralization at 30 min equals disappearance of the parent pollutant for TC, RhB, and phenol.
Links: scoped evidence ← O2

## H3 (limitation)
Statement: Performance at extreme pH and toxicity of accumulated intermediates limit broad environmental claims.
