# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?
System: 411 patients with confirmed superficial LNTB, Xi'an Chest Hospital, November 30, 2018 to June 17, 2024; tissue and purulent specimens tested with a Mycobacterium nucleic acid detection kit (PCR-fluorescent probe) on an ABI7500 real-time PCR system
Conditions: Retrospective extraction of electronic medical records; Blood for laboratory tests, including T lymphocyte subsets, collected within 24 hours of admission; PCR-fluorescent probe result as the dependent variable in logistic regression
Scope limits: Single center (Xi'an Chest Hospital); Superficial LNTB only; other extrapulmonary TB forms not studied; Observational retrospective design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Screen candidate factors (demographic characteristics, TB-related information, comorbidities, laboratory data, T lymphocyte subsets and number of samples) for association with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Explore the dose-response relationships of age, total T lymphocytes (CD3+), T helper lymphocytes (CD3+CD4+) and the T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models combined with logistic regression.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Specimen acquisition factors (how and how many specimens were obtained) are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result in LNTB patients.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Samples obtained through surgery, compared with samples not obtained through surgery, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Double samples, compared with a single sample, are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result.
Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.
Links: composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Without Sn, complete exfoliation of NCA90 into single crystals requires calcination at 900 °C, and Li/Ni cation mixing increases with calcination temperature.
Links: composition ← H8

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Sn loading, calcination temperature and hold time govern the extent of exfoliation and the resulting structure and performance of Sn-modified NCA90.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Layered structural ordering and Ni oxidation state of SC-Sn-NCA90 compared with PC-NCA90 (Li/Ni mixing, surface Ni2+ fraction, Ni K-edge local environment).

## H5 (claim)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 shows higher rate capability and 500-cycle capacity retention than PC-NCA90 in half-cells cycled to 4.5 V and to 4.7 V.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H7; proposed mechanism ← H6; proposed mechanism ← H8

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: The grain-boundary-free single-crystalline morphology suppresses intergranular microcracking under high-voltage cycling.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: The dual-site Sn modification, bulk Sn doping plus the residual surface Li2SnO3 layer, produces the improved high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 (Sn(OH)2-coated NCA90 precursor, 0.8 mol% Sn) calcined at 750 °C has higher high-voltage electrochemical stability than undoped NCA90 calcined at 900 °C, the conventional high-temperature single-crystal product, at 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism → H5

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2)

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.
Links: composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Without Sn, complete exfoliation of NCA90 into single crystals requires calcination at 900 °C, and Li/Ni cation mixing increases with calcination temperature.
Links: composition ← H8

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Sn loading, calcination temperature and hold time govern the extent of exfoliation and the resulting structure and performance of Sn-modified NCA90.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Layered structural ordering and Ni oxidation state of SC-Sn-NCA90 compared with PC-NCA90 (Li/Ni mixing, surface Ni2+ fraction, Ni K-edge local environment).

## H5 (claim)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 shows higher rate capability and 500-cycle capacity retention than PC-NCA90 in half-cells cycled to 4.5 V and to 4.7 V.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H7; proposed mechanism ← H6; composition ← H8

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: The grain-boundary-free single-crystalline morphology suppresses intergranular microcracking under high-voltage cycling.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5; composition ← H8

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: The dual-site Sn modification, bulk Sn doping plus the residual surface Li2SnO3 layer, produces the improved high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 synthesized at 750 °C (with Sn coating) is compared with conventional high-temperature single-crystal NCA90 (e.g., the 900 °C undoped sample from O2) to assess whether the lower synthesis temperature, enabled by Sn, confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn.

# Main hypothesis
Do mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles carrying the DPEP1 inhibitor cilastatin sodium and surface-modified with L-serine (CTT/MPDA@L-Ser NPs) accumulate in injured kidney tissue and mitigate cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury by suppressing DPEP1 and restoring GPX4/SLC7A11-dependent ferroptosis defence?

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether MG53 regulates corneal sensory nerve regeneration after alkali burn injury and define the macrophage-associated molecular route through which it acts.
System: Mouse alkali-burn corneal injury in wild-type, MG53 global knockout (mg53-/-) and tPA-MG53 transgenic mice, with bone marrow-derived and immortalized macrophage cultures and HEK-293T/HEK293 reconstitution systems.
Conditions: Central corneal alkali burn produced with a 2 mm filter paper soaked in 2 uL of 1 M NaOH for 30 s; Corneal readouts between 3 h and day 10 after injury; M2 polarization of macrophages induced with 20 ng/mL IL-4 for 24 h; Recombinant human MG53 (rhMG53) or modified RNA used to raise MG53 levels
Scope limits: Mouse cornea and cultured mouse macrophages, with human membrane proteins and tagged constructs expressed in HEK-293T/HEK293 cells; MG53 levels are varied by global genotype (mg53-/-, tPA-MG53), recombinant protein or modified RNA rather than by cell type-restricted manipulation; Macrophages are identified by surface markers (CD68, CD206, CD80, CD192, CD11b) without separation of CCR2+ and CCR2- subsets
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether MG53 abundance changes corneal nerve loss and regrowth after alkali injury in vivo. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Evaluate whether delivering MG53 as modified RNA improves corneal healing and nerve regeneration after injury. (aspects: H2, H3)

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether MG53 regulates corneal sensory nerve regeneration after alkali burn injury and define the macrophage-associated molecular route through which it acts.
System: Mouse alkali-burn corneal injury in wild-type, MG53 global knockout (mg53-/-) and tPA-MG53 transgenic mice, with bone marrow-derived and immortalized macrophage cultures and HEK-293T/HEK293 reconstitution systems.

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2, H8)

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2, H8)

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2, H8)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Coating the NCA90 precursor with Sn(OH)2 yields well-dispersed single-crystalline NCA after calcination at 750 °C, the schedule that yields polycrystalline NCA90 from the uncoated precursor.
Links: composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Without Sn, complete exfoliation of NCA90 into single crystals requires calcination at 900 °C, and Li/Ni cation mixing increases with calcination temperature.
Links: composition ← H8

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Sn loading, calcination temperature and hold time govern the extent of exfoliation and the resulting structure and performance of Sn-modified NCA90.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Layered structural ordering and Ni oxidation state of SC-Sn-NCA90 compared with PC-NCA90 (Li/Ni mixing, surface Ni2+ fraction, Ni K-edge local environment).

## H5 (claim)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 shows higher rate capability and 500-cycle capacity retention than PC-NCA90 in half-cells cycled to 4.5 V and to 4.7 V.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H7; proposed mechanism ← H6; proposed mechanism ← H9

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: The grain-boundary-free single-crystalline morphology suppresses intergranular microcracking under high-voltage cycling.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

## H7 (mechanism)
Statement: The dual-site Sn modification, bulk Sn doping plus the residual surface Li2SnO3 layer, produces the improved high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: SC-Sn-NCA90 made at 750 °C shows better electrochemical reversibility than undoped single-crystalline NCA made by conventional high-temperature calcination.
Links: composition → H2

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: The Sn-modified single-crystalline NCA90 synthesized at 750 °C exhibits both structural (grain-boundary-free) and electrochemical (higher rate capability and better capacity retention) advantages compared to conventional undoped single-crystalline NCA90 synthesized at 900 °C.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5

# Main hypothesis
Can coating the Ni0.90Co0.08Al0.02(OH)2 (NCA90) precursor with Sn(OH)2 yield well-dispersed single-crystalline LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2 at 750 °C, the calcination condition that gives polycrystalline NCA90 without Sn, through Sn-driven grain-boundary elimination; and does the incorporated Sn (bulk doping plus a surface Li2SnO3 phase) improve high-voltage (2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V) electrochemical stability?
System: Ni-rich layered NCA cathode powders (LiNi0.9Co0.08Al0.02O2) made from a commercial hydroxide precursor with LiOH·H2O (Li/TM = 1.05); DFT models of Sn-doped NCA
Conditions: Calcination 500 °C for 5 h then 750 °C for 24 h (main samples); temperature, Sn loading and hold-time series; 0.8 mol% Sn(OH)2 coating for SC-Sn-NCA90; Li-metal half-cells at 25 °C, 2.8-4.5 V and 2.8-4.7 V, 1 C = 200 mA g-1
Scope limits: Half-cell data only; no full cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare high-voltage electrochemical performance of SC-Sn-NCA90 with PC-NCA90 and identify the structural and interfacial origins of any difference. (aspects: H5, H6, H7)
- R2: Establish whether the lower synthesis temperature enabled by Sn confers structural and electrochemical benefits relative to conventional high-temperature single-crystal synthesis without Sn. (aspects: H2, H8)

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)

## H1 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity of NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH relative to the Pt/3D-Gr benchmark.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity and 12-h stability of NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: OER activity of NiFe/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH relative to the IrO2/3D-Gr benchmark.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: OER activity and 12-h stability of NiFe/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl.

## H5 (claim)
Statement: The comparable activity observed in 1 M KOH and 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl confirms the robustness of the catalysts (NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr and NiFe/3D-Gr) and their tolerance to saline environments.

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity of NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH relative to the Pt/3D-Gr benchmark.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity and 12-h stability of NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: OER activity of NiFe/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH relative to the IrO2/3D-Gr benchmark.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: OER activity and 12-h stability of NiFe/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl.

## H5 (claim)
Statement: In 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl, NiFe/3D-Gr showed OER activity comparable to 1 M KOH (309 ± 17 vs 318 ± 10 mV at 100 mA cm-2, comparable Tafel slope), whereas NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr remained HER-active but with a higher overpotential (221 ± 29 vs 155 ± 13 mV at -100 mA cm-2) and lower maximum current density; both changed by less than 30 mV over 12 h of chronopotentiometry at 100 mA cm-2 current magnitude in the saline electrolyte, supporting saline tolerance under these test conditions.
Links: scoped evidence ← O2; scoped evidence ← O5

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: HER linear sweep voltammetry in 1 M KOH of NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr, benchmark, preparation variants and a TCP-supported electrode.
Manipulation: NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr was compared with Pt/3D-Gr; with NiCo/3D-Gr (Ce(NO3)3 omitted from the electrolyte) and with NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr prepared without the intercalation step (same electrodeposition and thermal route otherwise); and with NiCo-CeO2 prepared on Toray carbon paper (NiCo-CeO2/TCP). Three-electrode cell, graphite rod counter, Ag/AgCl reference, 25 mL electrolyte.
Measurements: LSV; Tafel slope

Measurements: LSV; Tafel slope; Chronopotentiometry; Cyclic voltammetry (Cdl); EIS

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H4, H9)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H5, H6, H7, H8, H11)
- R5: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H10)

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Two-cycle surface modification of 3C-SiC nanoparticles (hydroxylation, then APTES silanization) and characterization of the powders.

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H4, H9)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H5, H6, H7, H8, H11)
- R5: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H10)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: APTES-functionalized cubic SiC nanoparticles added to the carbon paste raise the PCE of p-i-n C-PSCs from 14.75% to 18.43% (champion devices) by improving paste rheology and contact with the ETL, reducing series resistance and hysteresis.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9; composition → H10; composition → H11; composition → H13

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface without changing the SiC crystal structure, and SiC and APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Pristine SiC and SiC-APTES differ in how they change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES to the carbon paste changes the photovoltaic performance (PCE, JSC, VOC, FF, Rs, Rsh, hysteresis) of p-i-n C-PSCs relative to the pure carbon paste control.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H12

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the cross-sectional structure of the carbon electrode and its contact with the underlying C60/Cr layers.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the interfacial charge-transport resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon contact.
Links: composition ← H1

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change the bulk conductivity of the carbon electrode.
Links: composition ← H1

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: The additives change leakage and recombination behaviour of the devices (shunt resistance, reverse-bias dark current, recombination resistance, trap density).
Links: composition ← H1

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Average device PCE depends on the additive loading in the paste, with an optimal loading window for SiC and for SiC-APTES.
Links: composition ← H1

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: Stability of p-i-n C-PSCs made with and without additive-containing carbon electrodes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: APTES added directly (not anchored to SiC) to the carbon paste changes device performance.
Links: composition ← H1

## H12 (mechanism)
Statement: APTES functionalization disperses SiC and keeps the paste flowable, giving void-free carbon films in intimate contact with C60; the resulting reduction of contact resistance at the C60/Cr/carbon interface is the primary origin of the PCE gain.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

## H13 (aspect)
Statement: Adding SiC or SiC-APTES shifts the work function of the carbon electrode, changing energy-level alignment at the C60/Cr/carbon contact and thereby contributing to the device changes.
Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H4, H9)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H5, H6, H7, H8, H11)
- R5: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H10)

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Two-cycle surface modification of 3C-SiC nanoparticles (hydroxylation, then APTES silanization) and characterization of the powders.
Manipulation: As-received SiC nanoparticles (50 nm nominal, beta form; 200 mg) were activated in 0.5 M aqueous KOH, ultrasonically dispersed for 30 min, treated in a home-built vibro-heating reactor at 130 °C for 90 min, centrifuged and rinsed twice with water, redispersed in IPA and dried by rotary evaporation to give SiC-OH (~90% yield). SiC-OH was then redispersed by sonication in 3 mL 1-butanol, mixed with 1 mL anhydrous DMF and 1 mL APTES, vibro-heated for 90 min, washed with IPA by repeated centrifugation and dried to give SiC-APTES.
Measurements: FTIR (Jasco FT/IR-4700AC); Powder XRD (Rigaku MiniFlex-600, Cu-Kalpha); PYS (vacuum <10^-2 Pa); SEM (JEOL JSM-IT700HR, 5 keV) particle diameter

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H4, H9)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H5, H6, H7, H8, H11)
- R5: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H10)

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Two-cycle surface modification of 3C-SiC nanoparticles (hydroxylation, then APTES silanization) and characterization of the powders.
Manipulation: As-received SiC nanoparticles (50 nm nominal, beta form; 200 mg) were activated in 0.5 M aqueous KOH, ultrasonically dispersed for 30 min, treated in a home-built vibro-heating reactor at 130 °C for 90 min, centrifuged and rinsed twice with water, redispersed in IPA and dried by rotary evaporation to give SiC-OH (~90% yield). SiC-OH was then redispersed by sonication in 3 mL 1-butanol, mixed with 1 mL anhydrous DMF and 1 mL APTES, vibro-heated for 90 min, washed with IPA by repeated centrifugation and dried to give SiC-APTES.
Measurements: FTIR (Jasco FT/IR-4700AC); Powder XRD (Rigaku MiniFlex-600, Cu-Kalpha); PYS (vacuum <10^-2 Pa); SEM (JEOL JSM-IT700HR, 5 keV) particle diameter

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H4, H9)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H5, H6, H7, H8, H11)
- R5: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H10)

# Main hypothesis
Does adding APTES-functionalized cubic SiC (SiC-APTES) nanoparticles to a home-made carbon paste improve the performance and stability of p-i-n carbon-electrode perovskite solar cells (C-PSCs), and through which changes in paste and electrode properties?
System: p-i-n C-PSCs with stack FTO/MeO-2PACz/Al2O3/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3 (EDAI2-passivated)/C60 (20 nm)/Cr (5 nm)/bar-coated carbon electrode (~12 µm); carbon paste of ethylcellulose, graphite and carbon black in butanol, with or without pristine 3C-SiC or SiC-APTES nanoparticles
Conditions: Additive loading 0-60 mg per 373 mg carbon paste composite (0-16 wt%); J-V under AM1.5G pseudo-sunlight at 100 mW cm-2 with a 0.08 cm2 light mask; Device fabrication in a N2-filled glovebox
Scope limits: Single perovskite composition and single C60/Cr electron-transport stack; Laboratory-scale masked cells
Validation requirements:
- R1: Verify that APTES is attached to the SiC nanoparticle surface and that SiC/APTES signatures are present in the deposited carbon electrode. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare how pristine SiC and SiC-APTES change carbon paste viscosity across additive loadings. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the photovoltaic performance of p-i-n C-PSCs made with control, SiC-containing and SiC-APTES-containing carbon pastes, including the dependence on additive loading. (aspects: H4, H9)
- R4: Determine which paste and electrode properties change with the additives and which of them account for the device changes. (aspects: H5, H6, H7, H8, H11)
- R5: Assess the stability of the devices made with each carbon paste. (aspects: H10)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: APTES-functionalized cubic SiC nanoparticles added to the carbon paste raise the PCE of p-i-n C-PSCs from 14.75% to 18.43% (champion devices) by improving paste rheology and contact with the ETL, reducing series resistance and hysteresis.

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Two-cycle surface modification of 3C-SiC nanoparticles (hydroxylation, then APTES silanization) and characterization of the powders.
Manipulation: As-received SiC nanoparticles (50 nm nominal, beta form; 200 mg) were activated in 0.5 M aqueous KOH, ultrasonically dispersed for 30 min, treated in a home-built vibro-heating reactor at 130 °C for 90 min, centrifuged and rinsed twice with water, redispersed in IPA and dried by rotary evaporation to give SiC-OH (~90% yield). SiC-OH was then redispersed by sonication in 3 mL 1-butanol, mixed with 1 mL anhydrous DMF and 1 mL APTES, vibro-heated for 90 min, washed with IPA by repeated centrifugation and dried to give SiC-APTES.
Measurements: FTIR (Jasco FT/IR-4700AC); Powder XRD (Rigaku MiniFlex-600, Cu-Kalpha); PYS (vacuum <10^-2 Pa); SEM (JEOL JSM-IT700HR, 5 keV) particle diameter

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)

## H1 (aspect)

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: OER activity of NiFe/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH relative to the IrO2/3D-Gr benchmark.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: OER activity and 12-h stability of NiFe/3D-Gr in 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl.

## H5 (claim)
Statement: In 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl, NiFe/3D-Gr maintained OER performance comparable to 1 M KOH (309 ± 17 mV at 100 mA cm-2) with comparable Tafel slope, whereas NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr showed a slight HER performance decrease, with a higher overpotential (221 ± 29 mV at -100 mA cm-2) and lower maximum current density but a similar Tafel slope.

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show antibacterial activity against planktonic MRSA and E. coli and against their biofilms, with and without NIR. (aspects: H1, H5)
- R2: Show biocompatibility of the material in vitro and in vivo. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Show accelerated healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds with tissue-level bacterial clearance, repair and inflammation readouts. (aspects: H2, H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR kills planktonic MRSA and E. coli more effectively than the other material and irradiation arms.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR accelerates closure of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR reduces tissue bacterial burden and improves tissue repair (collagen, angiogenesis) in the infected diabetic wound.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: At the concentrations used for antibacterial treatment, Fe-WS2@GOx with and without irradiation is tolerated by host systems: viability of a normal mammalian cell line is preserved, erythrocyte lysis stays within an acceptable limit, and treated animals show no loss of body weight, no abnormal blood counts and no histological damage in heart, liver, spleen, lung or kidney.
Links: experimental target ← E2

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Fe-WS2@GOx with irradiation acts on biofilm-associated MRSA and E. coli as well as on planktonic cells, reducing biofilm biomass and the viable cells recovered from an established biofilm rather than only preventing growth of suspended bacteria.

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide

# Main hypothesis

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Chronic cadmium exposure protocol with in vivo follow-up of body weight, blood glucose and systolic blood pressure at week 0 and week 8.
Manipulation: Male Wistar rats of about 200 g were randomly assigned with a digital randomiser to control, CdCl2 40 ppm or CdCl2 80 ppm; cadmium chloride was given in the drinking water for 8 weeks. ## E2
Statement: Acetylcholine concentration-response curves in phenylephrine-precontracted aortic rings, with and without apocynin preincubation.
Manipulation: After ketamine-xylazine anaesthesia and euthanasia by thoracotomy, the thoracic aorta was cleaned and cut into 3-mm rings mounted between stainless-steel wires in 5-mL organ baths with Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2. # Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that the exposure protocol produces the intended hypertensive phenotype, with systolic blood pressure compared between week 0 and week 8 in each group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H2, H3, H4)

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).

Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show that Fe substitution produces a defect-rich (sulfur-vacancy) Fe-WS2 with altered electronic structure, that GOx is loaded, and that the material converts NIR to heat.
- R2: Show the enzyme-like catalytic activities of the nanozyme (POD-, GOx-, CAT- and GPx-like).
- R3: Show antibacterial activity against planktonic MRSA and E. coli and against their biofilms, with and without NIR.
- R4: Show that bacterial killing involves ferroptosis-associated changes and interference with the ETC and energy metabolism.
- R5: Show biocompatibility of the material in vitro and in vivo.
- R6: Show macrophage polarization from M1 toward M2 in vitro and in wound tissue.
- R7: Show accelerated healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds with tissue-level bacterial clearance, repair and inflammation readouts.

## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Iron substitution into WS2 produces a defect-rich material with additional sulfur vacancies and a changed electronic structure (surface electron density, states near the Fermi level, band gap) relative to undoped WS2.
Links: composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Glucose oxidase is loaded onto the defect-engineered carrier, and the loaded amount is quantified rather than inferred from a single spectroscopic feature.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The material absorbs 808 nm light and converts it into heat reproducibly, with the temperature rise measured as a function of concentration and laser power and shown to be stable over repeated irradiation cycles.
Links: composition → H15

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The defect-engineered material has higher peroxidase-like activity than the undoped material, converting H2O2 into oxidizing species, tested against the undoped material at matched concentration.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The loaded enzyme oxidizes glucose to gluconic acid and H2O2, shown by glucose-dependent acidification, oxygen consumption and H2O2 accumulation against a glucose-free comparator.
Links: proposed mechanism → H10

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: The material decomposes H2O2 to O2 (catalase-like activity), measured as dissolved-oxygen evolution against H2O2 without material in the same buffer.

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: The material consumes reduced glutathione (glutathione-peroxidase-like activity), measured as residual GSH over time and concentration against a material-free GSH control.

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: The material with 808 nm irradiation reduces the number of viable planktonic MRSA and E. coli relative to material alone, irradiation alone and untreated controls at a stated material concentration.
Links: composition → H9; proposed mechanism ← H10; proposed mechanism ← H11; proposed mechanism → H16

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: The same treatment reduces biofilm biomass and the viable cells recovered from established MRSA and E. coli biofilms, which planktonic killing does not predict because matrix penetration and biofilm physiology differ.
Links: composition ← H8

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: Treated bacteria show ferroptosis-associated biochemistry measured in the bacteria themselves: increased intracellular reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, oxidation of glutathione and loss of glutathione-peroxidase activity.
Links: proposed mechanism → H8; proposed mechanism ← H5; competing explanation ← H15

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Treated bacteria show impaired energy metabolism demonstrated functionally, by respiratory-chain complex activities or respiration rate and by ATP normalized to viable cells or total protein, rather than by transcript abundance alone.
Links: proposed mechanism → H8

## H12 (aspect)
Statement: The material at the treatment concentration is tolerated by host systems: normal mammalian cells remain viable, erythrocyte lysis stays within an acceptable limit, and treated animals show stable body weight, normal blood counts and no organ damage.

## H13 (aspect)
Statement: In stimulated macrophages in culture, treatment lowers the M1 surface marker and raises the M2 surface marker, quantified per cell by flow cytometry.
Links: proposed mechanism → H17

## H14 (aspect)

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10; composition → H11

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H6

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: The Al-doping level sets the rate of in-situ dry reforming of the adsorbed CO2.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping increases the CO2 capture rate of the DFMs (fast carbonation and diffusion through the CaCO3 product layer) relative to CaO and across x, in proportion to oxygen-vacancy content.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H12

## H12 (mechanism)
Statement: Oxygen vacancies in the Al-doped perovskite, in contact with CaO, provide O2− migration channels through the CaCO3 layer that speed carbonation of inner CaO (proposed).
Links: proposed mechanism → H11

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H11

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H6

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: The Al-doping level sets the rate of in-situ dry reforming of the adsorbed CO2.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Al-induced oxygen vacancies in LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO transport O2− through the CaCO3 layer during CO2 capture, accelerating CO2 uptake relative to materials without such vacancies.
Links: composition ← H5

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10; composition → H11

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H6

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: The Al-doping level sets the rate of in-situ dry reforming of the adsorbed CO2.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Whether Al-induced oxygen vacancies provide O2− migration pathways through the CaCO3 product layer that accelerate CO2 uptake during carbonation remains to be validated.
Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism → H11

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H11

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H6

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: The Al-doping level sets the rate of in-situ dry reforming of the adsorbed CO2.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Test whether the Al-induced oxygen vacancies in LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture relative to the same DFMs without vacancies.
Links: composition ← H5; proposed mechanism ← H2; proposed mechanism ← [unlisted]

# Main hypothesis
Does B-site Al substitution in LaNiO3 within one-pot sol-gel LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO dual-functional materials (DFMs) preserve the perovskite lattice so that Ni nanoparticles (NPs) dissolve into it during oxidative CO2 capture and exsolve from it during reductive CH4 conversion, create oxygen vacancies that speed CO2 capture, and thereby give high and durable integrated CO2 capture and in-situ dry reforming of methane (iCCC-DRM)?
System: LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5; La:Ni:Al:Ca molar ratio 1:(1-x):x:10) made by one-pot sol-gel synthesis and calcined at 800 °C, compared with impregnated Ni/CaO (5 wt% Ni) and a physical mixture of separately made LaNi0.8Al0.2O3 and CaO (about 5.0 wt% Ni), tested in a fixed-bed reactor
Conditions: H2 prereduction at 700 °C (10 vol% H2/N2, 2 h); CO2 capture from simulated flue gas of 10 vol% CO2 and 2 vol% O2 in N2 at 625–700 °C, 650 °C standard; N2 purge for 5 min; In-situ conversion with 5 vol% CH4/N2 at the capture temperature
Scope limits: About 0.1 g DFM per fixed-bed test; Cycling up to 25 cycles for the comparison DFMs and 50 cycles for LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO; Simulated flue gas of CO2 and O2 in N2
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish whether Al enters the LaNiO3 B-site lattice and how it changes Ni valence and oxygen vacancies. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Establish whether the perovskite survives reductive Ni exsolution and whether Ni dissolves and exsolves reversibly across the capture and conversion steps. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Determine how the Al-doping level affects CO2 capture and CO2/CH4 conversion at 650 °C. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Test whether oxygen vacancies created by Al doping provide O2− migration channels that speed CO2 capture. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R5: Determine cyclic durability and resistance to Ni sintering and coking compared with conventional Ni/CaO and the other comparison DFMs. (aspects: H6, H7, H8, H9)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Al-doped LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO DFMs give efficient and durable iCCC-DRM through reversible Ni exsolution-dissolution in a preserved perovskite lattice.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; composition → H10

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Al3+ substitutes into the LaNiO3 B-site, contracting the lattice, raising the Ni2+/Ni3+ ratio and increasing oxygen vacancies in the DFMs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping keeps the perovskite phase intact when Ni exsolves under reduction, whereas undoped LaNiO3/CaO decomposes.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Within one capture–conversion cycle on LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO, Ni dissolves into the perovskite under the oxidative CO2 capture step and exsolves as metallic Ni NPs under the reductive CH4 conversion step.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: At 650 °C the Al-doping level x sets CO2 and CH4 conversion efficiency, with an optimum at intermediate x, while CO2 capture capacity stays similar across x.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Cyclic durability of iCCC-DRM performance and resistance of Ni NPs to sintering and coking.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Over repeated cycles, Ni/CaO, undoped LaNiO3/CaO and the physically mixed LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO-PM lose CO2 capture capacity and CH4 conversion relative to the one-pot Al-doped DFM.
Links: composition ← H6

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO retains CO2 capture capacity and CO2/CH4 conversion over 50 cycles at 650 °C.
Links: composition ← H6

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Al doping strengthens the metal-support interaction of exsolved Ni NPs, limiting Ni sintering and coking over cycles.
Links: composition ← H6

## H10 (aspect)
Statement: The Al-doping level sets the rate of in-situ dry reforming of the adsorbed CO2.
Links: composition ← H1

## H11 (aspect)
Statement: Al-induced oxygen vacancies in the LaNi1-xAlxO3/CaO perovskite provide oxygen vacancies that act as O2− migration channels, speeding CO2 adsorption and uptake during the oxidative CO2 capture step compared with the same material without the vacancies.
Links: composition ← R4
