# Main hypothesis
Does joining electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nonwoven layers and solution-cast chitosan (CH) sheets by heating at the PCL melting range into trilayer films (PCL/CH/PCL or CH/PCL/CH), with PCL from a medical-grade (PCLm) or technical-grade (PCLt) polymer, enhance film properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film, particularly mechanical performance, for food packaging use?
System: Glycerol-plasticized cast chitosan film combined with electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwovens as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH and CH/PCLm/CH trilayers; comparator: monolayer chitosan film without PCL fibers
Conditions: Trilayers heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side; Laboratory film tests: tensile, gravimetric water uptake, contact angle, water vapor and gas permeability, SEM, UV-VIS, DSC, and mass loss in PBS at 37 °C
Scope limits: Film-level laboratory measurements; no food contact or storage trials are reported; Per-film values for several endpoints are shown only in Figures 4-8, 11 and 12; the text reports selected values
Validation requirements:
- R1: Hydrophilic properties: moisture content, swelling degree, total soluble matter and water contact angle. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Degradation: mass loss of films incubated in PBS at 37 °C over 72 h. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Trilayer films of cast chitosan and electrospun PCL nonwovens joined by heating have enhanced packaging-relevant properties relative to a monolayer chitosan film.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: PCL layers reduce the hydrophilicity of the films relative to chitosan.
Links: composition ← H1; composition → H3

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Trilayer films take up and lose less water than chitosan: lower moisture content, swelling degree and total soluble matter.
Links: composition ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Films lose mass during incubation in PBS at 37 °C, with the extent depending on composition and layer arrangement.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5

## H5 (claim)
Statement: The observed mass loss confirms the biodegradable nature of the developed multilayer films and supports their potential use in short-term packaging or coating applications, where moderate durability is followed by environmentally safe degradation.
Links: refinement ← H4

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Gravimetric moisture content, swelling degree and total soluble matter of the neat chitosan film and the trilayer films.
Manipulation: Neat chitosan film: solution-cast from 2% w/v chitosan in 1% v/v aqueous acetic acid with 30% w/w glycerol. Trilayers: 10 x 10 cm pieces of chitosan film and electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwoven stacked between aluminum foils as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH or CH/PCLm/CH and heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side (2 min total), then cooled to room temperature and the foil removed. Masses recorded as prepared, after drying at 100 °C for 24 h, after 24 h immersion in 100 mL distilled water, and after re-drying at 100 °C for 24 h.
Measurements: MC; SD; TSM
Comparison: groups: neat chitosan film (CH); PCLt/CH/PCLt; PCLm/CH/PCLm; CH/PCLt/CH; CH/PCLm/CH | endpoint: moisture content (MC), swelling degree (SD), total soluble matter (TSM) | varied: presence of PCL nonwoven layers; layer arrangement; PCL grade | held fixed: drying at 100 °C for 24 h; 24 h immersion in 100 mL distilled water | unit: film sample; replicate number not reported | window: 24 h drying; 24 h immersion; 24 h re-drying | units: %
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: Mass loss of films incubated in phosphate-buffered saline at 37 °C.
Manipulation: Neat chitosan film: solution-cast from 2% w/v chitosan in 1% v/v aqueous acetic acid with 30% w/w glycerol. Trilayers: 10 x 10 cm pieces of chitosan film and electrospun PCLm or PCLt nonwoven stacked between aluminum foils as PCLt/CH/PCLt, PCLm/CH/PCLm, CH/PCLt/CH or CH/PCLm/CH and heated at 180 °C for 1 min per side (2 min total), then cooled to room temperature and the foil removed. # Main hypothesis
How do graded zoledronate exposures affect PDLSC survival and osteogenic differentiation, and do Wnt/beta-catenin and MAPK signaling functionally mediate the pro-osteogenic response at low dose?
System: Human PDLSCs from three healthy adolescent donors, cultured in vitro and implanted on beta-TCP at ectopic subcutaneous sites in nude mice
Conditions: ZOL 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, or 10 µM versus vehicle/control; in vitro cellular and osteogenic assays; 12-week ectopic implantation
Scope limits: Not an orthotopic periodontal defect model; No long-term stability or native-tissue integration measurement; Figure pixels and supplementary files were not inspected
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare graded ZOL concentrations for osteogenic promotion versus cytotoxic or osteogenesis-suppressing effects. (aspects: H1, H2, H3)
- R2: Assess whether Wnt/beta-catenin and p38/JNK MAPK pathway activity contributes functionally to low-dose ZOL-enhanced osteogenesis. (aspects: H4, H5)
- R3: Separate ectopic preclinical evidence from unresolved orthotopic, inflammatory, integration, and durability questions. (aspects: H6, H7, H8)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: ZOL has a dose- and endpoint-dependent biphasic effect on PDLSC osteogenesis rather than a single uniform response.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Low-dose ZOL, especially 0.5 µM in vitro and 0.1–0.5 µM ectopically in vivo, promotes osteogenic outcomes.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Higher ZOL exposure produces cytotoxicity and suppresses osteogenic outcomes, with the boundary depending on assay and context.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Beta-catenin stabilization contributes functionally to 0.5 µM ZOL-enhanced osteogenesis in cultured PDLSCs.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: p38 and JNK MAPK activation contributes functionally to 0.5 µM ZOL-enhanced osteogenesis in cultured PDLSCs.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

## H6 (claim)
Statement: ZOL concentration changes ectopic bone formation by PDLSC/beta-TCP constructs after 12 weeks; 1 and 10 µM increase new bone formation relative to control.
Links: refinement ← H7; refinement ← H8

## H7 (limitation)
Statement: Ectopic subcutaneous implantation does not establish efficacy in anatomical, vascular, inflammatory, and microbial conditions of periodontal defects.
Links: refinement → H6

## H8 (limitation)
Statement: Long-term stability of ZOL-induced bone and integration with native tissue were not assessed.
Links: refinement → H6

# Main hypothesis
Does active immunization of mice with purified recombinant murine keratin 14 (K14) or keratin 17 (K17) fusion protein produce an antigen-specific psoriasis-like disease model, that is, psoriasis-like skin lesions together with the histopathological and antigen-specific immune features reported for psoriasis?
System: Female wild-type BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice, 6-8 weeks old at purchase, immunized with Escherichia coli-expressed murine K14 or K17 fused to a GST or a His-Trigger-factor (TF) tag.
Conditions: Primary immunization: antigen emulsified in complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), injected intradermally into shaved dorsal skin (about 25 uL per site, 200 uL total per mouse; 350 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Booster immunization 3-4 weeks later: same antigen emulsified in incomplete Freund's adjuvant (IFA), injected subcutaneously (450 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Comparator groups: tag-only protein with the same adjuvant, an adjuvant-only group injected with CFA intradermally or IFA subcutaneously without protein, mice only anesthetized and hair-clipped (C57BL/6J additionally depilated), and topical imiquimod (IMQ; 10 mg/day to the tail base in BALB/c, 62.5 mg/day to dorsal skin in C57BL/6J, 7 consecutive days); no outcome is reported for the adjuvant-only group in the retrieved text.; Five independent experiments per mouse strain (two with GST-tagged proteins, three with TF-tagged proteins); per experiment 5 mice in the control and in the tag-control group and 10 mice in each of the K14 and K17 groups.
Scope limits: Female mice only; applicability to male mice was not evaluated.; Proof-of-concept study; no T-cell depletion, transfer or blocking experiment was performed.; Systematic longitudinal clinical scoring was not performed.; Figure images, supplementary figures and the supplementary table were not inspected for this workspace; values are taken from Results text and figure captions.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Immunization with K14 or K17 must produce psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, scales) in immunized mice, recorded with incidence, onset and duration alongside the adjuvant/tag and untreated comparator groups. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Lesional skin of immunized mice must show the histopathological hallmarks attributed to psoriasis (epidermal hyperplasia or thickening and inflammatory cell infiltration) relative to skin from comparator mice sampled at the same anatomical site. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Immunized mice must show an antigen-specific T-cell response, and the systemic inflammatory cytokine profile after immunization must be characterized. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R4: The induced phenotype must be attributable to the keratin moiety rather than to the fusion tag used to express it. (aspects: H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization with K14 or K17 fusion protein induces psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, white scales) at skin sites the authors designate as non-injection sites.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Lesional skin of immunized mice shows psoriasis-like histopathology: epidermal hyperplasia or measured epidermal thickening together with inflammatory cell infiltration.
Links: scoped evidence ← O4

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization generates K14/K17-reactive T cells, shown as increased IFN-gamma release by lymph node and spleen cells restimulated with keratin antigen ex vivo.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization changes the systemic inflammatory cytokine profile in blood at 7 days after primary immunization.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The clinical and immunological outcomes are attributable to the keratin moiety of the immunogen rather than to the GST or His-TF fusion tag carried by the recombinant protein.

## E1
Statement: Female BALB/c mice were immunized intradermally into shaved dorsal skin with CFA-emulsified GST-K14 (n = 10), GST-K17 (n = 10) or GST (n = 5) at 350 ug per mouse, and boosted subcutaneously three weeks later with 450 ug of the same protein emulsified in IFA; a further control group received 10 mg imiquimod daily to the tail base, an adjuvant control group received CFA intradermally or IFA subcutaneously without protein, and the untreated control group was only anesthetized and hair-clipped. Mice were examined for psoriasis-like skin lesions every day after immunization. Two independent experiments per strain used GST-tagged proteins.
Manipulation: Injected immunogen: GST-K14, GST-K17 or GST alone in adjuvant, against topical IMQ and clipping-only controls.
Measurements: Daily visual inspection of the skin; Photography of tails at the indicated time points; Proportion of mice with psoriasis-like symptoms per group

## E3

# Main hypothesis
Does a glucose-oxidase-loaded, Fe-substituted, sulfur-vacancy-rich WS2 nanozyme (Fe-WS2@GOx), combined with 808 nm NIR irradiation, kill MRSA and E. coli by ROS-mediated interference with the bacterial electron transport chain (ETC) and amplified bacterial ferroptosis, and accelerate healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds through antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects?
System: Synthesized WS2, Fe-WS2 and Fe-WS2@GOx nanozymes; planktonic and biofilm MRSA and E. coli in vitro; L929 fibroblasts, mouse erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; STZ-induced diabetic rodents with MRSA-infected dorsal wounds (three animals per group).
Conditions: 808 nm NIR at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min in the in vitro planktonic antibacterial assays; irradiation parameters for the bacterial mechanistic assays are not stated; In vivo: near-infrared irradiation at 1 W/cm2 for 10 min (wavelength not stated); In vivo dose: 5 uL of 50 ug/mL material applied to the infected site 24 h after MRSA inoculation; Mechanistic bacterial assays compare Control, NIR, Fe-WS2@GOx and Fe-WS2@GOx+NIR; In vivo endpoints over 12 days after treatment
Scope limits: Enzyme-like activities measured in cell-free buffer assays; Mechanistic assays use four groups without WS2 or Fe-WS2 arms; RNA sequencing only in E. coli; In vivo model uses MRSA only with n = 3 per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Show antibacterial activity against planktonic MRSA and E. coli and against their biofilms, with and without NIR. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show biocompatibility of the material in vitro and in vivo.
- R3: Show accelerated healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds with tissue-level bacterial clearance, repair and inflammation readouts. (aspects: H2, H3)

# Main hypothesis
Can a 2 x 2 single-chip SnO2 MEMS gas sensor array whose four units run at different temperatures under one heating voltage, combined with a physics-informed Hierarchical Kolmogorov-Arnold Mixture-of-Experts (HK-MoE) model, detect target-gas presence, classify, and determine the concentration of the lithium-ion-battery thermal-runaway gases H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, including after aging-induced sensor drift and in gas mixtures?
System: Solution-synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles dispensed on a 1.8 x 1.8 x 0.5 mm3 2 x 2 MEMS microheater array (Pt heating electrode line widths 8, 12, 16 and 20 um), read out as four resistance channels and analyzed by the HK-MoE model
Conditions: H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 at 100-500 ppm in discrete 100 ppm steps, balance nitrogen, with background air between injections; Heating voltage 1.9 V during gas sensing; Laboratory gas delivery; 25 C and 60% RH unless otherwise noted; Fresh array (Source Domain) and the same array after 30 days (Target Domain) and 60 days of continuous operational aging; Four mixtures of the four gases at 1000 ppm total concentration
Scope limits: Laboratory gas-delivery conditions; no measurement during actual battery thermal runaway; Aging studied on one array up to 60 days
Validation requirements:
- R1: The array must respond to H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and produce distinct temperature-modulated response patterns across its four units.
- R2: The model must perform three tasks: target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination. (aspects: H1)
- R3: Discrimination must remain usable after sensor drift caused by aging of the array. (aspects: H2)
- R4: Discrimination must be demonstrated for multi-component gas mixtures.
- R5: The device must be miniaturized, low-power and single-chip.

# Main hypothesis
Can a 2 x 2 single-chip SnO2 MEMS gas sensor array whose four units run at different temperatures under one heating voltage, combined with a physics-informed Hierarchical Kolmogorov-Arnold Mixture-of-Experts (HK-MoE) model, detect target-gas presence, classify, and determine the concentration of the lithium-ion-battery thermal-runaway gases H2, CO, CH4 and CO2, including after aging-induced sensor drift and in gas mixtures?
System: Solution-synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles dispensed on a 1.8 x 1.8 x 0.5 mm3 2 x 2 MEMS microheater array (Pt heating electrode line widths 8, 12, 16 and 20 um), read out as four resistance channels and analyzed by the HK-MoE model
Conditions: H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 at 100-500 ppm in discrete 100 ppm steps, balance nitrogen, with background air between injections; Heating voltage 1.9 V during gas sensing; Laboratory gas delivery; 25 C and 60% RH unless otherwise noted; Fresh array (Source Domain) and the same array after 30 days (Target Domain) and 60 days of continuous operational aging; Four mixtures of the four gases at 1000 ppm total concentration
Scope limits: Laboratory gas-delivery conditions; no measurement during actual battery thermal runaway; Aging studied on one array up to 60 days
Validation requirements:
- R1: The array must respond to H2, CO, CH4 and CO2 and produce distinct temperature-modulated response patterns across its four units.
- R2: The model must perform three tasks: target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination. (aspects: H1)
- R3: Discrimination must remain usable after sensor drift caused by aging of the array. (aspects: H2)
- R4: Discrimination must be demonstrated for multi-component gas mixtures.
- R5: The device must be miniaturized, low-power and single-chip.

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: On the fresh array, HK-MoE performs target-gas presence detection, gas classification and concentration determination.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HK-MoE discrimination remains usable after aging-induced drift of the same array.
Links: composition → H3; composition → H4; proposed mechanism ← H8

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Task-wise HK-MoE performance on the 30-day-aged Target Domain relative to the fresh Source Domain and to baseline models.
Links: composition ← H2

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Task-wise HK-MoE performance after 60 days of aging.
Links: composition ← H2; refinement → H5; refinement → H6

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Few-shot calibration with a small number of labeled samples from the aged array recovers classification and concentration performance.
Links: refinement ← H4; refinement → H7

## H6 (claim)
Statement: Under the 60-day aging condition HK-MoE reached F1 of 94.83% (presence), 53.59% (classification) and 30.65% (concentration), indicating that prolonged drift primarily degrades classification and concentration determination while presence detection, the primary requirement for early warning, remains reliable.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Under the 60-day aging condition HK-MoE reached F1 of 94.83% (presence), 53.59% (classification) and 30.65% (concentration) on the 60-day dataset; with concentration-balanced sampling and k = 100 labeled samples, the F1-scores for gas classification and concentration determination recovered to 83.50% and 72.92%, respectively.
Links: refinement ← H5

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: Performance degradation after aging could arise from SnO2 grain growth, changes in oxygen-vacancy concentration, heater-resistance change, thermal-stress accumulation and slight changes in the temperature distribution across units.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2

# Main hypothesis
Can a stacking machine-learning model trained on a curated database of screen-printed p-MPSC fabrication records predict device PCE accurately, identify composition and processing features associated with PCE, yield molecular-fingerprint screening rules for precursor additives, and guide the fabrication of higher-PCE devices?
System: Printable hole-conductor-free mesoscopic perovskite solar cells (p-MPSCs; mp-TiO2/mp-ZrO2/porous carbon) fabricated by screen printing, and a database of in-house and literature device records
Conditions: 237 in-house experimental records and 841 literature entries; 54 features encoded from 15 process-related factors; Stacking ensemble of six tree-based base learners with a linear-regression meta-learner; SHAP interpretation of the stacking model; RDKit MACCS fingerprints for 231 precursor additives; Laboratory device fabrication with J-V measurement
Scope limits: Figures and supplementary tables were not inspected; only values stated in the main text are used.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the stacking model's PCE prediction accuracy with r, R2, RMSE and MAE.
- R2: Verify model predictions against devices fabricated for validation.
- R3: Identify key factors influencing device PCE through model interpretability analysis.
- R4: Formulate screening rules for precursor additives based on molecular fingerprints.
- R5: Use model-proposed strategies to fabricate a higher-PCE device.
- R6: Project the PCE attainable through model-proposed optimization strategies.

Can a stacking machine-learning model trained on a curated database of screen-printed p-MPSC fabrication records predict device PCE accurately, identify composition and processing features associated with PCE, yield molecular-fingerprint screening rules for precursor additives, and guide the fabrication of higher-PCE devices?
System: Printable hole-conductor-free mesoscopic perovskite solar cells (p-MPSCs; mp-TiO2/mp-ZrO2/porous carbon) fabricated by screen printing, and a database of in-house and literature device records
Conditions: 237 in-house experimental records and 841 literature entries; 54 features encoded from 15 process-related factors; Stacking ensemble of six tree-based base learners with a linear-regression meta-learner; SHAP interpretation of the stacking model; RDKit MACCS fingerprints for 231 precursor additives; Laboratory device fabrication with J-V measurement
Scope limits: Figures and supplementary tables were not inspected; only values stated in the main text are used.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the stacking model's PCE prediction accuracy with r, R2, RMSE and MAE.
- R2: Verify model predictions against devices fabricated for validation.
- R3: Identify key factors influencing device PCE through model interpretability analysis.
- R4: Formulate screening rules for precursor additives based on molecular fingerprints.
- R5: Use model-proposed strategies to fabricate a higher-PCE device.
- R6: Project the PCE attainable through model-proposed optimization strategies.

# Main hypothesis
Does oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, reduce infarct size after LAD ligation ischemia-reperfusion in Wistar rats, and do reductions in inflammation and oxidative stress account for the protection?
System: Adult Wistar rats (150-200 g; equal numbers of males and females) with LAD ligation (45 min ischemia) followed by reperfusion
Conditions: Preventive model: daily oral dosing for 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31; Treatment model: 45 min ischemia, reperfusion for 7 days; dosing from 4 h after reperfusion, once daily until day 7; Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg (preventive) and 90 or 180 mg/kg (treatment); combination Oxystorm 90 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (preventive) or Oxystorm 180 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (treatment); Controls: vehicle (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control, verapamil 10 mg/kg LAD positive control
Scope limits: Single rat LAD ischemia-reperfusion model; Endpoints: TTC infarct size, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, MDA, SOD and GSH
Validation requirements:
- R1: Measure TTC infarct size in each group of both models. (aspects: H3)
- R2: Measure IL-6 and TNF-alpha after ischemia-reperfusion. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Measure oxidative stress markers in heart homogenates. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Explicate the probable mechanisms underlying any cardioprotective effect. (aspects: H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, protects the rat myocardium against LAD ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: LAD ligation with 45 min ischemia and reperfusion produces myocardial injury relative to control animals (larger infarct, higher injury biomarkers, inflammation and oxidative stress).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce TTC-defined infarct size relative to the LAD control.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: TTC infarct size in the preventive and treatment LAD ischemia-reperfusion models.
Manipulation: In each model, 56 adult Wistar rats (150-200 g) were randomly assigned to 7 groups of 8 (4 male, 4 female): vehicle control (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control (ischemia-reperfusion alone), verapamil 10 mg/kg (LAD positive control), low-dose Oxystorm, high-dose Oxystorm, and Oxystorm + BCM-95. LAD ligation: 45 min ischemia, then reperfusion. Preventive model: Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg in water, orally, daily for 30 days; combination Oxystorm 90 mg/kg (in water) + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (in dimethyl sulfoxide), orally, 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31. Treatment model: Oxystorm 90 or 180 mg/kg; combination Oxystorm 180 mg/kg + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (2:1); dosing started 4 h after reperfusion and continued once daily until day 7 of reperfusion.
Measurements: Hearts sectioned horizontally into 4-5 slices, stained with 2% TTC (pH 7.8, 37 C, 30 min), fixed in paraformaldehyde and photographed; unstained and stained areas quantified in ImageJ as % of total myocardial area; Outcome assessment blinded to treatment allocation; one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc test
Comparison: groups: vehicle control (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose); sham; LAD control (ischemia-reperfusion alone); verapamil 10 mg/kg (LAD, positive control); low-dose Oxystorm; high-dose Oxystorm; Oxystorm + BCM-95 combination | endpoint: Infarct (TTC-unstained) area as percentage of total myocardial area | varied: treatment group (formulation and dose, verapamil, or none); LAD ligation versus sham surgery | held fixed: 45 min LAD ischemia in ligated groups; model-specific dosing and reperfusion schedule | unit: rat (4-5 horizontal heart sections per rat) | window: Preventive model: day 31, after 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion per the dosing schedule and Figure 1 legend (the infarct-size Methods paragraph refers to the end of a 7-day reperfusion); treatment model: end of the 7-day reperfusion | units: % of total myocardial area | uncertainty: mean +/- SEM (Figure 4 legend)
Observations: O1, O2, O3, O4, O5

# Main hypothesis
Does oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, reduce infarct size after LAD ligation ischemia-reperfusion in Wistar rats, and do reductions in inflammation and oxidative stress account for the protection?
System: Adult Wistar rats (150-200 g; equal numbers of males and females) with LAD ligation (45 min ischemia) followed by reperfusion
Conditions: Preventive model: daily oral dosing for 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31; Treatment model: 45 min ischemia, reperfusion for 7 days; dosing from 4 h after reperfusion, once daily until day 7; Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg (preventive) and 90 or 180 mg/kg (treatment); combination Oxystorm 90 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (preventive) or Oxystorm 180 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (treatment); Controls: vehicle (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control, verapamil 10 mg/kg LAD positive control
Scope limits: Single rat LAD ischemia-reperfusion model; Endpoints: TTC infarct size, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, MDA, SOD and GSH
Validation requirements:
- R1: Measure TTC infarct size in each group of both models. (aspects: H3)
- R2: Measure IL-6 and TNF-alpha after ischemia-reperfusion. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Measure oxidative stress markers in heart homogenates. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Explicate the probable mechanisms underlying any cardioprotective effect. (aspects: H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, protects the rat myocardium against LAD ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: LAD ligation with 45 min ischemia and reperfusion produces myocardial injury relative to control animals (larger infarct, higher injury biomarkers, inflammation and oxidative stress).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce TTC-defined infarct size relative to the LAD control.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce the inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-alpha after ischemia-reperfusion.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce myocardial lipid peroxidation (MDA) and restore SOD and GSH after ischemia-reperfusion.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: The test formulations protect the myocardium through inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3; competing explanation ← H7

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: BCM-95 contributes the protection: BCM-95 alone reduces infarct size and tissue damage, and the combination group is more effective than high-dose Oxystorm alone because BCM-95 provides the antioxidant component absent from Oxystorm.
Links: competing explanation → H6

# Main hypothesis
Does oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, reduce infarct size after LAD ligation ischemia-reperfusion in Wistar rats, and do reductions in inflammation and oxidative stress account for the protection?
System: Adult Wistar rats (150-200 g; equal numbers of males and females) with LAD ligation (45 min ischemia) followed by reperfusion
Conditions: Preventive model: daily oral dosing for 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31; Treatment model: 45 min ischemia, reperfusion for 7 days; dosing from 4 h after reperfusion, once daily until day 7; Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg (preventive) and 90 or 180 mg/kg (treatment); combination Oxystorm 90 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (preventive) or Oxystorm 180 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (treatment); Controls: vehicle (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control, verapamil 10 mg/kg LAD positive control
Scope limits: Single rat LAD ischemia-reperfusion model; Endpoints: TTC infarct size, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, MDA, SOD and GSH
Validation requirements:
- R1: Measure TTC infarct size in each group of both models. (aspects: H3)
- R2: Measure IL-6 and TNF-alpha after ischemia-reperfusion. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Measure oxidative stress markers in heart homogenates. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Explicate the probable mechanisms underlying any cardioprotective effect. (aspects: H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, protects the rat myocardium against LAD ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: LAD ligation with 45 min ischemia and reperfusion produces myocardial injury relative to control animals (larger infarct, higher injury biomarkers, inflammation and oxidative stress).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce TTC-defined infarct size relative to the LAD control.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce the inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-alpha after ischemia-reperfusion.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce myocardial lipid peroxidation (MDA) and restore SOD and GSH after ischemia-reperfusion.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: The test formulations protect the myocardium through inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: Increased endothelial Nitric Oxide Synthase (eNOS) activity via nitric oxide (NO) production from Amaranthus flavonoids and nitrate; NO mediates vasodilation and anti-inflammatory effects.

# Main hypothesis
Does oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, reduce infarct size after LAD ligation ischemia-reperfusion in Wistar rats, and do reductions in inflammation and oxidative stress account for the protection?
System: Adult Wistar rats (150-200 g; equal numbers of males and females) with LAD ligation (45 min ischemia) followed by reperfusion
Conditions: Preventive model: daily oral dosing for 30 days; 45 min ischemia and 60 min reperfusion on day 31; Treatment model: 45 min ischemia, reperfusion for 7 days; dosing from 4 h after reperfusion, once daily until day 7; Oxystorm 45 or 90 mg/kg (preventive) and 90 or 180 mg/kg (treatment); combination Oxystorm 90 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (preventive) or Oxystorm 180 + BCM-95 90 mg/kg (treatment); Controls: vehicle (0.5% carboxymethyl cellulose), sham, LAD control, verapamil 10 mg/kg LAD positive control
Scope limits: Single rat LAD ischemia-reperfusion model; Endpoints: TTC infarct size, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, MDA, SOD and GSH
Validation requirements:
- R1: Measure TTC infarct size in each group of both models. (aspects: H3)
- R2: Measure IL-6 and TNF-alpha after ischemia-reperfusion. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Measure oxidative stress markers in heart homogenates. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Explicate the probable mechanisms underlying any cardioprotective effect. (aspects: H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Oral Oxystorm, alone or combined with BCM-95, protects the rat myocardium against LAD ischemia-reperfusion injury.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: LAD ligation with 45 min ischemia and reperfusion produces myocardial injury relative to control animals (larger infarct, higher injury biomarkers, inflammation and oxidative stress).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce TTC-defined infarct size relative to the LAD control.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce the inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-alpha after ischemia-reperfusion.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: The test formulations reduce myocardial lipid peroxidation (MDA) and restore SOD and GSH after ischemia-reperfusion.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: The test formulations protect the myocardium through inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: Alternative explanation: The observed reductions in infarct size, inflammatory cytokines, and oxidative stress markers may be due to the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory constituents of the formulations (e.g., flavonoids, phenolics, pigments) directly reducing oxidative stress and inflammation, rather than through the specific inhibition of inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways (H6).

# Main hypothesis
Whether the HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x electrodes on nickel foam differs between 1.0 M KOH and 1.0 M KOH + seawater, and what explains the difference observed for NiFe-LDH-4.
System: NiFe layered double hydroxide grown on nickel foam (NiFe-LDH-x, x = 1, 2, 4, 6) by one-step hydrothermal synthesis with urea and NH4F
Conditions: 1.0 M KOH (pH 13.7); 1.0 M KOH + seawater (pH 13.51); three-electrode half-cell tests
Scope limits: Laboratory-scale electrodes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH + seawater. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Explain the electrolyte dependence of NiFe-LDH-4 HER activity. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x across precursor ratios and relative to Pt/C.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; refinement → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH + seawater (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl, EIS, Bode kinetics).
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (claim)
Statement: The HER activity of NiFe-LDH-4 at −10 mA cm−2 is higher in 1.0 M KOH + seawater than in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential lower by 88.5 mV, Tafel slope lower by 53.6 mV dec−1).
Links: refinement ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Cl− adsorption on Fe sites in seawater modifies the surface into chlorine-resistant NiOOH and FeOOH, giving a Ni3+-rich surface that optimizes hydrogen adsorption (lower ΔGH) and speeds proton transfer through hydrogen-bond networks, thereby lowering the HER Tafel slope.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

# Main hypothesis
Whether the HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x electrodes on nickel foam differs between 1.0 M KOH and 1.0 M KOH + seawater, and what explains the difference observed for NiFe-LDH-4.
System: NiFe layered double hydroxide grown on nickel foam (NiFe-LDH-x, x = 1, 2, 4, 6) by one-step hydrothermal synthesis with urea and NH4F
Conditions: 1.0 M KOH (pH 13.7); 1.0 M KOH + seawater (pH 13.51); three-electrode half-cell tests
Scope limits: Laboratory-scale electrodes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH + seawater. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Explain the electrolyte dependence of NiFe-LDH-4 HER activity. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x across precursor ratios and relative to Pt/C.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; refinement → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH + seawater (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl, EIS, Bode kinetics).
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (claim)
Statement: The HER activity of NiFe-LDH-4 at −10 mA cm−2 is higher in 1.0 M KOH + seawater than in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential lower by 88.5 mV, Tafel slope lower by 53.6 mV dec−1).
Links: refinement ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5; proposed mechanism ← H6

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Cl− adsorption on Fe sites in seawater modifies the surface into chlorine-resistant NiOOH and FeOOH, giving a Ni3+-rich surface that optimizes hydrogen adsorption (lower ΔGH) and speeds proton transfer through hydrogen-bond networks, thereby lowering the HER Tafel slope.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4; competing explanation ← H6

## H6 (alternative)
Statement: The lower HER overpotential and Tafel slope of NiFe-LDH-4 in 1.0 M KOH + seawater at −10 mA cm−2 reflect a difference between the electrodes measured in the two electrolytes, chiefly a larger electrochemically accessible area (HER-set Cdl 0.011 versus 0.0016 mF cm−2) or electrode-to-electrode variation, rather than a chloride-induced change in the intrinsic surface chemistry.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4; competing explanation → H5

# Main hypothesis
Whether the HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x electrodes on nickel foam differs between 1.0 M KOH and 1.0 M KOH + seawater, and what explains the difference observed for NiFe-LDH-4.
System: NiFe layered double hydroxide grown on nickel foam (NiFe-LDH-x, x = 1, 2, 4, 6) by one-step hydrothermal synthesis with urea and NH4F
Conditions: 1.0 M KOH (pH 13.7); 1.0 M KOH + seawater (pH 13.51); three-electrode half-cell tests
Scope limits: Laboratory-scale electrodes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH + seawater. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Explain the electrolyte dependence of NiFe-LDH-4 HER activity. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x across precursor ratios and relative to Pt/C.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; refinement → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH + seawater (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl, EIS, Bode kinetics).
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (claim)
Statement: The HER activity of NiFe-LDH-4 at −10 mA cm−2 is higher in 1.0 M KOH + seawater than in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential lower by 88.5 mV, Tafel slope lower by 53.6 mV dec−1).
Links: refinement ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5; alternative explanation ← H6

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Cl− adsorption on Fe sites in seawater modifies the surface into chlorine-resistant NiOOH and FeOOH, giving a Ni3+-rich surface that optimizes hydrogen adsorption (lower ΔGH) and speeds proton transfer through hydrogen-bond networks, thereby lowering the HER Tafel slope.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

## H6 (alternative)
Statement: For NiFe-LDH-4 HER at the reported low-current comparison, the higher Cdl measured in 1.0 M KOH + seawater than in 1.0 M KOH may indicate greater electrochemically accessible area and could contribute to the lower overpotential at fixed geometric current. This is a candidate partial explanation, not an established cause; the Cdl difference alone does not explain the lower Tafel slope or exclude the proposed chloride-induced surface change.
Links: alternative explanation → H4

# Main hypothesis
Whether the HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x electrodes on nickel foam differs between 1.0 M KOH and 1.0 M KOH + seawater, and what explains the difference observed for NiFe-LDH-4.
System: NiFe layered double hydroxide grown on nickel foam (NiFe-LDH-x, x = 1, 2, 4, 6) by one-step hydrothermal synthesis with urea and NH4F
Conditions: 1.0 M KOH (pH 13.7); 1.0 M KOH + seawater (pH 13.51); three-electrode half-cell tests
Scope limits: Laboratory-scale electrodes
Validation requirements:
- R1: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare HER activity of the four ratios and Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH + seawater. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Explain the electrolyte dependence of NiFe-LDH-4 HER activity. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity of NiFe-LDH-x across precursor ratios and relative to Pt/C.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; refinement → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl).
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: HER activity in 1.0 M KOH + seawater (overpotential, Tafel slope, Cdl, EIS, Bode kinetics).
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (claim)
Statement: The HER activity of NiFe-LDH-4 at −10 mA cm−2 is higher in 1.0 M KOH + seawater than in 1.0 M KOH (overpotential lower by 88.5 mV, Tafel slope lower by 53.6 mV dec−1).
Links: refinement ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H5; competing explanation ← H6

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Cl− adsorption on Fe sites in seawater modifies the surface into chlorine-resistant NiOOH and FeOOH, giving a Ni3+-rich surface that optimizes hydrogen adsorption (lower ΔGH) and speeds proton transfer through hydrogen-bond networks, thereby lowering the HER Tafel slope.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4; competing explanation ← H6

## H6 (alternative)
Statement: Proposed alternative explanation: The lower HER overpotential and Tafel slope of NiFe-LDH-4 in 1.0 M KOH + seawater compared with 1.0 M KOH arises from a general electrolyte effect, such as changes in ionic strength, pH, cation composition, or the presence of Cl−, rather than a chloride-induced surface change on NiFe-LDH-4.
Links: competing explanation → H4; competing explanation → H5

# Main hypothesis
Does SIRT1 act as the deacetylase for GAPDH lysine 254 in microglia, and does the K254 acetylation state thereby set glycolytic flux and pro-inflammatory output during LPS/IFN-gamma activation?
System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH
Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+
Scope limits: in vitro only; no in vivo, aged or chronic low-grade inflammatory model was studied; GAPDH replacement reaches 75-80%, leaving residual endogenous wild-type protein; acetylation states are represented by K254Q and K254R substitutions rather than by enzymatically controlled acetylation in cells; figure images and supplementary files were not inspected during this extraction
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how inflammatory activation changes SIRT1 protein, NAD+-dependent deacetylase activity and NAD+ cofactor availability in microglia. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Show that the reported treatment and genotype differences are not produced by loss of cell viability. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Does SIRT1 act as the deacetylase for GAPDH lysine 254 in microglia, and does the K254 acetylation state thereby set glycolytic flux and pro-inflammatory output during LPS/IFN-gamma activation?
System: BV-2 murine microglia and CD11b+ primary microglia from postnatal day 3-5 C57BL/6J pups, plus a cell-free reaction with purified recombinant human SIRT1 and FLAG-tagged GAPDH
Conditions: acute stimulation with LPS (E. coli O111:B4) 100 ng/mL plus IFN-gamma 10 ng/mL for 6 or 24 h; pharmacological SIRT1 modulation with SRT1720 (5 uM) or EX-527 (10 uM), 1 h before stimulation; replacement of endogenous murine GAPDH (3'-UTR siRNA) by siRNA-resistant FLAG-tagged human GAPDH WT, K254Q or K254R; cell-free reactions at 37 C for 60 min with 500 uM NAD+

# Main hypothesis
Can grafting sulfonate-type zwitterionic side chains onto the hard segments of an IPDI/PTMG/MDEA polyurethane (ZESTPU) and swelling it with the ionic liquid [EMIM]+[BF4]− give an ionogel (ZESTI) that simultaneously has high tensile strength, stretchability and toughness, autonomous self-healing under ambient conditions, and high ionic conductivity, and can this ionogel serve as the active material of self-reporting packaging and strain-sensing iontronic devices?
System: ZESTI: zwitterionic side-chain engineered polyurethane (ZESTPU, made by reacting PMPU with 1,3-propanesultone) containing [EMIM]+[BF4]− ionic liquid; references are the unmodified polyurethane PMPU, IL-free ZESTPU, and the non-zwitterionic ionogel i-PMPU (PMPU + IL).
Conditions: IL content expressed as IL/(IL + PU) weight ratio; 30 wt% IL unless otherwise specified (10, 30 and 50 wt% also prepared); Tensile tests at room temperature, 10 mm min−1, three independent specimens; Self-healing at room temperature (24 h for cut-and-rejoin tests); scratch tests at ambient 20–40% relative humidity; EIS at room temperature, 0.1 Hz–1 MHz, 10 mV; temperature-dependent conductivity over 293.15–353.15 K
Scope limits: Single ionic liquid ([EMIM]+[BF4]−) and a single hard/soft segment ratio and zwitterion grafting condition; Autonomous self-healing is stated to be mainly applicable under ambient conditions and strongly limited at sub-zero temperatures; Device demonstrations are described as proof-of-concept rather than optimized products
Validation requirements:
- R1: High tensile strength, stretchability, Young's modulus and toughness of the ionogel (aspects: H1)
- R2: Chemical and structural verification of zwitterionic side-chain incorporation, of its interactions with the IL, and of the resulting nanostructure (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Mechanical performance of ZESTI: tensile strength, Young's modulus, elongation at break and toughness
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Effect of zwitterionic side-chain grafting on the mechanics of the IL-free polyurethane (ZESTPU versus PMPU)
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H6

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Effect of IL incorporation and IL content on the mechanics of the zwitterionic polyurethane (ZESTI versus ZESTPU; 10, 30 and 50 wt% IL)
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Microphase-separated nanostructure and its change with zwitterion grafting and IL incorporation
Links: proposed mechanism ← H6; composition → H5

## H5 (claim)
Statement: XRD of PMPU, ZESTPU, i-PMPU and ZESTI shows only broad amorphous halos at similar positions and no new diffraction peaks after IL incorporation, so no crystalline phase or long-range order forms in any sample. Because the samples are non-crystalline, XRD does not resolve hard-segment stacking or where the IL resides; hard-phase organization after IL incorporation is indicated by SAXS, which shows a decreased average domain spacing consistent with partial disruption of hard-phase aggregation.
Links: composition ← H4; scoped evidence ← O1; scoped evidence ← O4

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Dipole–dipole interactions among zwitterionic side chains strengthen hard-segment cohesion and promote hard-phase aggregation, so that hard phases act as dynamic physical cross-links and energy-dissipating units
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; proposed mechanism → H4

# Main hypothesis
Do TPBE scaffolds with periodic mild NIR promote neuronal differentiation and neurite outgrowth of PC12 cells and primary DRG neurons, and which signaling pathway is involved?
System: PC12 cells and primary mouse DRG neurons cultured with T, TP, TPB, TPBE or TPBE+NIR scaffolds

## H1 (aspect)
Statement: TPBE scaffolds, further with NIR, shift neuronal differentiation markers in PC12 cells and DRG neurons toward a mature neuronal profile.

# Main hypothesis
Do TPBE scaffolds with periodic mild NIR promote neuronal differentiation and neurite outgrowth of PC12 cells and primary DRG neurons, and which signaling pathway is involved?

# Main hypothesis
Can a stacking machine-learning model trained on a curated database of screen-printed p-MPSC fabrication records predict device PCE accurately, identify composition and processing features associated with PCE, yield molecular-fingerprint screening rules for precursor additives, and guide the fabrication of higher-PCE devices?
System: Printable hole-conductor-free mesoscopic perovskite solar cells (p-MPSCs; mp-TiO2/mp-ZrO2/porous carbon) fabricated by screen printing, and a database of in-house and literature device records
Conditions: 237 in-house experimental records and 841 literature entries; 54 features encoded from 15 process-related factors; Stacking ensemble of six tree-based base learners with a linear-regression meta-learner; SHAP interpretation of the stacking model; RDKit MACCS fingerprints for 231 precursor additives; Laboratory device fabrication with J-V measurement
Scope limits: Figures and supplementary tables were not inspected; only values stated in the main text are used.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish that the stacking model's PCE predictions are accurate for the devices whose fabrication it is used to guide. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Identify key factors influencing device PCE through model interpretability analysis. (aspects: H4)
- R3: Formulate screening rules for precursor additives based on molecular fingerprints. (aspects: H5)
- R4: Use model-proposed strategies to fabricate a higher-PCE device. (aspects: H6)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: An integrated ML framework (stacking PCE model, SHAP and fingerprint interpretation, and experimental validation) can guide the design of high-PCE p-MPSCs.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The stacking model predicts the PCE of held-out database entries (the 20% test split) with high correlation and low error, evaluated by r, R2, RMSE and MAE.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The stacking model predicts PCE more accurately than each of its six base learners trained on the same data.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: SHAP analysis of the stacking model identifies the features with the largest contributions to predicted PCE.
Links: composition ← H1

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: MACCS fingerprints of precursor additives with the largest contributions to model performance define screening rules for selecting precursor additives.
Links: composition ← H1

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Adding MACl (Cl content adjusted to the model-indicated value) and 5% formamide to a PACl-containing Control precursor raises device PCE.
Links: composition ← H1

Bears on: H4

Bears on: H5

Statement: Device PCE increased from 17.27% for the Control to 19.36% for the Target, and Jsc from 22.13 to 25.32 mA/cm2, while Voc and FF remained consistent.

Bears on: H6

# Main hypothesis
Whether Liuwei Dihuang Pills (LWDHP) alleviate cognitive deficits in APP/PS1 transgenic mice, and whether this is accompanied by changes in synaptic integrity, mitochondrial dynamics and ultrastructure, and cerebral IRS-1/AKT/GSK-3beta insulin signaling.
System: Male APP(Swedish K670N/M671L)/PSEN1dE9 transgenic mice and age/sex-matched wild-type C57BL/6J littermates
Conditions: LWDHP 0.675 g/kg/day by oral gavage for 8 weeks (stated as equivalent to 3.75 g/kg/day crude drug); memantine 3 mg/kg/day oral gavage as positive control group; cortex and hippocampus analyzed by immunofluorescence, transmission electron microscopy and western blot
Scope limits: single LWDHP dose; single treatment duration (8 weeks); male mice only; one transgenic AD model
Validation requirements:
- R1: Expression and phosphorylation of IRS-1/AKT/GSK-3beta pathway components (aspects: H1)
- R2: Tau phosphorylation in cortex and hippocampus (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Investigate the photodetection performance of devices with untreated and cryogenically treated MWCNTs under solar illumination and under different UV, Vis and NIR wavelengths. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs improves the photodetection performance of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices with untreated commercial MWCNTs.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

Links: composition ← H1

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Investigate the photodetection performance of devices with untreated and cryogenically treated MWCNTs under solar illumination and under different UV, Vis and NIR wavelengths. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (claim)
Statement: Cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs improves the photodetection performance of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices with untreated commercial MWCNTs.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Structural, surface and morphological changes of the MWCNTs produced by the cryogenic thermal-stress treatment relative to the commercial MWCNTs.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: The Cryo-MWCNT interlayer improves the photodetector performance of the MWCNT/n-Si device relative to the C-MWCNT interlayer.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Cryogenic treatment improves the electrical conductivity of the MWCNT layer and the MWCNT/n-Si interface quality, which improves photogenerated carrier separation and collection.
Links: proposed mechanism → H3; proposed mechanism → H5

## H5 (alternative)
Statement: The sub-linear power-law exponent (m=0.3615) may indicate trap-mediated charge transport rather than performance degradation, as interpreted by the authors (i06).
Links: proposed mechanism ← H4

# Main hypothesis
Does cryogenic thermal-stress treatment of commercial MWCNTs (liquid-nitrogen immersion followed by return to room temperature) change the MWCNT structure and improve the electrical and optoelectronic properties of Al/MWCNT/n-Si Schottky photodetectors relative to devices made with untreated commercial MWCNTs?
System: Al/MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors with a spin-coated interlayer of either commercial MWCNTs (C-MWCNT/n-Si) or cryogenically treated MWCNTs (Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si) on phosphorus-doped n-Si (1-20 ohm cm) with Al back and top contacts
Conditions: Cryogenic treatment: 2 cycles of 20 min liquid-nitrogen immersion and 5 min at room temperature; I-V from -5 V to +5 V in the dark and under 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mW cm-2 solar-simulator illumination; Spectral response at 351-1600 nm with narrowband band-pass filters at a fixed 20 mW cm-2 and zero bias
Scope limits: One treatment condition (the previously optimized cycle) compared with untreated commercial MWCNTs; No temperature-dependent measurements; the temperature of the I-V, I-t and spectral measurements is not stated (Raman at room temperature; BET by N2 adsorption at 77 K)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize the structural and surface changes produced by the cryogenic treatment using BET surface area analysis, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM and CTEM. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Compare the electrical and optoelectronic properties of the C-MWCNT/n-Si and Cryo-MWCNT/n-Si photodetectors to evaluate the effect of the cryogenic treatment. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Investigate the photodetection performance of devices with untreated and cryogenically treated MWCNTs under solar illumination and under different UV, Vis and NIR wavelengths. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Whether the hemoglobin-containing formulations (HB-PDA@Gel, HPC@Gel) relieve hypoxia-associated neuronal stress in HT22 neurons cultured at 1% O2 and in the injured rat cortex.
System: HPC@Gel and component formulations; HT22 neurons at 1% O2; rat right parietal cortical cavity TBI
Conditions: In vitro: 1% O2, 5% CO2, 37 °C, 24 h; In vivo: implants placed immediately after injury; tissue at days 3 and 7
Scope limits: In vitro n = 3 independent experiments; in vivo n = 6 animals per group
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterize oxygen release, oxygen-binding responsiveness and radical scavenging of the composite materials. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Test intracellular oxygenation and HIF-1α accumulation in hypoxic HT22 neurons. (aspects: H3, H4)
- R3: Test neuronal hypoxia-associated stress, neuronal apoptosis and microglial phenotype in the injured cortex. (aspects: H6, H5, H7)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: HPC nanoparticles retain oxygen-binding responsiveness, and HPC@Gel releases oxygen, with release derived from the hemoglobin-containing component.

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: The composite hydrogels scavenge radicals through their HB-PDA and CCQD components.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: HB-containing formulations improve intracellular oxygenation of HT22 neurons cultured at 1% O2.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: HB-containing formulations reduce HIF-1α accumulation in HT22 neurons cultured at 1% O2.

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Hydrogel treatment reduces neuronal apoptosis in the injured rat cortex.

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: HB-containing hydrogels relieve hypoxia-associated neuronal stress in the injured rat cortex.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H8; refinement → H9

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Treatment shifts microglia in the injured cortex from iNOS+ toward Arg-1+ phenotypes.

## H8 (mechanism)
Statement: Oxygen released from the hemoglobin in HB-PDA or HPC raises oxygen available to neurons in the injured tissue, lowering HIF-1α accumulation and hypoxia-associated stress.
Links: proposed mechanism → H6

## H9 (claim)
Statement: The HB-containing hydrogels alleviated hypoxia-associated neuronal stress in vivo.
Links: refinement ← H6; scoped evidence ← O7

# Main hypothesis
Whether the hemoglobin-containing formulations (HB-PDA@Gel, HPC@Gel) relieve hypoxia-associated neuronal stress in HT22 neurons cultured at 1% O2 and in the injured rat cortex.
System: HPC@Gel and component formulations; HT22 neurons at 1% O2; rat right parietal cortical cavity TBI

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Riboflavin molecules captured electrons from S. oneidensis cells through MtrC and OmcA and then reduced NCM, which accelerated metal oxide leaching.

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7; composition → H8

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Reduced riboflavin transfers electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension, and MtrC and OmcA are required for NCM reduction by the SO3-BS3 consortium; that S. oneidensis loads electrons onto riboflavin through MtrC and OmcA during leaching is a proposal taken from an earlier report and was not measured here, so the share of leaching carried by the shuttle rather than by direct cytochrome contact remains open.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: The relative contribution of direct MtrC/OmcA contact with NCM and of riboflavin shuttling to metal oxide leaching can be separated, for example by supplying reduced riboflavin to a consortium lacking both cytochromes or by titrating riboflavin at fixed cell density.
Links: composition ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Riboflavin is proposed to act as an electron shuttle in the electron-transfer route used by the S. oneidensis-containing consortia, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM after the electrons have reached the consortium through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA.
Links: refinement ← H2

# Main hypothesis
Can brewing wastewater serve as the leaching agent for the NCM (LiNixCoyMn1-x-yO2) cathode black mass of spent lithium-ion batteries when a synthetic two-species consortium of engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 catalyses NCM reduction, and how far does leaching rise when the consortium is engineered in turn for ethanol catabolism, riboflavin-mediated extracellular electron transfer (EET) and resistance to the leached metal ions?
System: Anaerobic brewing-wastewater cultures at 30 C containing 0.2 g/L spent-LIB NCM black mass, with engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and Bacillus subtilis 168 strains as single strains or two-species consortia
Conditions: brewing wastewater collected from one brewing factory in Moutai Town, Guizhou, containing 1.8% (v/v) ethanol; 0.2 g/L NCM black mass, 1% (v/v) inoculum, anaerobic bottles at 30 C for 14 days; plasmid-borne expression with 0.2 g/L chloramphenicol and 0.5 mM IPTG induction; dissolved Li, Ni, Co and Mn quantified by ICP-OES; EET rate quantified as maximum power density in H-type microbial fuel cells
Scope limits: 14-day anaerobic batch operation without pH or aeration control; leaching of the four cathode metals Li, Ni, Co and Mn only
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify how much metal is leached from NCM black mass in brewing wastewater with and without a bacterial catalyst, and whether the dissolved metals come with reduction of the high-valence species. (aspects: H1, H3)
- R2: Identify the route by which electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM. (aspects: H2)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Metal oxide leaching from spent-LIB NCM black mass held in brewing wastewater rises when NCM reduction is catalysed by S. oneidensis-containing consortia rather than by the wastewater alone.
Links: composition → H2; proposed mechanism ← H3

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Electrons generated by S. oneidensis reach solid NCM through the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA and through riboflavin acting as electron shuttle.
Links: composition ← H1; proposed mechanism ← H4; refinement → H5; refinement → H7

## H3 (mechanism)
Statement: Leaching proceeds through reduction of Ni3+, Co3+ and Mn4+ in NCM to the more soluble lower-valence species Ni2+, Co2+ and Mn2+/Mn3+, with wastewater organics as the electron source.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H4 (mechanism)
Statement: Riboflavin cycles between reduced and oxidised states as an electron shuttle, with reduced riboflavin passing electrons to NCM.
Links: proposed mechanism → H2; refinement → H6

## H5 (claim)
Statement: MtrC and OmcA of S. oneidensis are required for NCM reduction during metal oxide leaching.
Links: refinement ← H2

## H6 (aspect)
Statement: Riboflavin in its reduced form can pass electrons to NCM in a cell-free anoxic suspension.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (claim)
Statement: Electrons from S. oneidensis reach riboflavin, which then transfers them to NCM, with the outer-membrane c-type cytochromes MtrC and OmcA required for this electron-transfer route.
Links: refinement ← H2
