# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization with K14 or K17 fusion protein induces psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, white scales) at skin sites the authors designate as non-injection sites.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization elicits antigen-specific serum antibodies against K14/K17, detectable as IgM early and as IgG1 and IgG2b at later time points.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization generates K14/K17-reactive T cells, shown as increased IFN-gamma release by lymph node and spleen cells restimulated with keratin antigen ex vivo.
Links: competing explanation ← H7

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The clinical and immunological outcomes are attributable to the keratin moiety of the immunogen rather than to the GST or His-TF fusion tag carried by the recombinant protein.

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Molecular mimicry: K14 and K17 carry 'ALEEANxxL' and 'GLRRxLD' motifs identical to motifs of the streptococcal M protein, which the authors propose may allow these keratins to trigger autoimmune responses.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H6 (claim)
Statement: The low sequence identity between the fusion tags and K14, together with similar results obtained with two different fusion-tag systems, indicates that immunization with the K14/K17 moiety is primarily responsible for the induction of the psoriasis-like phenotype.
Links: scoped evidence ← O2; scoped evidence ← O6

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: Keratin-independent T-cell activation by the fusion tag: the same IFN-gamma readout was used for cells from both immunized groups, which were stimulated with the GST-tagged keratin antigen, so the higher IFN-gamma release could reflect a response to the fusion tag rather than to the keratin antigen; this remains a proposal because the antigen presented by the antigen-presenting cells was not measured.
Links: competing explanation → H3

# Main hypothesis
Does active immunization of mice with purified recombinant murine keratin 14 (K14) or keratin 17 (K17) fusion protein produce an antigen-specific psoriasis-like disease model, that is, psoriasis-like skin lesions together with the histopathological and antigen-specific immune features reported for psoriasis?
System: Female wild-type BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice, 6-8 weeks old at purchase, immunized with Escherichia coli-expressed murine K14 or K17 fused to a GST or a His-Trigger-factor (TF) tag.
Conditions: Primary immunization: antigen emulsified in complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), injected intradermally into shaved dorsal skin (about 25 uL per site, 200 uL total per mouse; 350 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Booster immunization 3-4 weeks later: same antigen emulsified in incomplete Freund's adjuvant (IFA), injected subcutaneously (450 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Comparator groups: tag-only protein with the same adjuvant, an adjuvant-only group injected with CFA intradermally or IFA subcutaneously without protein, mice only anesthetized and hair-clipped (C57BL/6J additionally depilated), and topical imiquimod (IMQ; 10 mg/day to the tail base in BALB/c, 62.5 mg/day to dorsal skin in C57BL/6J, 7 consecutive days); no outcome is reported for the adjuvant-only group in the retrieved text.; Five independent experiments per mouse strain (two with GST-tagged proteins, three with TF-tagged proteins); per experiment 5 mice in the control and in the tag-control group and 10 mice in each of the K14 and K17 groups.
Scope limits: Female mice only; applicability to male mice was not evaluated.; Proof-of-concept study; no T-cell depletion, transfer or blocking experiment was performed.; Systematic longitudinal clinical scoring was not performed.; Figure images, supplementary figures and the supplementary table were not inspected for this workspace; values are taken from Results text and figure captions.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Immunization with K14 or K17 must produce psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, scales) in immunized mice, recorded with incidence, onset and duration alongside the adjuvant/tag and untreated comparator groups. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Immunized mice must mount a measurable antigen-specific antibody response against K14/K17, resolved by isotype and time point. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Immunized mice must show an antigen-specific T-cell response, and the systemic inflammatory cytokine profile after immunization must be characterized. (aspects: H3)
- R4: The induced phenotype must be attributable to the keratin moiety rather than to the fusion tag used to express it. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization with K14 or K17 fusion protein induces psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, white scales) at skin sites the authors designate as non-injection sites.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization elicits antigen-specific serum antibodies against K14/K17, detectable as IgM early and as IgG1 and IgG2b at later time points.

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization generates K14/K17-reactive T cells, shown as increased IFN-gamma release by lymph node and spleen cells restimulated with keratin antigen ex vivo.

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The clinical and immunological outcomes are attributable to the keratin moiety of the immunogen rather than to the GST or His-TF fusion tag carried by the recombinant protein.
Links: competing explanation ← H7

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Molecular mimicry: K14 and K17 carry 'ALEEANxxL' and 'GLRRxLD' motifs identical to motifs of the streptococcal M protein, which the authors propose may allow these keratins to trigger autoimmune responses.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H6 (claim)
Statement: The low sequence identity between the fusion tags and K14, together with similar results obtained with two different fusion-tag systems, indicates that immunization with the K14/K17 moiety is primarily responsible for the induction of the psoriasis-like phenotype.
Links: scoped evidence ← O2; scoped evidence ← O6; competing explanation ← H7

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: The clinical and immunological outcomes are attributable to the fusion tag rather than to the keratin antigen; the low sequence identity of the GST and TF tags with K14 (3.93% and 4.5%) and the similar results obtained with the two different fusion-tag systems support this alternative, and the visible readouts are compatible with it.
Links: competing explanation → H6; competing explanation → H4

Conditions: Primary immunization: antigen emulsified in complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA), injected intradermally into shaved dorsal skin (about 25 uL per site, 200 uL total per mouse; 350 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Booster immunization 3-4 weeks later: same antigen emulsified in incomplete Freund's adjuvant (IFA), injected subcutaneously (450 ug per mouse in the GST-tagged figure legends).; Comparator groups: tag-only protein with the same adjuvant, an adjuvant-only group injected with CFA intradermally or IFA subcutaneously without protein, mice only anesthetized and hair-clipped (C57BL/6J additionally depilated), and topical imiquimod (IMQ; 10 mg/day to the tail base in BALB/c, 62.5 mg/day to dorsal skin in C57BL/6J, 7 consecutive days); no outcome is reported for the adjuvant-only group in the retrieved text.; Five independent experiments per mouse strain (two with GST-tagged proteins, three with TF-tagged proteins); per experiment 5 mice in the control and in the tag-control group and 10 mice in each of the K14 and K17 groups.
Scope limits: Female mice only; applicability to male mice was not evaluated.; Proof-of-concept study; no T-cell depletion, transfer or blocking experiment was performed.; Systematic longitudinal clinical scoring was not performed.; Figure images, supplementary figures and the supplementary table were not inspected for this workspace; values are taken from Results text and figure captions.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Immunization with K14 or K17 must produce psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, scales) in immunized mice, recorded with incidence, onset and duration alongside the adjuvant/tag and untreated comparator groups. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Immunized mice must mount a measurable antigen-specific antibody response against K14/K17, resolved by isotype and time point. (aspects: H2)
- R3: Immunized mice must show an antigen-specific T-cell response, and the systemic inflammatory cytokine profile after immunization must be characterized. (aspects: H3)
- R4: The induced phenotype must be attributable to the keratin moiety rather than to the fusion tag used to express it. (aspects: H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization with K14 or K17 fusion protein induces psoriasis-like clinical skin lesions (erythema, crusts, white scales) at skin sites the authors designate as non-injection sites.
Links: proposed mechanism ← H5; scoped evidence ← H7

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization elicits antigen-specific serum antibodies against K14/K17, detectable as IgM early and as IgG1 and IgG2b at later time points.
Links: scoped evidence ← H7

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Immunization generates K14/K17-reactive T cells, shown as increased IFN-gamma release by lymph node and spleen cells restimulated with keratin antigen ex vivo.
Links: scoped evidence ← H7

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: The clinical and immunological outcomes are attributable to the keratin moiety of the immunogen rather than to the GST or His-TF fusion tag carried by the recombinant protein.

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: Molecular mimicry: K14 and K17 carry 'ALEEANxxL' and 'GLRRxLD' motifs identical to motifs of the streptococcal M protein, which the authors propose may allow these keratins to trigger autoimmune responses.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1

## H6 (claim)
Statement: The low sequence identity between the fusion tags and K14, together with similar results obtained with two different fusion-tag systems, indicates that immunization with the K14/K17 moiety is primarily responsible for the induction of the psoriasis-like phenotype.
Links: scoped evidence ← O2; scoped evidence ← O6; competing explanation ← H7

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: Candidate explanation (proposed, not observed): the difference between the two assays is partly explained by the difference between the GST and TF tags, rather than by the difference between the keratins K14 and K17. The GST and TF tags differ in sequence identity to K14 (3.93% versus 4.5%), and the two assays use different adjuvant schedules (CFA primary, IFA booster for GST-K14/K17; the same for TF-K14/K17), so the tag's sequence and the adjuvant schedule are confounded with the keratin antigen in the attribution claim.
Links: competing explanation → H6; scoped evidence → H1; scoped evidence → H2; scoped evidence → H3

# Main hypothesis
Can enzymatic hydrolysis of coconut kernel fiber (CKF), a coconut-processing by-product, yield a low-molecular-weight (1-3 kDa) hydrolysate fraction (LW-CKFH) that inhibits alpha-glucosidase, improves glucose metabolism in IR-HepG2 cells and in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, retains activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions, and contains identifiable alpha-glucosidase inhibitory peptides?
System: CKF protein hydrolysates (CKFH) and their ultrafiltration/gel-filtration fractions; in vitro alpha-glucosidase (pNPG) assay; HepG2 and insulin-induced IR-HepG2 cells; male Kunming mice with high-sugar high-fat diet plus streptozotocin (HSHFD/STZ) induced T2DM; simulated digestion and bread model; LC-MS/MS, in silico screening, molecular docking and synthetic peptides.
Conditions: Ultrasound-assisted sequential neutral then alkaline protease hydrolysis (8000 U/g, 2 h each); LW-CKFH = 1-3 kDa ultrafiltration fraction; Mice: oral gavage for 4 weeks with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, or LW-CKFH 200, 400, 800 mg/kg bw; n = 6 per group; Stability/matrix outcomes expressed as retention relative to untreated LW-CKFH (20 mg/mL, pH 7.0, 25 C) set to 100%
Scope limits: Single mouse strain and sex (male Kunming), one T2DM induction model, one 4-week treatment period; Insulin resistance and sensitivity assessed by HOMA surrogate indices from fasting glucose and insulin; Peptide binding assessed by molecular docking; synthetic peptides tested only for in vitro alpha-glucosidase inhibition; Food feasibility assessed in vitro (simulated digestion, one bread formulation)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Establish a hydrolysis and fractionation route that yields a CKF hydrolysate fraction with high alpha-glucosidase inhibitory activity. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Evaluate in vivo hypoglycemic efficacy of LW-CKFH in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice relative to untreated model mice and a metformin group. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Ultrasound-assisted dual-protease hydrolysis followed by ultrafiltration yields a CKF hydrolysate fraction with high alpha-glucosidase inhibitory activity.
Links: composition → H2

Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)

Links: composition → H4; composition → H5; composition → H6; proposed mechanism ← H7

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Ultrafiltration of CKFH into four molecular-weight fractions, each tested for alpha-glucosidase inhibition.
Manipulation: CKFH solution separated with centrifugal filters of 10, 3 and 1 kDa cut-off (8000 rpm, 10 min), giving four fractions; the most active fraction was freeze-dried.
Measurements: alpha-glucosidase inhibition rate (%)
Comparison: groups: four ultrafiltration fractions (including 1-3 kDa LW-CKFH) | endpoint: alpha-glucosidase inhibition rate (%) | varied: molecular-weight range of the fraction | held fixed: assay conditions of Section 2.4 | unit: fraction; replicate number not stated | units: % | uncertainty: mean +/- SD in Figure 1d
Observations: O1

## E2
Statement: HSHFD/STZ T2DM mouse model and 4-week oral treatment with LW-CKFH or metformin, with weekly body weight and fasting blood glucose.
Manipulation: Male Kunming SPF mice (4 weeks old, 20.0 +/- 0.2 g) acclimatized 1 week and randomized into six groups of six; controls fed standard diet, the other five groups HSHFD for 4 weeks; after a 12 h fast, model mice received intraperitoneal STZ 60 mg/kg (in 0.1 mol/L citrate buffer) twice at a 1-day interval, normal mice received citrate buffer; FBG >= 11.1 mmol/L (after a further 12 h fast) defined successful induction, and the number of mice failing this criterion is not reported. After induction, mice were again randomized into six groups (n = 6) and gavaged for 4 weeks: normal control and model with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, LW-CKFH 200 (L), 400 (M) or 800 (H) mg/kg bw. Body weight and FBG recorded every 7 days; the fast duration before these weekly FBG readings is not stated. Diet during the treatment period is not stated.
Measurements: fasting blood glucose; body weight
Comparison: groups: normal control (saline); T2DM model (saline); metformin 200 mg/kg bw; LW-CKFH-L 200 mg/kg bw; LW-CKFH-M 400 mg/kg bw; LW-CKFH-H 800 mg/kg bw | endpoint: fasting blood glucose (tail vein, glucometer) and body weight | varied: treatment and LW-CKFH dose | held fixed: strain, sex, induction protocol; 4-week gavage; tail-vein glucometer FBG (fast duration for weekly readings not stated) | unit: mouse (n = 6 per group) | window: every 7 days over 4 weeks of treatment | units: mmol/L; g | uncertainty: mean +/- SD; one-way ANOVA with Duncan test
Observations: O2, O3

## E3
Statement: Oral glucose tolerance test at the end of treatment.
Manipulation: After four weeks of treatment and a 12 h fast, mice received glucose 2.0 g/kg bw; blood glucose measured at 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 h; AUC = 0.25 x (G0 + G0.5) + 0.25 x (G0 + G1) + 0.5 x (G1 + G2). As printed, the second term of Formula (3) uses G0 where the trapezoidal rule would use G0.5, so the reported AUC values may not be standard trapezoidal AUCs.
Measurements: blood glucose at 0, 0.5, 1, 2 h; AUC (Formula 3)
Comparison: groups: six treatment groups of E2 | endpoint: blood glucose curve and AUC (0-2 h) | varied: treatment and LW-CKFH dose | held fixed: glucose load 2.0 g/kg; 12 h fast; sampling times | unit: mouse (n = 6 per group) | window: 0, 0.5, 1, 2 h after the glucose load, end of week 4 | units: mmol/L; mmol/L x h | uncertainty: mean +/- SD in Figure 3E,F
Observations: O5, O6

## E4
Statement: Serum glycated serum protein (GSP) at the end of treatment.
Manipulation: After 4 weeks and a 12 h fast, mice were anesthetized with ether, blood drawn from the eye, serum obtained (4 C 2 h; 2500 rpm, 4 C, 10 min); GSP measured with a commercial kit.
Measurements: serum GSP
Comparison: groups: six treatment groups of E2 | endpoint: serum GSP | varied: treatment and LW-CKFH dose | held fixed: sampling protocol | unit: mouse (n = 6 per group) | window: end of week 4 | uncertainty: mean +/- SD in Figure 3D
Observations: O4

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: The 1-3 kDa ultrafiltration fraction (LW-CKFH) showed the highest alpha-glucosidase inhibition among four fractions (74.49%).
Scope: Fractions compared at an assay concentration not stated in the text.
Comparison: groups: four ultrafiltration fractions | endpoint: alpha-glucosidase inhibition rate | varied: molecular-weight range | held fixed: assay conditions | unit: fraction | units: % | result: 1-3 kDa highest, 74.49% | uncertainty: other fraction values only in Figure 1d
Bears on: H2

## O2 (from E2)
Statement: Before treatment, HSHFD/STZ mice gained weight during induction relative to normal controls and had FBG above 11.1 mmol/L, which the authors took as successful T2DM model construction.
Scope: Model validation before treatment.
Comparison: groups: normal control; HSHFD/STZ mice | endpoint: FBG and body weight | varied: induction | unit: mouse | window: end of induction | units: mmol/L | result: FBG > 11.1 mmol/L in model mice | uncertainty: Figure 3B,C
Bears on: H3

## O3 (from E2)
Statement: After 4 weeks, FBG relative to the model group was lower by 38.7% (metformin), 32.0% (LW-CKFH-H), 27.0% (LW-CKFH-M) and 23.1% (LW-CKFH-L); the authors describe a dose-dependent effect with the high dose comparable to metformin.
Scope: Percent reduction versus model group means.
Comparison: groups: model; metformin; LW-CKFH-H; LW-CKFH-M; LW-CKFH-L | endpoint: fasting blood glucose | varied: treatment and dose | held fixed: 4-week gavage | unit: mouse (n = 6) | window: end of week 4 | units: % | result: -38.7%, -32.0%, -27.0%, -23.1% versus model | uncertainty: Figure 3C
Bears on: H4

## O4 (from E4)
Statement: Serum GSP of the model group was 326.8% of the normal control; LW-CKFH lowered GSP significantly, the high dose by 27.7% (p < 0.05), described as 'reaching 72.32% of those in the metformin group'.
Scope: The meaning of the 72.32% metformin comparison is not specified.
Comparison: groups: normal control; model; LW-CKFH doses; metformin | endpoint: serum GSP | varied: treatment and dose | held fixed: end-of-study serum | unit: mouse (n = 6) | window: end of week 4 | units: % | result: model 326.8% of normal; H -27.7% vs model | uncertainty: p < 0.05
Bears on: H5

## O5 (from E3)
Statement: LW-CKFH reduced the blood-glucose peak after the oral glucose load, with the high dose showing the best result among LW-CKFH groups.
Scope: Curve values available only in figure.
Comparison: groups: model; LW-CKFH doses; metformin | endpoint: post-load blood-glucose curve | varied: treatment and dose | held fixed: 2.0 g/kg glucose | unit: mouse (n = 6) | window: 0-2 h | result: lower peak with LW-CKFH, best at high dose | uncertainty: Figure 3E
Bears on: H6

Bears on: H6

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4).
- R2: Obtain compositional profiles of the deposited layers for all six samples by SEM (Figures 3-5).
- R3: Determine the elemental distribution of Zn and Fe within the layers by EDX mapping (Figures 6-8).
- R4: Measure microhardness at several points within the Fe and Zn layers (UNE-EN ISO 6507-1:2024; Table 5, Figure 10).
- R5: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11).

# Observations

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4).
- R2: Obtain compositional profiles of the deposited layers for all six samples by SEM (Figures 3-5).
- R3: Determine the elemental distribution of Zn and Fe within the layers by EDX mapping (Figures 6-8).
- R4: Measure microhardness at several points within the Fe and Zn layers (UNE-EN ISO 6507-1:2024; Table 5, Figure 10).
- R5: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11).

# Observations

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Links: composition → H1; composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; composition → H5
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4).
- R2: Obtain compositional profiles of the deposited layers for all six samples by SEM (Figures 3-5).
- R3: Determine the elemental distribution of Zn and Fe within the layers by EDX mapping (Figures 6-8).
- R4: Measure microhardness at several points within the Fe and Zn layers (UNE-EN ISO 6507-1:2024; Table 5, Figure 10).
- R5: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11).

# Observations

# Main hypothesis
How do lavender-extract AgNPs and LEO compare in the concentrations at which they inhibit growth and biofilm formation of multidrug-resistant, biofilm-forming staphylococci?
System: In vitro microtiter-plate assays with two S. aureus reference strains (CCM 4750, methicillin-resistant; CCM 4223, strong biofilm producer) and two multidrug-resistant, strong biofilm-forming NASM clinical isolates from animals (Mammaliicoccus sciuri, S. pseudintermedius); lavender-extract AgNPs and commercial L. angustifolia essential oil.
Conditions: Modified BHI broth with 1% glucose and 2% NaCl; 37 °C, 24 h exposures; AgNPs 25–200 μg/mL; LEO 0.001–1% (Methods); Triplicate wells; one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's test against the positive control
Scope limits: In vitro only; Four strains, one isolate or strain per designation; Biofilm eradication and nanoparticle characterization are outside this workspace
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the growth-inhibitory concentrations of AgNPs and LEO for each strain. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Determine the concentrations of AgNPs and LEO that inhibit biofilm formation for each strain. (aspects: H3)
- R3: Compare the effective concentrations of AgNPs and LEO for growth inhibition and for inhibition of biofilm formation across the four strains. (aspects: H4)

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)
- R2: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)

Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)
- R2: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Vasomotor function of isolated thoracic aortic rings is altered in cadmium-exposed hypertensive rats relative to controls.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4; proposed mechanism ← H5

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Endothelium-dependent relaxation to acetylcholine in phenylephrine-precontracted aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H1

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Alpha-adrenergic contraction to phenylephrine in aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H1

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Contraction to the TXA2 analogue U46619 in aortic rings differs between cadmium-exposed and control animals.
Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H6; scoped evidence ← H8

## H5 (mechanism)
Statement: NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species within the vascular wall mediate the altered vasomotor responses of cadmium-exposed aortas; the proposed mechanism is probed by incubating rings with the NADPH oxidase inhibitor apocynin.
Links: proposed mechanism → H1; composition → H7; composition → H8; composition → H9

## H6 (claim)
Statement: TXA2 induces hypercontractility in aortas from cadmium-exposed hypertensive animals, an effect associated with oxidative stress and reversed after NADPH oxidase inhibition.
Links: refinement ← H4

## H7 (aspect)
Statement: Branch of the oxidative mechanism, endothelium-dependent relaxation: an apocynin-sensitive oxidative component limits acetylcholine-induced relaxation in aortic rings from cadmium-exposed animals at both 40 and 80 ppm. Supported by the reduction of relaxation Emax to 0.5 in non-incubated exposed rings and its return to about 0.7, indistinguishable from control, after apocynin incubation.
Links: composition ← H5

## H8 (aspect)
Statement: Branch of the oxidative mechanism, TXA2-receptor-mediated contraction: an apocynin-sensitive oxidative component amplifies U46619-induced contraction in aortic rings from exposed animals. Supported at 40 ppm by a response indistinguishable from control preparations after apocynin, and at 80 ppm by a fall in Emax relative to matched non-incubated rings, a comparison that differs from the one used at 40 ppm.
Links: composition ← H5; scoped evidence → H4

## H9 (aspect)
Statement: Branch of the oxidative mechanism, alpha-adrenergic contraction: an apocynin-sensitive oxidative component contributes to phenylephrine-induced contraction only at the higher exposure. Evidence is weaker than for the other branches, since 40 ppm rings did not differ from control before incubation and the reported 80 ppm increase in Emax is stated in the text without a corresponding significance marker in the table.
Links: composition ← H5

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Acetylcholine concentration-response curves in phenylephrine-precontracted aortic rings, with and without apocynin preincubation.
Manipulation: After ketamine-xylazine anaesthesia and euthanasia by thoracotomy, the thoracic aorta was cleaned and cut into 3-mm rings mounted between stainless-steel wires in 5-mL organ baths with Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2. Rings were precontracted with phenylephrine 1 x 10^-6 M and exposed to cumulative acetylcholine concentrations from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M. Selected rings were incubated with apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction.
Measurements: isometric tension of aortic rings; Emax of acetylcholine relaxation; pD2 of acetylcholine relaxation

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)
- R2: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)

# Main hypothesis
Determine whether thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor-mediated signalling contributes to aortic hypercontractility in rats made hypertensive by chronic cadmium administration (HICAD), and whether such an effect is associated with an oxidative imbalance involving NADPH oxidase.
System: Male Wistar rats (~200 g at start) given CdCl2 at 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks, compared with untreated controls; isolated thoracic aortic rings and aortic tissue homogenates from the same animals.
Conditions: CdCl2 40 or 80 ppm in drinking water for 8 weeks; control group without CdCl2; Systolic blood pressure by non-invasive tail-cuff plethysmography in conscious rats at week 0 and week 8; Aortic rings (3 mm) in Krebs-Henseleit solution at 37 degrees C, aerated with 95% O2 / 5% CO2; Cumulative agonist concentration-response curves from 1 x 10^-9 to 3 x 10^-5 M; Apocynin 300 micromol/L for 15 min before curve construction in selected rings; Contractile responses normalised to the maximal contraction induced by 80 mM KCl; Aortic homogenates in potassium phosphate buffer for spectrophotometric redox assays
Scope limits: Thoracic aorta only; no resistance-sized vessels were studied; Male rats only; One exposure duration (8 weeks) and two exposure concentrations (40 and 80 ppm); NADPH oxidase involvement probed only with the pharmacological inhibitor apocynin; No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
Validation requirements:
- R1: Characterise endothelium-dependent relaxation and agonist-induced contraction of aortic rings from exposed and control animals, reporting maximal effect and sensitivity for each agonist. (aspects: H1, H2, H3, H4)
- R2: Test whether inhibiting NADPH oxidase with apocynin changes the vasomotor responses of aortic rings from exposed animals. (aspects: H5)

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: The 3D-Gr structure must function as a support platform for catalyst preparation. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H3, H5, H8, H9, H10, H11)
- R3: The two supported catalysts must operate together in a two-electrode overall water and seawater splitting cell with long-term stability. (aspects: H12, H13)

Filament conductivity was measured by 4-point probe on up to ten 40 mm filaments; compressive strength on six printed cylinders (10 mm x 10 mm, 1 perimeter, 50% infill) at 0.05 mm s-1; morphology by SEM.

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: The 3D-Gr structure must function as a support platform for catalyst preparation. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H3, H5, H8, H9, H10, H11)
- R3: The two supported catalysts must operate together in a two-electrode overall water and seawater splitting cell with long-term stability. (aspects: H12, H13)

# Experiments
## E1

Manipulation: A 60 wt.% solids paste (graphite:graphitizable binder 47:13 in 25 wt.% Pluronic F127 hydrogel) was extruded through a 610 um nozzle at 10 mm s-1 into 10 x 15 x 2.7 mm grids (six layers, 50% infill, 26% overlap), dried at 60 C for 24 h and carbonized at 800 C for 1 h under N2. Filament conductivity was measured by 4-point probe on up to ten 40 mm filaments; compressive strength on six printed cylinders (10 mm x 10 mm, 1 perimeter, 50% infill) at 0.05 mm s-1; morphology by SEM.
Measurements: 4-point probe conductivity; Uniaxial compressive strength; SEM

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: The 3D-Gr structure must function as a support platform for catalyst preparation. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H3, H5, H8, H9, H10, H11)
- R3: The two supported catalysts must operate together in a two-electrode overall water and seawater splitting cell with long-term stability. (aspects: H12, H13)

# Main hypothesis
Can 3D-structured all-carbon graphite grids fabricated by direct ink writing (3D-Gr) serve as supports for electrodeposited non-noble electrocatalysts, NiCo-CeO2 for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and NiFe for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), giving active and stable electrodes in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes and in two-electrode overall water splitting?
System: DIW-printed graphite/graphitizable-binder grids (10 x 15 x 2.7 mm, carbonized at 800 C) carrying electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2 (cathode) or NiFe (anode); Pt/3D-Gr and IrO2/3D-Gr benchmarks; NiCo-CeO2 and NiFe on Toray carbon paper (TCP).
Conditions: 1 M KOH; 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl; 1 M KOH + synthetic seawater; Three-electrode and two-electrode cells, 25 mL electrolyte (measurement temperature not stated); Geometric current density, 85% iR compensation
Scope limits: Proof-of-concept study with a single grid geometry; Catalyst synthesis routes adapted from prior reports; Synthetic seawater, not natural seawater
Validation requirements:
- R1: The 3D-Gr structure must function as a support platform for catalyst preparation. (aspects: H2)
- R2: Electrodeposited NiCo-CeO2/3D-Gr (HER) and NiFe/3D-Gr (OER) must show catalytic activity and stability in alkaline and alkaline-saline electrolytes. (aspects: H3, H5, H8, H9, H10, H11)
- R3: The two supported catalysts must operate together in a two-electrode overall water and seawater splitting cell with long-term stability. (aspects: H12, H13)

# Main hypothesis
Can a physics-based Monte Carlo simulator (BioElectroSynth) that combines electrochemical noise, cardiac/muscular bioelectric interference and instrumental noise predict, from in vitro EIS parameters of AZ91 in simulated body fluid, (1) for which electrode areas and coating resistances passive zero-resistance-ammetry (ZRA) noise monitoring of an implanted Mg electrode pair in a mouse is feasible, (2) the smallest coating breach fraction that can be statistically distinguished from the intact state and how it depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings, and (3) which signal processing metric extracts the most information?
System: BioElectroSynth simulation of a two-electrode ZRA corrosion sensor made of AZ91 Mg alloy in a mouse anatomical phantom
Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the combinations of electrode area and coating quality for which ZRA-based monitoring is feasible, given that corrosion noise, ECG interference and the instrumental floor scale differently with area. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H3)

Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E2

Links: composition → H4

Links: composition ← H3; proposed mechanism ← H6; experimental target ← E3

Conditions: Two-time-constant equivalent circuit (film Rf/CPEf in series with Rct/CPEdl) for all Monte Carlo work; AZ91 in SBF early-exposure interface: Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, Cdl = 25 uF/cm2; Stern-Geary B ~ 0.03 V; Baseline coating Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2, Cf = 800 uF/cm2 (stated worst-case swollen/porous hydrogel-like state); Amplifier noise 0.05 uA RMS and ADC step 0.05 uA in the Monte Carlo study; Breach factorial: 5 areas x 11 breach fractions x 2 sampling rates (10, 100 Hz) x 30 seeds, 30 s recordings; Operating-window analysis assumes a fully restrained animal (EMG excluded; ECG retained)
Scope limits: All thresholds, NSR values and working windows are model outputs, not measurements; Electrochemical and coating parameters are time-invariant in vitro values; Mouse body approximated by nine homogeneous ellipsoids; bioelectric parameters taken from literature; No in vivo or in vitro ZRA recordings are reported in this paper
Validation requirements:
- R1: Determine the combinations of electrode area and coating quality for which ZRA-based monitoring is feasible, given that corrosion noise, ECG interference and the instrumental floor scale differently with area. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Determine the smallest coating breach that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state and how this threshold depends on electrode design, sampling rate and number of recordings. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Operating window: the electrode areas A and area-specific coating resistances Rf,sp for which simulated median corrosion-noise RMS exceeds both the ECG-induced current and the amplifier noise floor (SNR > 1) in a fully restrained animal.
Links: composition → H2; proposed alternative → H7

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: Upper coating-resistance bound of the operating window set by ECG interference, which the coating does not attenuate while it suppresses corrosion current.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E2

## H3 (aspect)
Statement: Minimum detectable coating breach fraction (two-sample test against intact baseline, alpha = 0.05) and its dependence on electrode design, sampling rate, coating resistance and number of recordings.
Links: composition → H4

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: Dependence of the minimum detectable breach on coating resistance Rf,sp across electrode areas at N = 30 recordings.
Links: composition ← H3; proposed mechanism ← H6; experimental target ← E3

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: Relative magnitudes and temporal structure of the simulated signal components (corrosion noise, ECG, EMG, thermal and amplifier noise) in a representative digitized ZRA record.

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Authors' explanation: for high-resistance coatings the impedance contrast between intact and breached zones is large, so a small bare patch produces a large noise current relative to the intact surface, allowing small breaches to be detected.
Links: proposed mechanism → H4

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: High-resistance coatings may reduce ECG interference by increasing the impedance contrast between zones, allowing corrosion noise to dominate over bioelectric signals.
Links: proposed alternative ← H1

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: Decomposition of one synthetic ZRA record into six components (total digitized current, corrosion noise, ECG, EMG, Johnson-Nyquist thermal noise, amplifier white noise), labeled by the authors as model validation.
Manipulation: Simulator components generated independently and displayed separately for A = 0.50 cm2, Rct,sp = 300 ohm cm2, breach theta = 0.1, heart rate 400 bpm, EMG burst rate 0.3 per s; total current digitized by an ideal 10 Hz ADC (LSB 0.05 uA); corrosion noise also shown at the 10 kHz internal bandwidth.
Measurements: ECG-induced current peak-to-peak and R-peak frequency; EMG burst amplitude; Johnson-Nyquist noise RMS; amplifier white noise RMS; visibility of 1/f^2 and bubble transients at 10 kHz versus 10 Hz

Observations: O1

## E2
Statement: Monte Carlo SNR phase diagram over coating resistance Rf,sp and electrode area A (Figure 5b).

Links: experimental target → H2
Observations: O2

## E3
Statement: Coating-resistance sweep of the minimum detectable breach (Figure 7): Rf,sp from 35 to 5000 ohm cm2 at five electrode areas using residual RMS and N = 30 recordings.

Measurements: minimum detectable breach fraction versus A and Rf,sp

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: In the simulated record (A = 0.50 cm2, theta = 0.1, 400 bpm), ECG interference is ~0.1 uA peak-to-peak at geometric gain 0.15 with R-peaks at ~6.7 Hz; EMG bursts are sporadic broadband transients with amplitudes comparable to ECG; Johnson-Nyquist noise (~0.1 nA RMS) and amplifier white noise (~0.01 uA RMS) are negligible; 1/f^2 fluctuations and hydrogen-bubble transients visible at 10 kHz are smoothed out by the anti-aliasing filter of the 10 Hz ADC.
Scope: One synthetic realization at one parameter set; descriptive, not compared with measured signals.
Comparison: groups: signal components | endpoint: component amplitude | varied: component | held fixed: single parameter set of E1 | unit: single realization | window: one synthetic record | units: uA, nA
Bears on: H5

## O2 (from E2)
Statement: In the simulated SNR phase diagram the SNR > 1 region shrinks steeply as Rf,sp increases; below A ~ 0.01 cm2 even a bare electrode does not reach the amplifier floor; beyond Rf,sp ~ 10^3 ohm cm2 the corrosion signal falls below the ECG + noise background at any electrode area and the SNR > 1 region disappears.
Scope: Restrained-animal assumption (no EMG); SNR is an absolute-magnitude criterion, not a breach-detection test; Rf,sp grid read from text only.
Comparison: groups: SNR > 1; SNR < 1 | endpoint: log10(SNR) | varied: A; Rf,sp | held fixed: EMG excluded | unit: MC median per configuration | window: 10 s realizations | units: dimensionless
Bears on: H1, H2

## O3 (from E3)
Statement: Figure 7 sweep (residual RMS, N = 30): for coatings above 1000 ohm cm2 a 2-4% breach is detectable even at 0.05 cm2 electrodes.
Scope: High-resistance coatings; values read from the Results text, not figure pixels.
Comparison: groups: Rf,sp > 1000 ohm cm2; lower Rf,sp | endpoint: minimum detectable breach (%) | varied: Rf,sp; A | held fixed: residual RMS; N = 30 | unit: configuration | window: 30 s recordings | units: % breach
Bears on: H3, H4

## O4 (from E3)
Statement: Figure 7 sweep (residual RMS, N = 30): at the baseline Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2 the threshold at 0.05 cm2 is approximately 25%, attributed to the deliberately weak impedance contrast of the worst-case scenario.
Scope: Baseline coating, smallest area.
Comparison: groups: Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2 | endpoint: minimum detectable breach (%) | varied: Rf,sp | held fixed: A = 0.05 cm2; residual RMS; N = 30 | unit: configuration | window: 30 s recordings | units: % breach
Bears on: H3, H4

## O5 (from E3)
Statement: From Figure 7: at A = 1.0 cm2 and Rf,sp = 1200 ohm cm2 the framework resolves a minimum detectable breach of approximately 2% from N = 30 recordings, corresponding to 0.02 cm2 of bare metal.
Scope: Single configuration reported in the Discussion.
Comparison: groups: A = 1.0 cm2, Rf,sp = 1200 ohm cm2 | endpoint: minimum detectable breach (%) | varied: Rf,sp; A | held fixed: residual RMS; N = 30 | unit: configuration | window: 30 s recordings | units: % breach
Bears on: H3, H4

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H5)
- R2: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H3)

# Main hypothesis
Can electroless Ni-P plating, preceded by Sn/Pd sensitization-activation and with the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) added to the bath, form a uniform Ni-P layer selectively on the exposed faces of polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi-Sb-Te TE elements that prevents Cu from an electroplated Cu layer from diffusing into the TE element and forming intermetallic compounds during heat treatment?
System: Hot-extruded cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 (x = 1.56) thermoelectric (TE) elements (diameter 1.3 mm, height 5 mm) whose side surfaces are spray-coated with a TiO2-containing polymer paint, leaving the top and bottom faces exposed; Sn/Pd sensitization-activation, electroless Ni-P plating (80 °C, 20 min, pH 8.5) in baths without SDS (Bath A) or with 0.5 g/L SDS (Bath B), and Cu electroplating on the Ni-P layer
Conditions: Electroless Ni-P plating at 80 °C for 20 min at pH 8.5 (ammonia-adjusted); SDS at 0 g/L (Bath A) or 0.5 g/L (Bath B); Cu electroplating at -60 mA/cm2 for 8 min on the Ni-P-plated element; Heat treatment of Cu/Ni-P-plated elements at 100 °C and 200 °C under Ar
Scope limits: Specimen counts per condition and the heat-treatment duration are not stated in the text.; Work function, barrier height and contact resistance of the Ni-P/TE element interface were not measured.
Validation requirements:
- R1: Ni-P deposits selectively on the exposed TE element surface and not on the adjacent polymer-coated region. (aspects: H5)
- R2: The effects of SDS addition on plating selectivity, on the surface and interfacial chemical states of the Ni-P-plated TE elements, and on Cu diffusion barrier performance are examined. (aspects: H3)

## H4 (aspect)
Statement: SDS in the plating bath changes wetting of the bath on the TE element surface and on the polymer surface.
Links: composition ← H3; experimental target ← E2

## H5 (aspect)
Statement: SDS concentration governs Ni-P coverage of the TE element surface and the selectivity of deposition relative to the adjacent polymer region.
Links: composition ← H3; proposed mechanism ← H6; experimental target ← E3; experimental target ← E4; proposed mechanism ← H7

## H6 (mechanism)
Statement: Wettability contrast drives selective deposition: SDS lowers the bath surface tension, the higher-energy activated TE element surface becomes nearly completely wetted, and the low-energy, chemically inert polymer surface stays poorly wetted, so Ni-P deposits on the TE element and not on the polymer.
Links: proposed mechanism → H5; competing explanation ← H7

## H7 (alternative)
Statement: SDS changes the surface energy of the deposited Ni-P layer: it lowers the bath surface tension and adsorbs on the electrode surface during deposition, which lowers the Ni-P surface energy and makes it more attractive to the bath. The lower-energy Ni-P surface then becomes more wettable, so the bath spreads on it and deposits more Ni-P, while the higher-energy polymer stays wettable and deposits less. This would predict that SDS lowers the Ni-P surface energy, and that the same SDS concentration changes the Ni-P/TE element and Ni-P/polymer contact angles.
Links: competing explanation → H6; proposed mechanism → H5

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?
System: S235JR steel wire (Ø3.25, 2.50 and 1.50 mm) hot-dip galvanized in a pure ZnZ1 zinc bath and wiped by one of two techniques; six samples 1a, 2a, 3a (wax) and 1b, 2b, 3b (Teflon pads).
Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)
Scope limits: one steel grade and one pure-zinc bath composition; one sample per technique-diameter combination; pad clamping pressure and wax-wiping operating parameters not reported; accelerated salt-spray corrosion only; no statistical tests reported
Validation requirements:
- R1: Quantify the deposited zinc layer thickness for all six samples (Table 4). (aspects: H2)
- R2: Evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings in an Erichsen salt-spray chamber (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023; Table 6, Figure 11). (aspects: H3, H4)

# Sub-hypotheses
## H1 (aspect)
Statement: Replacing charcoal-wax wiping (technique a) with non-asbestos Teflon pad wiping (technique b) after hot-dip galvanizing changes the zinc coating of S235JR wire and its protective performance; the study asks whether zinc use can fall without compromising anticorrosive performance.
Links: composition → H2; composition → H3; composition → H4

## H2 (aspect)
Statement: At each of the three wire diameters, Teflon pad wiping yields a lower zinc coating mass per unit area and thickness than wax wiping.
Links: composition ← H1; experimental target ← E1

Links: composition ← H1; refinement → H5; experimental target ← E2

Teflon pad wiping therefore reduces coating zinc at the cost of a shorter time to red rust in this test; equivalent anticorrosive performance is not supported.

# Main hypothesis
Can wiping hot-dip galvanized steel wire with non-asbestos Teflon pads (technique b), instead of conventional charcoal-wax wiping (technique a), reduce the zinc coating (and hence zinc consumption and cost) without compromising the coating's integrity and its anticorrosive performance?

Conditions: bath 450 °C, immersion 90 s, line speed 50 m/min for both techniques; identical annealing, HCl pickling and rinsing pretreatment; coating characterization on as-produced wire; corrosion by neutral salt spray (UNE-EN ISO 9227:2023)

Statement: In neutral salt spray, the two wiping techniques gave the same time to white rust (24 h on all six samples), but Teflon-wiped wires reached red rust earlier than wax-wiped wires at every diameter: 120 h for 1b (Ø3.25 mm) versus 264 h for 1a (wax), 120 h for 2b (Ø2.50 mm) versus 192 h for 2a (wax), and 120 h for 3b (Ø1.50 mm) versus 168 h for 3a (wax). # Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?
System: 411 patients with confirmed superficial LNTB, Xi'an Chest Hospital, November 30, 2018 to June 17, 2024; tissue and purulent specimens tested with a Mycobacterium nucleic acid detection kit (PCR-fluorescent probe) on an ABI7500 real-time PCR system
Conditions: Retrospective extraction of electronic medical records; Blood for laboratory tests, including T lymphocyte subsets, collected within 24 hours of admission; PCR-fluorescent probe result as the dependent variable in logistic regression
Scope limits: Single center (Xi'an Chest Hospital); Superficial LNTB only; other extrapulmonary TB forms not studied; Observational retrospective design
Validation requirements:
- R1: Screen candidate factors (demographic characteristics, TB-related information, comorbidities, laboratory data, T lymphocyte subsets and number of samples) for association with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using univariate and multivariate logistic regression. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Explore the dose-response relationships of age, total T lymphocytes (CD3+), T helper lymphocytes (CD3+CD4+) and the T helper/T suppressor ratio (CD4+/CD8+) with the PCR-fluorescent probe result using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models combined with logistic regression.

# Main hypothesis
Which specimen-related, demographic, clinical and immunological factors are associated with a positive PCR-fluorescent probe result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) nucleic acid in patients with superficial lymph node tuberculosis (LNTB), and what is the shape of the dose-response relationship between age, T lymphocyte subsets and the probability of a positive result?

# Main hypothesis
Does Ni electrodeposition on HNO3-activated CF fabric followed by vacuum heat treatment improve the tensile behaviour of the resulting epoxy CFRP, and how does the change relate to the Ni-C interfacial structure?
System: PAN-based T300 3K carbon fiber plain-weave fabric, sizing removed and HNO3-etched, Ni electrodeposited from a Watts bath at 0.02 A/cm2 (LD) or 0.04 A/cm2 (HD), vacuum heat-treated, and cured into 4674 epoxy CFRP panels
Conditions: LD 0.02 A/cm2 and HD 0.04 A/cm2 electrodeposition; IH at 500-900 °C or LH to 700 °C, 2 h, vacuum; EMI in the X band; quasi-static tensile tests of cured panels
Scope limits: LH applied only at 700 °C
Validation requirements:
- R1: Improve the mechanical properties of the CFRP relative to pristine CFRP. (aspects: H1, H2)
- R2: Characterize the Ni/C interfacial structure that accompanies the tensile changes. (aspects: H3)

# Sub-hypotheses

Links: refinement → H4

# Main hypothesis
Can enzymatic hydrolysis of coconut kernel fiber (CKF), a coconut-processing by-product, yield a low-molecular-weight (1-3 kDa) hydrolysate fraction (LW-CKFH) that inhibits alpha-glucosidase, improves glucose metabolism in IR-HepG2 cells and in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, retains activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions, and contains identifiable alpha-glucosidase inhibitory peptides?
System: CKF protein hydrolysates (CKFH) and their ultrafiltration/gel-filtration fractions; in vitro alpha-glucosidase (pNPG) assay; HepG2 and insulin-induced IR-HepG2 cells; male Kunming mice with high-sugar high-fat diet plus streptozotocin (HSHFD/STZ) induced T2DM; simulated digestion and bread model; LC-MS/MS, in silico screening, molecular docking and synthetic peptides.
Conditions: Ultrasound-assisted sequential neutral then alkaline protease hydrolysis (8000 U/g, 2 h each); LW-CKFH = 1-3 kDa ultrafiltration fraction; Mice: oral gavage for 4 weeks with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, or LW-CKFH 200, 400, 800 mg/kg bw; n = 6 per group; Stability/matrix outcomes expressed as retention relative to untreated LW-CKFH (20 mg/mL, pH 7.0, 25 C) set to 100%
Scope limits: Single mouse strain and sex (male Kunming), one T2DM induction model, one 4-week treatment period; Insulin resistance and sensitivity assessed by HOMA surrogate indices from fasting glucose and insulin; Peptide binding assessed by molecular docking; synthetic peptides tested only for in vitro alpha-glucosidase inhibition; Food feasibility assessed in vitro (simulated digestion, one bread formulation)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Evaluate in vivo hypoglycemic efficacy of LW-CKFH in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice relative to untreated model mice and a metformin group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Assess resistance to simulated gastrointestinal digestion, processing stability (heat, pH, metal ions), food-matrix effects, and glucose release from a food containing LW-CKFH. (aspects: H5)

# Main hypothesis
Can enzymatic hydrolysis of coconut kernel fiber (CKF), a coconut-processing by-product, yield a low-molecular-weight (1-3 kDa) hydrolysate fraction (LW-CKFH) that inhibits alpha-glucosidase, improves glucose metabolism in IR-HepG2 cells and in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, retains activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions, and contains identifiable alpha-glucosidase inhibitory peptides?
System: CKF protein hydrolysates (CKFH) and their ultrafiltration/gel-filtration fractions; in vitro alpha-glucosidase (pNPG) assay; HepG2 and insulin-induced IR-HepG2 cells; male Kunming mice with high-sugar high-fat diet plus streptozotocin (HSHFD/STZ) induced T2DM; simulated digestion and bread model; LC-MS/MS, in silico screening, molecular docking and synthetic peptides.
Conditions: Ultrasound-assisted sequential neutral then alkaline protease hydrolysis (8000 U/g, 2 h each); LW-CKFH = 1-3 kDa ultrafiltration fraction; Mice: oral gavage for 4 weeks with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, or LW-CKFH 200, 400, 800 mg/kg bw; n = 6 per group; Stability/matrix outcomes expressed as retention relative to untreated LW-CKFH (20 mg/mL, pH 7.0, 25 C) set to 100%
Scope limits: Single mouse strain and sex (male Kunming), one T2DM induction model, one 4-week treatment period; Insulin resistance and sensitivity assessed by HOMA surrogate indices from fasting glucose and insulin; Peptide binding assessed by molecular docking; synthetic peptides tested only for in vitro alpha-glucosidase inhibition; Food feasibility assessed in vitro (simulated digestion, one bread formulation)
Validation requirements:
- R1: Evaluate in vivo hypoglycemic efficacy of LW-CKFH in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice relative to untreated model mice and a metformin group. (aspects: H1)
- R2: Assess resistance to simulated gastrointestinal digestion, processing stability (heat, pH, metal ions), food-matrix effects, and glucose release from a food containing LW-CKFH. (aspects: H5)

# Main hypothesis
Can enzymatic hydrolysis of coconut kernel fiber (CKF), a coconut-processing by-product, yield a low-molecular-weight (1-3 kDa) hydrolysate fraction (LW-CKFH) that inhibits alpha-glucosidase, improves glucose metabolism in IR-HepG2 cells and in HSHFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, retains activity under digestion, processing and food-matrix conditions, and contains identifiable alpha-glucosidase inhibitory peptides?

# Experiments
## E1
Statement: HSHFD/STZ T2DM mouse model and 4-week oral treatment with LW-CKFH or metformin, with weekly body weight and fasting blood glucose.
Manipulation: Male Kunming SPF mice (4 weeks old, 20.0 +/- 0.2 g) acclimatized 1 week and randomized into six groups of six; controls fed standard diet, the other five groups HSHFD for 4 weeks; after a 12 h fast, model mice received intraperitoneal STZ 60 mg/kg (in 0.1 mol/L citrate buffer) twice at a 1-day interval, normal mice received citrate buffer; FBG >= 11.1 mmol/L (after a further 12 h fast) defined successful induction, and the number of mice failing this criterion is not reported. After induction, mice were again randomized into six groups (n = 6) and gavaged for 4 weeks: normal control and model with saline, metformin 200 mg/kg bw, LW-CKFH 200 (L), 400 (M) or 800 (H) mg/kg bw. Body weight and FBG recorded every 7 days; the fast duration before these weekly FBG readings is not stated. Diet during the treatment period is not stated.
Measurements: fasting blood glucose; body weight
Comparison: groups: normal control (saline); T2DM model (saline); metformin 200 mg/kg bw; LW-CKFH-L 200 mg/kg bw; LW-CKFH-M 400 mg/kg bw; LW-CKFH-H 800 mg/kg bw | endpoint: fasting blood glucose (tail vein, glucometer) and body weight | varied: treatment and LW-CKFH dose | held fixed: strain, sex, induction protocol; 4-week gavage; tail-vein glucometer FBG (fast duration for weekly readings not stated) | unit: mouse (n = 6 per group) | window: every 7 days over 4 weeks of treatment | units: mmol/L; g | uncertainty: mean +/- SD; one-way ANOVA with Duncan test
Observations: O1, O2

## E2
Statement: Oral glucose tolerance test at the end of treatment.
Manipulation: After four weeks of treatment and a 12 h fast, mice received glucose 2.0 g/kg bw; blood glucose measured at 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 h; AUC = 0.25 x (G0 + G0.5) + 0.25 x (G0 + G1) + 0.5 x (G1 + G2). As printed, the second term of Formula (3) uses G0 where the trapezoidal rule would use G0.5, so the reported AUC values may not be standard trapezoidal AUCs.
Measurements: blood glucose at 0, 0.5, 1, 2 h; AUC (Formula 3)
Comparison: groups: six treatment groups of E1 | endpoint: blood glucose curve and AUC (0-2 h) | varied: treatment and LW-CKFH dose | held fixed: glucose load 2.0 g/kg; 12 h fast; sampling times | unit: mouse (n = 6 per group) | window: 0, 0.5, 1, 2 h after the glucose load, end of week 4 | units: mmol/L; mmol/L x h | uncertainty: mean +/- SD in Figure 3E,F
Observations: O4, O5, O6

## E3
Statement: Serum glycated serum protein (GSP) at the end of treatment.
Manipulation: After 4 weeks and a 12 h fast, mice were anesthetized with ether, blood drawn from the eye, serum obtained (4 C 2 h; 2500 rpm, 4 C, 10 min); GSP measured with a commercial kit.
Measurements: serum GSP
Comparison: groups: six treatment groups of E1 | endpoint: serum GSP | varied: treatment and LW-CKFH dose | held fixed: sampling protocol | unit: mouse (n = 6 per group) | window: end of week 4 | uncertainty: mean +/- SD in Figure 3D
Observations: O3

## E4
Statement: Glucose release from bread with or without LW-CKFH during simulated digestion.
Manipulation: Bread from high-gluten flour with 1.2% dry yeast, 1.2% salt, 1 egg, 30% milk, 4.8% butter, plus 1.2% (v/w) LW-CKFH solution (solution concentration not stated); baked 35 min at 210/200 C. 5 g bread + 15 mL simulated saliva 2 min; pH 2.0 + 30 mL simulated gastric juice 2 h; pH 7.0 + 15 mL simulated intestinal fluid 2 h at 37 C; 2 mL aliquots at 0, 15, 30, 60, 120 min of intestinal digestion boiled 10 min; glucose by colorimetric kit. Bread without LW-CKFH served as the blank control.
Measurements: glucose content (mmol/L)
Comparison: groups: bread without LW-CKFH; bread with LW-CKFH | endpoint: glucose content of digesta | varied: LW-CKFH addition | held fixed: bread recipe and baking; digestion protocol | unit: digestion sample; replicate number not stated | window: 0-120 min of intestinal digestion | units: mmol/L | uncertainty: figure only
Observations: O7

# Observations
## O1 (from E1)
Statement: Before treatment, HSHFD/STZ mice gained weight during induction relative to normal controls and had FBG above 11.1 mmol/L, which the authors took as successful T2DM model construction.
Scope: Model validation before treatment.
Comparison: groups: normal control; HSHFD/STZ mice | endpoint: FBG and body weight | varied: induction | unit: mouse | window: end of induction | units: mmol/L | result: FBG > 11.1 mmol/L in model mice | uncertainty: Figure 3B,C
Bears on: H1

## O2 (from E1)
Statement: After 4 weeks, FBG relative to the model group was lower by 38.7% (metformin), 32.0% (LW-CKFH-H), 27.0% (LW-CKFH-M) and 23.1% (LW-CKFH-L); the authors describe a dose-dependent effect with the high dose comparable to metformin.
Scope: Percent reduction versus model group means.
Comparison: groups: model; metformin; LW-CKFH-H; LW-CKFH-M; LW-CKFH-L | endpoint: fasting blood glucose | varied: treatment and dose | held fixed: 4-week gavage | unit: mouse (n = 6) | window: end of week 4 | units: % | result: -38.7%, -32.0%, -27.0%, -23.1% versus model | uncertainty: Figure 3C
